paragraphs.text: THE WORKS OF ST PAULINUS OF NOLA, SECOND PART: POEMS.

It is an insult, I admit, to offer something earthy and rustic to a householder well supplied with the delicacies of the sea. But I wanted a reason to talk with you, my kindred spirit, and to seem to add some small gift to this message. So I have sent a few of the very few figpeckers that the boys bring in at evening. Since I blushed at how few they were, I also added rather more words in verse, as if I meant to make up the number with talk. Both are faults, but if you kindly and as a friend pardon both, you will keep the small number from seeming ungracious and the chatter from seeming tiresome.
I. PAULINUS TO GESTIDIUS, A LORD RIGHTLY TO BE HELD IN HIGH ESTEEM.
Take, then, these birds, fattened in the bushy countryside,
which the cunning fowler, hiding under the cover of ferns,
mimicking the birds and fooling them with a whistle like their own,
catches in their trusting flocks on limed twigs.
Then, bringing home his slender catch as no slender gift,
he lays out the day's fowling on platters. The first row
gleams with plump birds, and they thin out gradually toward the bottom of the board,
so that the leanness may offend less: the charm of the fattened ones set in front
pleases eyes that the plump birds have won over first.
II.
If a poor friend's gift is to please you and be dear to you,
do not weigh against it the rich gifts you send to us.
For what could I send you that would be a worthy return for those fish
which the shore near you, with its rich waters,
supplies, marvellous and varied in appearance and form?
But here, through the rocky shallows of the deep, there is scarcely
a rare spondylus to be found growing in the dark seaweed.
Sharing these with you, I have sent you twice five and twice three
shells, fragrant with the nectar of the sea,
filled with very sweet flesh and two-coloured marrow.
Please accept them gladly and do not scorn these cheap things,
which are small only in size, for I have measured them out with great love.
III.
Europe and Asia, the two greatest limbs of the earth,
to which Sallust, with some doubt, adds Libya
as joined to Europe, though it could be called a third,
were ruled by many kings whom fame has blotted out and whose
barbarian names do not pass into the Roman tongue:
Illibanus, Avelis the Numidian, Vonones the Parthian,
and Caranus, who gave Pella its line of kings,
and Nechepsos, who taught the magi their empty mysteries,
and the one who reigned without a name, and soon after him Sesostris.
the bold one who gave his name to the Icarian Sea,
and the one who, keeping a middle course, swam through the air to the Chalcidian heights.
IV. A PRAYER.
Almighty Father of all things, you who hold the highest power,
hear me, if what I ask is just. Let no day be sad
for me, and let no night break my peaceful rest.
Let me take no pleasure in what belongs to others; instead, let what is mine help
those who ask of me. Let no one wish to harm me,
or have anything that could do me harm. Let me have no capacity
for wishing evil, and let me have the quiet power to do good.
Let my mind, content with its own and not given to shameful gain,
and with a clear conscience about a chaste bed, overcome the body's
allurements. Let it hate base jokes and obscene talk
and the harmful tongue, so welcome to malicious
ears, always guilty of pouring out poison.
Let me not be laid low by anyone's death, or grow rich by anyone's funeral.
Let me never envy anyone, and never lie.
Let me have a cheerful household; at meals I have not had to buy
let the well-fed home-born slave make merry, with a faithful companion and a neat servant,
and an obliging wife, and dear children born of that wife.
These things God grants to chaste ways of life, and such ways
promise themselves everlasting life in the ages to come.
V. A PRAYER.
Almighty one, known to me only through the worship of the mind,
unknown to the wicked and unknown to none of the godly,
without beginning or end, older than all time
that has been or will come, whose form and measure
no mind can grasp and no tongue can tell;
the only one who may rightly see you and hear you face to face as you command,
and sit beside the Father's right hand,
is the maker of all things himself, himself the cause of all creation,
himself the Word of God, the Word who is God, existing before
the world he was to make, begotten in that
time when time did not yet exist, brought forth before
the sun's radiance and the ruddy Morning Star lit the sky;
without him nothing was done, through him all things were made;
his throne is in heaven, and as he sits there the earth is subject to him,
and the sea, and the unconquerable chaos of dark night;
never resting, he himself moves all things and gives life to what is inert;
God from an unbegotten Begetter, who, offended by the treachery of a proud
people, called the Gentiles into the kingdom,
to be worshipped by the better offspring of an adopted stock;
our forefathers were allowed to see him, and in seeing his divinity
they were granted to see the Father too; he bore our contagion
and, having suffered the mockery of a dreadful death,
taught that there is a way back to eternal life,
and that not the soul alone returns, but enters the heavenly regions
with the whole body, and leaves the empty
secret place of the tomb lying open in the abandoned earth.
Son of the highest Father, bringer of salvation to our age,
to whom the Father handed over all his powers,
withholding nothing out of envy, so that you are full of his gifts,
open the way for my prayers and carry them to your Father's ears.
Grant me, Father, a mind unconquered against every sin,
and turn away the viper's wickedness and its harmful poison.
Let it be enough that the serpent ruined Eve long ago
and deceived Adam to share her fate. Let us, the late-born seed
of their descendants, the age foretold by truthful prophets,
avoid the snares that the death-dealing snake twists together.
Open the way that, after the bonds of this sick body,
will carry me on high, where the milky path of the pure heaven
rises above the drifting clouds of the windy moon,
where the godly patriarchs have gone, and where once,
caught up whole in a four-horse chariot, Elijah passed on high [?],
and Enoch, who went before him with his body intact.
Grant me, Father, the breath of eternal light I hope for,
if I do not swear by stones as gods, and if, looking up to the one altar
of awesome sacrifice, I bring the offerings
of an undefiled life; if I know you as the Father of the Lord and God,
the Only-begotten, and know the Spirit, joined with the two,
who hovered over the waters of the sea.
Grant me pardon, Father, and cleanse my tormented heart,
if I seek you not in the entrails of cattle, not in shed blood,
and do not guess at the divine will from hidden innards;
if I keep from crime, though I am prone to error, and
hope, rather than trust, to be found good and pure.
Deign to receive my confessing soul, if I loathe these perishable limbs,
and if I silently repent, and deep
dread torments my senses and anticipates the late torments of Gehenna,
and my wounded mind suffers its own punishment.
Grant, Father, that these wishes, made known in my prayer, may be fulfilled:
let me fear nothing and desire nothing; let me count as enough
whatever is enough. Let me want nothing shameful, nor be a cause of shame
to myself. Let me not do to anyone what, in the same situation,
I would not want done to me. Let me not be harmed by a real crime,
nor stained by a doubtful one; little seems to separate
the suspect from the truly guilty. Let me have no capacity to do evil,
and let me have the quiet power to do good.
Let me live simply in food and dress, let me be dear to my friends,
and always be a father without hurt to that name.
Let me suffer no pain of mind or body; let all my limbs
perform their duties in peace, and let my body, wounded in no
part, never miss any function it has lost.
Let me enjoy peace and live free from care, and think nothing on earth
a marvel. When the last hour of my day comes,
let a life with a clear conscience neither fear death nor long for it.
When, by your kindness, I am seen to be cleansed of hidden faults,
let me look down on all things, since my only pleasure will be
to hope for your judgement. And while it puts off its
appointed time and the day lingers, drive far away the savage
snake that lies in wait with its alluring errors.
These godly prayers, though they tremble with sorrowful guilt,
plead for them, Son, before the eternal Father, for you can win his favour:
Saviour, God and Lord, Mind, Glory, Word,
Son, true from true, Light from light,
abiding with the eternal Father, reigning for ever,
whom the harmonious songs of melodious David celebrate,
and the Amen strikes the air with answering voices.
VI. IN PRAISE OF ST JOHN.
Highest Father of all things, eternal power of heaven,
and you, Christ, with whom are our salvation and the glory of the saints,
and Spirit, joined equally to Father and to Son,
you who rule minds and tongues and supply the strength
that faith alone has earned, you who have full power
to pour wit into the dull and voice into the mute,
grant that John, drawn from the gospel spring,
may run down into my songs, though their channel is dry.
He is indeed as great as He could make him for the world
who commanded that such a one be born through new miracles;
but it is allowed to spend slender efforts on great things,
and heavenly things do not scorn humble praise.
It is itself part of merit to celebrate the merit of the godly;
nor shall I now sing things new or my own: the prophets told
all of it beforehand, and holy men in prose
have hallowed his promise, his birth, his life and his death,
if that was death which earned heaven by blood.
I have vowed only to unfold their words in tuneful measures
and with verse to ease the minds of those who read.
So (for one may compare great with small, ancient with new,
perfect with unlearned, eternal with perishable)
by God's inspiration, whatever earlier men had said
David, that venerable name, set to the lyre,
composing harmonious strains with a heavenly plectrum.
We too may rightly remember God, and, though our hearts
are buried under many sins, admit a heavenly understanding.
Zechariah, once a priest of the Syrian nation,
tended the temple entrusted to him with solemn ritual.
The man's life, in piety, faith, gravity and modesty,
was worthy of God's service; his kindly wife,
Elizabeth, born of the ancient stock of holy men,
was in virtues equal to so great a husband.
But—what our forebears counted a reproach to mothers—
she had no child, and sadly led a barren old age,
and her spent years had shut out all hope of offspring.
It happened that the whole people were offering a solemn sacrifice to God,
and the devout high priest had kindled the sacred fires,
adorning the inner altar with divine flames;
behold, beside the holy altar a heavenly messenger
stood, and, distinguished by his raiment, venerable in face,
showed by look and bearing that he was sent from heaven,
then opened his holy breast in such words as these:
"Receive, O priest beloved of the heavenly Lord,
the commands of the eternal God, whose care for the godly
is everlasting, who, a constant guardian in the pure heart,
has known how to bestow on the holy the love they have earned.
First, he does not will that your line should perish here
with its seed extinct, and he has made fruitful the womb
of your wife, which was already failing in worn-out age.
Yet why do you doubt, you too, with mortal understanding,
that God can do all things? But you will believe; he will prove it.
There will be born, worthy of so great a guarantor, a blessed
and enduring boy, who from his very first days
will hold, greater still, sacred strength in his unconquered breast,
more by the gift of his Maker than of his father.
Nor indeed is it in your choice or right
what first name you give your son; God himself, surely,
who orders him to be born, likewise orders him to be John.
This is the title of his name, offshoot of immense merits,
which, before he was born, he alone could foreknow
who will give him and grant you joy in so great a son.
Nor will he grant it to you alone; small is the glory
shut within one house; but the whole world, as far as it stretches
from the sunrise to the bounded twilight of the evening light,
will rejoice with you in your offspring.
What wonder? He will be free of all the dregs of vice,
leading a heavenly life without stain or sin,
keeping his heart abstinent from maddening wine
and shunning every cup of ill-counselling juice;
and though he will promise salvation to the human race, even after its errors,
for whoever is renewed by the holy water,
he himself will have nothing in him to be cleansed.
And not to tell you more with long windings,
you, a learned priest, cannot be ignorant of the merit
of Elijah, who, released from the law of hateful death,
lives an eternal life in his own body,
whom a fiery chariot carried up to the lofty heavens,
borne by the swift straining of a team of flaming horses;
your son will equal him in the lineage of merits
and will have just as much praise and virtue.
So, to give fitting thanks for so great a gift,
do not hold your faith in doubtful suspense, lest the anger
of a favouring God be stirred and impose a deserved penalty after rewards."
So he spoke, and glided away on wings into the thin air,
and filled the air far around with holy fragrance.
The priest stood rigid, confounded in his trembling mind,
and while his hesitant heart turns over the promise,
while he doubts that he has earned so great a favour,
that he should be the care of the highest God, that a messenger
sent from high heaven should bring such clear commands
from the Lord to his servant, and fears he is being mocked,
and thinks it all a dream, while he values his own conduct
more meanly than is fair and will not admit that he has earned it,
his very faith makes him faithless; while he will not believe himself
worthy, he earns punishment by unbelief.
At once the doubter's tongue was bound fast to his palate,
and, forgetting its own motion, as it strove
to shape the sound of a voice, it stuck in sluggish numbness;
and while he longs to tell his people the wonders,
he tried in vain and fell silent, his mouth fixed shut.
Sadly he departs, turning his grief within his closed mind,
and in his secret heart begs pardon for his error.
How great is God's kindness, how easily his godhead is entreated!
To repent is enough. The order of time that brings fulfilment
rolls on, and—wonderful to tell—Elizabeth swells with pregnant womb,
and her devout womb carries a holy burden,
and a youthful gift comes in exhausted age.
Next, holy Gabriel, the same who had been messenger
to Zechariah, pondering far greater things,
makes his way on another errand to Mary, who, betrothed to a husband
but chosen rather by God, destined to bear the salvation of the world,
a chaste virgin, kept her modesty unblemished.
When he, distinguished in form with heavenly beauty,
stood before her eyes, she lowered her modest face
and dyed her glowing cheeks with a rush of blood.
He said: "O maiden, in all the world the sun's orbit encircles,
among all who were before, who are, and who shall follow after,
happier than every virgin on earth,
chosen by great God, that you may be called the mother
of him whose Father He also is! Come, happy one, conceive the burden,
undefiled by man and free of all intercourse,
made fruitful by the Word of God; let your womb provide a body
for him who made heaven, earth, sea and stars,
who always was, and now is, and through all time
will always be Lord of the world and Creator of light.
He, the very light of heaven, will through you put on mortal limbs
and come before the eyes and the company of men.
Lift up your heart, undisturbed, to the reward of such great praise;
he will give you strength and faith,
who willed (for he rules all things and governs them by his nod)
to be your son, though he was the Lord's Son."
He spoke, and left her sight and the earth together,
and with easy flight sought his accustomed heaven.
God's commands are fulfilled, and the maiden believes
at once, and her ready faith adds to her merit and her former life.
By silent causes hidden elements
shape the divine body, and the burden to be hallowed grows;
the devout womb cherishes the heavenly Lord.
Meanwhile her child, though not yet born, urges
holy Mary in her pregnancy to set out and visit
Elizabeth, who, venerable now with long age,
was carrying a boy beloved of the Lord, soon to be born.
The mother heeds her son—so great is the power of faith—
and goes where she is bidden; John stirred his mother's
womb and filled her breast with divine understanding.
Already a seer, though unborn and shut in the womb,
already a prophet, he saw things past and things to come.
When she saw Mary far off, shining with the light she had conceived,
she was stirred and hastened from afar with swift steps
to meet her, stretching out her arms in reverence.
"Hail, mother of the Lord," she said, "hail, holy virgin,
free of the marriage bed and knowing no union with man,
yet about to bear God; so much was it worth to be chaste
that, untouched, you bear the titles and rewards of a wife.
Why is the honour of this service granted to me, undeserving
and unworthy of so great a gift? Why does the glory of heaven,
brought down to our household and humble roof,
bring so great a light into our obscure inner rooms?
But may he be gentle and kind to those who worship him,
and, once born, grant the favour he has granted before."
She spoke, and folded her in her embracing arms,
and, already worshipping God, kissed the holy womb.
Come, tell me now, guilty Judea, stained with the blood
of your own king: if no faith is to be given
to the words of those of old, if you believe the holy seers deceive,
and Moses himself, if the impious harshness of a perverse race
thinks that David deceives,
then believe the unborn: shut in his mother's womb,
John teaches through his mother's holy mouth what he sees.
Who, I ask, taught him whom the virgin held in her chaste womb,
and how great a birth awaits the new ages?
But hidden things lie open to the holy, unseen by the profane.
But my track has strayed beyond its bounds and seeks wide plains,
and, forgetting me, dares to run on too far.
I hope a day will come when, my strength made firm,
I may drive strong four-horse chariots over this course too.
Now let us take up again the road we began; let a mortal page
speak of mortal things; let divine pages speak of the Lord.
And now, when the time that nature required
was complete, the glorious boy is born from the ripe womb,
and God's great promises, disbelieved at the cost of punishment,
sure faith fulfils and the newborn infant confirms.
The kinsfolk gather together, as the custom was,
to give the boy a name drawn from his ancestors,
sought out by weighing reasons together;
but the mother, made aware through her son of heaven's command,
denies that the choice has been left to the relatives.
So they resolve to consult the father, long silent
with his voice shut off; the only way of giving
the sign his tongue cannot is if a letter marks it.
He is consulted, takes the tablets, and writes "John."
All are amazed, and recall that none of their forebears
in the family line had borne that name before.
How much belated faith prevailed! Because his right hand wrote
what his mind had believed, the penalty for his sin was remitted.
The bars of his bound tongue are loosed and released;
the old man now answers aloud and reveals to his kin
God's commands, long hidden, and foretells what is to come,
while proving what is past. Who would doubt that he would be such a one,
seeing that he could be born at the Lord's command, the law of nature set aside,
by so unaccustomed a birth?
An example of unbelief, to be proclaimed to all,
was set before the eyes of all by the father's punishment
or by his pardon, and on their minds press fear on one side, hope on the other.
Meanwhile the time of the cradle slips by; even in it
a clear sign of divine strength stands out.
Coaxing and laughter are silent, and uncertain babbling
ceases; a seriousness that outran playful sense
already shapes his tender face to his future character.
Then, when the boy had planted his first steps with steady effort
and his words had shaped sure speech,
his habit was either to listen to the sayings of his holy father
or to learn by heart the famous deeds of the ancients,
or the laws which God himself, with Moses as interpreter,
had established, which the writing on the sacred stone preserves.
These, and whatever else would strengthen a tender mind,
he studied and pondered; for he must not be thought ignorant of the past
to whom the Lord had given knowledge of the future.
But when age had brought strength to his limbs
(for his mind, full of God, had outrun the slow years),
he resolved even then that he must learn what men
cannot teach, and at the same time must flee the harmful contagion
that food and drink bring to a holy life.
So he leaves the house of his holy father, spotless though it was,
and flees the crowds of men and their harmful gatherings,
and makes for lonely lands and pathless places,
where his undefiled mind might see itself alone
and, free from cares, give itself to sacred precepts.
His garment was woven of the bristles of the humped camel,
to harden his soft limbs against luxury
and to ward off heavy sleep by pricking his body.
A cheap belt bound it to his rigid loins.
Wild honey supplied easy food,
with fruits and herbs sprung from untilled rocks,
and running water relieved his parching thirst.
What room is there here for vices? What entry could depraved desire
find among these things into the sanctuary of a holy mind?
How can he sin who desires nothing? How can one who lacks nothing
make his way into the lurking places of wicked thought?
So lived the first men, and when the world was new
the Creator had given them these ways for ages to come,
until ill-counselling pleasure crept in
and brought with it luxury and the love of possessing.
Hence hatreds, hence quarrels, hence fraud, hence envy and anger,
slaughter, arms, bloodshed, conflict, battles, deaths;
hence offence against God, which cruel Tartarus will expiate.
But why do I rebuke our common faults too much,
forgetful of myself, who ought not to press charges
but to hope for pardon? Rather we shall marvel,
more fittingly, at the unconquered example, inimitable by any
of the ancient age, of a man who by his toil surpassed human limits,
a demigod, who, free from every stain,
though he tormented his body with such harsh penalties,
prescribed what befits us, at least after our sins.
But when, strengthening his unconquered mind by such means,
he had spent a long time and had settled what he had found,
the things that had to be sought, a voice was sent to him from heaven:
"Enough time has now been spent, beloved prophet,
in profiting yourself; now is the time for what you know has been given you
to profit others and to save what is already lost.
Go, then, to the holy waters of the pure Jordan.
There, whoever among men repents of the sins
of his former life and at last turns his mind to better things,
wash him once he has confessed; whoever with faithful mind
believes that you blot out sins with the holy washing,
he will be born again, provided such a life follows
as proves that the washed have condemned their former life."
John obeyed what he heard with a servant's mind
at once, and went down to the banks of the river as he was bidden.
There he preaches God's precepts in words that command awe
and pours new salvation into the hearts of believers.
With the waters poured on them he washes away believers' sins,
frees men from their fears and remits their penalties,
and quenches fire with water; he urges them to forget
their errors, and grants new bodies for a new life.
O Father, O eternal Creator of men and of all things,
by how many steps your love spares us! What father ever
bears to forgive an erring son so often?
You give our race understanding to know good and evil.
Not content with that, you bind on us the bonds of a law to be kept,
and set punishments before the wicked and rewards before the just.
Whoever has spurned these too may return whenever he will;
pardon is at hand; see, the holy washing lies open,
to renew life and blot out old deeds
and make men new. What more do we seek?
And yet there is further pardon, should anyone violate
even this gift, fallen again with defiled body.
Though his error has already gone far too far,
let him stop and return. When he has condemned himself,
he has earned acquittal; if he repents, the guilt is void.
Truly, as you say, the burden is light and the yoke that clings to us
is sweet, when one man is forgiven so many times;
and yet we go astray, and there is no end of sin
for the human race. But your praise grows; for the greater
the guilt of the accused, the greater the glory of the one who spares.
So let every mind give you thanks, and let every
tongue sing, and let the human race, as far as it can,
if it cannot be pleasing, at least strive to be grateful.
A boundless deep opens, if we spread our sails,
for your praises, kindly Father; but my mind, aware of so great
a burden, trembles, and, not unaware, weighs its own strength
and leaves what must be said to worthier men.
Let us return to our theme: this is your work, holy John,
to renew pure minds by washing the body.
It was not first given by that word of the Lord with which he
admonished you, sending a clear voice through the clouds;
many ages before, God spoke through the mouth of the holy
prophet Isaiah, greatest of the ancient age:
"I will send before your face, O Son, a servant
who, clearing the tangled growth of thorny roads,
will make the high mountains sink before your steps,
and likewise make the sunken valleys rise;
he will straighten what is crooked and smooth what is rough; he will soften
what is hard and make the whole world level."
Is it you, I ask, gift of the highest Father, kindly John,
promised along with Christ, who come, and does he count you as his gift too
who sent his Son? Is it you, foretold by the prophets,
you who share the honour of the angels' name?
Through you God's mercy first shows itself;
to you first was granted the power to give pardon.
When the new people sought many miracles,
Christ said of you: "It has been granted you to see such a prophet
as no ages before have ever seen.
I say this, who alone know what has been done and what is to be done:
among the mortals whom woman has borne
and will bear, begotten in the ordinary human way,
there will be none who can set himself above John."
This he declares of you, who sees through every inmost secret
of the human heart and all the tracts of the ages in their order,
as we see what lies before our eyes.
VII.
Blessed is he who has kept his life far
apart from the gatherings of the ungodly,
and has not lingered in the way of sinners,
nor sat in the seat of pestilence,
but, fixed with his whole heart on the law of God,
turns over [?] the precepts of life night and day
and cultivates his mind with chaste teachings.
He will be like a tree that, close by a river,
is fed by the nourishing moisture of the bank,
and, laden, yields its fruit in its season,
and, ever green with leaves that never fall,
will stand, living wood with unfading foliage.
No such glory will attend the wicked;
but as the wind snatches away ash and dust,
so wrath will sweep the wicked from the face of God.
Therefore in this order will be divided
the flocks of men scattered across the world:
the ungodly, who denied God the worship due to him,
will not rise again to be judged,
but to be punished; for their evident crime
will need no inquiry to be uncovered,
since they will bear the threatening mark of death,
not bearing the sign of salvation on their foreheads.
But the sinner who is not, however, ungodly—
and that is a great crowd—will not rise to glory,
but will rise to be assigned to examination.
For he cannot sit as judge with the godly,
since he must render account of his own deeds
and, as his deeds vary, be approved or found guilty.
Those ignorant of the law will fall everywhere without law;
he who fell under the law will be judged by the law.
Fire will run as judge through every work;
whatever the flame does not burn up but proves,
that will be repaid with an everlasting reward.
He whose works must be burned will suffer loss,
but he himself will escape the flames and be saved;
yet, wretched, bearing the marks of a scorched body,
he will keep life, but he will not keep glory.
For, though overcome by the flesh, yet not turned away in mind,
even if he has denied the law the faith it was owed,
often tumbling down through many sins,
yet, bearing the eternal name of faith,
he will never be exiled from the bounds of salvation.
Therefore let us all, now in this world,
while our time runs on and the day of life lies open,
walk straight paths with steady foot
and not be carried down the slippery broad road;
it is better to struggle along the narrow track
and enter in with toilsome effort.
God gladly acknowledges the ways of the good,
but the downhill road of the ungodly will be destroyed.
VIII.
Why have the nations raged, and why have the peoples
plotted vain things? The princes, driven on with the kings, have taken their stand
against the Lord and his Christ, raging in madness:
"Let us burst their bonds, let us shake off their yokes."
He who abides in eternal rule over all the heavens
will laugh at them, and speak in his just anger,
and with a terrible, menacing word confound the wicked:
"But I, made king by him with equal dominion,
proclaim the Lord's decree upon holy Zion.
The Lord himself said to me: You are my Son;
today I have begotten you. Ask; be my heir among the nations,
and let your possession be founded over all the earth.
Yours is a rod of iron, for with mighty right you rule
the swelling peoples through all the world, breaking hearts like vessels
shaped of fired clay, so that you may remake them better."
And now, see, all you kings, give heed with humbled
minds, and all you who rule the serving hearts of men
by your judgment and hold the reins of affairs:
serve God with trembling, and, faithful, exult with fear
mingled in; let there be a harmonious discord,
joining unlike feelings in a single breast,
so that fear may not crush minds nor joys unnerve them,
if the fearful lack joy, or the joyful the dread of death [?].
Speak justice and take up upright ways,
and tremble before God as just, rejoice in him as kind,
lest God at some time be angry with the world, as it deserves,
and you, driven from the just way, justly perish.
From now on, hasten to turn back from the wicked way;
see, soon, when the great wrath of the Mighty One has blazed up
to winnow the whole world with divine sifting
and separate the chaff for the fire, the grain for salvation,
then blessed are all whose faithful hope is in him.
IX.
We sat as captives by the unknown rivers of dread Babylon,
a band of Judah, weeping piteously,
as we called up our fathers' Zion from remembering hearts
and sighed over the exile we had earned
from a just wrath, where the bank, planted with pliant willows,
gave friendly shade to the stranger peoples.
There, in the heart of the Assyrian city's walls,
forgetting our glad voices in sorrowful silence,
we hung our instruments on the branches of the willows.
For a heavy wrath dealt us bitter pain,
since the songs we used to raise in the holy temple
he ordered us to sing for his own amusement,
that impious enemy who had led us away from home.
Shall we, then, sing divine praises and songs fit for chaste
choirs among barbarous rites and foul tombs,
among altars kindled with deadly fires,
and, alas, wickedly sing for revellers out of our grief,
turning holy ritual into unholy revelry,
tuning mystic songs to an enemy's sport?
With what mouth shall we wretches now sing the sacred hymns?
Or in what place does Babylon demand the songs of Zion for herself?
No, a foreign land is not fit to earn
the Lord's song; the sacred voice turns away from unworthy ears.
Yet if you press on us captives as a harsher master,
and if you are so eager to learn the holy songs
of Zion, if you go on forcing me to utter what is not yours,
and what the divine songs of Zion may be for you,
hear what the avenging God pledges to the captured city,
so that you may not hope to rejoice long in that triumph,
impious one, in which you order the sacred hymn to be laid bare for you.
Behold the hymn of the Lord, behold the songs of Zion:
"If I forget my walls, you, my care,
city of Jerusalem, may my right hand never
remember me, and may my tongue cling parched
to my throat, unless I embrace you with eternal love,
and unless, at the beginning of the kingdom promised for ever,
in the first year of my joy, I remember
to set you, Jerusalem, above all lands.
Remember then the offspring of Edom, so that, the tables turned,
they may look on our day in confusion, when your people will dwell
in glorious Jerusalem within everlasting walls,
the city on which a nation forgetful of you now threatens cruel
destruction, saying: 'Tear down the hated city to its foundations
and empty it by force, until no trace
is left, its walls reduced to nothing.'
Unhappy daughter of wretched Babylon, happy
is he who will repay you on our behalf for what you did to us.
No less blessed will he be who will seize your little ones
and dash your offspring against the solid rock."
If you long to be blessed by the destruction of Babylon's stock,
then the sins swelling within yourself in their first flames
break by faith. Christ, the rock, is close at hand; against him
dash the viper's brood with strong arms.
For the name Babylon means confusion, and her daughter
is the flesh, the mother of sins, a throng harmful to salvation,
that draws evil seeds into the body's fibres.
These you must conquer if you wish to overcome death;
for such enemies, shut up within your bones,
if they are allowed to gather strength as they grow,
you will conquer only by a hard struggle. Forestall them while they are small,
while the raw infancy of the vices, born from the womb of the heart,
still creeps with tender limbs through the captured breast.
Unless you guard against them, this earthly brood, its strength increased,
will kill the soul that consents to the vices.
So do not spare to slaughter such a band.
It will be no crime for you to destroy a race bent on harming you
and to drench the avenging rock with evil blood;
for the righteous rejoices when the impious offspring falls,
and the godly man is cleansed more and more by this slaughter,
if he kills the sins that lord it over his members
and triumphs once the people of vices has been broken in Christ.
X. Paulinus to Ausonius
This is now the fourth summer returning to the hardy reapers,
and as often has winter stiffened with hoary frost,
since any letter came to me from your lips,
or I saw any writing traced by your hand,
until at last a happy sheet, with a health-bringing little book,
gave me the gifts so long denied, and multiplied them.
For a threefold letter flowered in varied texture,
and each of the three pages was a song in measured verse.
Your affection, anxious to censure, had mingled certain sweet things
beneath bitter ones in complaints of many kinds.
But the father's mildness weighed with me more than the censor's harshness,
and I weigh the harsh words against the gentle ones in my mind.
Those charges, however, must be answered in their own place, and handled
in the weightier sound of the vindicating heroic verse.
Meanwhile the lighter iambus will run ahead in a few lines,
returning words in exchange with its own distinct foot.
For now the elegiacs bid you greeting, and, having said their greeting,
having given the others their start and their pace, fall silent.
Why, father, do you bid the Muses I have renounced
return to my care?
Hearts devoted to Christ refuse themselves to the Camenae
and are closed to Apollo.
Once there was this concord, not of equal power but of equal zeal,
between you and me:
to summon deaf Phoebus from the Delphic cave,
to call on the Muses as deities,
and to seek the gift of speech, which is granted by the gift of God,
from groves or mountain ridges.
Now another power drives my mind, a greater God,
who demands another way of life,
claiming back from man his own gift,
so that we may live for the Father of life.
To spend ourselves on vain things, in leisure or in business,
and on the literature of fables,
he forbids, so that we may obey his laws
and behold his light,
which the cunning force of the philosophers, the art of the rhetoricians,
and the fictions of the poets cloud over;
they steep hearts in false and empty things
and train only tongues,
offering nothing that might bring salvation
or clothe us in truth.
For what good or true thing can they hold
who do not hold the head of all,
God, the kindling and the fountain of the true and the good,
whom no one sees except in Christ?
He is the light of truth, the way of life,
the might, mind, hand and power of the Father,
the sun of justice, the fount of good things, the flower of God,
born of God, the sower of the world,
the life of our mortality and the death of death;
he is the teacher of the virtues;
God for us, and for us made man,
he stripped himself by putting on our nature,
joining in himself an eternal exchange between men and God
in both natures.
So when he has flashed his radiance from heaven
into our hearts,
he wipes away the sickly mould of the sluggish body
and renews the condition of the mind;
he drains away all that pleased us before,
putting chaste delight in its place,
and by a lord's right he claims wholly what is ours,
our hearts, our lips, our times;
he wills to be thought on, understood, believed, read;
he wills to be feared and loved.
The empty agitations stirred by the toil of life
along the path of this present age
are abolished by faith in the life to come with God.
That faith does not cast away the riches we seem to scorn
as profane or worthless,
but, holding them more precious, bids that they
be stored up in heaven, entrusted to Christ our God,
who has promised more than was given,
so that what is now despised, or rather deposited with him,
he may repay with rich interest.
A guardian without fraud, a good debtor,
he will return their money to his creditors increased,
and God, more generous still, will restore
the money we scorned with abundant interest.
One who is free for him, eager and devoted,
storing up everything in him,
do not, I beg you, think sluggish or perverse,
nor accuse him of impiety.
How can piety be lacking in a Christian?
For each is the proof of the other:
to be a Christian is the proof of piety, and of impiety
not to be subject to Christ.
Once we learn to hold to this piety, could I
fail to show it to you, that is, to a father,
to whom God willed that I should owe
every sacred duty, every dear name?
To you I owe my learning, rank and letters,
the distinction of my tongue, my toga and my fame;
by you I was promoted, raised and taught,
my patron, teacher, father.
But why do you reproach me for living so long far away,
and grow angry out of loving concern?
Either this is profitable, or necessary, or pleasing:
whichever of these is the case, it is pardonable.
Forgive me, loving as you are, if I do what is expedient;
rejoice with me if I live as I please.
That I have been absent from my native land for three whole years,
and chosen another world in wandering travels,
forgetful of the companionship of your life which I once cherished,
you reproach me in holy complaints, moved by affection.
I embrace the feelings of a father's heart, worthy of reverence,
and an anger I must welcome, since your affection is unharmed.
But I would rather, father, that you asked for my return from the one
who could grant it. Am I to believe that you will call me back,
when you pour out barren prayers, not to the divine,
but as a suppliant to the Castalian Muses, whose godhead turns away?
Not by these deities will you bring me back to you and to my homeland.
You call on deaf things and ask of nothings (a light breeze will carry off
what is given to nothing): the Muses, names without godhead.
Windy storms snatch away these useless vows,
which, not addressed to God, stick fast in empty clouds
and never reach the starry hall of the King on high.
If you care for my return, look to him and pray to him
who with his thunder shakes the fiery heights of highest heaven,
who flashes with three-forked fire and mixes no empty rumblings,
who lavishes from heaven both suns and rains on the sown fields,
who, above all that is, and wholly everywhere in all things,
rules all things through Christ, who is poured into all,
through whom he holds and moves our minds, through whom he orders our times
and places. And if he should decree what goes against our wishes,
it is he who must be turned by prayer toward
what we desire. Why do you accuse me? If the course displeases you
that I follow at God's prompting, then, if one may say so, the author is the first defendant,
since it is his pleasure either to form or to change my mind.
For if you consider my former ways, the ones you knew,
I will freely confess that I am not now the man I was
at the time when I was not thought perverse
and yet was perverse, seeing through the fog of falsehood,
wise in what is folly to God, and living on the fodder of death.
All the more right that I should be forgiven, since from this
it is the more readily recognized that what is not done in my usual way
is a renewal by the supreme Father. I shall not, I think, be said
to have confessed here a culpable error of a mind
changed for the worse, since I have freely professed
that it was not by my own mind that I changed my former life.
A new mind is mine, I confess, a mind not my own, not mine once,
but mine now, with God as its author; and if he saw anything in my conduct
or my character worthy of his service,
the first thanks go to you, to you the glory due is yielded,
by whose teaching was produced something Christ could love.
So you should rejoice rather than complain
that this man of yours, sprung from your studies and your character,
Paulinus, whose parent you do not deny you are,
even now, when you believe him perverse, has had his counsels
so turned that he has earned the right to be Christ's while he remains
Ausonius'. He will bring his own rewards to your praise,
and offer you first the fruit of your own tree.
So I pray you, think better of it, and do not lose the greatest
rewards by cursing the good things that sprang from your own springs.
For mine is not a crazed mind, nor do I lead a life fleeing
the company of men, like the life you write
the rider of Pegasus lived in the caves of Lycia; though many,
at God's prompting, dwell in pathless places, just as famous philosophers once did
for the sake of their studies and their Muses, so now too
those who have received Christ into chaste souls often spend their lives there,
not poor in spirit, nor choosing out of savagery
to dwell in deserted places, but, turned toward the lofty
stars, gazing upon God, and intent on seeing into the depths
of truth, they love a leisure free from vain cares,
and shrink from the din of the forum, the tumult of affairs,
and all business hostile to divine gifts,
out of regard for Christ's commands and love of salvation;
and in hope and faith they follow God for a promised reward,
which the sure author will pay to those who do not despair,
provided only that present things do not win out with their emptiness,
and that the fiery mind scorns what it sees so as to earn what it does not see,
penetrating the secrets of heaven.
For perishable things lie open to our sight; eternal things are denied
to our eyes, and for now we pursue in hope what we see with the mind,
scorning the varied forms that are the spectacles of the world,
goods that wickedly tempt the bodily eyes.
This judgment, at any rate, was seen to be settled among those
to whom the whole light of the true and the good has already been revealed:
that the age to come is eternal, and the present one empty.
But why should I, who have not the same glory, have the same
reputation? My faith is equal to that of the famous, but since I still live
in pleasant places, settled on the charming strand
of a rich coast, why this hasty spite
about where I live? Would that a just envy
would begin to pluck at me! Under the name of Christ, reproaches will please me.
A mind made firm by God does not allow tender shame,
and the praise scorned here returns to me with Christ as judge.
So do not, revered parent, rebuke me as one gone astray
in these pursuits, nor carp at me either over my wife
or for a defect of mind. Mine is not the anxious mind of Bellerophon,
nor is my wife a Tanaquil, but a Lucretia.
Nor do I seem to myself now to have forgotten my native sky,
I who look up to the supreme Father; whoever worships him alone
is truly mindful of heaven. Believe then, father, that we
are neither unmindful of heaven nor living out of our wits,
and that we dwell in places inhabited by men. The very pursuits of the godly
bear witness to the characters of men; for no impious
race could know the supreme God. Grant that many places,
many men are uncouth in their pursuits and without laws:
what region is free of rustic ways? And how does
another's wickedness harm anyone in such places? Why do you cast at me the vast
forests of Vasconia and the snowy lodgings of the Pyrenees,
as though I lived fixed on the very threshold
of the Spanish land, and had no place anywhere,
in country or city, where rich Spain
stretches out to the edge of the world, watching the suns go down?
But suppose it were so. Has it been my lot to live on the ridges of brigands?
Have I grown rough in a barbarous home, changed into the very likeness
of those among whom I had my dwelling, sharing their savagery?
A pure mind does not take in evil, nor do stains
sprinkled on smooth fibres cling to them. So in the Vascon forest
whoever lives pure of crime, upright and just,
draws no contagion of manners from an inhuman
host. But why should I be charged on account of that name,
when I dwell, as I have always dwelt, in quite different places, near proud
cities and thronged with men in happy cultivation?
And if my life had indeed been spent on Vascon shores,
why would the barbarous race not rather be shaped by my ways,
lay aside its savage customs, and pass over to ours?
As for your setting my dwelling in the ruined cities
of Spain, and picking out deserted towns in your verse,
and taunting me with mountainous Calagurris, and Bilbilis hanging
on its sharp crags, and the hill of fallen Ilerda,
as though I lived in these, an exile from home and city,
far from the roofs and roads of men: do you think these
are the riches of the Iberian land, ignorant as you are of the Spanish world,
where Atlas once stood under the heavy weight of the sky,
now a mountain, the last remnant of him and the boundary of the earth,
who with his lofty peak sets apart Calpe between two seas?
Are only Bilbilis, Calagurris and Ilerda to be noted in a land
which has Caesaraugusta, which has lovely Barcino,
and Tarraco looking down on the sea from her famous height?
Why should I list the cities outstanding in their lands and walls,
where happy Spain stretches out toward the twin seas,
where she swells the Ocean with the Baetis and the Tyrrhenian Sea with the Ebro,
and fills the broad divide between the distant waters,
setting with her circuit a boundary at the edge of the world?
Or would you, illustrious lord, if you had a mind to write
of the region where you live, like to say nothing of shining
Bordeaux and prefer to describe the pitchy Boii?
And when you lavish your leisure on the baths of Marojallia
and grant yourself a life among shady groves,
dwelling in happy places and in houses wonderful for their buildings,
is it in black huts and straw-thatched hovels that you live,
in wildernesses fit for the skin-clad Bigerri?
And you, the consul, who in your power scorn the proud walls of Rome,
do you not disdain the sandy Vasates?
Or, because your fertile estate flourishes in the fields of the Pictones,
shall I lament that the Ausonian curule chair has, alas, come down to Rauranum,
and that the consular robe grows shabby in an old shrine,
that robe which, in the august city of Latin Quirinus,
among the emperors' palm-embroidered robes, with equal title,
shines long venerable with its unworn gold,
keeping the flourishing honour of living merit?
Or when you linger at the heights of your Lucanian estate,
living under a roof that rivals the halls of Romulus,
are you to be said, because the place gives an opening and marks its neighbourhood,
to live in the village of Condate?
Let much be open to jesting; let it be allowed to play with fictions.
But to strike in a heavy tooth while the tongue soothes,
to play with burning blandishments, and to sour
sweet jests wickedly with the vinegar of biting satire,
is often the way of poets, but never fitting for parents.
For faith and affection demand that what rumour, weaving evil,
whispers into chaste ears, a father's mind, good and prayerful,
should not let fasten on the heart and stick there,
fixed. And the crowd, malicious in its perverse rumour,
[?] former ways; to change one's life is not always
a crime; indeed, to turn for the better deserves praise. When you hear
that I am changed, ask what my pursuits and duties are.
If I have turned from right to crooked, from holy to profane,
from frugal to extravagant, from honourable to base,
and live sluggish, idle and obscure, pity your companion
turned to evil; then let anger rouse even a gentle parent
to restore his fallen friend to right
ways and repair him for better things with stern rebuke.
But if perhaps you hear instead what I have chosen and what I follow:
that I have vowed my heart to holy God, following the venerable
command of Christ with a teachable faith,
and persuaded by God's warnings that eternal
rewards are prepared, bought by mortals with present losses,
then I do not think this has so displeased a holy parent
that he believes it an error of mind to live for Christ
as Christ ordained. This delights me, and I do not repent of this
error. I do not mind being a fool to those who follow
other paths, so long as my judgment
is wise in the eyes of the eternal King. Brief is whatever man is; he is of a sickly body,
of a passing time, and without Christ, dust and shadow;
what he approves or condemns is worth only as much as the judge himself.
He himself dies, and his error goes along with him,
and his opinion passes away, dying with its judge.
But unless, while the present time is given us, we take anxious
care to live by the precept of Christ the Lord,
too late will man lament, once stripped of his limbs,
that while he feared the light reproaches of human tongues,
he did not fear the heavy wrath of the divine judge,
who sits on the throne at the right hand of the eternal Father,
set as king over all, and who, as the years slip by,
will come to judge all nations with an even
scale and repay each varied deed with its due reward:
this I truly believe, and in fear I labour with hurrying zeal,
if it may be granted, not to be released by death before I am released from sin.
At the thought of his coming my believing heart trembles
in quaking fibres, and my soul, already wary of the future, is restless,
fearing beforehand that, bound by sickly cares for the body
and weighed down by the burden of affairs, if the sky should open
and the vast trumpet ring out, it might not be able to rise
into the air on light wings to meet the King,
flying in heaven among the honoured thousands of the saints,
who, light through the void, their feet unbound by the shackles of the world,
will lift them with easy effort to the lofty stars,
and, borne on soft clouds, will pass among the stars
to worship the heavenly King in mid-air
and join their bright ranks to Christ whom they adore.
This is my fear, this my labour: that the last day may catch me
asleep in black darkness, at fruitless work,
spending lost time on empty cares.
For what shall I do if, while I drowse over sluggish vows,
Christ, revealed to me from the citadel of heaven, should flash forth,
and I, dazzled by the sudden rays of the Lord coming
through the opened heavens, confounded by the light that falls on me,
should seek the gloomy refuges of dark night?
So that neither distrust of the truth nor love of present life,
nor pleasure in things, nor the toil of cares should bring this upon me,
I resolved to forestall that fate
by my purpose, and to end my cares while life remains,
and, trusting in God, who is shared by all ages to come,
to await cruel death with an untroubled heart.
If this pleases you, rejoice in your friend's rich hope;
if not, leave me to be approved by Christ alone.
XI. Paulinus to Ausonius
That my tongue's silence has gone on unbroken
you complain in words that are never silent, and you reproach me
with an idleness that delights in hiding; on top of this you add
the charge of neglected friendship, and you taunt me
with a wife I supposedly fear, and hurl a harsh verse into my very heart.
Spare, I beg you, to wound your own, and do not choose to mix bitterness
into a father's words, like wormwood into honey.
It has always been, and still is, my care to honour you
with every duty and to respect you with faithful affection.
Never has your favour been stained by me
with even the slightest blemish; I always feared to hurt you even by a look,
or to offend you by an unguarded expression.
Whenever I approached you in reverence, I composed my face with care
and shaped my brow with a cheerful eye,
so that no false suspicion might read a cloud gathered even in a silent heart
as turned against my holy parent.
Following this example my household has honoured you and honours you still,
and our agreement in love for you is as great
as our united mind in worshipping Christ.
What jealousy, I ask, has clouded your heart against your own?
By what rumour has easy gossip broken in through your loving ears
and struck your mind, and, against a long-standing faith
proven by affection, opened new wounds,
so that, ill-counselling, it should turn a gentle parent against his children?
But my mind, conscious of unfeigned simplicity,
and my affection, guilty of no neglect of my father, reject everything
undeserved and will not bear to be grazed by a false charge,
being truly innocent; for a mind as tender to offence as it is free from guilt
is the more gravely hurt by an unjust wound.
You complain that I have thrown off the yoke by which I was joined
to you in learned studies. I claim I never even bore
that yoke; for it is equals who go under the yoke; no one couples the strong
with the weak, and the reins are not in harmony
if the pair yoked together are of unequal measure.
If you match a calf with a bull or a horse with a wild ass,
if you compare coots with swans and the nightingale with the magpie,
hazels with chestnuts, and make the wayfaring tree equal to the cypress,
then pair me with you; even Tully and Maro could scarcely bear
an equal yoke with you. If I am joined to you by love,
in that alone will I dare to boast myself your yoke-fellow,
in which [?] with great reins
sweet friendship binds me to you in an eternal covenant,
ever fair by the equal laws of returning love.
This yoke no perverse tale has loosed from our necks,
no long absence in distant lands has broken,
nor will it destroy it. Though I be drawn away by the whole world or by the whole of time,
I shall never live parted from you in spirit; life itself will leave
my body sooner than your face will leave my heart.
Through all the time that is given
and appointed to mortals,
as long as I am held within the enclosing body,
whatever world may separate us,
I shall hold you, never far off in the world nor removed from my sight,
implanted in my inmost being;
I shall see you with my heart, embrace you with a loving mind,
present to me everywhere.
And when, set free from the prison of the body,
I fly away from the earth,
in whatever region of the sky the common Father places me,
there too I shall bear you in my soul.
The end that frees me from my body
will not also release me from my love for you.
For the mind, which outlives the fallen limbs
and endures by its heavenly origin,
must keep its senses and its affections
just as it keeps its life;
and as it cannot die, so it cannot forget,
ever living and ever mindful.
XII.
Renowned confessor, Felix in merit and in name,
a soul mighty in devotion, a soul that dwells in highest heaven,
yet a power proven no less throughout all the earth;
you who confessed Christ the Lord with an unfettered voice
and by scorning savage torments earned your escape from them,
and, when you were bidden to give back to Christ, through every torment, your devoted soul
of your own free will, your limbs set loose,
left to the raging lictors your limbs, [?],
and were borne up to heavenly honor, a martyr without blood:
O father, O lord, grant to your servants, unworthy though they are,
that at last, while we drag out this life in a frail body,
in the dwelling we long for, in the hall where you rest,
we may celebrate this day, and pay in your presence
our devout vows, and rejoice amid the rejoicing throngs.
Let it be enough now, I beg, to have borne for our deserved ungodliness
this penalty: that we have lived so many years now without you,
far, alas, from your dwelling, though not distant in mind.
Now take thought for our longings, wearied by endless time;
now, though late, remember your own and have pity on them;
and across the world, which parts us by so vast an expanse
of the great sea, crush whatever hostile things hold us back,
and open easy ways; and if, as we hasten to you,
the envious enemy stands in our way, drive back the bars he sets against us,
being stronger than our adversaries, and speed us on a friendly course.
If the road by land should please us, be a companion on the safe highway
to your own; or if great trust in you
should persuade us to go by the long sea, grant us to run over gentle waves,
and supply to your servants winds that serve them from the stern,
so that, as soon as we have reached the Campanian shores with Christ as our guide,
we may be swept on in swift course to your rooftops
and find at your threshold a calm harbor.
There we shall bear a sweet yoke, a light burden, and a pleasant
servitude under you as master; and though, being just, you have no need
of unjust servants, yet you will both bear with and love
those dedicated to you by Christ's gift, such as they are,
and you will allow them to serve at your doors, to tend your threshold in the morning
by keeping it clean, and in turn by night
to guard it with devout vigils, and in this duty
to close, with weary body, a life that has earned its reward.
XIII.
Felix, as happy in merit as in name, and in name the same
as in merit, the kindly day returns on which Christ took you to himself,
his confessor, into the highest hall of the homeland;
the time is here to pour out thanks to you with full vows.
O father, O lord, best of masters even to unworthy servants,
at last our prayer has been granted, to celebrate within your threshold
your birthday. Three lustres have run their long course
since, at these solemn rites,
I dedicated my vows to you in your presence, in your presence my heart.
Since then, what toils by land and sea
have kept me from your dwelling, far off in a distant world,
you know; for I called on you, always near me everywhere,
amid the hardships of the road and the uncertainties of life.
And I entered upon the seas with you as guide, because fear of danger
gave way to love of you; nor was it without you, for I felt
your protection in Christ the Lord as I overcame the roughness of the sea;
always, because of you, I go safe on land and wave.
Ask, I pray, that this day be bright with everlasting devotion and peace
for your own, Felix, you who stand in his great name.
Now it is a delight to set loose our hearts, poured out in joy,
since at last the dear day has dawned here for us who are present,
the day we always celebrated across a foreign world,
which hallowed you for the earth and gave you to the stars.
See, a motley people paints the roads with varied throngs;
we marvel at countless cities in a single city.
O Nola, happy in Felix, your own patron,
renowned for your holy citizen, made strong by your heavenly protector,
and allotted honors second only to Rome herself,
which once was first only by empire and victorious arms,
but now is first in the world by the tombs of the apostles too!
Be kind and favorable to your own, and entreat the mighty Lord
that, by the gift of Christ appeased, we may,
after the waves of the sea, and once the waves of the world too are past,
come to rest at your anchorage in a calm harbor.
On this shore I have hauled up my fleet safely and made it fast;
in you let the anchor of my settled life be fixed.
XIV.
The festal day has come, a feast in heaven and most celebrated on earth,
keeping the birthday of Felix, on which in body
he passed from the earth and was born to Christ among the stars above,
a martyr who won heavenly honor without blood.
For he died a confessor, spared the torments not by his own choice,
since God accepted a faithful mind in place of blood;
for he who searches the silent heart counts those ready to suffer
equal to those who have suffered, and, content to have tested what is within,
in just mercy remits the torment of the flesh.
Martyrdom without slaughter pleases him, if a mind and faith ready to endure
burn for God; a will prepared to suffer
suffices, and is the highest witness to proven merit.
So the day which by so great a gift set
Felix in high heaven is this one, kept with sacred rites,
which, after the solstice on which Christ, born in the body,
changed the season of icy winter with a new sun,
and, granting mortals a saving birth,
bade the nights dwindle with him as the day grew longer—
the twentieth light to rise for us from that day—
marks the starry honor of Felix's merit.
Indeed, in no way unequal to those witnesses who poured out their blood,
received alike in title and in power,
he shows the merit of a martyr when with mighty right
he harries demons and frees bodies held in bondage.
For the pestilent princes confess with doleful outcry that Felix
presses on them with unseen punishments,
and they bear witness to hidden crosses with open groans,
and betray him, veiled from mortal eyes yet plain
to the ears, and present in great power,
when, caught within the bodies they hold captive, they cry out and acknowledge
that Christ shines in his saint,
by the trembling shudder of limbs and the whirling of heads
and by their own torments; yet it is not their own bodies they torture,
crying out their own pains through others' mouths
as they beg for pardon; the avenger is hidden, the punishment is seen.
Then, if the enemy has bound any more violently with a heavier evil,
this day sets them free by divine power.
Now one may see everywhere hearts cleansed by the sacred remedy
lying prostrate at the threshold, now restored in mind,
now giving thanks with their own voices; a gaping crowd
of people runs together trembling; amid the joy, tears spring
from all, mingled together; God is believed to be present to all
there; Felix is the glory of the boundless Christ.
The kindly day is celebrated by great gatherings; all
dedicate their fulfilled vows at the sacred doorposts; all things
of earth and heaven rejoice; the sky seems to smile with the heavens
thrown open, the breezes, their blasts gone still, seem to breathe of spring,
and the milky band to gird the glad sky.
There is no end to the peoples gathering in dense column,
nor any rest; they hurry from night into light, and to wait for the day
irks them; the delay of night is broken by their eager prayers,
and torches overcome the night with their flames.
It is a joy to see one city thronged with many cities
and so many swarms driven together by a single vow.
The Lucanian peoples gather, the Apulian youth gather,
and the Calabrians, and all whom either sea washes,
the waves that sound round Latium on left and right;
and glad Campania, through her twice thirty cities,
rejoices as at her own feast: those whom wealthy Capua holds
within her broad walls, those whom lovely Naples, or those whom
Gaurus nourishes, those who work the fruitful Massic slopes, and those who
drink of the Ufens and the Sarnus, those who till the dry fields of the Tanager
and the fertile tilth of the well-watered Galaesus,
those whom mighty Atina, whom mother Aricia sends.
Rome herself, mighty in the sacred tombs of the heavenly princes
Peter and Paul, is glad to be thinned out
in honor of this day, and from the mouth of the Capene Gate
pouring forth thousands toward the walls of friendly Nola,
sends them out over twelve times ten miles in dense
column; far and wide the Appian Way lies hidden beneath the packed crowds.
No less, by peoples setting out from another region,
the rough paving of the mountainous Latin Way is traversed:
those whom lofty Praeneste, whom fertile Aquinum feeds,
those whom ancient Ardea sends from the lands near Rome,
and those who have left Cales and twin Teanum,
the one dwelt in by the stern Auruncan, the other by the rough Apulian;
here too a crowd runs together from olive-bearing Venafrum,
and the hardy Samnites leave their mountain towns.
Devotion has conquered the hard road; love of Christ conquers
all things, and kindly faith persuades those hardened in mind and by their homeland
to endure bitter hardships, and at the same time to lay aside their rough hearts.
One day calls them all, and one Nola receives them,
full of them throughout her whole extent, yet spacious for all,
so that you would think her walls were widened for countless
guests. So, Nola, you rise up in the likeness of Rome,
[you too allotted honors second after the City;
for she was once first only by empire and victorious arms,
but now is first in the world by the tombs of the apostles too.]
You too have embraced, under a twofold honor, the everlasting crowns
of your Felix, first as priest, then for all ages as martyr;
well do you reach heaven by a twin
merit, mother of a friend of God.
First, as a presbyter, he honored your kindly altars with devout worship,
ordered your life, and ruled you with gentle governance.
Now too Felix adorns you with his everlasting name.
For, hallowed in your bosom, he draws honor from his merit,
his holy bones laid to rest in a fragrant tomb.
Now the golden thresholds are adorned with snow-white curtains,
the bright altars are crowned with crowded lamps,
fragrant lights burn on waxed papyrus wicks,
and glitter night and day. So the night shines with the brightness of day,
and the day itself, illustrious with heavenly honor,
gleams the more, its light doubled by countless lamps.
We too are happy, who are granted to see this day face to face
and to celebrate it, to behold the rewards of our patron,
to give thanks to Christ who grants such great things to his own,
and to rejoice amid the joyful throngs.
Bring praise to God, boys, fulfill your devout vows,
and together offer festal songs with chaste dances;
strew the ground with flowers, fringe the doorways with garlands.
Let winter breathe out purple spring, let the year burst into flower
before its time; let nature yield to the holy day.
You too, earth, owe crowns to the martyr's tomb.
But the sacred glory of the heavenly threshold surrounds him
as he flourishes with the double crown of war and peace.
Ask, I pray, that this day be bright for us with everlasting peace;
may we rejoice again when it returns,
and here pay yearly both vows and songs at your festivals,
with Christ appeased and his power at peace.
This is our love, this our labor; receive these vows of your own
and commend them to God, so that when, with diligent care,
our service has been paid to you for a long age,
then at last you may release your nurslings, pleasing to you in the devotion of their labor,
sending them forth with your hand, and that you may not refuse to carry the souls of your own,
set before your face, in your fatherly
bosom to the face of the shining Lord,
whom, kind in goodness yet dreadful in majesty,
you must entreat, that he may graciously, at your prayers and for your merits, forgive
us our debts. When you too, a great part of the righteous,
attend the reigning Lamb, Felix,
ask that we be placed in the flock of sheep, so that the sentence of the supreme
Judge may give us to you again, this time also as a gift,
and may not assign us to the left among the ill-favored goats,
but rather, setting us on the right among the righteous,
may join us to the bountiful flock and the praised lambs.
XV.
My yearly vows come round again, and with them the yearly debts
of my tongue: your birthday, Felix, most illustrious to Christ,
dearer to me than my own birthday. On this day,
though the joy is shared by countless crowds,
there is something special for your own, because Christ granted
that we should be yours, bestowing worthless men on his dear friend.
It was not that you deserved such worthless servants,
you whom God deems worthy to walk as a companion in eternal triumphs;
it was because we were poor in righteousness and in need of salvation,
and the good Father chose to enrich us in this way: that we, wickedly rich
in sins, with the lot of our riches turned for the better,
in place of all our wealth and all our attachments, and in place of
noble titles and empty honours, should take as our all
Felix: our wealth, our homeland and our home.
You are father and homeland and home and substance to us;
our cradles have been moved into your lap,
and your bosom is our nest. Warmly cherished there
we grow, and, changing our bodies into another form,
we shed our earthly stock, and as our wings spring up
we are turned into birds by the seed of the divine Word.
Because you lift it, we find Christ's yoke gentle; in you
Christ is kind to the unworthy and sweet to the bitter.
So we too must keep this day as a feast,
the day that is your birthday, because, as you wipe away our evils,
we die to the world so as to be born into good things in Christ.
Rise up, then, my lyre, and strain with all your strings;
awake, power of my soul! Let my inmost being, with silent song,
and the heart's sounding-shell, which is not silent, with the teeth for its struck strings,
be plucked by love, and let the mouth's lyre ring out with the tongue for its plectrum.
I will not summon the Castalian Muses, mere phantoms of invention,
nor deaf Phoebus from the Aonian crag;
Christ is the one who inspires my song, and by Christ's gift
I, a sinner, dare to speak of holy and heavenly things.
Nor is it hard for you, Almighty, to loosen my lips
into skilful measures, for you command the mute to speak, the dry to flow, the hard
to melt. You made a she-ass bellow out in speech,
and made sucklings fashion perfect praise for you;
you dissolved a solid rock into rivers,
and bade the waterless earth gush with sudden streams,
watering the deserts as a hope for the peoples,
into whose parched souls holy grace has flowed,
whom Christ, the Rock that pours out a living spring, has refreshed.
So I, the least of men, relying on this gift
of your dew, O Christ, and parched as I am, pray for living draughts.
Give me a word from your spring. I cannot tell of your works
without you, for the praise of your martyr is your praise as well.
You, almighty, make men strong for divine deeds,
and you overcome the strong through the weak, triumphing out of the flesh
and conquering the princes of the air in our body.
So be with me, that with you as my guide I may go back to the beginning
and tell of your Felix. His noble family
came from the East; for no other land
was a more fitting homeland for Felix than the one that had borne the patriarchs
and the holy prophets, those sacred vessels of Christ,
the land from which, pouring out its rivers through the tongues of the apostles,
the sound of the gospel flowed out over the whole world.
From there Felix, destined for God, came to Italy when his father set out;
not yet begotten, he still came, in his father,
so that he might spring up a citizen of our shores in affection
and remember that he had been born for no one but us.
So father Abraham, following the Lord's commands,
exchanged his ancestral lands for foreign soil
and planted his holy seed in the fields of Canaan;
and from there, as his offspring went out into foreign lands,
a mystic lineage sent Felix across to us,
whom perfect faith, sprung from that root,
brought forth to be for us a holy vein of faith.
Even now, though Felix has laid aside the flesh and rests,
he lives as a spirit in Christ, and through the working merits of his lofty
power he, as Abraham's seed, changes
the hardness of stones, which he raises up to the good things of life.
So, born in this city to a Syrian father,
he cherished beloved Nola as the likeness of his homeland,
blessing it with the dwelling he chose; and, left much gold,
he flourished, rich in wealth, though he was not the only heir.
With his brother Hermias, who bore their father's name,
he divided the earthly wealth; the heavenly wealth Felix alone
obtained. A clash of choices parted
the two brothers: the world carried Hermias off,
Christ took Felix up for himself. The one preferred
what passes away, the other what endures; the one clung to the present,
the other turned his soil into heaven and his inheritance into kingdoms;
the one was heir only of his own father, the other co-heir
with Christ. But who would wonder that offspring so unlike came from one
blood, if he rereads, among the holy records of our ancient forebears,
how Rebecca, fruitful with the stock of two peoples,
suffered the battles within her womb
and complained to God of the wrestling in her pregnant belly?
For even then there raged within the holy mother's womb
the discord that now rages within the womb of the world:
for the Jews, who follow the bristling faithlessness of hairy Esau,
a harsh one, since they are bound over to serve the younger people;
but for us a gentle one, gentle Jacob, through the smooth ways of peace,
where the way of light leads those who follow with a better birth.
So, from the same blood of brothers, a different blood:
Hermias, like rough Edom, pursued earthly things
and wasted away, a captive to the empty image of the world;
he chose the harsh laws of his Idumaean forebear,
living by his own sword, and endured the toil of empty
and barren soldiering, in which he submitted to Caesar's arms,
while to the service of Christ he remained a stranger.
But my Felix, born to take up the arms of the eternal King,
passed into the name of father Israel,
and from boyhood, his holy mind devoting itself to heavenly things,
he set himself to serve God. Nor did grace come to him
sparingly: as much as his soul thirsted, gaping
for light with a capacious heart, so lavishly did it drink in the inflowing
gifts of God. In his first years he served as a reader;
from there he rose to the rank whose task is, with faithful voice,
to adjure evil spirits and drive them out with holy words.
And because he performed this with the manifest power of his merit,
he rightly obtained the venerable insignia of the priesthood,
and with a mind worthy of the office he adorned the honour he had earned.
But so that the priestly fillet should not be the only adornment of his sacred head,
there arose a stronger reason for a double crown:
the dread rage of profane fury broke out,
when the holy Church was shaken by sacrilegious war
and impiety demanded, out of all the people,
above all those whose piety was most conspicuous.
At that time the aged Maximus was shaping the city of Nola by holy laws
as its bishop, with gentle speech,
strong in his priest Felix, whom with a father's heart
he embraced as a son and intended as heir
to his see. But, driven off by the sudden storm,
with his faith unyielding, he made for desert places.
Then, as the bishop was hunted, Felix shone out
more and more, set against the swords, and alone he became
the target of hatred for the faith; nor was it his rank they looked at;
his faith was greater than his rank, for the faith was the only charge.
Then he is sought, as the envious dragon rouses his arms,
eager to overthrow that by which we rise and he himself falls.
So, with the bishop in flight, for cruel punishment Felix alone,
or first among the people, like the head of the body,
is hunted down. All strive to overcome him,
and as men attack a towering citadel on besieged walls
with siege-works heaped up, so that, once its defences are overcome,
the rest of the city may fall, laid low in easy ruin.
O madness worthy of the faithless! They believe that in one man
they can extinguish the faith in which the whole world has believed.
Alas, wretched impiety, blind in hellish darkness,
where are you rushing? At whom do you aim your weapons? Do you believe that God
exists in one mortal, and that if you destroy bodies
the divine power and mind can be abolished along with them?
That power passes through the limbs of the world; by it you yourself are born
and, unworthy as you are, are nourished; on its will depends
conquering or being conquered; by its might even one man
is stronger than countless others. Armed with unarmed piety,
he faces men armed with steel but with hearts unarmed by Christ,
and lays them low by the triumph of faith, which, knowing the true
heavenly life, purchases the life to come by present death,
and, when the body is conquered, carries the conquering mind
joyfully back to God and bears it up to the rejoicing stars.
What good is it, then, madman, that with such a weight of fury
you attack holy Felix? Within, hidden, there remains
a mind unconquered for God. Nor is it now merely
the nature of an earthly man that resists you: God himself fights back,
the very one you attack; and to your poisons, ancient serpent,
Christ himself offers himself through the bodies of his servants,
and, binding you in your own snares, in the slaughter of his own people
he lays you low, triumphing over death through the semblance of death.
But their own error, with goads of fury, drove their savage hearts
to burn with a thirst for blood and to demand holy blood
as though it were the prize for their crime.
So when Nola was gripped by the sacrilegious frenzy
and trembled at the swords aimed at its devout citizens,
the venerable Felix was searched for throughout the ransacked city.
Nor did he flee. Already breathing the stars with lofty spirit
and sharpening his mind for battle with silent goads,
the fearless shepherd guarded his trembling fold,
ready, after the Lord's example, to give his life for the flock.
So he stands eagerly, like a wall, against the savage enemy,
and in his white-haired years grows green again with flourishing faith,
wholly among the stars in spirit, mindful of Christ, unmindful of his age,
bearing God in his heart, his breast full of Christ.
Now he can no longer contain himself: holy, he seems greater,
his eyes like stars, glory shining in his face.
At once he is seized, rejoicing, and by the savage hands of the raging men
he is dragged away. But, as is the way of the wicked enemy,
whose greater concern is to destroy our souls rather than our bodies,
he holds back the sword and first assails him with terrors,
and climbs towards death by stages of torment.
The first stage of punishment is woven from prison.
Iron chains are added to the dark confinement;
