steel holds his hands and neck, and his feet grow stiff in the stocks
that force them apart; broken potsherds are strewn about
so that his bed of punishment might keep off sleep with its sharp edges.
Yet the confessor was neither without rest nor deprived of light,
for Christ, now joined with him in all things,
suffers with him; and the heavier his punishment, the more it multiplies
his green crowns, as with roaming mind he travels the heavens.
Though his body is bound, his spirit, free,
flies on ahead into the inner sanctuary of Christ most high,
his soul rehearsing its rewards in confident prayer.
So a blessed passion pressed Felix with holy punishments,
with heavy chains and a dark prison;
and as many punishments as his subjected flesh had borne from men,
so many palms did his endurance receive from Christ.
Meanwhile Maximus, sick and alone in the mountains,
content to have escaped the hands and the deadly faces
of the executioners, was bearing a different but no lighter
martyrdom on his cross than if he had given his neck to the sword
and his limbs to tortures or flames. A keener
care for his flock burned and afflicted him; he is burned by the fire
of cold and stiffens under the icy dew of the sky,
without bread and shelter alike; night and day
he keeps watch, joining both times together in earnest prayer;
lying on the brambly ground, he is pierced in his limbs
by briars and in his mind by cares; within and without
he struggles: he bears the thorns of the field in his body
and suffers the thorns of grief in his mournful breast.
Covering hardship with hardship, by the bitter torment of his mind
he eases the torments of his limbs, and the pain of his mind
shuts out the sense of bodily pain. And yet the sick
earthly matter, though the strength of his soul remained unshaken
as his faith scorned the failings of the flesh,
overcome by winter and hunger and worn down by the hard bed,
was letting go of his mind as the body failed,
and the cold, drunk deep into the empty marrow of the weary old man,
was driving out his life as his blood froze.
The loving-kindness of the Father most high, moved for so great a bishop,
would not allow his body to waste away in an obscure death.
He could indeed have fed him as he fed Elijah,
sending food-bearing birds through the hungry wilderness,
and could have hidden him, like Moses, in a secret tomb;
but God had granted this gift to one friend alone,
to be hidden in secret ground, because such honour rightly befitted
that body which had shone from meeting face to face
the mouth and speech of God, so that, having paid the debt of mortality,
he should have God alone as the witness of his tomb.
So the gentle Father, looking with serene gaze
on the priest and confessor wasting away in the silent woods,
would bear it no longer; and since he was preparing to join to this worthy man
a companion of equally worthy merits,
he chose Felix out of the whole company in the prison
to add this work to his merits: that he should lift up the limbs
of the kindly old man, call back his soul, carry him home restored,
and give back to the stunned sheep the comfort of their dear
shepherd. So in the silent night there came, shining,
an angel, and among the whole crowd of chained prisoners
he addressed Felix alone, whom holy piety had made
a criminal; and the horror of the dark prison fled.
Roused at once by the voice and the light of the holy messenger,
Felix trembles and drinks in the word with a faithful ear.
At first, as if he were receiving God's commands in the image
of a mocking dream, he is bewildered and anxious, and
pleads that he cannot follow, since the chain prevents him,
and that he is held besides by both the bolt and the guard
of the watched prison. But the divine voice, rebuking his delay,
commands him to shake off his chains and rise.
And suddenly, as the chains slipped softly from his hands,
his neck, freed of itself from the iron yoke, is lifted,
and his feet spring out as the wooden stocks loosen.
Wondrous faith! The prison is opened with its bolts unbroken;
the guard is lulled to sleep; fearless, he goes out through the doors,
and a way is made through the very men by whom the way is barred. The angel went
ahead, and through the friendly silence of the quiet night
he was light and path for Felix. Is not the one Christ
present in every saint? Just as the same Spirit thrives in all
who are born in Christ, so the grace of the devout itself
is in harmony. I see an ancient pattern return in a recent
story, as in the account where, bidden to depart,
Peter, exalted in the band of the twelve disciples,
as his chains fell away of their own accord, came out
of a locked prison, where the angel went before him
and led him on, having stolen Herod's prey.
So my Felix, with God leading him out through the twofold darkness
of prison and of night, dark to the rest but lit
for him alone, passed unharmed through the very
guards, pressing on with steady step,
and, guided along unknown paths, made for the place he had been sent.
And after he had crossed hidden glades and trackless
country, he found the place where the weary old man lay, and sorrowfully saw him
drawing sick sighs with a faint breath.
As soon as he recognized the body of his dear father,
he threw his arms around him and kissed the familiar face,
and tried by warming him to call heat back into the cold
limbs, and with frequent breaths from his panting mouth
to restore living sensation to the body once it was warm.
But the body would stir neither at calling nor at shaking;
it was already like a corpse, yet a faint breath
and a trembling deep within betrayed the last of life.
At such a sight Felix, anxious in his loving heart,
is torn; he sees the bloodless limbs and the face
livid with hunger, and has nothing with which to help
in such need: no fire far off, no food close by,
to revive the wasting man with food and the frozen man with fire.
As he searched, and besought Christ with many prayers
to show by what help or by what means he could fulfil the service
laid on him, the Almighty suddenly brought forth a cluster of grapes from the briars
and made it hang close above his head,
so that he could easily pluck from the nearby branch
food that had grown of its own accord. So, refreshed by heaven,
Felix rejoices with devout heart in the gift offered,
and, picking the cluster with his hand, he brings it to the dying man's lips;
and since the old man, his teeth now clenched,
could neither taste nor take the sweet food,
he squeezes the juicy grapes and lets the flowing juice
drip in, parting the dry lips with his finger,
until, with God breathing on his feeble efforts
and his struggling hand, he loosened the rigid jaws
a little and made a narrow opening in the parted mouth,
through which the crushed grape could pour in a little moisture.
From this, feeling returns to his soul, warmth to his bones, light to his eyes,
and all his life comes back; and the tongue, which had stuck, coated, in his dry
throat, now resumes its accustomed speech,
once the slippery moisture had opened a path for his voice.
So, reviving, he sees close by a face he knows so well,
the face of his own Felix, and embracing him in turn
he complains that he was slow: "The Lord had promised me," he says,
"long ago that you would come, Felix, my portion;
Felix, my dearest pledge, tell me, what such long delays,
or where, held you back? If in body I gave way
for a while, being frail, yet in my heart I held firm
and stayed faithful. The place and my very state show,
in which you see me drawing out the last dregs of this life,
that I did not flee from fear of death, and that I put Christ
before my own life. I fled not from love of the light
but from fear of the frailty of this weak body; indeed,
I could have sought shelter in another city and lived safely,
if faith had been cheap to me and this life dear.
I made for unknown mountains and bare wilderness,
laying my neck in the lap of my sweet Lord,
so that I might die with him as my witness or be fed by him.
And this trust of ours, as you see, was not in vain:
the Almighty was at hand and chose to send you to me,
through whom he might bestow his gifts on me. Obey, my son,
the commands of love that lay this task on you, and
take me on your shoulders and carry me back to our common fold."
Tireless, rejoicing in the longed-for task, Felix
takes up the dear burden as the light load of Christ, and carries it
so swiftly on his way that he seemed rather to be carried himself
than to carry; and truly Christ himself carries the carrier,
and God gave wings to feet made quick by love.
In the same night Felix alone receives so many tasks
and carries them all out together: bidden to break his
chains, he revives the priest, carries him back revived,
and sets him down safe under the roof of his own house,
which a lone old woman looked after. So lofty, by this very
merit, did Maximus stand out as a confessor, that
an empty house was all he had and a single old woman his whole estate.
Knocking at the door, Felix wakes her. She,
startled at the first sounds, barely recognizes the familiar
voice, and, opening the house, takes in her master,
trembling in voice and step as fear shook her old age.
Felix says to her: "Take this deposit, which the stars of night,
witnesses with me, and the hands of angels under Christ their prince
hand over to you as I hand it over. Receive into your faithful
bosom this jewel of the Lord, and at the last day
return him to us unharmed before the Lord as judge,
the same Lord before whom you now receive him." Maximus took up these words,
and calling his Felix back, he said, "You too, receive
the reward for your service, my son, which he commanded me
to give you, laid up in store, he who commanded you to come to me,
his charge." Then on the head of his beloved Felix
he laid his holy right hand, asking at the same time for all the gifts
of Christ; and just as Isaac, venerable among the fathers,
blessed his son with the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth,
so Maximus, blessing Felix for Christ with a father's
and an apostle's lips, and enriching him,
crowned him with the honour of an unfading crown
and endowed him with everlasting riches, which we still see today.
XVI.
Times give way to times; one age departs and another comes;
each day flees by thrusting on the next, and turns the world's circle;
all things pass away; the glory of the saints endures
in Christ, who makes all things new while he himself remains.
At last, then, day come round again, dawn for me, day longed for through the whole
year, you who renew my sweet festivities
and my vows, who demand of me the solemn
offerings as you bring back the birthday in which thousands,
countless peoples, rejoice, in which a joy all my own
touches me, in which I owe the appointed offerings of my servant tongue,
to be poured out to my Felix, to whom with dedicated mind
I am devoted in Christ the Lord; to celebrate this saint
also with the service of my lips in yearly songs
is my duty. I shall tell, then, his merits and the grounds of those merits,
by which he won the rewards of heavenly praise,
and eternal days, and the name of great honor.
Already the earlier book has set forth for you the first deeds
of the martyr: where his home was, what his family, in what studies
he was reared, then by what rank, called through holy
offices, he chose to serve the everlasting Christ
rather than stray along his father's paths through the byways of the world;
for his father had lived as a veteran soldier under Caesar.
We also told of the punishments borne in a foul prison,
which he underwent as confessor, ready to suffer death as well,
had not God, forestalling the swords, released him and set him free
from his unjust chains, and called him to other tasks,
so that first Bishop Maximus might return to the holy hall,
he who in the lonely woodlands, at the end of his life,
lay sick and gasping, driven out by the raging enemy;
at God's command Felix carried him off on his own body,
brought him to the dwelling of a poor house and settled him there;
and, repaid for his services by the holy lips of the blessed old man,
he departed with a blessing, and for a few days
lay hidden in silence beneath the roof of his own house,
though not silent in mind, as he wearied the heavenly Lord,
piercing beyond the stars with prayer sent straight upward, and
knocking with merit that drew near, begging that peace might come forth.
Meanwhile the days slipped by; peace seemed to have returned.
Felix left his hiding-place, and at last, trusting a clear
sky, he had begun to give himself back, joyful, to his joyful
brothers, and to entrust himself to the now peaceful city.
Christ's sheep rejoiced at their shepherd's return.
He soothed the flock, frightened by the recent storm,
with heavenly counsels, and, guiding anxious hearts with the word
as their leader, strengthened them with love of the faith,
teaching that both the bitter and the sweet of the world must be scorned;
he urged them not to yield to terrors, but readily to offer their breasts
to meet the very fires or swords;
and he himself added weight to his words,
a confessor who had suffered what he taught must be endured,
a teacher to all by word and example alike.
That evil one did not bear this for long; he bristled his black
locks and swelled his neck with raging venom,
and sent his poison into wicked breasts,
so that the grace of Felix might burn their dark minds.
He planted his goads, and in unjust minds there blazed
the fury of viperous envy; shameless anger makes first
for his house; in all of them an impious passion burns for crime.
Impiety thirsts for Felix; but, away from his home,
he happened to be standing, unconcerned, in the middle of the city,
surrounded as usual by his brothers and friends,
sowing holy words in the ears of the believing people.
See, they arrive, seeking him with drawn swords,
when suddenly either the hearts of the enemies or his face
were changed; in their fury they did not recognize the man they knew,
and they asked him for Felix. Felix is seen, and not
seen; he is himself and not himself; though near, he is far away.
The same man becomes both unknown and known to his fellow citizens:
for believers, faith discerned his face, and he was himself;
to his enemies he was another. He himself perceived the plan
of Christ's favor, and, smiling, said to those questioning him:
"I do not know the Felix you are looking for." At once they
pass him by; and he leaves the square,
the Lord mocking the gaping dogs he had foiled.
They had gone no great distance, asking everyone
in what quarter Felix might be, when someone scolds them and gives
them a clue, not knowing the reason, and believing them mad
with rage, not to have seen the man himself face to face,
with whom they had exchanged words in close conversation.
Struck by the strangeness of the trick and raging more fiercely,
they soon return and run along the man's very tracks.
And now they were drawing near, but the uproar of the city running ahead,
and the shouts of the astonished crowd on every side,
warned Felix, and with a turn he dodges the threatening wounds,
and, slipping aside, takes himself far out of the open
ground; and finding a place which by chance opens
as an escape for a frightened man, withdrawn from the busy city,
even so he was not far from his black pursuers,
a man who, barely withdrawn from the sight of those chasing him,
had somehow escaped the hostile swords he feared;
and he was about to be caught, for that place had no barrier of any bolt
to stand in the way and keep the wicked out.
For, with no doors, there opened onto the public platform
an untrustworthy wall, a broken fragment of half-ruined masonry.
But the divine hand set itself between the saint and his enemies,
and fenced the place with a wondrous defense:
not a pile of stones, nor bolts provided by iron-bound doors,
with which, by human skill, we close our halls;
but suddenly a filthy mound of rubble grew up,
and the spider, at command, stretched out its swaying webs,
and with trembling folds built up the unprotected opening,
and gave it the squalid look of a deserted ruin.
As soon as this met the threatening men, they stood amazed,
and, halting in their tracks, said to one another:
"Is it not madness to try this entrance, or to believe that any
man has gone in here, where the tiniest worms have left their
signs? Little flies break these nets;
are we fools to think a man has got through this closed way,
and the delicate weaving not torn by so large a body?
Rather, that informer is now owed to our hands,
who cunningly, with deceitful craft, led us
into this wasteland, and, turned in another direction, lied that
Felix was hiding in this spot, so that with malicious
trickery he might divert our weapons, a friend to the fugitive's life.
So let us withdraw, for to stand here any longer
will make us the laughingstock of the crowd, and it will be branded a mad error
to press our steps here to search out a man's hiding-place,
where, by rotting rubble or the coverings of little spiders,
the untrodden ground shows recesses no one has entered."
Without delay they hurry off in different directions, growling;
but God, as Scripture sings, as they uttered their mad threats,
Christ laughed at them from his heavenly citadel,
and had veiled his Felix beneath his holy wings.
Safe in the Lord's bosom, he struck aside the fiery darts,
triumphant with the helmet and the shield of faith,
and the confessor carried in his mouth the sword of the word.
His hands armed with godliness, full of God, he covered his chaste
breast with the breastplate of outstanding merit.
O divine wisdom, rich in so many ways,
ever confounding the strong things of the world by the weak!
Scarcely [?] do walls with lofty ramparts defend peoples,
and more often the enemy crushes those who trust in strong defenses,
and overthrown cities expose them to death.
But now a spider protected the saint from armed men,
with God defending him; the enemy stood driven off by delicate
nets; iron force yielded to an airy thread.
Vain is the safety men give; my strength is no strength to me
if I lack the strength of God. Where now is the vast might of the giants?
Where are Egypt's kings? Where is great Jericho?
For all of them the glory in which they swelled was the cause
of their ruin; and divine power shattered them, not by the valor of heroes,
but rather by the weak.
That giant met his death by the sling of a shepherd boy,
like a dog; the sound of trumpets brought that city down;
that proud king lay on the sand of the shore,
paying for the riches of his kingdom with a naked corpse.
So, when Christ is with us, even a spider's web is a wall;
but for one from whom Christ is absent, even a wall [?] will become a spider's web.
So when the crowds had gone and silence had fallen,
and deep night offered trusty darkness for a secret flight,
Felix comes out and changes his hiding-place,
singing this to the Lord: "Though I walk in the shadow of the dead of night,
I will fear no evil, for your right hand is with me;
through hell itself I shall go, not without light."
So, led by God, he finds in a remote quarter
a narrow nook in a courtyard open to the rain, among low dwellings,
where an old cistern lay dry beneath a deep covering.
Nearby, in the adjoining building, there lived
a woman holy to God, who, unaware of the hidden confessor,
fed Felix as though she shared Christ's secret.
I shall sing of wonders: the Lord's skill in feeding his nursling
while the woman who fed him knew nothing of it. Diligently, now loaves,
now other food she had cooked for herself as usual,
she, in a trance of mind, acting by divine arrangement,
would carry in to where Felix lay hidden,
veiled by the Lord; but neither when she went there
did she know she had gone in, nor when she had left
did she remember having entered; and when, prepared,
she had busily brought it in, although she served the saint
with her own hands in feeding him, yet, unaware of so great
a service, she could not know in her own heart
that she was acting not by her own mind but by the power of Christ;
and, going to the place of hiding, above the mouth of the built cistern,
she would leave the food she brought, and
believing she had set it down at home, she would always go away so,
mindful of setting down the food, and soon unmindful that she had set it down.
O woman blessed by God, like one of the birds
which once fed the prophet withdrawn from the world,
you too fed a martyr under a secret roof,
obeying the Lord like a bird; and, unaware of the holy
service you shared in, what you did and whom in the end
you served, you will learn with joy at that time
when God himself, Christ, will give you, for his confessor's sake, the crown
of righteousness; then Felix himself
will repay you your meals before Christ the judge,
meals which God transferred to the sweet use of the holy martyr,
as once he sent food cooked for reapers,
the prophet hanging in the void by an angel's hand,
to the fasting prophet amid the raging beasts;
their wildness was wild no longer, for their prey and his holy fasting
bridled the savage lions' greedy jaws.
They say he lived six whole months on end
apart from the company of men, beneath that hiding-place
under a roof both dark and narrow,
needing no human help, always abounding
in Christ's comfort; who, it is said, at that time
often deigned to visit him with his speech,
often fed him with his own hand, and gave him from heaven
drink, not of rainwater, which the clouds pour out everywhere
on all alike, but the dew which grace, for him uniquely,
poured down from the heavens upon Felix;
for then, as happens, summer, scorched by excessive suns,
had dried up even the well that had given scanty
drink to the hidden man. But lest bodily thirst should burn him,
who in thirsting for Christ was bearing this
punishment of an afflicted body, a cloud, brought down from a clear sky
and gathered into a small ball, through the narrow
opening of the courtyard poured sweet liquid into the thirsting man's mouth,
as though squeezed by a hand, and refreshed the one destined to be called to heaven
with the milky juice of a heavenly fleece.
What wonder if now Christ feeds him, freed from earthly stain,
whom, while he still dwelt in the body, the Holy Spirit fed,
and for whom bread was the Word, God himself,
the bread of heaven on which every angel feeds?
When this time had passed, restored peace sheathed the swords,
and God told Felix to come out of his hiding-place,
he who had long since closed his peaceful ears to the clamor of the world,
drawing oblivion over human affairs.
As he comes out into the light, like a new man, to those who had already despaired,
and is seen in his native city as if returned to life,
many hesitate to recognize him, and first ask him:
"Is it truly your face? Are you then that blessed one,
Felix, given back to us after so long a time?
From what region do you come? Were you given to heaven, or, returned
from paradise to earth, are you revisiting our dwellings?"
He assures them that he stands before them in the body,
that he had lived, preserved by God; joy was granted to all,
and he is celebrated by all the people with praises for his merits.
Bishop Maximus had died, having completed a long life,
and the flock lacked a shepherd's guidance.
The whole fold bleated the name of Felix,
whom the glory of a confessor crowned for Christ,
and whom his tongue promised as a saving teacher,
and his life in harmony with his teaching; but so that in this too he might carry off the palm
of righteousness, keeping his lofty merit down with a quiet
heart, as though unworthy he does not dare to rise in honor,
and declares it is rather due to the elder Quintus,
because he had been first to earn the rank of the shared office
of priest. The whole difference amounted to seven days.
So under this bishop too Felix lived
as a priest, and grew in merit because he refused to grow
in rank; Quintus himself, as though the lesser, deferred to him
in all things, and his mouth had Felix for its tongue.
Quintus ruled the flock with his services, Felix with his preaching.
The grace of Christ enlarged holy Felix with many other virtues,
and in peace he won battles no less great
than those the confessor had waged with strong arms.
In the grim storm he had scorned bodily safety;
and likewise he was a despiser of wealth and honors alike
in untroubled peace. Nor was he
careless about keeping his merit, but more cautious, so as to guard
the good things of life he had gained, now that he had overcome
the dangers of death; and amid the calm he feared the reefs.
We have told how he trampled on death and ambition;
now learn of another palm of the confessor.
He conquered avarice; for he had possessed many estates and houses,
an heir rich in his father's wealth.
As a confessor he had been proscribed, but once peace was restored
he was free, if he wished, to claim back his rights;
yet he preferred to heed the Master's word:
"All things are lawful, but not all things are helpful." He puts the helpful before the lawful,
and, as if it meant contracting the infection of earthly stain,
he shrank from claiming his lost lands back by law.
Many pestered him, above all one with an ancient name,
Archelais, as renowned for holy faith as for her name,
a widow rich in means, who revered holy Felix with faithful
devotion and was dear to him in turn.
She honored him with the reverence his merit deserved,
and, as they say, presuming by right of fellowship that his mind
was at one with hers, she often wearied his devout heart
with frequent complaints: why did he refuse to have restored
the rights that were owed and ready to hand, which, once recovered, he could
distribute to the needy, earning the interest of a great reward?
She also often offered him many gifts from her own
property. He, content in all things with a devout spirit,
smiled with a calm heart at her womanly concern,
well aware himself of the heavenly goods
which he held as repayment in exchange for earthly ones.
So, strong in this, he would answer his dear friends when they pressed him:
"Are you forcing me to seek back earthly things and lose eternal ones?
Better that wealth be lacking while I am saved, than that life be lacking to the rich man;
rich, I would be in want of God; but poor, I shall have Christ.
The grace of Christ will make the needy rich with riches."
Holding to this resolve, three acres of a small plot,
not even held under his own title but rented, he as a tenant
tilled with his own hand, without a servant, the owner of a poor man's
garden; but even these riches from the soil he, rich man that he was, poured out
for the needy, lending to the Lord, always sharing with the poor
the vegetables he gathered, sharing his table with the poor.
A single day used up his concern for possessions;
a single garment covered him, and often scarcely a single one.
If he had two, he warmed a naked man with the better.
Often he exchanged wretched rags for new clothing,
and the poor man, transformed by Felix's garment, shone out
from his gloom; Felix, on the other hand, in a beggar's covering
looked squalid, adorning his mind while his body went unkempt.
Living with this piety, ripe for God in both years
and merit, he closed his lifetime in the fullness of days,
and changed, but did not close, the ages of his holy life.
XVII.
Are you leaving already, hurrying off and abandoning us,
though you leave us only in place,
us who will always be bound to you, without end,
in mind?
Are you departing already, as the land you serve
calls you back from afar? Yet you remain here too,
holy Niceta, for even when you have set out
we hold you in our heart.
Go, remembering us, and in going remain
present in spirit; planted in turn
within our souls, draw and carry with you
those whom you bear in [?]
O land and peoples blessed beyond measure,
whom you will now reach on your way back from us,
whom Christ will visit as you come
with your feet and with your mouth!
You will go far, all the way to the northern Dacians;
you will go to be seen by both Epiruses,
and through the Aegean surges you will make your way
to Thessalonica.
But first the road will carry you through Apulian lands,
broad across its long plain,
where at Canusium fleeces steeped in dye
glow bright.
But when the road has carried you on a little further,
may Christ, I pray, grant you mild heat,
and may a light, cloudless breeze blow
over parched Calabria.
Just as, at the hands of the ancient prophet,
through the mystery of the cross, the water, when wood was thrown in,
grew sweet, and Marah put away
its bitter streams,
so may the sky now be tempered for you,
and the air, thinned to a light, clear sky,
breathe gently in pure breezes
and turn to healthful airs —
that air which, heavy with marshy breath
and carrying the foul stench of snakes,
is wont, with its thick wind, to break down swollen bodies
into sickness.
May the mighty Lord of all things command it to be driven off
or changed, and now for his own
priest supply the kindly breezes
of health.
Just as once, when Egypt was perishing
and covered in the darkness of thick night,
there was light for the world where the holy nation
of the living God dwelt —
a pattern now proven throughout the whole
world, since the devout portion of the holy faith
shines in Christ, while error overwhelms the rest
with darkness —
so, in whatever region his journey bears him,
may the Lord prosper everything for my Niceta,
until he is carried, rejoicing, to his longed-for
native city.
Go on, Niceta, and run well your homeward,
prosperous course with Christ as your companion —
you for whom your people have long been wearying heaven
night and day,
demanding you back, as a field, when its crops need relief,
thirsts for rain, and as tender
calves, when milk is held back,
seek out their mothers.
So, by the just prayers of your own people,
who rightly claim back their father,
we are forced, though unsatisfied, to yield,
our wish defeated.
And since the hope of keeping you is now snatched away,
affection urges us to favour what has been decided;
now, although we may hate those roads
that snatch you away —
we hate them, yet we love them too.
We hate them because they draw you back; we love them
because from far away they brought us
the sight of your face.
Bound fast by overpowering love,
we now pray that these roads may be laid smooth and easy for you
on land and sea, with the name of Christ
Most High leading the way.
May he make your whole road into level plains for you,
press down the steep mountains, fill
the hollow valleys, smooth the rough places,
and bridge the gaps.
As you are carried through Otranto and Lecce,
choirs of celibate brothers and sisters alike
will throng about you, singing to the Lord with one
voice.
Who would give me wings like a dove,
that I might swiftly join those choirs
which, singing of Christ as God with you as their leader,
strike the stars?
But though we are held by the sluggish bond
of a sick body, yet we fly out
in mind after you, and with you we sing hymns
to the Lord.
For, entwined within your
inmost feelings, whenever you sing and pray,
then with your prayer and with your voice
we too are uttered from you.
Then, when the sea takes the place of land,
the levelled gulf of the Adriatic will obey you,
the waves will lie down, and in the gentle west wind
the sails will swell.
You will go gliding over the calm sea,
and in a ship armed with the sign of salvation,
victorious with the yard of the cross, you will go, safe
from waves and south winds.
The sailors will joyfully sing their usual shanty,
its rhythms turned into hymns,
and with holy voices will draw the breezes as companions
out onto the sea.
Before them all, like a resounding trumpet,
Niceta's tongue will sing of Christ in measured strains;
David, the eternal harpist, will sing psalms over the whole
sea.
The whales, trembling, will hear the Amen,
and to the priest singing to the Lord
the sea monsters will come gladly from afar,
swimming in frolic.
On every side green dolphins will play
with gaping mouths, and though they have no voice,
they will still express joys that rival
human tongues.
For what does not know God and live for him,
by whose word all things were sown?
Hence the depths of the sea know the praise of God,
and mute things cry aloud.
Our witness is the ancient prophet's
beast, roused from the deep at the Lord's nod
to catch him when he was thrown overboard, and afterwards
to give back what it had swallowed.
But now that same wild creature, beside our own prophet,
will devour only with its ears the holy
songs; it will fill its unfed belly,
feasting on song.
Wherever you go on your way, over the waves
and over land, and even through enemies,
you will go armed with the helmet of salvation,
with Christ as your head.
May Raphael be sent and fly to you; as once
he was to Tobias among the Medes, so, escorting him,
may he be Niceta's companion all the way to the Dacians,
an angel at his side.
May that same leader likewise lead this servant of his,
the God who once, when he fled the face of his proud
brother, brought into safety
Jacob.
For Niceta too is a fugitive:
what the patriarch did once, he
does always, fleeing the world for the walls
of high heaven;
and those steps on which Jacob saw
angels going up and down in turn —
these Niceta strives to climb by a life
that rises above the clouds,
hastening to the stars by the ladder of the cross,
from which God, leaning toward the earth from his gleaming
throne, watches the varied toils
and battles of the mind.
And you, Niceta, are rightly named
conqueror of the body, just as Jacob was called
Israel because he saw the highest
Creator with an exalted heart;
so my Niceta is proven
a true Israelite, without guile,
who sees Christ as God by the light
of solid faith.
May this our God, our way forever,
be our companion and go before us,
a light for our paths, and for our feet
his word a lamp,
so that through the blind shoals of this dark world
we may be guided by the torch of the true light,
until we are allowed to reach the longed-for harbours
of salvation,
which we now seek across a billowing sea,
tossed on the surge of a wandering mind,
carried in our earthly body as if
in a fragile hull.
But with the cross as rudder steering
this ship within us, we now spread the holy sails
of the heart, while Christ carries us home rejoicing
on a favourable wind.
So may the same guide now escort
you on the road by which you now hasten back
home, Niceta, and restore you safe
to your native threshold.
But when the sea is crossed, the toil of travel remains
once more on land, until you are carried
all the way to the happy regions to which you have been given
as their priest.
You will walk through the Philippian fields of the Macedonians,
through the city of Tomi,
and you will go to Scupi, near your homeland,
a Dardanian guest.
O with what joys that land
will resound even then, when you teach stubborn
peoples to bow their wild necks
beneath gentle Christ!
And where, on the Riphaean coasts, the north wind
binds the rivers in thick frosts,
there you melt minds stiff with frost
with heavenly fire.
For the Bessi, hard in land and soul alike
and harder than their own snow,
now made sheep, are gathered under your leadership
into the fold of peace.
And the necks which, never subdued in war,
they always refused to yield to servitude,
they now rejoice to bow down,
subdued to the yoke of the true Lord.
Now the Bessian exults, richer
in the reward of his labour; the gold he once sought
in the ground and with his hands, he now gathers
in heaven with his mind.
O change of fortune! O shape well transformed!
Mountains once trackless and bloody
now shelter robbers turned into monks,
nurslings of peace.
Once a land of blood, it is now a land of life;
the robbers' violence, made holy, is turned toward heaven,
and Christ favours the plunder
that seizes the kingdom above.
Where once the ways of wild beasts prevailed,
now the rites of angels flourish,
and the righteous man hides in the caves
where the robber himself once lived.
That old plunderer becomes plunder for the saints,
and the murderer groans at losses turned against him,
rightly stripped, as Christ despoils him,
of the weapons of crime.
By Satan's fall, in turn,
envious Cain perishes; Abel, restored to life,
feeds lambs redeemed at the price
of shed blood.
Well done, Niceta, good servant of Christ,
who grants you to turn stones into stars
and to build holy temples out of living
stones.
You range through pathless glades and vast ridges
as you seek the way, and, conquering the barren forest
of the untilled mind, you turn it into
rich fields.
The whole region of the North calls you father;
at your words the Scythian grows gentle
and, at war with himself, under your teaching lays aside
his savage heart.
The Getae come running, and both kinds of Dacian,
the one who dwells in the heart of the land, and the one
in the felt cap who lives beside the riverbank
rich in cattle.
This is to make calves out of wolves,
to feed the lion on straw, yoked to the ox,
and to open the vipers' holes
safely to little children.
For you persuade beasts, their savagery driven out,
to join the gentle flock,
you who imbue the wild minds of men
with your refined speech.
In the mute region of the world, through you
barbarians learn to sound forth Christ
with a Roman heart, and to live the tranquil peace
of chastity.
So the wolf is gentle toward your fold,
the calf grazes in harmony with the lion,
and the little child plays with the asp drawn out
of its grim den.
The cunning gold-gatherers you turn into gold,
and imitate them at their own work:
from them, digging with the word,
you unearth living gold.
Storing up this wealth for the everlasting Lord,
heaping up the holy talent with these gains,
you will hear: 'Enter, rejoicing, into the joys
of the everlasting Lord.'
Among these, I pray, when the kindly house
has received you into the numerous holy company of brothers
in their choirs, add us too, by the devotion
of your dear heart.
For thanks be to God, who with such great love
has bound us to you by hidden bonds
that no force could avail to break
that inner chain.
So, embracing your dear heart without end,
we cling to it with a faithful cord,
and wherever you press on, we shall be your companions
with following minds.
The love of Christ, poured richly from heaven
into our hearts, binds us so closely within
that we are not torn away from one another, even when removed
to a land far apart.
No age, no ruin
of the world, no other world, not even death will tear us from you;
when the life of the body dies, the life
of love will live on.
While we dwell in these heavy limbs,
we shall always honour you with a mindful heart;
and you will pray that we may be together with you
for all eternity.
For precious virtue will set you, exalted by your merits,
upon the lofty summit,
and in the city of the living above will add you
to its great towers.
We, as far removed in place as in merit,
lowly and far below our exalted patrons,
shall look up from afar at you, the companion
of the holy hosts.
Who will grant us this on that day:
that we may stand in the shade at your side,
and that the breeze of your rest
may cool the fire for us?
Then, I pray, remember us dearly,
and, reclining in the bosom of the holy father,
with a dewy finger shake off from us
the raging flame.
Now go, and fare well; yet even as you withdraw,
always run back here to us in spirit;
be with us, even when you have reached
your fathers' city.
For God has granted you to be the teacher not of one people
only, nor the citizen of one
land only; see, our homeland
claims you as its own.
Now divide your affections with equal devotion
between both: be with us in love,
with your fellow citizens in person; dwell on two
shores as a citizen [?].
Perhaps this homeland should even be thought the greater,
where you are held not in dwellings made by hands
but in the dwellings of hearts, and you inhabit people,
a living city.
As you are a bishop, so you are a worthy guest
of kindly Christ, since in Christian
minds you dwell as a sharer, a resident
of the Master's temple.
Now farewell to us; and loving us
for all time, good man, to the very end
run your good course, and take the crown
laid up for the just.
XVIII.
The law laid on me by a holy duty, to celebrate this day each year
with the service of my speech, demands its solemn
gift from my lips: to tell of Felix in verse,
to set my joy to music in a votive song,
and to sing the great merit of my dear patron,
who by a hard road, where the way lies open to few,
seeking the heights through narrow paths, made his way to the citadels above.
Join in harmony with my songs, I pray, brothers, and applaud them,
and pour out your hearts in chaste festivity.
Holy joys and chaste songs befit the faithful;
for what man is there, for whom Christ is both love and fear, who may rightly
fail to rejoice today, and come forth empty of his offering,
by whatever means of talent, tongue or wealth he can,
when heaven's ministers rejoice with Christ, as
even the very elements reveal by their festive color?
See how the world's joy, in the brightness of the day,
shines out with holy emblems; a joyful whiteness
holds all things; a dry rain like ashes from the clouds
is laid down, and the earth is veiled in a snowy mantle;
covered with snow, its ground, its woods, its rooftops, its hills
adorned with snow, it bears witness to the white-haired honors of the holy old man;
and with angelic signs they teach that Felix enjoys both light and peace,
glorious in the tranquil region of the righteous,
where milk-white fleeces glide across the silent sky.
Christ, God of Felix, be present; give me now the word,
you who are the Word and God; give me, O Wisdom, a clear mind.
Human eloquence has no power to tell
your praises; for your saints are your glory.
I yield: let others bring precious offerings and
outdo me in the cost of their service, who bring fair
curtains to hang over the doors, either shining with pure linen
or woven and painted with colored figures.
Let these polish light inscriptions with pliant silver
and overlay the holy thresholds with plates fixed upon them.
Let others kindle lights on painted candles
and fit many-holed lamps to the hollow coffered ceilings,
so that the hanging lamps quiver with trembling flames.
Let these be eager to drench the martyr's tomb with nard,
so that they may carry back healing ointments from the holy sepulcher.
I yield indeed, my purse empty of gold, to the many who are wealthier,
whose pockets, heavy with coin, are lightened as the needy are filled,
who with lavish hand throw open their well-stocked storerooms
and stand pledging their souls with various gifts,
alike in mind, different in means; and let them no less zealously
dedicate rich dishes of food, candles, hangings, lamps,
gifts generous indeed, but mute: I, with the gift of my tongue,
possessing no wealth, do my service, paying my dues from myself,
and offer myself for myself, though a poor victim.
Nor shall I fear to be scorned, since not cheap to Christ
are the offerings of a poor man's homage; for he gladly
received and praised the two coins, the whole fortune of the devout widow.
Then too the rich were bringing many gifts to God,
filling the holy treasury with great talents;
but Christ was watching, and, looking into the hearts
of the givers, gave the palm to the widow; she had cast
her day's living, two coins, all the substance she had,
into the sacred chest, untroubled about her body's needs.
Therefore from the very mouth of the Judge who is to come
she earned, before the day, a foretaste of praise for her deed,
and to be preferred to those whose gold her mite had surpassed,
a poor old woman in her gift, but lavish in her faithful heart.
So, good brothers, to whom the honor has been granted both here and there,
turn your ears to me with calm minds,
and listen gladly, not to who speaks, but to whom I speak of.
I shall tell of things to be despised, yet also to be wondered at:
to be despised for my poor talent, to be wondered at for the merit of blessed
Felix, which cannot be told without the praise
of Christ, since whatever we wonder at in him comes from Christ,
from whom comes strength to the faithful, and through whom life to the buried.
In earlier books I sang of his homeland, his family, his deeds,
and, going back to the very beginning, I told of holy
Felix, until he closed the span of a life made perfect
and, laying down his body on the earth he left behind,
made his way to the fellowship of the eternal kingdom he had earned.
But since tombs do not hide the merits of the righteous
along with their limbs, the life of souls, surviving
when bodies are spent, experiences the fruits it sought in the body,
and after bodily death, not dead itself, feels them,
the good with joy, the wicked with torment; and these, called back again into the body itself
in the time to come, with the body joined to it once more,
it will reap in common, undivided in what it receives.
Long, then, is my subject; and as long as time endures,
so long will there be words on this theme for anyone free to tell the deeds
of Felix, if he had as great a store of speech
as there remains of his works and merit. For from that time
when this day first laid Felix to rest in a blessed end
and gave his flesh to the earth, his soul to the stars,
from then on almost every day the confessor of God
is seen at work, and Christ proves him alive even without the body,
to show that a greater power remains in the righteous in death
than the force of the wicked in life.
See, you behold the tomb that covers the martyr's sacred bones,
and the silent body kept under the marble laid over it;
nothing of him stands before human eyes as we see with the body;
the limbs of the one laid here lie hidden, the flesh rests in peaceful death,
buried in the hope, not empty, of life restored.
Whence, then, does such great terror surround this threshold?
Who drives such crowds here? What hand presses
the demons and seizes them against their will, and drives them, vainly protesting
with rebellious voice, right up to the tomb
of the martyr, and halts them at the holy boundary as if fixed there?
I look back to this day long ago: how sorrowful it was for the world
left behind, how joyful for heaven, when Christ, as God,
taking up the soul that was his friend, drew it from those chaste lips.
He added adornment to heaven, yet did not rob the earth
of its pledge; those above enjoy the spirit of Felix,
we his body; the spirit of his mighty soul lives there,
and his merit here. But it is a joy to set before you the whole honor
that Nola paid to his kindly funeral.
For it had lost its priest in holy things and its father in years,
but, destined to have him as its patron in heaven,
the devoted city consoled its love for the holy man with hope.
So with all the crowds that throng it, streaming together,
the city runs to pay its respects, pouring forth its faithful people.
Then grief and devotion meet in the hearts of all;
faith, mingled with devotion, both rejoices and grieves.
And though it believes that Felix, summoned by Christ, is raised above the heavens,
still it grieves to be left without so great
a teacher; and since the one consolation for love that remains
at a holy funeral and amid the rites
is this, once the bier was set down at the place of burial,
the people, pressing round in rivalry of devotion,
crown the laid-out body from every side in a dense throng,
and a religious battle of loving hearts is piously fought.
Each, outstripping another, strives to stand nearer
to the remains, and rejoices to touch the body with his hand.
Nor is it enough to have seen him once; they love to linger long
and fix their gaze, and, where allowed, their kisses
on the exposed limbs; the people with one voice give due praise to Christ
and prepare the sacred honor of Felix's resting place.
Where the area lay empty of walls and far from houses,
there a spreading field smiled with happy turf,
the spot blooming more richly, as though even then, foreknowing
a tomb to be honored forever by the world's veneration,
it rejoiced to be blessed by the holy body; and,
lovely in its spring attire, so as to be more worthy to receive
the martyr's burial, the earth strewed itself with fragrant grasses.
But him, as he climbed the heights in gentle flight,
taken up from his chaste body, the joyful throng
of the righteous had come out to meet and receive through the clouds of the upper air;
and the angelic choirs, the hosts of the sevenfold heaven,
running to meet him from all the gates where heaven opens,
into the sight of the King and before the face of the supreme Father
joyfully bore him in his flight in starry triumph.
Then they adorned his holy head with a snow-white crown,
but the Father, with Christ as judge, added a rose-red one too,
and doubled his snowy robes with a purple garment,
since both honors were his by merit. For he received bright
garlands as one carried into heaven by a peaceful death,
but he equally earned the purple of a slain martyr,
though he died a confessor. So he holds the rewards of one who suffered,
because he was ready in courage, yet does not lack the honor
and adornment of peace, because he did not die in combat.
So when the due rites had been performed, they laid the holy body
in the tomb; but the grace divinely implanted in the holy limbs
could not die and be buried with the flesh;
at once a light shone out from the bones laid there,
which, by its healing riches, has never ceased from that time
until now to give signs of his mighty merit.
And through all the age that the world endures there will shine
that same light, guardian of the holy ashes through the centuries.
This proves that the departed martyr lives, and, working Christ's
blessings at the tomb of Felix, spreads into all lands
far and wide the wondrous name of Felix,
and ennobles Nola, alone of all cities deemed worthy
of so great a guest; Nola, which the grace of Christ
has so enlarged through Felix's merits that, increased
with new citizens and walls, here too there is now a city,
where at first there was a poor tomb, which, in a savage time,
when profane threats made religion a crime,
the Lord's people, trembling amid swords and fires, had built
in narrow compass, as the ancient age handed down to later
generations. It had shut a vast light under a small roof,
and once a sacred little corner was the sole possessor
of so great a deposit; aware of the hidden light within,
it rose up like a spring into spacious buildings,
and remains in their midst like a gem set among the roofs,
spreading out the spacious courts of the holy tomb
through five basilicas, whose rooftops, seen
from far away, present to the eye the look of a great city.
Yet these roofs, spacious though they are, are outdone by the crowds,
because, as faith grows, the grace of Christ overflows,
which, through his healing gift, makes Felix live
for the peoples. He, enduring even beyond the lifetime of the body,
presides in holiness over his own bones; and the bones of the holy
body, from the tomb, not covered with the dust of death
but endowed with the hidden seed of eternal life,
breathe out the life-giving fragrance of his victorious soul,
through which powerful medicine is given to the sick who pray.
How great the power and glory that will surround the saints when they rise
we may guess, when such great grace attends them
in the grave, and with what beauty their restored bodies will shine,
when there is so much light in their dark ashes!
What will the crowns of these men be able to bestow on us, the least,
when even their ashes give blessings to the living?
It is often a delight to see wonderful scenes of every kind:
people greeting the saint, and each asking for what suits
his own prayers; you may even see farmers from the countryside
not only carrying their children in a father's lap,
but often leading sick cattle in by hand with them
and freely entrusting them to the saint as though he were visible,
and soon, trusting that healing has been granted to their prayers,
rejoicing in God's proven help and already believing them sound;
and indeed, often healed in a short time right at
the threshold, the beasts are led back joyfully to their homes.
But since it would be long and idle to run through all
the miracles that Felix works by the power of Christ,
I shall bring forth one wonderful deed out of many,
like countless others; but from this one, weigh those left untold,
which the same power performed, though differing in their occasions.
Open your hearts, I pray; the burden on you is brief,
while I tell a great work in few and humble words.
And, remembering the widow spoken of at the start,
whom God, judging by the worth of her mind, not of her gift,
preferred to those who gave much, since she gave all,
bear with me too as I tell great things in a slight account.
For my words too are rivals of those tiny coins
to which devotion gave value, making even cheap things golden.
There was a man poor in means, of humble birth, rustic
in his ways, who supported his narrow poverty with two oxen
by the wages of their yoke; now he was accustomed to put them to wagons
to haul loads over an agreed distance,
now he earned his poverty's income by the fee for hiring them
out under other men's ploughs; that pair was the anxious hope
and the whole wealth of the needy man. Not dearer to him
were his children, or he himself; rather he counted them as his children
and as himself; nor was his care to feed his bullocks full less
than to raise his sweet children; indeed, he was more sparing
to his children than to his dear cattle; not with cheap grass
or barren straw did he feed them, but with a warm shelter,
himself cold, and with grain denied to himself and his children,
himself hungry; poor for himself, rich in them,
whose fruitful labor filled the needy man.
These, then, so dear a comfort of his life,
the wretched man, buried one night in heavier sleep than usual,
lost, driven off by the theft of a silent robber;
and rising at the return of day to yoke them as usual,
the unhappy man searched first inside, in the empty stalls,
and soon outside, in vain, in the familiar fields;
but then, worn out by fruitless wandering this way
and that, when he sees no tracks made certain
by any signs, his hopes dashed and his search come to nothing,
he despairs of human help, and, filled with devotion,
by God's inspiration he lifts to heaven the mind bowed down
in his broken heart; and soon, his heart restored,
with faith running ahead, he drinks in the hope of gaining his wish [?]
and makes for the holy courts of Felix at a swift run;
and, entering the sacred hall with loud weeping,
he throws himself down before the doors, presses kisses on the doorposts,
and waters all the floor with tears, before the holy threshold
stretched on the ground; and the bullocks snatched by the night's fraud
he demands back from holy Felix as from their guardian,
reproaching him, and mingling prayers with complaints:
"Felix, holy to God, sustenance of the poor, ever
a blessing to the wretched and ever rich for the needy,
God has set you as rest for the weary and relief for the afflicted,
as healing for the wounded hearts of the sorrowful;
therefore, as if trusting in a father's lap,
poverty lays down its head and rests on you.
Holy Felix, who have always pitied my labors,
why now, forgetting me, I ask, do you desert me, stripped
to my very skin? I have lost my dear bullocks, your gifts,
which I used so often to commend to you as a suppliant,
which your care kept with constant favor
and fed for me. For your guarding kept them safe,
and your bountiful right hand made them sleek;
and this night has taken them from wretched me. Alas, what shall I do now?
Where shall I go, cheated? Whom shall I accuse? Or shall I complain to you
about you, and accuse my patron of forgetting me,
who let so heavy a sleep steal over me as I slumbered
that I did not hear the robbers breaking my bolts,
and did not break their hard hearts with any fear,
nor bring light upon the darkness and the theft?
Or did you take care to betray the runaways by any sign?
Where shall I run now? Where shall I turn? Everything
is hidden from me in blind darkness; now even my own house seems
shut to me, where, desolate, my nurslings carried off,
I have nothing I would want to have, nothing to give me sweet,
not fruitless delight, sweet to look on, sweet as I labor,
cheering a poor man with the sight and the profit of his little property.
Where shall I, pitiable man, look for them now? Or where and when
shall I find such others, or how shall I get them, even if found,
I, a rustic, who had these alone as the wealth of a contented
poverty? Give me back these very ones, then;
I do not want others. Nor shall I search for them in any region;
they are owed to me here; this threshold will give them back,
where as a suppliant I lay hold of you yourself and cling
to you. Why should I hunt for robbers I do not know, or where?
Here is my debtor; I shall hold the guardian himself
in place of the thief. You, holy one, are answerable to me, an accomplice with them.
I have you; you know where they are, you who by the light of Christ
see all things, even hidden ones, and behold things far away,
and grasp them, since God, who holds all things, encloses them.
And so the hidden thieves, in whatever hiding place they are,
are not concealed from you, nor can they escape you,
since one hand holds them all [?]. God is one everywhere,
the right hand of Christ, gentle to the devout but avenging to the wicked.
Give back, then, give me back my oxen, and punish the thief.
But no, I do not seek the guilty; let them go. I am not ignorant of your ways,
holy one; you do not know how to repay wrongdoing; you would rather
correct the wicked with pardon than destroy them with punishment.
So let us come to terms: divide with me in this way
what is yours and what is mine: let my interest stand unharmed
through you, and let clemency likewise claim
your share, and let your judgment stand with balanced
scales: release the guilty for yourself, give back the bullocks to me.
There, you have the bargain; now you have no reason
to keep your servant waiting; hurry to free me from such great cares.
For my resolve stands firm never to leave
until you help me, nor to be torn from this doorpost;
unless you hurry, I shall lay down my life on this threshold,
and then you will find no one to give them back to, brought back too late."
As he wept like this, with a complaining voice but a faithful mind,
and prayed all day without end,
the martyr heard him gladly, though the suppliant was hardly flattering,
and, sharing the jest with the Lord, laughed at his abuse;
and, moved by the petitioner's faith, not by the grieving man's outspokenness,
he hastens his help; the delay is drawn out only a few hours.
Meanwhile, as the day slipped away and evening drew on,
he set no limit to his prayers or his tears; one
cry came from him as he clung to the doors: "I will not be dragged from here;
here I will die, unless I receive here at once
a reason to live." At last, however, as the deep
night required the sanctuary to be closed and secured, and he,
forgetful of the hour, mindful of his loss, pressing the doors with his face
bowed down, blocked the entrance with his whole body,
after his ears had been assailed in vain by many voices urging him,
a forceful hand seizes him, and at last the crowd
tears him away, struggling, and drives him far from the holy hall.
Driven out by the sacristans, he weeps more bitterly and, mourning,
makes for his home; the silence of the night resounds with his lament,
and the lonely places far and wide echo with his loud complaints,
until he arrives, though unwillingly. And entering the dark
inner rooms of his silent hut, again, from the very
entrance of that silent roof, when he saw the stalls
bare of oxen, and the bells giving no sound,
as they used to jingle when the oxen tossed their necks,
or more softly strike their hollow bronze with slow tongues
while the herd chewed the returning cud in its throat:
at this, as though the wound were torn open again, he renews
his lament more heavily; and though care denies the sick man rest,
yet it gives this comfort to his wakeful grief:
that he lies stretched out, his body pressed upon
the places where his oxen were stalled; nor do his limbs ache, broken by the hard bed;
the very hardship pleases him; nor does he shrink from the filth
of the dirty stable, since it gives back the familiar smell
of his beloved cattle, and to a lover a stench does not stink.
Any tracks they had left with their last steps
he looks at, and feeling over the trodden spots with groping hand
he groans and rubs over the now cold hoofprints
with his whole body; and his mind, though he is far away
in body, he sends to the sacred hall of Felix,
calling on Felix with his tears, on Felix by name,
and neither despairs of help nor stops pouring out prayers.
Night, now borne to mid-heaven, had flooded the world
with sleep-bringing peace; all things on earth were silent;
only he was kept awake by his hope and his care.
Suddenly he hears a noise at his doorposts
and the doors resounding with knocks; terrified at this, beside himself,
he cries out, believing the thieves were coming for him again:
"Why, cruel men, do you want to break down empty doors
for nothing? I have no ox left; what more do you want?
Others got here first; only my life is left,
which remains, worthless as plunder, for your comrades."
So he spoke in fear; but the sound at the door went on
without end. As it grew more frequent, and no
voice of those knocking answered him, he draws near,
in suspense, with hesitant step, and puts an anxious ear
to the doorposts, and through the cracks of the gaping bars
where the pale color of the sky glimmers through the darkness
he puts his eye and peers a long time, and still does not trust himself
as to what he sees; for in the dim light of night
the eyes have no clear certainty; yet through the shadows the very
shapes of the knockers, though uncertain, began to remove his trembling fears
and, by their unexpected forms, to promise hope of good.
He sees that it is not men knocking; but what he sees to be
true, he does not dare believe. I shall tell of great
wonders, though small for God, at whose will every
living creature has sense, as far as the Creator himself has ordained,
beasts of every kind. See, bearing a mind with God as guide,
the fine pair of oxen, through trackless ways unknown to them by night,
had come to the familiar house with no one driving them,
of their own accord, as it seemed, and yet not of their own accord, since by divine power
Felix, snatching them from the robbers with a stronger hand,
had driven them, steering them with hidden reins.
And after they had reached the familiar thatched roof
of their home, rejoicing in their return and fearing the hands
they had experienced, with terror enough in their memory, as though they feared
a thief pressing close behind them, they began to shake the doors with their
foreheads together, and to use their horns like hands,
to rouse their master with the noise. But he, terrified
again, as if by a hostile uproar around his bolts,
feared even what was safe; again wisdom inspires the dumb
beasts to perceive the cause of his delay
and to read the mind of their fearful master,
and to let out a lowing, so that, his fear driven off,
he might, now reassured, open the way to his shut-out nurslings.
He, seeing the unlooked-for signs of the divine gift,
still hesitates, and even his joys throw his trembling heart into confusion.
He does not dare to believe, he fears not to believe; he sees them
close at hand and thinks his eyes are deceived; when he looks at himself,
he doubts that he could have deserved so much;
but, reflecting on the other hand on whom he had hoped in, he dares
to believe, recognizing the work of his patron Felix.
And now the twilight was reddening as morning broke
through the night, and as the last stars fled and thinned,
in half-dark light or shadows shot through with light,
it had begun to reveal the uncertain colors of things.
Then at last, the oxen plainly revealed to him in their familiar form,
as soon as their hides began to grow clear to his eyes,
he leaps for joy, now sure, and, drawing the bolts from the bars,
he opens the doors, which creak as the hinge gives way.
While he does this, the bullocks, side by side, burst in
and forestalled his efforts as he was still unbarring the door.
With the bar removed, the doorposts readily gave way,
and soon they recognize their lord, there before them on the very threshold,
and joyfully lick him in turn as he, joyful too,
strokes them; and with their lips they drench the hands that pat them,
and soil all his clothing with frothy kisses,
while, as their master embraces their dear yoked necks, they press
gently against his kindly breast, fawning on him in turn.
Nor do the horns of his beloved cattle hurt him,
and he draws their foreheads to his breast as though they were soft,
and to his hands their tongue does not seem rough,
though in licking it scrapes up even the fodder of the woods.
Yet even amid all this, with no empty heart, the faithful
peasant remembered his duty, and does not care
to lead his panting oxen into their stalls first, and after their toil
and hunger refresh them with food, before leading them with him
to the place from which he had obtained them. So he comes, leading them
back, and does not hide his joy in silent prayers,
and, telling his story, draws dense crowds to his words,
and enters the sacred building as all look on in wonder.
The very oxen whose loss the wretched man had wept for yesterday
he leads today in person, and displays to the people the triumph
of the holy martyr; and the bullocks themselves are led
through the midst of the throngs, lately the thieves' plunder,
and now the spoils of Felix; the vast crowd makes way
for them as they pass, and the glory of Christ is celebrated in dumb
cattle. And he, who had been the reason for so great a gift
from the Lord on high, standing out among the thousands
and weeping again, but now for joy, renders to the saint
his due vows, not with heavy coin nor with a voiceless gift,
but pouring forth the living gift of tongue and mind,
the poor man testifies with devout voice to his abundant love,
a debtor, and with this pledge pays Christ in full,
for whom the spotless sacrifice of his praise suffices:
"See, holy one, before all the people, I lead your captives
to you in victory, and the vanquished I entrust to you again to guard;
keep safe the returned ones, since you deigned to restore them when stolen.
But now, good martyr, look upon me myself;
for you see that something still remains for you to do, but in me,
who stand close at your threshold with eyes almost blinded;
for I have drowned my eyes in much weeping,
weeping not only at my loss but also amid my joy.
You have removed the cause of my tears; now take away what has arisen
the wounds my tears have caused; holy one, you pitied the loss
of my oxen: now pity in the same way the loss of my eyes.
You have given me back my beasts; now give back to them
my eyes as well. For what good is it that they have been brought back,
if, with my sight failing, I am present yet absent from what is present?"
The people standing by laughed at him as he made such complaints.
But the ears of the hidden martyr, turned toward him from afar,
took in the devout words of the simple suppliant,
and soon his restored eyes felt the touch of that holy right hand.
Then he made his way home rejoicing, his eyes and his oxen recovered,
while the people joined in praising God, and
the glad victory of his twofold prayer went along with him.
XIX.
If the stars can fail from the sky, if the grass from the earth,
honey from the combs, water from the springs, milk from the udders,
then could the praises of the godly cease from our tongues,
in whom lie both the virtue of life and the glory of death —
God himself, for whom they chose to barter away their life
and by dying to seal the holy faith of the peoples
and to purchase the sacred kingdom with precious blood,
the blood with which the martyrs, sprinkling the whole world,
became heavenly seed for countless nations.
From the number of these princes, a confessor given to this
city, Felix, has shone out far and wide across the world
through the fame of his name. But Nola, made the home of the buried saint,
applauds herself as though over a star of her own.
For every martyr, wherever he lies, entrusted to some region,
is at once the star of the place and the medicine of those who honor him.
For the Creator, pitying a world darkened by ancient gloom
and the languishing souls upon it,
so arranged the holy tombs of the godly across the earth
as he scattered the lights of the stars across the night sky.
And though one faith, equal grace and matching power
belong to all the martyrs, yet in these same martyrs
we see differing forms of works stand out.
In one place we reverently honor sublime merit
in silent tombs; elsewhere we marvel at signs that cry aloud
and at conspicuous powers. Where, I believe, a harsher impiety
holds more evil in its grip, there a graver disease
demands greater help; or where a blinder error still drags out
the deep night of unbelief, and faith lies sick and struggling
among a wavering people, there it is altogether fitting
that greater lights be kindled, that the darkness of the world
be destroyed as God sheds his light, and that minds,
dazed and trembling, with dulled eyes, be turned toward the very
rays of divine truth — that they be freed from the foul gloom
and anointed with the eye-salve of Christ the healer.
This salve, for the healing of the senses, by apostolic arts
is ground on a holy whetstone, since Christ's yoke is gentle and his burden
light for those already turned to Christ with clear sight
and whose hearts are steeped in the juice of the gospel,
by which the mists are thoroughly purged — the mists with which
the loves of a deceiving world cloud the inner eye,
loves that drive the senses, wandering without an oarsman, through the great void,
and dull them, held captive in heavy gloom,
with soft allurements, so as to break the strength of life
and make men chase hollow pageants through slippery pleasures.
Wishing, then, to turn these diseases away from us,
the all-healing Lord brought forth saints as physicians for sick mortals
among various nations, in his wholesome compassion;
and so that divine power might display its care
more clearly, he brought them into the more important
cities; and though small towns may keep certain
martyrs, yet God brought the leaders themselves into great walled cities
and, after their death, divided them among a few regions,
though before their death he had given them as teachers to the whole world.
So he fixed Peter and Paul in the city of Rome,
since the head of the world needed chief physicians,
mad as it was with many vices and blind with darkness.
But since God is stronger to restore our salvation
than Satan is to hold his captives even now by fraud,
the world's darkness thins, and now over almost all
godliness has prevailed and life has subdued death.
As faith grows, error is conquered and slips away,
and with scarcely anyone now left to sin and death,
all Rome is counted under the holy name of Christ,
laughing at the fictions of Numa and the oracles of the Sibyl.
And when the godly throng returns a joyful Amen to its holy shepherds
throughout the many sheepfolds of the reigning God,
the holy shout in praise of the eternal Lord strikes the heavens,
and the Capitol totters, its summit shaken.
In the empty temples the squalid idols tremble,
struck by godly voices and battered by the name of Christ.
The demons flee in terror from their deserted shrines.
The livid serpent rages in vain with bloody mouth,
mourning with hungry jaws the salvation of mankind,
and himself now cheated of the blood of cattle as well;
the robber, groaning, circles the dry altars in vain.
So God, granting his holy gifts to the remaining lands too,
scattered his members everywhere throughout great cities.
So he gave Andrew to Patras and John to Ephesus,
to heal Europe and Asia together through them
and to dispel heavy darkness through such great lights.
Parthia embraces Matthew, India Thomas,
the Libyans Lebbaeus; the Phrygians received Philip,
Crete took Titus, and Boeotia Luke the physician.
Mark was given to you, Alexandria, so that, with the bull driven out
along with Jove, mad Egypt might no longer worship cattle in Apis,
nor Crete wrongly worship a buried fellow-citizen in Jove,
nor the Phrygians perform Cybele's rites with castrated Galli,
consoling the impure Mother with a foul wound;
so that at last Ida might put forth leaves on chaste mountains,
bearing untouched pines upon her untroubled summit,
and vain Greece no longer consult Delphi, now mute,
but, scorning it, trample her own Olympus,
climbing higher into Zion, where Christ, the nursling of that hill,
raises his gentle yoke to a lofty summit.
Diana too fled from Ephesus as John drove her out,
following her brother, whom Paul, commanding in the name of Christ,
put to flight when he drove out the Python.
Satan fled from Egypt too, where he had taken a thousand shapes
and a thousand names to suit his various monsters,
so as to turn holy Joseph into Serapis,
hiding a venerable name under a deadly one,
although the very form of the idol revealed the truth,
with a grain-measure set upon its head; for once, with the crops
gathered in before the famine at the Lord's prompting,
he fed countless nations from the plenty of Egypt
and filled the barren years with the years of abundance.
But so that the saint should no longer be worshipped with profane honor,
the secret mind of God sharpened the hearts of the devout people
with goads sent upon them, and put an end to the cult of the wicked
demon when Serapis was overthrown and smashed.
No longer does wandering Isis seek Osiris through the Pelusian glades
with bald-headed soothsayers who, beating their breasts,
bewail another's lamentations with grief of their own,
and soon, just as madly, when the wailing is hushed,
put on an empty joy, pretending he has been found, with the same fraud
with which, wandering about, they sought one they had never lost.
Alas, into what gulf of folly are minds plunged
that lack the light of God! For what, I ask, is blinder than those
who seek one not lost, find one who abides nowhere,
and mourn on another's behalf what causes them no grief?
Choose what you will do, wretched error. What do you worship, or what
do you mourn? The things you join do not fit together; grief does not
go with honor; you worship lamentations, and believe that things to be mourned
are divine. If they are gods, they are not wretched;
or if they are wretched, they are not gods, but are men,
and wretched ones. So either pity those who have suffered mortal things,
or venerate gods who are happy; for plainly blind
is this madness, to worship the wretched or to mourn the blessed.
Is Isis, then, a goddess? A woman a goddess? If she is a goddess, she has
no body; and without a body there is no sex, and without sex
there is no childbirth. Where, then, did she get the Osiris she seeks?
And does a goddess not know where to look for him? But a deity can never
be a mother or a woman. For God is one,
a threefold power: one God the Father, and one in him
the Son, and from him, one with the Father, the Spirit
of the Word; these three names are always one God.
The nature of God alone is God, which the Son and
the Spirit and the Father are; but the Son is born of the Father,
the Spirit proceeds from the Father. In this no nature
among created things has anything in common or alike.
But mighty Carthage flourishes with the martyr Cyprian,
from whose mouth and blood alike poured fountains
that made fruitful the sands of thirsty Libya.
Not far from there the White Mass, its martyrs gathered together,
raised Utica on high with a great heap of venerable slaughter;
for a single mound of blessed turf,
covering many bodies, lifted its head high above the fields
and by the mountain of its tomb bears witness to their lofty merits.
Hence Africa, long since fruitful for God and Christ,
multiplies rich harvests from such seed
and bears outstanding teachers in word and faith.
Nor has lesser grace shone forth in the western lands.
Ambrose stands out for Latium, Vincent for the Spaniards;
Gaul received Martin, Aquitaine Delphinus.
And many other seeds of saints besides, scattered abundantly
through these same regions where their tombs are laid,
light up the whole world with heavenly powers
and thrust the ancient dragon out of the whole world —
the dragon who, through the thousand names of gods
(names taken from dead mortals, which the snake both assumed
himself and gave to his followers), shakes the human race with his art of harm,
holds a foul kingdom as prince in the empty air,
and roams about as head of the demons and our enemy.
So too this Nola of ours, through the love of merciful Christ,
was found worthy to be fortified by the tomb of Felix
and cleansed at the same time; for, caught up in the blind ruin
of the world, she too lay dying in the night,
long polluted by worshippers of stones, a city in which
the brothel of Venus and the madness of Bacchus
were gods to the wretched, and with foul ritual
lust, allied with frenzy, celebrated its wicked rites.
And what room was there here for life, where there was no shame anywhere
and no fear at all? For who would fear to sin
here, where bloody frenzy and unchaste lust
were religion? Crime took the place of divinity
for those who had believed that there was any divinity in crime;
and in the whole crowd he was reckoned the holier worshipper
who had burned more foully at the rites of Venus,
so that he was held to be full of the god and more blessed than the rest
who, with the demon poured more deeply into him, raving more savagely
against himself and offering frenzied rites with his own
wounds, had earned the loss of his sound mind.
O mind worthy of blind souls, and gods worthy of them!
For those who turn away from serving God, let Venus and a grove
be their god; let mad drunkenness and impious love
sanctify them; let them worship severed parts, and call the wretched shame
of their foul error the mysteries of the Mother.
A fitting faith for those who, in the kindly light of truth,
in chaste laws and the great name of Christ,
have no faith and no love, and so for their unworthy life
there is no ransom in the blood of Christ.
Let their belly be their god, or the other pleasures of the flesh,
those for whom God himself is not God, for whom in the cross of Christ
there is no glory, since the power of the cross does not deign
to approach degenerate souls. Hence blessed
Felix, like the other martyrs in different parts of the world,
was a physician to the people of Nola, and is so forever by this power;
and not only to the people of Nola, but to all by whom
he is entreated, he will by this right give health,
if the kindly faith of the cross is present in the suppliant's heart.
This faith both heals and cleanses the human race;
where this medicine is lacking, there will linger
the whole kingdom of evil, and in that man Cypris will never
cease to reign through adulteries, nor Lyaeus through frenzies —
in whom the modesty of Christ and the ardor of the cross are lacking.
For divine fire is within, where the power of the cross, inside,
as faith blazes up, torments guilty hearts
and gives life to the soul once the vices of the flesh are slain.
Long crushed by these enemies and corrupted by such
