plagues, Nola needed a mighty remedy,
and so, as God weighed the danger and the help required,
she received Felix as her physician, to overcome every
ruin, however ancient, in the black hearts of the wretched,
and, more powerful through the strength of his merit, to cut through
the hard skin grown over the rotting ulcers of deep wounds,
to squeeze out the pus gathered by the hidden infection
from the opened cavities, and then to let a scar,
drawn over with smooth skin, fill the pit of the wound.
So when Felix shone on the people of Nola like a star in the darkness,
coming from the mouth of God and bearing the word of healing
in his own mouth — just as, calm before the coming sun,
Phosphorus puts forth his glad radiance at the morning rising
and shines fresh above the setting stars,
herald of the approaching day as night gives way —
so now, with the gospel shining through the whole world,
and God soon drawing near as judge for all lands,
Christ holds out everywhere the banners of his coming
and makes his signs flash through his friends.
Of these, whom did he wish to shine before him in this region?
Felix, to strip away our shadows with this
star and to drive the ancient demons from this city too,
so that, once such tenants were driven out of men's hearts,
God might enter pure minds to dwell in them,
and, the roles reversed, now that we have been set free by his mercy,
our former chains might now hold down our lions,
raging in vain, their ferocity fettered, against the sheep of Christ.
And this grace remains to us even now, which looses
us from our sins through the intercession of the saints,
and, with these same saints as avengers, binds
and torments those enemies who used to bind us.
These now, like thieves caught when a lamp is brought in
and thrown into chains, now endure the fiery scourges of the godly,
as they deserved, or else, already thrust down wretchedly into the infernal
prisons, they tremble, confessing that close at hand
is the judgment of the Lord, grievous to them alone and to all
their followers, whom a perverse will has turned to Satan's side
and a life imitating Satan has made his allies —
men who are their partners in wickedness here, and in punishment there.
Behold the day acceptable to God; now the true light of salvation
shines out; we see all things now turned to good for us;
deceits have scattered, Bel has fallen, error is perishing,
and the demons who were worshipped as gods in whole temples
are tortured, defenseless, throughout the churches of God;
and those who dared to take divine honors to themselves
are now punished, brought into subjection by a human law.
For these, whom we now see in the thronged hall of Felix
being tortured, crying out, and hurled about through the bodies they have seized,
are held bound within those very bodies
into which they thrust themselves, and of their own will
found their punishment in human form. So now, in the role of defendants,
they howl under their punishments — they who by false divinity
had been gods, and who by feigned divinity had made living men
their devotees, men who before the worship of God saw nothing heavenly for themselves;
these now, when by the light of Christ
the true faith has been revealed, cannot bear the presence of the buried saints.
But to make it plainer that these demons who are now tortured
before the doors or before the tombs of the godly
are the very same to whom once the enslaved race
of men sacrificed and madly poured out sacred honors,
the very character of their voices shows it; for very often
they groan in that old voice, so that you recognize the familiar frenzy in their cry.
So frequently, as if their mouths had fallen loosely open,
they gnash their teeth, foam at the lips, their hair stands on end,
and, as though a hand had seized them by the hair, they are jerked aloft
and hang by their locks with feet dangling; meanwhile, there,
remembering the old rites in which they used to
lick the entrails of slaughtered cattle or feed on libations
and lead wanton dances in ivy-wreathed processions,
now too, bearing witness that those rites were their own,
in which the drunken crowd raised its mad uproar,
they pant out "Euhoe," the cry of Bacchus, imitating it with broken
voices, and toss their necks in slow circles.
But since the lifetime of a single mortal could not
suffice to wash away contagions drawn out over long ages
in the few years that he lived in the body —
Felix, confessor and presbyter, a teacher by his words,
a martyr by his record, a priest by merit and office —
the almighty Lord made the finished span of his bodily life
continue for Felix in a better way,
prolonging the healing works of the toiling martyr,
so that he might, though buried, perform the same miracles
that he had worked by the power of Christ while still in the flesh;
and so, even dead, he would not be absent in body from the city
that had received him, since the spirit of the one laid to rest would be fully present as healer,
and though the face of the dear patron would be hidden for a time,
withdrawn from the longing of those who loved him,
yet medicine would always be ready at hand for the health of the sick.
Hence everlasting honor and glory surround holy
Felix, with merits flourishing without end;
and though, hidden in his tomb since long ago,
he lies, so far as he was mortal, beneath the covering of earth,
yet a living grace, quickened by God and outliving the limbs,
makes the martyr's bones, which breathe of the divine, glorious
before the people, since the merit of the buried man lives on;
and a crowded throng from various lands continually
venerates the small throne of the great confessor.
But God, as the sower of all mankind, allowed this help
to go forth from the saints to all lands,
so that now the blessed martyrs might bestow holy gifts from their tombs
and, though buried, might heal the living.
Nor was this gift enough for the Lord, that the martyrs should
illumine only their own places with their name or their powers;
from those same tombs, multiplying the memorials of the godly as well,
the merciful one granted those same martyrs to many
nations. And I shall relate from the beginning the various causes
from which this blessing arose for various lands.
For since the first faith had not spread evenly
across the whole world, many regions of the world
had been without martyrs; and for this reason, I think, as a great gift
it pleased Christ — at times by inspiring the powerful,
as first happened under the emperor Constantine,
at times by revealing it to his servants — that from their former resting places
martyrs should be summoned and transferred to new
lodgings on earth; as we know was done not long ago
by the holy bishop Ambrose, who, upheld by such a gift,
after he had moved martyrs previously unknown, and then
discovered through Christ's revealing, to a new hall of his own,
confounded the raging queen with the light so readily revealed.
For when Constantine was founding the city of his own
name, and was the first among those who ruled under the Roman name
to bear the name of Christian, he conceived in his mind a divine
plan: since he was then raising, with magnificent undertakings,
walls to rival the walls of the city of Rome,
he would follow the city of Romulus in these endowments too,
and gladly fortify his walls with the bodies
of apostles. So he brought Andrew from the Achaeans
and Timothy from Asia; thus with twin towers stands
Constantinople, the rival head of mighty Rome,
more truly like the walls of Rome in this eminence,
that God, with equal munificence, made up to it for Peter and Paul,
since it was found worthy to receive Paul's
disciple together with Peter's brother. Now how great a benefit,
through this long journey of the saints across the far reaches of the earth,
has grown up for the needs of our life
the very places show even today, where that blessed
carriage, bearing its load, halted and rested
at every stage of the way — wherever there was a lodging for the holy
bodies and a rest for those who carried
those sacred ashes — places that cry out with wondrous signs.
For the divine hand is at work there with healing power
along every road where the holy bodies
left living footprints in their sacred passage.
Then, at faith's urging, leave was granted to the faithful
zeal of the escorts, so that they might take for themselves some pledges
plucked from the holy bones as a deserved reward,
so that, as wages for their service and payment for their labor,
each might carry home safeguards for his own private use.
From that time the sacred ashes, like seeds of life,
have been scattered in different places; and wherever, from a tiny bone,
from a small coin of the sacred body, a slender dew
has fallen among the nations, there holy grace has made a drop
of that ash bring forth springs and rivers of life.
From there Christ's abundance has dripped even upon us,
rich even in the smallest things; for we too have received here
sacred pledges of apostolic flesh in a little dust,
which the holy lord and father of our dwelling,
the guardian of our soul and the protector of our salvation,
Felix, has received close beside him in a neighboring church,
which, newer in age than his other halls,
keeps tiny ashes and great honors,
and is itself kept rather by its patrons as guardians;
for far be it that they should ever seem to need keeping
who are accustomed to keep others; yet they deign to care
for the welfare of their foster-children with fatherly love
and to cherish the safety of the places dedicated
to them; that this zeal of devotion dwells in the holy
spirits, proofs of wondrous faith have shown.
So I shall tell, after a few opening words, of a recent deed too;
for it is fitting to set forth the gifts of holy Felix on his very
birthday in words of thanksgiving.
I shall not tell of things foreign in place or ancient in time;
I shall relate a deed done lately in our own territory and in this
very place, which it will perhaps be easy for us
to recognize, since the thing was done openly in full light.
I believe that of this company hardly any of you
will be hearing it for the first time, for flying rumor must have gone
far, to distant places. Certainly some of you were present in this
city at the very time when it happened that a thief,
driven in his mind by unlawful goads, laid greedy
hands upon the sacred gifts, and out of all
the adornments of the venerable hall, wicked and mad,
chose the cross as the shape of his plunder, not knowing that it
would turn informer against him rather than spoil — which, like a hook,
he swallowed like a greedy fish, to be caught by the bait he caught.
Who, I ask, drove the robber on, armed him, blinded him, and hurled him headlong
into so great a daring of spirit,
that neither at the watches of the guards nor — what is more — at the very
altars that cover the reverend, sacred ashes
and breathe forth the fragrant power of the holy dust
did he flee with stricken heart, and that he should carry off
things outstanding not only in holiness but also in beauty and value?
For there were many other ornaments at hand, as you know, in that very
place, which he might have taken and so spared the gold
of the cross; for within lay hidden the mystic vessels
set apart for receiving the sacraments. But besides these, in the space
of the hall itself, gifts distinguished by various forms
had been placed, as is customary — those you see there
available every day, or fixed around all the columns
at measured intervals, like candelabra,
which bear painted candles on projecting spikes,
so that fragrant light may be given off from the papyrus wicks within.
And in the middle space, fastened to the high coffered ceiling,
hollow lamps hung on bronze chains,
which, shaped like trees, flinging out arms as of vines with pliant
shoots, bear on the topmost tip of each branch
little glass cups as their fruit,
and, as though in springtime, blossom when the light is kindled,
and imitate crowded stars with their many-tressed flames,
and dapple the heavy darkness with their many lights,
and paint the delicate air with blossoming little fires;
and while they quiver their liquid tresses and flicker incessantly,
scattering the gloom of night with their unceasing flames,
they make a wavering appearance, mingled between light and shadow,
and unsettle the air, uncertain to the trembling sight.
So although this man saw these things lying ready for him in the open
and safer to steal — since it would have been a lesser
crime and of lesser value to carry off a lamp hanging
farther from the edge of the altar, light with its silver —
yet the wretch, ambitious and proud even in his fraud,
scorned to steal silver, as though it were a cheap crime,
and stretched out his bold right hand to the golden things,
which he had seen were also skillfully set with various stones,
and had swelled his heart with great hopes
of rejoicing, rich in gems and gold alike.
But, loaded with the unjust weight of so great a crime,
he remained heavy with sin and light in money;
his punishment awaits the sacrilegious man; his plunder has deserted
the robber. Stripped of the spoil of his theft, but not of his crime,
he lives destitute of profit, but rich in the wound of his fraud.
And yet I would think that it was not without the great will
and counsel of Christ that he was allowed to approach this crime,
so that, since he had resolved in his mind to take anything at all
from sacred things, he was allowed to reach those things
in which the impiety of his deed would be the more conspicuous.
A few days before, this same man had fled there for refuge,
pretending to be fleeing military service, and was received kindly
as a guest by the sacristans who look after the holy hall.
Lying hidden there for almost a whole month, he had scouted out the beds, the sleep
and the hours of the guards; and when
he had found hours suited to the crime he had planned,
in the silent night he seized upon the wicked deed, and without effort
or noise, shut in behind closed doors as if he were one
of the keepers whose guest he was — when the watchmen, no longer
watchful, began amid the silent shadows
to snatch their first sleep and, their cares overcome, to sink into oblivion —
he, seizing his chance for the crime, where he knew from habit
there had been placed, for the lamps to be made ready through the night as usual,
provided a ladder with steps ready for climbing,
and that it was now left within his reach by a careless, overconfident guard,
where stood the likeness of a cross (as it still stands now), on a continuous rod
set upright, bearing on a crosswise bar two
little vessels, while a small chain hanging from its foot
supports a third. In these three little cups lights are set and shine
when a feast day comes round; but at that time, not being used
for light, it hung there only for show.
But a little in front of the ornament of the cross, on the same
continuous bar, there is a silver cup fitted for use.
This one, gleaming with a light that was unwelcome to him, the robber
at once puts out; for he also knew
that it often went out of itself, when the parched wick, the oil used up,
buried the light in the long night,
and that the watchman would not be surprised if by chance he saw
darkness creep over the roof once the lamp was out,
but would think the night had come about by custom, not by crime.
So not like a thief, though a robber was what he was, but like a guardian,
the robber carries off his unlawful plunder without a care,
and he does not flee but stays, unafraid. One cell hides him in his hiding,
one of the many that, set all along the sides of the great
buildings, offer the buried secluded
lodgings. In one of these the thief conceals himself; and when in the morning
he sees the doors standing open, he slips out of the unbarred hall
and, leaving his hiding place, carries off his crime. He was preparing to go
to the city of Romulus, as he later told when he was caught,
to carry on the trade of his unspeakable fraud there.
Meanwhile, while our people knew nothing, that night and the whole
day passed; late in the evening, attending to their usual duty,
they set up the ladder; as one began to climb
to light the lamp, he found nothing: the rod of the cross
stood bereft, stripped of its accustomed lovely necklace.
The poor men turn pale and dare not report the loss caused by the crime,
knowing that the blame would rightly fall on them as well.
They go off in alarm and hurry away after the robber,
pursuing the fugitive. Nowhere do they find any trace
of where he slipped away. They all go along different roads
and search the harbours lying on different shores.
Eight days slipped by for the searchers in vain,
or ten, and all had now returned from a fruitless hunt;
one of the searchers, a lad, his own labour likewise fruitless,
was coming back after ranging in vain over a wide region,
and, coming now close to Nola, he stops right on
the highway, and with loud groaning and a flood of tears,
calling on Felix, he resolves with a faithful heart
not to return home except with the cross; and at once he readily
retraces the road he had already travelled. And straightaway there meets him
a certain man who knew the thief, not as a thief, but as a fellow townsman.
Our lad first asks him where he had come from
on his journey; he tells him. Then he is asked about the thief,
whether he had seen him; and he replied that he was staying in places
near there, and that the district he indicated, close to the very spot
where they were talking, lay next to Mount Vesuvius,
at the fifth milestone from the city of Nola. But the coming on of evening
puts off their plan. They agree that the next day's light
should bring the two together again. Morning comes; the informer returns;
he leads our men there; the thief is caught; the plunder is brought back.
As it happened, that day had dawned as a holy day, recalling the birthday
of blessed Priscus, whom Nola also celebrates,
although he was bishop of Nuceria and had his see
in another city. And behold, into the very hall of holy Felix,
which the people were then thronging in solemn honour,
after the rites, just as the bishop was dismissing the devout assembly,
at a moment foreseen by God, face to face with the people
as they came out, he is suddenly brought in,
his thieving hands tied in knots behind his back.
The people are filled with joy, the robber with terror,
and the whole city runs together as if to some strange new monster.
The crowd, raging with the hatred of the mob, went for him;
joy and anger mingled in a confused uproar.
I was terrified, I confess, that the devil, with that
envy that is his habit, might stain the festival with blood
and heal the earlier wound with a worse wound.
He is snatched from the people and shut up in the very cell
(so it happened by chance to the captured culprit then) in which
he had hidden after seizing the cross; now that the cross was found, he himself
is shut in there, so that he might live. Then, when he had recovered his wits,
the culprit himself began to recount his crime and the obstacles he met,
in a marvellous way, and confessed that through those
eight or ten days in which he had been preparing to go to the city
of Romulus, he had been driven back, his feet entangled,
so that, always preparing to go, he always came back, drawn back
by someone, he knew not whom, and returned again to that region
of Vesuvius, where he had been ordered to be shut in as if in a prison,
bound by an angel's hand. Yet he thought,
poor wretch, that he was his own master, because in body
he seemed free, though, with no chain to be seen,
a stronger right hand held him with hidden bonds.
Felix the avenger bound him with a fitting bewilderment
and drove him round, out of his mind, in such a whirl
that, always going away, he never got away, and when
he had begun to leave with hurried step, he came back.
A thing hard to believe! He went by standing still and stayed by going,
unaware that the very thing on account of which he was preparing to flee
was what kept him from fleeing, that his chains stayed with him,
and that his own crime was an unbreakable chain upon him.
For he had entrusted the weight of the plunder, set with its fittings, to the closed fold of his garment,
and so, greedy and as if out of his mind, looking for
a hiding place, he yet wandered by daylight in the open fields
and, thinking himself hidden, stood out on the bright plain.
His guilty impiety had so blinded his mind that
in fleeing he did not escape, and in straying he was not concealed.
With conflicting feelings, fear on the one side and stupor on the other
had thrown his guilty soul into confusion; he avoided the paved roads,
yet in his helplessness was afraid to go into the lonely woodlands,
fearing that even in the forests the very silence might
cry out his crime, or thinking that grim monsters, avenging beasts,
would come at him in their dreadful shapes.
So the wretch, drawn aside from the busy highway, was wandering
in some countryside near by [?],
pretending to those who did not know to be free of care, but keeping fear down in his heart
just as he kept his crime under his clothing; for in the folds of his garment,
girded up high, he had shut away the gold.
For he had not dared to entrust the stolen goods even to the silent earth
or to hollow caves, as robbers do,
fearing discovery, too greedy to trust his loot to anything.
And so the wicked man had entrusted his thefts to his tunic alone,
where he had knotted his garment tight,
hitching up the flowing cloth to bare his knees.
This storehouse of his crime the robber had then built on his own person,
and he was fittingly bound by such fear
that he would trust no one with a share in the wretched theft,
so that he alone should bear the contagion of so great a crime,
and the fold of his garment should become the keeper of the stolen goods
whose sacrilegious seizure his hand had dared,
so that he would carry his own burden himself, and the deadly load
of his plunder would weigh down and pollute him alone,
so that no part of him remained free of impiety,
since, shutting in the spoil of crime carried off from the holy building,
he bound himself up in his girded garment
and himself put on a foretoken of his own chains.
For soon, when he was caught, he exchanged his girdle for bonds,
and as the gold fell out of the loosened folds
of his ungirt garment, with the very strap with which he had been girded
he was bound; and the hands that the bold robber had stretched out
to holy gifts, now caught in the knot of his own belt,
he brought back empty of plunder and full of rope.
But if we wish to look closely at the whole
course of events as they unfolded, more and more in every
respect, both where the crime lay hidden and where, disclosed,
it came to light, we shall see that Felix worked marvellous hidden things by the hand of God.
Much we have already told above:
how in fleeing he did not flee, and how, his steps turned back,
he retraced in his own footprints the ground he had covered,
so many times in vain, as his course wheeled round,
shut out from distant places and driven back to nearby ones.
Now I will recall another work of Felix, which the right hand of Christ
brought about to show the merit of his dear foster-son,
a marvellous proof, equal to the other sign,
which the culprit himself, trembling, disclosed when he confessed his daring deed.
But first, since the matter demands it, I will describe the shape
of the cross itself, such as painting too is accustomed to depict in two forms,
either two-horned on an upright staff
or with its five arms spread out across three rods.
The form of the cross is made up in a twofold shape: at one time
it stands and displays the look of a yardarm, like a ship's mast,
or of the letter the Greeks use to signify three hundred,
when it is fixed on a single upright
and, where it has its top, is yoked to a crosswise bar;
at another time the same cross, put together in a different arrangement,
proclaims the Lord Christ as in a monogram.
For the sign by which Latin reckoning marks twice five
is written by the Greeks as chi, and through its middle runs rho,
whose top also contains a sigma, which, curving back to the staff itself,
makes an O, as though a circle were completed.
For the upright stroke makes what in Greece is iota.
Then the stem itself, drawn back a little from the top,
makes tau; and so six letters, by which the name higher
than every name is expressed, come together in one
sign, and one letter is formed from three rods.
So one sign expresses six letters at once, so that one sign of three rods
signifies that the Lord is at once three and one,
and that God is in Christ, whom the harmony of the threefold mind
willed to be born for us, taking a body.
And there is a mystery in this: that the twin rods on either side,
as they spread apart, tilt back their tops to equal ends,
while below they stand on equal feet, set at matching distance,
and fastened together they hold fast at a central joint,
and their separate tops face one another at equal height.
Between these, set at the point where they meet in the middle,
a rod rises more proudly, like a royal sceptre,
signifying that Christ God reigns over all things,
who, through the cross spread out to the four extremities of the wood,
reaches the world measured out in four parts,
to draw peoples to life from every shore.
And since by the death of the cross Christ God is all in all
for the beginning of life and the end of evils,
alpha and omega stand round the cross, each letter
forming its different figure from three rods by a threefold reckoning,
because what is perfect is one mind and threefold power.
Christ, too, is for me alpha and omega, who, embracing alike the highest
bounds of heaven above and of the depths below,
as victor took possession of both hell and heaven,
and, having broken open the abysses, passed into the opened heavens,
bringing back victorious salvation after overcoming death.
And when victory had joined him to the Father's right hand,
he set up the trophy of his body in the heavenly seat
and planted the standard of the cross above all the stars.
That ornament, then, which the thief, driven by greedy
frenzy, had in vain unhooked from its hanging hook
and with polluted hand had carried off from the holy hall,
is made with such workmanship that, wondrously put together,
it represents both forms of the eternal cross,
as now, if anyone wishes to see it close at hand,
his eyes may readily confirm; for, restored, it shines in the very
place where it was fitted before, and, in front of the veil that encloses
the altar, it adorns its face with the sign of devotion.
So the same ornament displays that form of the cross
which marks out a balance poised on an even beam
and, in harmony, pictures a yoke on an upright pole,
or, with its crosswise arms, imitates the eyes joined across the face
by the brows of the forehead: that lofty tree
on which the Lord hung while the world trembled,
pouring out his innocent blood for the sinner.
Beneath this cross, which a double bar of solid weight
holds together, at the lowest foot of the extended metal
hangs a small crown set round with various gems.
With this, too, the Lord's cross, as though wreathed with a diadem,
shines out in the image of the eternal, life-giving wood.
This alone, out of the whole body of his theft, that thief
left untouched by the iron with which he had broken up the rest;
and when, once he was caught and ungirt and his clothes were let loose,
the pieces of plunder slipped out and fell,
the sight of it threw the hearts of the very men who found it
into confusion with mixed emotions. They rejoice
at what is found but grieve at what is broken; when they begin to ask the reason,
wondering that the robber was at once cautious and bold,
blind in what he broke and cautious in what he left,
then he confesses to the astonished men his crime and the divine power;
for his mind had collapsed entirely, yet this one thing
he had spared by divine will, because the cross set within forbade it
to the robber, however bold, by a power that left him helpless.
He himself confessed the crime of his mind and, bearing witness
to the power of the cross, told how every time he had armed his hands against
the crown joined to the cross in a single structure,
every time they had fallen as if broken, the blow recoiling,
and his arms had gone sick and numb, their sinews slack.
Here I would like to rise up briefly against the wretched thief:
Unhappy man, what great madness had turned your mind
that, rebuked by so great a light of truth,
you did not hurry back at a run to forestall the whole
search, so as to return the stolen goods of your own accord?
Did such force overwhelm your greedy mind with darkness
that you dared to hide in your bosom that part
which, with God preventing you, you so often feared to violate?
Tell me, where did that fear of yours flee to, and from where
did it return, while headlong boldness so wickedly hardened
your fearless senses? Fearful and scornful at once,
did you go off divided toward the very same form of crime,
mingling faith with faithlessness in a divided heart?
Did you believe in the power of the cross and the inviolable sign of Christ
while fearing to touch it with the iron,
and deny by carrying it off what you acknowledged by fearing it?
But your impiety did you no good, and you
who confessed your folly and the divine signs
have made us exult in a great triumph of the cross.
So let us stop assailing the thief, now that he is caught,
for whom the loss of the spoils of his fraud is punishment enough.
Now to you, venerable cross of God, I turn my words,
and, giving thanks, I will close by speaking your praise:
O cross, great love of God; cross, glory of heaven;
cross, eternal salvation of mankind; cross, terror to the wicked,
strength to the just and light to the faithful! O cross,
who granted that on earth God in the flesh should serve our salvation,
and that in heaven man in God should reign;
through you the light of truth has shone forth and the impious night has fled.
You have destroyed the shrines, torn down for the nations
who believe; you are the harmonious clasp of human peace,
reconciling man through the covenant of Christ the mediator.
You have become the ladder for man, by which he may be carried up to heaven.
Be always a pillar to the faithful and an anchor to us,
so that our house may stand firm and our fleet sail well,
resting on the cross, by faith, and winning from the cross its crown.
XX.
Often good masters serve their dear household slaves
with a loving mind, and with a father's love they protect
the servants subject to them, and favour with closer care
those whom their searching affection sees to be more in need
of help and lacking in strength. And if one of them,
as the customary practice of human life requires,
wishes to celebrate some vow and cannot
accomplish it from his scanty means, the poor slave
is cared for by his master's zeal, and the master, rich in wealth,
bestows on him what the poor man lacked: the cost of heaping up the table.
This is the lot given to me under Felix my patron;
let nothing be mine from myself, so that all may be mine through him.
For now, at his birthday feast, as indeed before
in past years when this day has blossomed for me,
I had nothing with which to prepare the customary banquet for my vows,
and the day was pressing on, and as yet no ready means
was at hand from any source. Suddenly, see, my bountiful patron
gave me the means to lay out a lavish feast: two pigs,
together with a heifer. And when the poor had been fed on their flesh,
I took my theme from those same animals,
since God recently produced miracles with remarkable signs
through those very beasts, by a deep design
urging men to give heed to Christ
and not to prefer the craving of the flesh to faith.
For, to the lamentable shame of our greed,
the course of my story will show that through cattle lacking human reason
the most high God has given signs.
I shall not sing fictions, though I use the art of poetry;
I shall narrate with a historian's fidelity, without a poet's deceit,
for far be it from a servant of Christ to utter lies.
Let such arts please the pagans, as worshippers of falsehood;
but for us the one art is faith, and Christ is our music,
who taught a wondrous peace to come together in himself
out of a harmony once discordant. He brought it into one body
by taking on manhood, he who by infused power blended
the kindly God with man, so as to fashion the two in himself
and make natures far apart into one.
That man might be God, God was made man by him
who is God, begotten of God the Father; and it is not by grace
but by nature that he is the only heir of the supreme Father,
alone possessing as his own what he grants as a gift to possess
to those whom kindly faith has enabled to merit divine things.
He, then, is truly for us the author of music;
he is the true David, who restored the lyre of this body
that had long lain with its frame decayed;
and the lyre made silent, its strings broken by the ancient sin,
the Lord by taking it on repaired for his own use,
and, having joined mortals to God, he made all things
grow green again in the likeness of their first form,
so that all things might be new, as the old decay departed from all.
To renew this lyre, God himself, the master,
himself hung his own body upon the tree of wood
and renewed it by the cross that slew the sin of the flesh.
And so he fashioned a mortal lyre fit for heavenly measures,
one lyre made out of various nations,
joining peoples of every race into one body.
Then, its strings struck by the plectrum of the Word,
the voice of the gospel lyre fills all things
with the praise of God; through the whole world Christ's golden lyre
resounds in countless tongues with a single melody,
and new songs answer God on matching strings.
But I will turn my steps back to my undertaking, for it is time, the hour has come
to offer the promised feast and set before you
a meal to be taken chastely through attentive ears.
I shall not fetch what I am about to tell from some bygone age;
I shall recount things seen here a few days ago.
A man had come here to fulfil a vow he had made,
a stranger to our dwellings from the territory of the city
of Abellinum. He had brought a pig, raised with diligent care
and long kept back, so that it might grow in years and fatness alike;
he had brought it here from there, and when he arrived,
he slaughtered the fat beast of his vow, as is the custom of those who vow.
The report of the pig had kindled sharp hunger in the mouths
of the needy, and all the old men, in hope of a large share,
stretched their gaping jaws towards the rich banquet.
Meanwhile the stingy giver divided the cut-up meat
in unequal shares: he cut off half of the pig's head
and cooked only the innards of its opened belly,
and to the poor he distributed only the vital organs
of the slaughtered pig, and left the whole body for himself to keep.
He thought he had fulfilled his vow, and joyfully began
to return, daring to load onto his beast along with himself
those remains, and, wrongly trusting, to carry home in them
the holy pledges of his accepted vow, while in them the miser
was carrying both the ruin of his soul and the snare of his journey.
In short, he was not allowed to go even a mile
along the road—in broad daylight, on a level highway,
with no darkness to alarm him and no rough ground to trip him—
before he fell from his horse, and as if fixed to the ground
he could not raise himself again, though he tried with renewed strength to stand;
and he began to cry out that his feet were bound,
and, lying there, to show it, his soles joined as if by a fetter.
Here another marvel was joined to that same mishap.
For while, around him lying in such disability,
a sorrowful crowd of his relatives was standing,
the beast of burden, which now carried only the pork as its load,
left empty of its rider and without its leader,
of its own accord, with no one turning it, reined itself in,
as if it recognised unbidden the cause of the stumbling,
or had seen someone barring the road on which it had begun to go;
so it fled, turned back its route and course,
and at a hurried pace ran back to the lodging,
flying ahead of all those whom anxious care for the fallen man
held fast, along the road by which, little by little—as one with a broken body,
straining, his stiff knees refusing to go forward,
and confessing both the unseen bonds on his feet and the deserved cause
of his fall and punishment with a tearful voice,
in open daylight, their hands bearing up the sick man's heavy
body—the faithful company was carrying him back to the holy halls,
as he begged to be brought back to the very threshold of Felix the physician,
soon to find a sure remedy there.
As men carried him among hands and crowds
into the holy courts, with the throngs marvelling,
the old men, ranged in a threefold company along the long benches,
gazed at him in astonishment, along with the pitiable multitude of the poor
and the grey-haired mothers seated in a rank beside them.
Besides, many whom their devotion had brought to the holy
buildings from various distant regions
saw the notable sign of mercy, since at the same time,
indeed on the same day, there came so wonderful a reversal of things.
The same man who a little earlier had left these same
thresholds on his own feet now, returning, was carried in on the feet
of others, hanging with his body held up.
Elsewhere, saddled, with none of the company guarding him,
before the door of the host, still laden with pork,
stood the horse, and no one who knew him
stood by to take care to relieve him, weighed down
by his burden, and lead him back into the familiar stable on his return.
Yet he, as if filled with human reason,
stood there like one seeking his own people and waiting for them at once,
keeping his hooves fixed
in one set place, twitching his ears and snorting through his nostrils,
as he sought the familiar scents of the men he knew.
The hosts wondered what that flight was, and what was the state
of the horse; the strange shape of the affair made the familiar animal
a puzzle to his friends, and there was no one to tell
what had happened, since all were crowding around inside the man
who had been carried by hands into the holy hall
of the martyr, where the sick man, prostrate before the holy threshold,
his body flung down, clinging to the doorposts and embracing them,
pressed kisses on them as a suppliant and washed them with weeping,
and, recognising himself as the source of his own pain,
uttered such complaints, accusing himself:
“Woe is me, who have deserved to incur such a penalty,
wretch that I am, in this place where, if any wretch arrives,
he is made happy! But I confess that I have met and suffer
a ruin that is just and equal to my wicked deserts,
so that, guilty, I am punished here among these very thresholds, burning
with a pain that at once scorches and grips my feet;
for in this—alas, madman that I was!—the gifts of my offered vow,
violating my pledge by fraud, I turned into the loss of my well-being.
Yet there is, there is something, I confess, that I can say:
that now for me sorrow is turning, by a welcome exchange, into joy,
and that, as my mind now looks to happier things,
the very punishments, with my troubles broken, have begun to grow sweet;
from them this very favour has now come to me for my good,
by which it has come about that so soon again I, wretched as I am,
may touch the venerable threshold of Felix.
For if there had been no fall, or only a slight one,
so that I could have pressed on with the journey I had begun,
then I would have been more unhappy through my good fortune,
because the harmful guilt would have remained, and I would not have felt
the wound driven deep into the bones of my soul, while my flesh rebelled.
For the vigour of an unharmed body would have hidden the peril
of my wicked deserts, and a hardened mind would have bound me, inert and guilty,
had not punishment fettered me in my fall.
Therefore, mighty physician in the name of Christ the Lord,
Felix, let this now be enough for you and for the mighty Lord:
that not wrath but a kindness friendly to my salvation
has brought forth my punishment, so that, binding my body, it might loose
my guilt. See, the wicked slave, the greedy runaway,
you have rightly dragged back, casting chains on him for his crime.
An unhappy debtor, I am held, bound fast, burned,
set before all as an image of the fear of God.
All of you, consider with trembling minds what you now
see me, wretched as I am, bearing as a lesson for the rest.
For are any free of this error? But it was God's will that in one man
an example should be made, so that my punishment
might be a warning in advance to those who do not amend.
But now spare your wretched servant, I pray, most excellent Felix;
spare me willingly, help me with your favour. Extreme pain drives me
to repeat my clamorous prayers. Come quickly,
lest swift death forestall a physician who delays.
But I know that this hand of the Lord, which strikes and which
will spare, lies in your mouth. Only hasten now
to loosen for me, exhausted and now failing, the chain
which you, holy one, see and I feel. Just as with a hidden
bond you secretly and silently bound the limbs of the runaway,
so with invisible medicine release him now that he has returned.”
As he cried out such words, clinging to those very doorposts
of holy Felix, licking them and wiping them with his kisses,
the devout throng, in astonished assemblies, both saw and heard
him. He himself, still lying there, was lifted up by hope,
and he chided every delay and the slowness of his people
in serving him. He ordered the pig to be brought, and all its parts
to be given back at once to the poor; he asked only to be granted
his life, and to be nourished by the filling of the needy.
His companions vied with one another to carry out his faithful orders swiftly.
They went to the familiar lodging; there the load
was taken off the beast, the meat was cut into pieces,
and the fire cooked the portions in foaming cauldrons.
Once cooked, they were brought in, many of them, on wide platters.
The hunger of the needy, fully satisfied, gave grateful
words to God and, appeased, asked pardon for the giver.
Without delay, at once, the account of the vow being settled,
that debtor inside was loosed from the fastening of his deserved chain,
and, his feet restored by the Lord's mercy,
like a horse set free, or a bird when the nets are broken,
he flew out and ran like a leaping stag.
A wonderful proof was set before their eyes. All rejoiced
at God's mercy so readily given, and at the merit of Felix,
so mighty that Christ is present in person in him,
governing powerfully in either direction according to men's deserts,
so as to be physician to the repentant and avenger to the wicked.
For see how great was the wrong of that fraud
by which that wretched man had first divided the pig
between the needy and himself; and here, where he ought
to have paid the whole vow, he had plucked off only the head and entrails of the pig
for them, and had made the rest, the whole body, his own,
foolish and wicked as he was; and yet, through the very fraud
by which he had become wretched, he was soon made blessed,
as God transformed his guilt by the lash of mercy.
For such is God's judgment; so does God, judge and father and king,
temper the weights of his lofty judgment,
that he balances a gentle justice for all
with measured scrutiny, and power, made lighter by mingled goodness,
first warns the guilty with a goad rather than destroys them with a thunderbolt,
so that, if the stroke of the warning lash has done its good,
salvation may return unharmed to the man who repents of his offence.
But if anyone, warned by the terror of the sacred scourge,
refuses to feel the blow, he will go away uncured,
and, kept for death, will feel the full force of wrath.
That man, then, was first wretched, and soon afterwards blessed,
healed in flesh and soul by such a remedy.
Because he recognised the cause and, acknowledging it as he lay there,
repented, he found in himself the ground
of his cure, and in a short time experienced both things which, by a just law,
await all men: the right and the work of divine peace and wrath,
so that avenging punishment justly awaits the proud
who are guilty, and compassionate mercy saves those who confess.
So, his feet nimble once the bonds were loosed,
the same man—quickly crippled after being sound, and quickly free
after being a captive only moments before—went back with a joyful voice,
leaping like that man of old who, limping
from his mother's womb, was commanded by Peter and John in the word of the Lord
to spring up on strong feet.
This poor man too was worthy of the threshold of the Beautiful Gate;
for God himself, the God of Peter and of Felix, by the same
power of his word, has now healed him among us,
lamed by a fall just now, by which he had once healed
the man lame from the womb; by that help this man went away rejoicing.
And he who inside had poured out sorrowful prayers in his affliction,
see, outside, with his body sound, was giving thanks:
“What can I render to Felix my patron?
What thanks shall I worthily return to him for so great a gift,
healed so quickly from so grave an affliction?
I did not set a fee with a physician, nor did I endure the dreary
weariness of a sickbed; nor through scalpels or cautery
or the harshly biting juices of various herbs
did a medicine fiercer than diseases and wounds
assail my body, as happens to those
whom a human hand visits with its untrustworthy art
and ever soothes, anxious as they are, with uncertain comfort.
See, I was carried just now a short distance to the very
throne of holy Felix, and flung down on the very
threshold, broken on marble as cold as it was hard,
I lay in pain, and my only speech was prayer,
my only medicine was faith. I saw no physician present,
and yet I felt one. Who was this physician, then, but Christ
himself, or Felix, made mighty by Christ in Christ's name
and power? Neither did I perceive at that time,
and yet he was present in both, so as
quickly to rebuke me when I sinned and to heal me when I grieved.
The Lord's way with me was the same under different forms,
as he chastised and as he spared. The healer and avenger
lay hidden from my eyes; the punishment and the cure shone forth.
Now, with the signs fulfilled in full order,
I shall go home rejoicing, safe with Felix as my physician and patron
forever. No longer shall I fear any
dangers of the road that might meet me, as before;
for danger will be far off, since the cause of danger has been removed.
My pledge unpaid had bound me, and now my pledge,
duly paid, has set me free. Yet, I pray, let your love
always bind me, Felix. Fasten on me that chain
by which neither death nor life may ever loose me from you.
But all who saw my sufferings
and, through your merit, beheld in great signs the lofty
hand of Christ, ought to recognise
how much good my punishment has secured for them, so that from now on
they may beware of hoarding earthly goods for themselves
and, while they grasp at gain, acquiring the loss of their salvation.
For if it was an evil for me to have cheated the poor of food
from the flesh of a worthless beast, what then of those
who wickedly embrace riches with a vain love,
and brood over metals buried together with their heart,
and by hiding them betray that they are superfluous,
guarding them, stored away far from their own use?
What will they do? What will they say for themselves to you, O Christ,
those who have seized the share of so many poor and have not
laid up for themselves any salvation from their surplus?”
One course has been served. Now we shall set out the welcome dishes
of a second table; but although we shall again bring the same
meat, it will be seasoned with a different sauce.
For I shall unfold for you, with wonderful novelty, another
marvellous work that Felix playfully wrought concerning a pig.
In time this event came earlier, but it was passed over in my
earlier little books; kept for the present time, it shall now be sung.
Nor does it matter at what time any work was done,
since through the various years there is one worker,
who works diverse miracles in praise of his saints
in all lands: Christ.
Certain farmers, far from our region,
who till Apulian fields beyond the city of Beneventum,
picked out for themselves from their bristly herd, among many young, one
still nudging the milky teats with its tender snout,
and, having tended it for a long time,
they fed the pig for their vow; and when it was ready, they began
to lead it to the hallowed hall of holy Felix,
so that, once slaughtered, it might feed many needy people from its great body,
and the martyr might rejoice in the poor well fed.
But the pig, heavy with fat that outweighed the strength of its legs,
could not carry itself for long, and at the very start of the road
it collapsed under its own weight, and from then on it could not be moved
by voice, hand or goad. Its owners, grieving,
left it lying there and entrusted it, left behind,
to their hosts. Their anxious minds wavered in doubt;
for their devout hearts were unwilling to abandon the journey of their vow,
yet, going far to venerate the threshold of Felix,
they were ashamed to go empty of their devoted gift. So
this decision settled in their uncertain minds:
that they would choose, from the same breed, as many smaller ones
for their vow as the years to which that pig had grown,
the one that stayed behind, inert, weighed down by its own bulk;
devout faith, eager to hasten the payment of the vow by which it was bound,
thought out this plan,
to make up for one fat pig with many modest ones.
So they came to this holy place and, their vows performed,
went back to their lodging, which was not close by;
for at that time, as it happened, the houses around the martyr's hall
had been filled by the usual dense press of crowds.
Therefore, far from here, in secluded countryside, they had contentedly
taken shelter in a remote cottage, from which in the morning they were preparing
to set out on their return, as the first dawn, reddening,
was bringing forth the day. The door of the hut was opened,
and one of the guests came out of the house, and the man
saw the familiar pig standing before the door, ready in a wondrous way,
as though saying that it had been sent to its master and was present;
and, like one giving a greeting, it licked the feet
of its rejoicing master and with gestures grunted softly to its keeper,
fawning, and sniffing, it gave him kisses with its moving snout;
and as if recognising that it was owed for its master's vow,
it pressed forward and offered its throat to the slow knives.
Under what guide, I ask, did it make its way through unknown lands,
or what feet did it acquire, to be able to run so far,
this pig that, after a short distance, at the very start of the road,
had given out, weighed down by its mass of flabby fat?
Surely no hand carried so large a beast along the long highway,
nor any lap; nor did its own mind compel it to travel so long
a road through an unknown region,
since even men, strong in the reason of the mind
and easily guided through unknown parts with the help of language,
if they lack a guide to light up the way for them,
are entangled by blind wandering in foreign regions.
Who, then, directed the pig's journey? Where did it get the will
to follow its masters, or the sense to be
aware that it had been raised for the vow over a long time?
Where did a beast get this concern, which seldom
stirs the faithful, so that, as if guilty by its own act
of having lazily stayed behind, the pig, struck with holy fear,
took care by coming to atone for the fault it had incurred by staying,
and to make amends for the vice of idle
sloth by attending, though late, in service on the masters who had set out?
Plainly a wondrous portent
was granted by heavenly power to a pig that dared so much,
that it went alone on a long journey, and that the pig
had such intelligence as to direct itself by a straight path
through unknown spaces. And how great is this too, that as it
came here from the lands beyond Beneventum,
whether it boldly took the paved public road along the middle of the highway,
and yet the busy traffic nowhere caught it,
or whether it made its way through hidden woods,
no hand met it with iron, and no wild beast with its bite.
What hand led it alone, or protected it as it went?
Surely, hidden by some cloud, it escaped men's eyes,
or, snatched up into the air, it came by wind rather than on foot,
and, set down by a sudden breeze at its master's lodging,
it stood, a four-footed guest, before an unknown threshold.
I shall tell of another marvel, close kin to this neighbouring sign.
For a heifer—a different kind, a beast of the herd—
certain men, who had likewise set out from a distant home,
had separated at first from the udder of its suckling mother
and reared, pledged by a votive gift to our
poor, whom, gathered here in a great multitude,
the grace of Felix feeds through the generous wealth of many.
So when the calf was now exulting in full-grown limbs,
her body now developed and fit for the vow,
they set out from home. But, as seems to be the custom
of those who bring from afar the vows they must pay to the holy
martyrs, to harness a beast to a cart in which they might ride,
they set about putting her under the yoke, though
she was unaccustomed to it, thinking her gentle, her spirit now tamed
to human uses, for which her masters had taken her
when small from the company of the herd and made her share their houses and food.
So, thinking that her wildness was tamed
and that she would readily yield to the yoke with a docile neck,
they coaxed her with stroking hands and tried to bring her into
harness; and she, trusting that the familiar touches were in play,
at first consented and followed them when they called.
But when, brought close to the yoke, she saw the reins
and sensed the straps being made ready for her neck,
indignant at the trick and suddenly changed,
she turned wild, and would accept neither yoke on her neck nor bonds on her throat,
and, overpowering their hands and shaking off the straps,
she leapt away from the group holding her and sought far-off, pathless
solitudes, fleeing her masters and the familiar dwellings.
Yet not far from men's sight, in the manner of a wild beast,
she rushed off and hid herself, a runaway, in dark thickets;
for, fleeing her departing masters, standing off at a distance,
she fled in such a way as not to let herself be left behind in the countryside.
At last, when she saw the cart moving off, yoked to a pair of oxen,
she showed a human understanding and, as though aware that she was owed
to the vow, she began to accompany the travellers.
Nor was she a companion for long: she scorned to go along
with the slow wheels, and, darting out as if in mockery, she passed
the groaning wheels and looked back at the laboriously creeping train
as she flew on ahead, no longer fearing to be forced under the yoke;
and to the cart she had hated before she became a friend and forerunner,
until they came to the hallowed hall of Felix.
There she halted of her own accord, came up to the one
who called her, and, as if bound by the vow, rejoiced to stand
in the very place to which, as a victim, she owed her own slaughter.
She who was rebellious and would not submit to human bonds
was led to a peaceful death without any struggle;
offering to the axe the neck that yokes had never touched,
about to provide food for the poor from her slain body,
she gladly poured out her blood for her masters' vow.
To what end are these things told? Is it for cattle, as the apostle says,
that God cares? But he who made all things for our sake,
the Author, works all things in all for us,
and through unknowing beasts he performs signs
that work for us, by clear tokens stirring dull minds
to strengthen their faith and to trust in the truth,
so that men, being teachable, with tongues loosed into words,
may not keep silent about the Lord whom dumb creatures proclaim by signs.
XXI.
Bright peace, by a welcome turn of the times, leads in our year
with tranquil light now that the winters are past,
and the day marked out by the honor of holy Felix
it opens to peoples free from care. To rejoice with cloudless
minds, now that the gloom of dreadful war is wiped away,
Felix urges in triumph, because he too, as a patron of peace,
together with the fathers Paul and Peter, and with his kindly brothers
the martyrs, besought the King of kings, whose divine will was favorable,
to prolong the times of the Roman realm,
to drive back the Getae, who were pressing already at the very jaws of the City,
and to turn destruction and chains back upon those very men
who were threatening the Roman realm with final ruin.
Now, therefore, with fear driven off, just as, when the rains are past,
one likes to look back at the clouds driven away, so it pleases us to compare the present state of things
with the past. How foul a night there was through those
days that have flowed by, in the year now slipped away,
when fury, kindled by the stirrings of divine wrath,
blazed in the cities of Latium as the enemy was let loose upon them!
Now behold, in the same way, the mighty gifts of Christ, now appeased:
with the enemy slaughtered together with their profane king,
the victory of the boy Augustus has restored
peace; and he, tender in years yet strong in arms,
prevailed by the power of God and broke the mortal
strength of the sacrilegious tyrant, for Christ won the victory.
But why should I say more on this now, when the commonwealth shows
that it was not the particular work of my Felix?
For this cause was taken in hand by many patrons,
so that Roman safety and the life of the state might endure.
Here Peter, here Paul, the chief princes, here all the martyrs
whom, countless as they are, the circuit of the great City holds together,
and those whom, across countless nations over a wide-spread territory,
the Church venerates within the bounds of Romulus,
together kept anxious watch with earnest
prayer. My Felix, as one among them,
had a great part in the prayers; but the sum of the gift requested
is credited to them all, and to no one privately.
So I will draw back my step; it is enough for me to have said a little
on a matter in which nothing belonged peculiarly to Felix's merits;
and yet I could not keep silent, since a share of praise
lay here too for Felix, in that the supreme Power,
Christ God, the mighty King of kings, had granted assent to all the saints
together, and among them, mingled in the suppliant flock,
He kindly heard Felix with equal favor.
I will refrain, then, from joining public gifts to his own
favors, and will sing the private honors of Felix,
and I will set forth what he does here in his dwelling as properly his own.
Where, then, shall I begin the weaving of my song?
Which blessings of Felix shall I recount? Shall I rather unfold the many things
he does everywhere for all, or shall I speak of the domestic
gifts for which I am his particular debtor?
Let me rather recount these, which I well remember were conferred on me
and mine; and since in earlier books I spoke rather of those things
which he granted partly to others and partly to us along with them,
now, from these riches which he has lavishly
bestowed on us, I will weave this little book with a grateful heart,
and, against custom, in varied measures —
just as he too each year brings forth varied
themes for me — I will change my meters, and in a single sequence
I will move on the feet of a song not bound by a single law.
For, as if in the fruitful field of holy Felix,
new flowers have sprung up, two shoots of Christ:
Turcius with his devout speech, Suerius in the flower of his youth;
and likewise holy mothers and girls like them,
such as was Apphia, that noble sister of Philemon long ago,
whom Paul's letter names in its address;
and with them Eunomia, a maiden already betrothed to the eternal
bridal chamber in heaven, whom, snatched from her mother's breast,
Christ with eager love consecrated as pleasing to Himself
and anointed with the ointment of His name, so that,
the tresses of her soul perfumed and the chaste head of her mind anointed,
she breathes from it the sacred fragrance of the heavenly Bridegroom.
She is the sister of Melania and at the same time almost her daughter; at her
side she clings rejoicing, having found a teacher in her kinswoman.
Both of them, bound together by divine dowries,
wear the varied jewels of the virtues like living necklaces
upon their lovely breasts, in well-cultivated minds.
They are followed by a numerous company of nobles and by the holy throng
of a virgin band, all of one color, as though of one fleece.
Here Christ, in His beloved Lamb, listens with joy
to Eunomia, taught under Melania's leading voice,
as she shapes those vessels with the modest measures of the psalms,
because, with God setting the tune, the little leader
guides with chaste voice the blessed choirs, the companions of the saints.
This grace, then, as I pondered, persuaded me fittingly
with a song playfully woven in manifold meters
to imitate a garden picked out with various flowers,
just as I marvel that the bosom of Felix is blooming, filled
with diverse light like a rich countryside,
with many guests sent to him under Christ's leading
and with children born to father Felix in a crowded throng
of offspring, so that he rejoices that suddenly his dwellings, with all their cells,
have grown throughout his bounds, and that his sober
roofs ring at last with chaste measures in voices fitting for him;
and in his guest-quarters, both in body and in speech,
he himself, with full bosom, marvels at his worthy nurslings,
souls equal in virtue though unequal in sex;
just as on a fruitful hill the aged planter
rejoices at the young olive shoots from the divine seed of Christ,
seeing settlers among his own fields.
So let the threshing floor of my song flower for me as a new meadow,
and in praise of the Lord, who is the maker of speech and of every
art, let music run in His service on varied feet.
And now let the elegiac follow, interwoven with iambics,
and let the heroic verse be the head and foundation of the little book.
The holy day, to be kept with chaste joys and offerings,
has shone forth in praise of Felix.
When I said “praise,” understand that I meant “death,”
since the death of the godly will rightly be called praise,
being precious when it is rendered back to the Lord God.
Hence the prophet too says in the word of God
that praise is given to a proven life at its departure,
and that no one is to be praised before death
the divine word teaches by the mouth of Solomon,
although some do praiseworthy things in this life,
and the praise that is to be sung at one's departure can be prepared
nowhere else than in this present age.
But I believe that, because the whole business of this life
hangs, wavering and uncertain, on slippery footing,
and a wheel swiftly turns our age about,
rising and falling along the rough roads
by which the course of this life must be run out —
for this reason Providence, our teacher,
warns us that before the end no one ought
to applaud or trust in himself or another;
though a man walk upright on an honorable road,
he must still always fear the stumbling of his foot,
until, with his courses run right to the turning-post,
he grasps the palm of the glory he has sought.
That is why the blessed martyrs, whom perfect
virtue has raised to the heavenly crown,
with just proclamations of the honor due them
we all celebrate, we who are their descendants
in the confession of the Christian name,
for whom they, by shedding their blood for the holy faith,
sowed beforehand the blessing of an eternal harvest,
so that, if we walk in the footsteps of the martyrs,
we may enjoy rewards equal to those of our forefathers.
Hence, then, for the saints, whether confessors
or witnesses consecrated by suffering,
the sacred days on which, having finished the day
of their mortal life by a life-giving death,
they passed from the stain of the world to God —
these the faithful peoples, with solemn joys,
rejoicing in the honor of Christ, devoutly keep;
as with this day of holy Felix's peace,
on which long ago, an old man, he closed the life of the body;
having earlier fought the battles of confession,
but consecrated by a bloodless departure,
a victor after wars, taken up on a day of peace,
at Christ's call he left the earth exulting
and made his passage to the mansions above,
not cheated of the martyr's crown,
since in his mind he had fulfilled the vow of suffering.
For often the mighty soldier entered the contest,
and always, the enemy defeated, returned a confessor;
but God, content with the readiness of his mind,
preserved him, not denying him the martyr's crown
but adding the crown of a priest as well,
so that, having won the palm in a bloodless battle,
he might possess the reward of one who had fought,
the purple laurel of confession,
and, wreathed with the fillet of peace upon the priest's stole,
the same man might be twice crowned,
Felix, confessor and presbyter of God.
This day, then, which we recall with yearly vows,
is the day not of his contest but of his burial,
on which, the two substances parted from each other,
that of the soul flew to God, while the flesh, returned to the earth,
came to rest hidden in the tomb.
And rightly is this marked as the birthday
of the saints, the day on which, having fulfilled the law of the flesh,
they are stripped of the bonds of mortality
and are born to God into the realms above,
carrying with them the joyful hope of rising again.
I have always honored this day in such a way
that I would sooner think it my own birthday
than the day on which I was born to no purpose.
For that day is more fittingly mourned by me
on which, created into this world,
I fell, a sinner, from the womb of a sinful woman,
conceived in dark iniquities,
so that my mother bore me already guilty.
Cursed, then, be the day on which I, wretched one,
was brought forth by the iniquitous into iniquities.
But blessed be this birthday for me as well,
on which my patron, born in heaven,
Felix, rose up to that power
by which he could cleanse me of my dregs,
loosen my chains, and, having redeemed me, set me free
from the mournful death of my own birth.
This same day always comes round again for all
when the year has run through the world in its circles;
but since every year grace renews
the diversity of the gifts which Christ gives
to His companion, so that Felix may give them to me,
it changes, and is not the same day that comes to all,
bringing varied themes for my songs.
Let us see, then, what new thing this year
has brought me, that I may burst into spring with new strains.
I will not go far, nor take for myself from afar
things past in time or absent in place.
They are here; the gifts themselves are held close at hand;
you all see the gifts granted this year
to us, joined together in the one bosom of Felix:
servants of Christ, formerly nobles of the earth,
but now inhabitants destined for heaven,
whom Christ Himself, who had made them rich,
has made poor in this world, so that into His kingdom
He may carry them, cast down from the citadel of earthly honor:
Apronianus, the glory of the Turcian family,
a boy in age, an old man in the senses of the flesh,
noble by an ancient lineage of the toga
but more illustrious by the Christian name,
who, with the glory of old and new birth mingled,
is an old senator of the Curia, and new to Christ.
Close beside him, a companion under an equal yoke,
younger in age, is Pinianus, his equal in faith,
himself also a boy illustrious from ancient blood,
of the stock of the first consul in the chief City.
That Valerius of consular lineage
who holds the first name in the Latin Fasti,
whom Rome, after driving out the kings, joined with Brutus,
is, for this Valerius, now a Christian consul,
the remotest founder of his race, far back in time.
O happy vein! Although that man, having died
in pagan error, does not enjoy this blessing of his stock,
sunk in the black lake of hell,
yet we, beholding with the light of faith
the past and present of the human condition,
marvel at the works of the lofty Creator,
and at those prepared from ancient ages
along the lines of mystical successions —
godly sons of ungodly men — we stand amazed;
yet in the darkness of ungodly minds
we see that seeds of light flashed forth
even in the very time of the ancient night,
in those whose mind and will, pagans though they were,
were approved by the law of nature.
Hence in some of their descendants now
the vein of the ancient fathers answers once again;
just as that man of old, the furthest ancestor
of my Pinianus now, chosen to restore his fellow citizens
to liberty after the harsh rule of kings,
foreshadowed the rising of this descendant of his,
who, pursuing pride with his ancestral spirit,
in a better cause has driven slavery away
from himself, the conqueror of his own body;
and with the devil's kingship driven out of his members,
now, in spiritual peace, the yoke of sin
is trodden down by the chaste freedom of a faithful soul;
and in this the boy reflects something of that ancestor,
as he serves as a soldier in the consulship of Christ:
that, taking thought for those to be set free, he dispenses the holy service
of the work of redemption for God,
an emulator of his ancient forefather so far as this,
that he frees his household from slavery,
as that man freed the citizens. But what that man had done
in a single city, and a small one, still in the first
years of Rome, this one does now in many
cities set in different parts of the world,
generous everywhere, both to his own people and to strangers.
For from the necks of many free men too
he drives off the servile yoke with his holy wealth;
those bound by debt in the darkness of prison
he releases with gold from the chain of usury.
These, then, Felix has hidden in his bosom
and, at Christ's command, lodged under his roofs,
and with me has received them as everlasting guests.
Now, glad of these helpers on either side,
I dedicate the vow of three under one voice,
one spirit speaking with the affection of three.
Magnify God with me, and wisely, in honorable
songs, boys of one mind, sing your psalms.
As ten-stringed psalteries sound when their strings are plucked,
and strings of different pitch join in matching measures,
so let the holy lyre of our fellowship resound,
as though a threefold tongue sounded from a single lip.
For we are three in number, yet one in mind,
and still more souls join together in these three,
whose names, written within it, the heavenly book preserves:
first of the choir is Albina, with her peer Therasia;
to this yoke her sister is joined, so that the third leader
of the hymn-singing choirs is the mother Avita.
These three mothers have two children, both of one sex,
a twin flower, the shoot Melania and Eunomia.
These same are children to us men as well; for those whom
sex divides, devotion unites.
Along with father Paulinus, this Turcius is likewise a father,
but age makes me a father, offspring makes him one.
From different sources we are joined in one name:
not both old men, yet both fathers.
So this whole company together: the mothers make three names,
there are four among the children, and two among the fathers.
For here is the boy, Melania's husband in the body of Christ,
to whom God granted a name taken from the pine,
so that, born a child of eternal life, he might take his name
from that tree which is green without end.
For the pine, standing always with a flourishing crown,
always loving to spread its foliage high on lofty ridges,
does not change its appearance with the seasons (for in heat
and snow alike it stays the same with its green foliage),
and, fertile too with the fruit of a hard nut, inside it, for food,
like a mother it holds tender milk under a crinkled covering;
its rich pitch-wood sweats a fragrant liquid,
so that even in its very timber the tree is not barren.
This tree, then, is a type of the eternal body:
beautiful, fruitful, long-lived, lofty, fragrant, green.
This blessed boy will be, in the Lord, the likeness
of this tree, so that grace may remain with him forever.
And now, planted by God, he thrives, and with holy progress
raises his fruitful head like a lofty pine.
He stands out as my first son in my own flock;
but I have another light, his equal, in Asterius,
whom his parents, of one mind in true devotion,
together dedicated as an infant to Christ,
so that, like Samuel, marked out from his first years,
he might grow up vowed among the saints, with God to nourish him.
He first let loose his babbling in the name of Christ,
and the name of the Lord was his first speech;
and now, born to the heavenly kingdoms with God as his parent,
he shines alike with his starry name and his face.
Holy grace has made this boy a brother to his father as well;
for they were born together from the holy stream.
Those whom nature had separated by rank, God by His kindly
gift will carry into His kingdom as brothers.
So let all nine of us, parents together with our shared offspring,
be like a single lyre with harmonious hearts;
let all of us make of ourselves one cithara for a single
song, composed of diverse strings.
Let Aemilius come as the tenth. Then at last, with the number full,
the mystic law will sing within us.
For with this number of heads, on the lyre of peace
the living string will tell forth the work of salvation.
For this cithara Felix will be the plectrum; with this quill
Christ in triumph will strike the ten-stringed cithara.
This cithara in us, with Christ playing, will sound
a harmony full in its perfect senses,
if our peace is in tune with God in every fiber,
so that we are united in body, mind, and faith.
For that person fills out the cithara with holy laws,
tuned in all its measures toward life,
whose life accords in all things with the sacred law;
for every string will sing with unbroken thread.
Now to you, revered father, eternal patron,
my protector, Felix most dear to Christ,
I will turn my speech and offer words of thanks.
You have bestowed many favors on me in various gifts;
all that brings forth the substance of the present life and the hope of the life to come
I remember that I owe to you, to whom
Christ gave me as a servant from my earliest years.
If eloquence ran for me in river floods,
and I had a thousand mouths, each sounding with a hundred tongues,
perhaps not even when filled with these resources, their fountains pooled together,
could I run through all the gifts of Felix,
all that Christ the Lord has given to His friend
and the confessor has passed on to me, his servant and nursling.
Which shall I put before which? Diverse in kind, but equal
in weight, many great gifts crowd together, and among them
I could not decide which I should rather choose to recall;
abundance confounds what would be an easy choice.
If I go back to the very beginning and unroll everything
he has granted me with equal love at different times of my life,
I could sooner number the hairs of my own head
than recount your gifts to me, good Felix.
You it was who first cast into me, for saving purposes, the seeds
of heavenly things, if only I could attain them.
For as a boy, brought from the western shores of the Gauls,
as soon as I touched your threshold with trembling step,
seeing the wondrous proofs of holy works
teeming before your doors, where, your body buried,
you are enclosed, and by your lofty merits spread far and wide,
I drank in with my whole heart faith in the divine name,
and, rejoicing in your light, I came to love Christ.
Under your guidance, in my early youth, I bore the honor of the fasces,
and with you directing my hand and preserving my salvation
I remained pure of the peril of human blood.
Then too, as a boy, I cut the first offerings of my beard
before your throne, as though you yourself were clipping it;
already then, having sent ahead a pledge of residence through my office,
I fixed dwellings to be laid out in Campanian lands,
you laying the foundations of the future lodgings of your servant,
when, silently inspiring my mind, you bade me take care
that a road leading to your buildings be paved and laid,
and that, adjoining your roofs, a covered building should rise in a long stretch,
under which formerly the needy had their
dwelling. After this the house grew, built up with a second story,
which now remains as a hostel for our cells;
below it a portico serves the sick poor,
which supports us, living in the rooms added above it
as lodgings, and affords us the healing companionship of the needy
for our wounds under one roof,
so that we may render friendly benefits to one another in turn:
they strengthen our foundations with their prayers,
we shelter the brotherly bodies of the poor under our roof.
So when, relieved of the sixfold fasces of authority,
I laid down the axe stained by no slaughter,
at your recall I was restored to the shores of my native soil
and to my anxious mother. From there I went as a traveler
across the ridges of the Pyrenees to my kinsmen the Spaniards.
There you allowed me to be joined in marriage by human law,
so that you might gain the life of two,
and so that, through the yoke of the flesh, the doubled salvation of souls
might make up for the delayed salvation of one.
From then on, although my life ran along another path
and I dwelt far away in another region of the world,
where Gaul is beaten by the surge of the resounding Ocean,
yet in mind I was never torn away from this
seat, and I always clung to the bosom of Felix,
and in turn I felt Felix standing by my
affairs for every good, in all that had to be done at home and abroad.
My property and the defense of my property
was Felix alone, with Christ's power appeased,
always both warding off adversity and granting prosperity.
You, Felix, always “felix,” happy, for me, so that I should not be wretched,
were father and guardian to me with unfailing love.
And when I was in trouble over the blood of my murdered brother,
and my brother's case brought peril upon me, his kinsman,
and the confiscator was already moving against my estate,
you, father, rescued my neck from the sword and my patrimony from the treasury,
and kept me and mine for Christ the Lord.
For with what purpose Christ then brought help to my property
and my life, and the care of Felix was mightily
at hand, the great outcome of events afterwards showed,
when the lot and purpose of my life were changed,
as faith renounced the world, country, and home.
Faith carried on trade, selling off property in different lands,
and, with everything sold, bought a cross to carry.
So earthly wealth bought the hope of the heavenly kingdom —
for the hope of faith is stronger than the wealth of the flesh. This hope,
resting on God, brings forth an everlasting wealth; but fleshly
wealth destroys heavenly hope. Yet hope, as for wealth,
if it prevails through victorious faith, does not simply take it away,
but, happily transformed, remakes it by divine right,
turning it from frail to eternal, and, removed from earth,
establishing it in heaven, where Christ, the faithful guardian, holds
what is entrusted to Him; nor does He keep the deposit only in the amount
in which He received it from here, but with multiplied
interest He will repay the talents entrusted to Him to those who entrusted them,
and will make Himself the wealth of those who believe.
And what wealth could be more precious than this wealth?
If the whole world had been my private property,
would that possession be worth more than Christ the Lord?
