And who made me the possessor of so great a wealth,
even if only in hope? Who compelled me to spurn that
wealth for Christ, so as to turn Christ into my wealth?
Who but you, Felix, always my great power,
enemy of my sins and friend of my salvation?
You exchanged my homeland for me for a better provision,
giving me yourself in place of a homeland. You broke
our fleshly bonds. You set us free from the stain of perishable
blood and made us move from the shores of our native land
to your own race, and breathe heavenly things with lofty
spirits. You, changing our lineage
from mortal ancestors, will cause our names, among the friends
of the heavenly Lord and marked in the everlasting book,
now that the birth of our mortal origin has been transferred,
to be blotted out for death and written over for salvation.
What did I have like these things when I was called a senator,
such as I have here now, when I am called a pauper?
See: throughout the many halls of the blessed martyr,
ample in space and lofty in their roofs,
and splendid with deeply coffered ceilings,
watered with fountains and garlanded with porticoes —
everywhere and all at once, whatever throughout these, in the name
of blessed Felix, is tended, celebrated, and possessed —
in all these spaces is my home. Nor is there any place
joined to and set within his buildings
that does not lie open to me as my own. But why should I boast
of this gift, if, as a home-born guest, I possess
the property of beloved Felix under a visible roof of stone?
How much more is it for me that Felix
himself, by the gift of God, is my home, in whom my living
life possesses a house that will not fall for any length of years?
For that Felix's house is also my house, since he himself
allows me the reins of his authority,
our boldness proves by these services too:
that we have received companions into these hospitable buildings, and now
we all hold Felix's rights with equal right,
and are cherished, joined together in the lap of father Felix,
as children — those you know, whom you see even now in these very
buildings of Felix, keeping with me the lodgings marked out for them,
forgetful of the lofty roofs of their ancestral houses,
and dwelling more safely in narrow cells near the martyr,
in a small space, with ambition spurned.
For Christ is near to the lowly and turns away from the lofty,
and visits the narrow thatch of a poor man's hut more often
than the towering gables of proud estates.
So, that I may compare the roofs I dwell under now, having left
the lofty ones, what I have now with what I remember having had,
please, compare them yourselves with just judgment.
What house so beautiful, what field so fertile, was ever
mine in mortal possession, as the one which now, in this
poverty, Christ has granted me, through whom I have in abundance
Felix, a rich estate with inexhaustible returns?
But if I look back over my estates from my former wealth,
whatever was once great to me in anything at all
was earth, the windy semblance of an empty shape;
whether it was gold or gems, that finery was
a cheap price to the good and a precious poison to the greedy.
But now, stripped of wealth—or rather not of wealth, but more truly freed
from damnable burdens—free from the urge to possess, I enjoy
a carefree poverty, and hostile chains have no scrap of cloth
by which to hold me, naked as I am. Light and nimble-bodied
goes the one whom the alluring image of the deceitful world does not stifle with any loves
through its many shifting appearances.
O poverty of Christ, venerable to me and more precious than the whole world!
You enrich with heavenly treasure
those you strip of wealth; you cleanse them as if of the rubble of earth;
you tear down what is earthly in us and in its place
build what is eternal; by a new law you turn the losses of earth
into the price of life, reversing the roles of loss
and gain, so that money kept brings us loss
and money not kept brings gain; yet the same money poured out
in the wrong way is loss. For it profits no one to pour out his goods except in the name of Christ
and at God's command;
for what is spent on profane vices truly perishes.
Extravagance and ambition, so dangerous is their disease,
weigh as heavy as the crime of avarice, since in both lies
an equal cause of death, which stained lust brings about
just as surely as does the ill-counselling desire for the things of the world.
You wish me poor in these riches, best Felix,
so that you may make me rich in life, and by a poor way of living
set me free from the death to be paid without end
by the rich of this world, for whom the deadly use of gold
breeds eternal fires, with worms for company.
You wish us joined to you not only by living under your roof,
for you are preparing to nurture us for partnership with you in eternal life
and to lead us to that pattern
which you, made perfect in the image of the Lord Christ,
bore on earth, once a man who from rich became poor.
For who does not know of your poverty, which, for the holy Name,
you entered joyfully as a confessor when your wealth was confiscated,
and in which, right up to old age,
you always worked a rented garden, Felix?
That is why you strive to make like yourself, in holy poverty,
all whom you receive under your hospitable roof;
for a form unlike yours could not be joined to you.
For as far as the wolf is at odds with the lamb, and light with darkness,
so far apart are the way of the rich man and the way of Christ.
For the broad way lies open, slippery on its downward slope,
sinking into hell; it drives the greedy rich,
pushed on by their own bulk, to be carried down into Tartarus.
But the way that is Christ's, which lies open to holy confessors
and martyrs, is steep, and opens its path to few.
So this way does not admit the stuffed; it shuts out the laden.
Therefore it is fitting that the servant and follower of the blessed
martyr be tightly girded and, stripped of troublesome
fetters, be made slender by wholesome poverty
and light, so that he can pass through the narrow gate
and climb the lofty mountain of the Lord.
But why do I, unskilled at weighing the worth of things,
set these down as your great gifts, best father?
However great these too may be to me, they are small
if I speak of greater things. For how small a share of your works
toward us is the reckoning of this gift,
that you gave us land to dwell on and allowed us to build
houses to live in, when you, father, have offered us even your
very heart? For what else but your inmost heart
did you bring out for us, when, deigning to open the inner depths of your tomb,
holy one, by occasions stirred up from the hidden dust,
you wished to show by so great a sign that we
are grafted onto you by a special love,
willing that the silent resting place of your body, fixed through so many ages past,
gracious one, should, as the ash of the dust suddenly came forth,
be unsealed in our own time?
So in his praises I shall pass quickly over
those riches of Felix, as lesser gifts:
the many things he has zealously bestowed on us, now that we are received into his lap;
and in his lavishness he will not stop
flowing toward us continually with countless gifts of rich bounty.
Supplying not only what the body's needs require,
he has also added those things by which the favour of praise is sought now
and an honoured name is kept after us,
so that he, buried so many ages ago, allowed his halls—as never before—
to grow or be renewed through our labour, with porticoes
and houses built around them.
He also revealed to us the holy secrets
of his own tomb. In a few words I shall tell of this venerable gift,
so that the measure of his great kindness may shine out,
by which he deigned to love us, unworthy as we are, so much
that, letting our eyes come close to that awesome secret,
he disclosed his bones to us as though to his own marrow.
So I shall tell in full order the occasion
by which he granted us to see things close to his limbs
and to touch the very coffin in which his body lies.
The appearance of the place is well known to all: over the very
sarcophagus of the hidden martyr, where a railing closes off the tomb,
there lies in the middle a broad slab
of marble, overlaid with fixed silver plating.
The surface of this slab opens with two mouths,
offering holes underneath for pouring in nard.
This nard a spirit, coming from the hidden resting place of the holy ash,
sanctifies, healing it with a secret breath.
Suddenly the liquid poured in, in the usual way,
was drunk up by these little vessels, as earth rose up from the tomb;
and those who had put nard into the place, getting ready to draw it out
to take home with them, found, to their astonishment, the vessels filled
not with nard but with a heap of sand bursting up,
and in alarm they drew back their hands, full of dust,
from the mouth of the tomb. The strange event stirred everyone
and kindled an eagerness to search out the cause of the sudden
portent. So it was decided to fix a set day
and, with the marble removed, to examine the inmost resting place.
For this, I confess, was what our overanxious care feared:
whether perhaps the dust contained something of the holy body—
the dust which hands had drawn out of the tomb through the open holes
and carried off, clotted with all kinds of filth
and mixed with little bones, potsherds and rubble.
So people in their fear, talking among themselves, wondered
whether perhaps some little creature shut up in hidden hollows
was spitting up from deep below
the sacred ash of the holy flesh, just as, across deserted fields,
creatures are wont to dig into the earth with their sharp snouts
and pour out black heaps around their burrows—
so too from the inner recess of holy Felix.
And to make it all the more wondrous, this wondrous eruption of heaped-up earth
occurred at intervals of several days.
So on the appointed day the work, useful in many ways,
was taken in hand. The bishop sent all his
priests to us. As they looked on, the workmen pressed on
to carry out the priests' orders; and their first task
was to remove the railing from the spot, and their next
to loosen the nails and lift the fixed slabs.
But when we saw the coffin, set deep beneath the marble covering,
still standing with the joints of the sarcophagus unbroken,
then confident faith drove from our doubting hearts the danger
of error, as it proved by touch and sight—
the sarcophagus intact, the tomb nowhere cracked—
that the body of the veteran martyr, walled in on every side by strong defences,
had been exposed to no sacrilege,
and that the holy bones kept the honour due to his flesh—
bones to which the holy Spirit never ceases to be present,
whence a living grace abides in holy tombs,
proving that those who have died in Christ are buried without death,
their bodies lulled for a time in peaceful sleep.
So, having restored the honour of Felix's tomb,
we left everything carefully secured, so that now,
until the day of the Lord, when the glory due to them under Christ their prince
will shine on the saints raised up together,
the bones may rest undisturbed in their bed,
and the same peace that awaits the holy soul in the realm above
may keep the venerable body here on earth.
What remains for me still to tell? As if indeed I had
worthily set forth even what I have sung, or recounted in full
all the gifts of our lavish patron!
Many are hidden by their very number, yet all of them sit fixed
in our mindful hearts; very many have already been told,
and more still remain to be told. But the rule of keeping a book within bounds
bids me pick out the greatest from the many.
When all the works had been built which are seen to stand
in their various artful forms, the lofty buildings, with their halls
and forecourts surrounded far and wide by long
colonnades, all seemed together to beg for one thing only, the gift of water,
for their sorrowing inhabitants.
I confess that I even used to accuse, in a complaining voice,
my Felix himself, as if he were too sluggish in pressing
these wishes, since he allowed a share of water
to be denied us for so long by our neighbouring city.
But by a wiser counsel he was holding us back as we hurried on with rash minds,
linking the delays to fitting times;
for the right order of the works rightly demanded
that completion should come first to those undertakings
which, around the holy halls of the venerable martyr,
busy care was preparing with manifold effort;
and when divine grace had put the finishing hand to the works,
then, with our prayers fulfilled in their full order,
it would channel springs brought into the finished courts.
And indeed, as soon as all the work here stood complete in its fittings,
the parched thirst of our longing was not long drawn out,
and soon, as God willed [?], the people's hearts, once harsh,
gave their ready consent with willing minds.
So now I shall tell of the gift of water. Grant me now, Felix,
by your prayers to the Lord, that my words may run
with as easy an eloquence as the abundant stream with which you made springs
flow into your forecourts and houses.
All that the kindly Lord has granted us through your intercession
he has adorned and increased with this gift,
by which he brought springs to the thirsting [?].
Christ, that Rock, has once again poured more from his holy breast,
renewing the gift of his ancient kindness, so as to
bedew with unwonted water all the sand that was dry before,
and make waterless land flow with sudden streams,
and so that into the holy halls of his Felix,
for the guest peoples gathered from many nations,
through wells and pools and capacious basins,
new drinks might run in abundantly flowing channels.
O highest Fount, who would grant that you water my deserts
and break through the pumice rock of my heart,
and that I build my house on the rock and drink from you the water
that would bring forth in my dry breast a living vein
of water springing up for ever? Yet even this slender drop
of eloquence with which I speak of you is surely drawn
from the place whence the source of the rivers also overflows.
For who could speak of you even a little, Christ, highest power of the highest
Father, without you? Your own Spirit
inspires us to speak of you, in whose light we see the equal light
of both Father and Son, so that, with the Holy One leading us
and breathing upon us, we may confess Christ as God with the Father.
But since, as I bear the name of the living Fount on my lips,
a drop from the river of the Word has trickled into my mouth,
perhaps my lips will from now on carry some taste of it,
and now my tongue will speak of the gift of water, not parched
with a dry throat, but as though more richly moistened.
With all the works furnished, which are seen to be many,
this point demands that I set the name of devoted Abella
into my verses; for she seems worthy of the honour
of being named, so that in the praise of Felix she too
may be praised, because for Felix's honour she willingly
took on a labour, and to sweat in the heat
among sheer crags she counted rest and reward.
Small indeed in its walls, this city will be called great
for this holy work. Six miles from our Nola
it lies among high-ridged mountains, from which it draws, close at hand,
the waters that rise there, and gathers them into a single basin,
from which, through inserted pipes, it first claims the streams for itself,
and with the rest of the flow runs on to the city of Nola,
watering many estates here and there in the fields as well.
But let me return to the thanks owed for the gift of labour;
for to restore the aqueduct, which long age
had broken, to its vessels and channels once more,
she supplied workers abundantly, labouring for nothing. The place, set among high
cliffs, with no path or road,
could not be reached even by pack animals,
and so the steeps of the vast mountain made it hard
to find a ready workforce even for wages;
all the greater, then, is the honour of reward that enriches Abella,
because, readily serving the sacred honour of Felix,
she gave her unhired hands with lavish devotion.
One could see eager throngs from the whole populace,
council and people together, gathered with one mind,
roused at early dawn, run gladly to the work,
and hurry eagerly, vying with one another, up to the highest peaks,
and, with necks bowed beneath the heavy load of baskets
and of bound-up stones, over the thorny steeps
make trip after trip under the blazing sun,
and stretch the whole of the long summer day
from dawn into the late hours of evening,
and, wakeful in spirit, their bodies scarcely refreshed by a short night,
rise again before daybreak to their workmen's tools
and feel no weariness, for God gave them strength.
In short, the grace of the great work so advanced
that, as if in play, the whole work in a few days
reached its end, complete and its task accomplished;
and the channel from the distant mountains, in a full column,
where it had long ago been broken off by long neglect,
taking in little springs on every side from the various rocks,
brought back the gathered water to cities long thirsty,
and with a full course through the channels over many miles
of road, flooding even the buildings of our Felix,
filled the new basin with the Summus [?] brimming over.
And, as proof of the divine gift,
the water ran here more abundantly in the summer months
than it used to come before from the winter rains.
Here, my Nola, I shall now rightly arraign you
before our common patron, and, out of the anger of a gentle love,
while remaining calm at heart, I shall pretend our patron is displeased,
scolding his little daughter in the words of an old complaint.
For why, Nola, when I asked for a just share
in your spring, did you, troubled by fear, harshly refuse
the hospitality of water held in common? Forgetting to regard
divine laws, you thought my wishes were for human
uses, and, forgetting Felix, you believed you would be giving to me;
and you lamented sadly that if you granted it, your homeland
would soon be dry, its drink taken away,
and you often shouted this too amid stirred-up uproar,
not knowing that springs would be at the service of divine bounty,
as you have since learned by experience. For soon God the Creator himself
rebuked minds faint enough to distrust Christ,
when, after peace had been agreed, you now held the use of the stream
piously shared with Felix as your partner,
so that by his surpassing goodness he might rebuke your complaint
all the more. He did not, as you feared, make you thirst
by dividing the water; but as author and sustainer
of things and of men alike, who created all things by his word,
he showed you that the thing was his, which you, distrusting the Lord of things,
were refusing his friend as though it were your own.
You saw it for certain, for the fact itself compelled you
to acknowledge the sublime laws of the eternal Father
and the powerful merit of Felix, when the water flowed forth abundantly
in the heat, and, through the holy loss by which you had given
a part to the martyr's halls, its channels suddenly increased,
and, with the spring's abundance released in its outlets,
the streams, at his command, were given back to you with ample interest
and flowed into your walls; and at the very season
in which you, owner of the water, used so often to go short,
God repaying many times over what he had taken from you,
water flowed in abundance for your drinking and your baths.
What gift, then, Abella, poor in wealth,
shall I give you in return for so great a gift? At least, while in my poem
I proclaim and record your service and your name,
I shall pay you this price by way of an honourable reward:
that you be written down for ever as joined
to the praises of holy Felix, and be remembered as the nursling of so great a patron,
of whose gifts the greatest share has fallen to you.
Now this labour of yours, to which the spirit of Felix drove you,
so that, with your whole people and council in harmony,
you undertook a work to be achieved with great sweat,
while the summer season doubled the hard toil:
the channel of the ancient structure, running over rugged peaks,
known in past ages but now without use
since the water had failed, lying hidden among the vast ridges
with forests heaped over it on every side in a great mass,
you strip of its dense mounds, and you restore its long-forgotten
functions; and the veins scattered through trackless places,
which were being swallowed deep in pumice sands,
you gather up, and force each water to follow its own tracks again,
and bring it back into the mouth of the mother channel,
and make the conduits, long empty since the flow had ceased,
overflow with the returning stream,
and the city, long complaining of its withdrawn springs,
Nola, you now flood with the Summus [?] long despaired of.
Nola enjoys the waters of Felix, for this abundance
is no longer the city's own, which it lately gained
through Felix's zeal: in return for the gift of a modest drop,
it has been enriched by divine bounty with plentiful streams.
So you too, Nola, together with me, cherish little Abella
as a mother would, since, as you know, though she herself
is your daughter, she is still the mother of your waters,
from whose native mountains flows to you all the abundance
in which you once took pride in your prosperity,
and which afterwards, with a better zeal, you came to serve.
Rejoice, then, my Nola, and congratulate yourself, exulting
with all your strength in Christ, who through his friend
and beloved Felix has fashioned you, and whose hand on high
has increased your beauty, with nature as its servant.
Look at your face, with which you now shine forth renewed,
so that you may know whether you have given anything to Felix's honour,
or are rather adorned and loaded with gifts by Felix, God's own.
Where rough pebbles lay parched on bare fields,
now a changed loveliness grows green on the watered clods.
Not only these springs, Nola, has the rich grace of Christ
poured out for you through the merit of Felix;
it has also brought springs flowing from heaven here to your
walls, and, placing them in the rejoicing bosom of Felix,
has bidden them flow out from your city to many cities
in outpoured rivers. I mean those servants of Christ,
a pair illustrious before God, a pair ennobled by the name of Christ,
who with their mother Albina have lately arisen in your territory,
darlings of all the saints and joys of heaven:
Pinianus joined in bond with Melania, a blessed pair.
God has made them both children of Felix and breasts to nurse others,
breasts of divine goodness flowing with milk,
from which every poor person takes flowing nourishment,
and every rich person likewise takes wholesome lessons.
See, these are springs from the holy river of Christ,
which do not flow through the earth in a visible flood,
but abound with the living water of compassionate love.
Grant, O Christ, that these springs may gush forth for you
in unfailing richness in the bosom of your Felix,
and that these veins may never dwindle under any star.
Flow into hearts dedicated to you for ever, O Christ,
and grant to your Felix himself, to whom we sinners
have been entrusted, that your love may never withdraw
from our hearts the spring of this help, and that Felix himself,
a spring from your spring, may flood us generously,
so that your spring, O Christ our King, may always leap up within us,
and that Felix may win for us, wretched and needy as we are,
to live from now on as happy men, as the lot of his name foretells.
XXII.
Now I promise myself that you will set your songs among sacred books
and that, set aflame by the divine power of Christ, God,
you will open your eloquent lips to the supreme Father.
Only begin to give your heart to divine things
and to raise your senses, lifted up toward God, from the earth.
Soon, as heaven opens, a new light will rise before your eyes,
and the Holy Spirit will enter by a silent passage through hidden ways
and stir your inmost being with a joyful breath.
Come, then, tune your lyre and rouse your fruitful heart,
proclaiming great things. Let go the skill you have spent on your usual
poems; a greater order of themes is being born for you.
No longer do you sing of the judgment of Paris or the wars of the Giants,
false tales as they are. That game of yours may once have belonged
to your boyhood years; trifles suited you when you were small.
Now, graver in mind as you are further on in years,
spurn the gentle Muses with a mature heart,
and take up such a subject as an age now suited to chaste conduct
and the venerable dignity of your countenance demand:
take up this matter, and conceive divine thoughts.
If you have won some glory from falsehoods and a great name
from empty matters, when you sang fictions in old-fashioned
poems or when you recounted earthly
deeds, praising the insignia of triumphant kings,
you were not, in truth, the one to take praise from those
whom you rather adorned with the gift of your rich speech.
How much greater glory will come to you from these undertakings,
in which, while exercising your tongue, you will also train your mind
in holiness and lay hold of praise and life at once?
And while you read with insight and write of the true miracles
of the most high God, you will learn to be nearer and dearer
to God himself; and while you marvel at him in belief, you will begin
to love him, and by loving God you will be loved in return by Christ.
Until now that trumpet of your voice has sounded
for vain uses; now let it thunder more loftily the deeds of God.
You are stirred to know the causes of things and the beginnings of the world:
do not go wandering after countless worlds, the dreams of Epicurus,
which in his madness he brings forth through the void, with atoms as their parents,
searching fruitlessly into emptiness with a mind that roams at large.
Moses, the lawgiver, venerable for his ancient name,
who tells how the world was framed from its first origin
by God's ordaining, will free you from empty cares;
and, telling how man was formed from clay and breathed upon
with the holy breath, by whose gift you stand higher than all
that breathe on earth, he himself will teach you.
Do not look down on yourself as though you were Pyrrha's stones or Prometheus' clay,
you, clay that the supreme hand fashioned, lofty in face and in mind,
deigning to shape it in its own image.
You will learn likewise, so that you do not go on handing over
our free will to the Fates, what sentence bound us to death
and under whose law we drag out our life.
If you cast your mind higher than heaven, and above the stars
you desire to know what is, or what was before time began,
John teaches what lies beyond both the world and the ages.
"In the beginning," he says, "was the Word"; God rejoiced in the Word as his pledge,
and the Word was with God, and at the same time that same Word
was God. This is the Word without whom nothing was made, through whom all things
that were made flourish, who rules all things, to whom all things are subject
and obey; and all nature, in eternal service,
lying prostrate before God the Son, adores the name of the Father who begot him.
And every tongue throughout the nations now confesses
that the Lord Jesus reigns in the Father's majesty,
the name on which our salvation stands founded and our faith
rests, reaching out toward the ages of eternal life.
Upheld by his divine gift, we mortals
succeed in overcoming our frail nature by chaste deeds,
in breaking the bonds of rigid death,
and in living, while in the body, by laws not of the body,
following the divine footsteps of Christ, God,
with the mind governing soul and body under sacred arms;
for the mind that is subject to God takes up the arms of salvation
and gains dominion over its soul and its flesh, and each man
becomes rightful master of himself; devoted to the one
eternal Lord, he is made ruler over his own limbs,
unconquered by vices and a hater of wickedness,
stronger than adversity through his virtues, and, in right order,
a true man; for, strong in mind, in which he holds the light
of reason, he governs his senses as servants without any struggle
and guides his heart with gentle reins.
You, whose noble mind burns with the fire of the heavenly seed,
climb in spirit into the recesses of the sky
and lay your head on the Lord's bosom; soon, as you open your mouth in longing,
Christ will generously give you breasts flowing with holy milk
and flood your mind with divine light,
so that, with the darkness driven away, you may see the great
laws of the awesome God, by which Christ, the all-begetting Wisdom,
abiding ever in himself, makes all things new.
And as he wills, God, himself the judge of his own works,
preserves and changes forms, and lengthens or shortens
the span of life, ruling heaven, sea, stars and winds
by the same power by which he made them. (The great exodus
from Egypt teaches this, and the tyrant drowned in the returning sea,
who had himself earlier felt grievous upheavals through all the elements.) He it is
whom all things fear and all things serve.
For at one time a single land was shared
by the Jews, then the only nation chosen by God, with others;
and yet that heavy wrath of God against the proud enemies
ran among the intermingled peoples, distinguishing between them.
Now I know you will not say that uncertain chance drives the storms
and that accident moves the sea, when you read that the sea, ordered to part,
did part, and that a dry road lay open between the waters
as the waves stood stiff, and that the sea, released again
at the command and the rod of the holy prophet,
flowed back into its liquid hollows. In both cases the power of the sea
obeyed, so that the holy might be given both passage and vengeance.
What of the prophet who fled toward Tarshish, whom, when he was cast into the sea
by the lot drawn in danger, a beast with wide gaping jaws
swallowed and then spat out unharmed from its vast belly?
Does he not teach that sea and stars are moved by God's command?
For by fleeing in vain from God, whom no one escapes,
since he holds all things, he roused the anger of sky and sea alike.
For nature, recognizing a rebel against the almighty Lord,
was afraid to carry the guilty man safely through itself, as though it were
his accomplice, and bound the fugitive with winds and waves.
This prophet, chosen by God to terrify the sinful peoples
with threatening warning, after he had proclaimed grievous
destruction, broke the guilty and turned aside the wrath
of heaven; washing away its crimes with lavish weeping,
Nineveh, turned to good, escaped its final day.
Was that king subject to fate who, as death drew near,
prayed to the Lord, whom he knew to be the only one
able to bend his own laws, that he might stretch his spent life
further, and earned fifteen more years, outliving
his own years and living a lifetime not his own?
Should we now admire Plato as he weaves his three Fates,
or the numbers of Aratus, or the painted stars of Manetho?
Let them tell me, I ask, where they then placed the swift hours for those being born,
and which stars were moving through which signs,
when pious Hezekiah, praying with the power of faith,
reversed the courses of the stars and disturbed
the movements of the heavens by command, turning back the light of the sun?
Or when, at the command of the holy leader, that same
sun held back the night and halted the day, so that the victory of the holy
people might be carried through, the balance of the sky stood still
with its orb turned back, so that the lengthened light might witness great triumphs?
What of Christ, the offspring, power and wisdom of God?
Does he not fully take away your concern with vain errors?
Does he not teach us, by his precepts and his deeds alike, that the one
God rules all things, so that we may think nothing exists apart from the mind
of God the sovereign, when he says that not a leaf from a tree,
not a bird from the air, falls without his command? And when
the Almighty calms the sea with a word or treads upon it with his foot,
drives out diseases with a word or hounds demons,
or sends souls back to return into dead bodies,
and orders those long lifeless to come out of opened tombs,
and makes the rotting dead whole as life returns to them,
does not the Creator plainly show his own power,
he who alone governs all nature and life?
To these, I pray, to these rather devote your zeal and effort, reading
and writing of them; sing the great works of the Thunderer,
write of the beginnings of things created by the Word,
the chaos before day and the twilight of the first light,
and whatever, from then on, through the various ages and through all the elements,
you will learn from the holy books was said or done by God:
what Moses taught, set down on the tablets of the law,
or what the new law of the Gospel testament
seals, unveiling the mysteries of Christ that were hidden before.
Then I shall truly call you a divine poet
and drink your poems like draughts of sweet water,
when they offer me nectar-sweet draughts from the highest springs,
echoing Christ, the Lord of all things,
and bearing witness that your mind is strong in God;
so that I may take from you riches of speech and of mind alike,
and may rejoice that you, whom I am glad to have joined to me by the bond of kinship,
are also close to me under holy religion,
and, with bonds that will not be loosed along with the mortal body,
may embrace you as a holy brother by an everlasting pledge.
Read this, and may you be blessed, Jovius, in Christ Jesus our Lord.
XXIII.
Spring opens the voices of birds; my tongue has its own spring:
the birthday of Felix, in whose light even
winter blossoms for the rejoicing peoples; and though, with black
frost, the wintry season still draws out the time amid the hoarfrosts,
the year frozen stiff on whitening lands,
yet on this day holy joys make a glad
spring for us. Cares are driven from the breast, and grief gives way,
the winter of the soul; from the cloudless heart flee
the clouds of sadness. Just as the gentle swallow
recognizes the friendly days, and so does the white bird with black wings,
and that turtledove, kin to the gentle dove;
and the thickets ring with goldfinches only in the new spring;
and the birds that only now wandered mute beneath the bristling hedges
soon rejoice everywhere as spring returns,
as varied in their tongues as in their many-colored wings:
so I too recognize this day, which every year the holy
feast renews with the honor due to great Felix.
Now gentle spring is reborn for me as the year rejoices;
now I delight to open my lips in measures and my songs in prayers,
and to burst into spring with new voices. O God, flow into my heart,
Christ, and fill its thirst from the springs on high.
But even a drop from you, sprinkled on my inmost being,
will be a river. For what wonder is it if with a little dew
you fill the smallest soul, you who, in a small body
made man, filled the world with eternal seed
and saved the whole earth with a drop of blood?
Grant it, fountain of the Word, Word who are God, and like that
bird of spring make me now melodious with a sweet voice,
the bird that, hidden beneath green leaves, rare and in pathless places, is wont
to charm with many kinds of measures, and through a single tongue
to pour out voices that are not single, changing its song,
a bird of one color in plumage, but painted in its speech.
Now it rolls out smooth measures, now draws out shrill
whistles in long notes, then begins again as if a mournful
song, and, suddenly cutting its lament short,
beguiles astonished ears with its broken melody.
But for me, Christ, let your grace flow from you unceasingly.
And yet I pray that, like that bird,
it may be granted me to vary my measures, and to bring forth the songs
pledged every year, changing my speech though with one mouth,
because rich grace always adds diverse
themes through the wondrous mighty works of the Lord,
which God, Christ, performs again and again in his dear Felix,
bringing forth glorious miracles in health-giving signs.
We see those that are usually witnessed every day,
when he presses hard the savage demons, the viper's brood,
and with hidden hand flogs the clamorous foes;
yet in this very power a marvel is noticed:
that although throughout the whole year he harries the tormented demons
and orders them to depart from human limbs,
he nonetheless prolongs many cases, either so that a longer
punishment may harass the wicked foes, or so that those who deserved
to become vessels for evil spirits, the cure being delayed as they merit,
may pay more fully for all their guilt over a lengthened time;
or else he is eager to show this favor to his birthday,
giving help to few at other times, so that in his kindness
he may give more gifts on his birthday. For when this day draws near
as the year slips away, then he presses on more often
and more heavily. Then you may see the sick throngs gathered
more densely, and sure health sought again as the feast draws near.
Then the demons, inflamed more than usual, burn,
and howl more piteously, and, subdued by greater force,
groan at what are now their final torments; nor are they allowed to leave
by an easy exit, but first, harried by wondrous
and varied punishments, they are cruelly lifted on high,
suspended higher than usual, and are shaken
in the void of the air and cling to hidden chains
in a penal suspension through empty space; though through bodies not their own,
it is their own punishment that wears down the tormented foes.
The people are free of punishment even when they seem to bear punishment
in the body, and their souls, unharmed, watch another's
torments in their own limbs; with the demon taken captive, the man
remains free; there is only the appearance of punishment in the body;
feeling is absent, because the cross belongs not to the man but to the demon.
Bitter foe, why do you mock? With what hope do you rush upon us?
Look, wicked one: by the craft of our Redeemer you in turn
are mocked, mocker; your trickery turns into your own
chains: catching, you are caught; binding, you are bound.
The ensnared man becomes a snare, and his own prey
deceives the robber; and, made captive by the body he captured, while he seeks
its forbidden bait, he swallows the deadly hook.
Things still greater than these, yet witnessed, I will declare:
above all, that man whose limbs an ancient foe
besieges—how, sick, at the holy martyr's sacred threshold
he was snatched up, flung out from the crowd, and, brought close to the sacred
railings before the saint's doors, his body turned over,
was hung up by his upturned feet, facing the roof;
and, what is more wonderful and holy, his clothes did not fall back over his face,
but, as though stiff or sewn to his feet,
every sacred part of his body stays veiled in chaste covering,
so that reverence for the divine work might remain, the bodies
being covered, and the demon might not exult in the very punishment
by which he is tormented, by exposing shame through naked
limbs; he is tortured the more heavily because decency is unharmed,
since the coverings sit straight though the limbs are inverted.
These things are wondrous and great (who denies it?), and yet, being known
more through familiarity, they seem less marvelous to hear about,
however awe-inspiring to see and great in the doing.
So listen, I pray, to the small yet new deeds of my patron,
which Christ the Lord performs in him
with manifold power, by all of which he strives
to strengthen one faith in us, so that through open
proofs we may see that the hidden God is present,
and that with fatherly care the heavenly Lord looks after the affairs and minds of men,
he who founded all things by his Word.
Let my brother Theridius give me the first beginnings of my tale;
for what work of Felix could I more fittingly or sooner
take up to sing than what, under my own roof,
he himself did for me—he who is master of that same house?
From that night the year has just now come round to this day.
You know the custom by which we usually fast
before the day, and, when the rites have been offered late in the evening,
each returns to his own home. So then, when the assemblies
had dispersed from the Lord's temple, and rest had been given to our weary
bodies with a meal, we began to raise hymns
joyfully to God and to prolong the night with psalms.
Meanwhile this brother of mine, stepping away from the friendly choir
to drive off in the breeze blowing outside the heat
that the room, smoky with wax-coated papyrus candles, gave off,
went where the portico stretches in a narrow-roofed line;
though the path lay hidden, blind in the night without any light,
he still walked there with fearless step through familiar doorways,
heedless, alas, of the danger already close at hand.
Right in his way, in the middle of the passage, between ceiling and floor,
swung the rope that usually held the lamp suspended,
fastening a three-pronged iron to its lowest strand,
into which the pierced handle of the glass lamp is inserted,
and the eared cup is fixed all round by three hooks.
At the bottom water gleams white; above the water, olive oil shows gold.
Liquid stands on liquid; the slippery fluid floats on the pool
beneath it, and the mixture of the liquids does not join and blend.
And it is a marvel that the fat floats; the dense substance does not
break through the thin element, but the light supports the thick,
as the thinner water, with its steady flow,
lying beneath the oil, becomes the foundation for the liquids.
And so great a discord shines out among the juices mingled within
that you can see the mixed liquids stay apart,
and in the shared hollow of the cup, with a clear division,
the nature of each liquid keeps its own color.
In the middle a three-footed piece of lead is sunk, and from it a hollow
tip stands out, packed with a wick of oiled flax.
The soaked tow catches the fluid fire in a slender flame,
and, surrounded by the expanse of the pooled oil,
the thin wick flickers in the glassy shallows,
and, quivering, from its tremulous tip a sharp light
gently casts a shadowy glow into the inner rooms
and with calm brightness opens up the dense darkness.
But this lamp had been taken down when the night was already far spent,
since, through the hours the boys had prolonged in their vigil,
the thirsty light had failed, its oil used up.
But the boy who had taken away the lamp when its light went out
had slackened the rope to lower it, and that same rope
he neglected to draw up and tie fast with the usual knot.
So the line, too loose, dangled with a low reach,
bereft of welcome light and full of unseen danger.
For the end of the cord was armed with menacing toothed hooks,
and with these it then met my brother to his harm—
almost to his harm, or rather, by Christ's will, to his good, for Christ well turned
a deadly mishap into joys for us to remember.
So (see the hand of Christ) that ill-hanging
rope, lower than usual, hung in the darkness below
its accustomed place in the air; and so,
brought exactly level with his head,
such was his height, with its triple point, alas, it caught
the unsuspecting face of the man as he came, and with a hook
it met and entered his eye, and, slipping deep, the point
darted in under the tender lid, where the cautious hand of the healing art
can scarcely guide a light probe with trembling control
and slide it under the eyelid with a gentle stroke.
Struck suddenly by the blow of so hard a lash,
he cries out and, distraught, brings his trembling hands
to the eye itself; and he holds the iron enclosed together with the eye,
to press it back, or, should it fall, to catch the slipping
eyeball, which, guarding the inner parts of sight
within its smooth sac, with fluid poured between,
lies hidden, white beneath the glassy image of the black pupil.
This, like a root, with the marrow running beneath it, supports
the eye and feeds it with the moist nourishment of the veins,
so long as the fountains of the eyes stay matched in brightness.
But if by chance, burst by grave disease or a blow,
alas, the membrane of the liquid eye should split apart,
this globe leaps out and, abandoned by the nourishing juice,
leaves behind a dried-up socket emptied of light.
Meanwhile the boy, roused by the cry of the man in pain,
runs up, leaving his bed as sleep flees,
and holds a lighted lamp in his hand up to his face.
He had covered his face with his hands and, with his forehead tilted back,
like a young man [?], was gazing upward,
so as to keep the rope motionless by holding his body balanced,
governing his trembling limbs as the wound dictated,
fearing to tear the wound open by a movement against it;
and with the one eye that was still free
he watched, as its partner, over the danger to the captive eye;
yet he did not dare to touch the iron to draw it out,
lest by pulling the point he should draw out with it the eyeball
clinging to it; nor could he any longer bear the delay
of the weapon fixed beneath his eye. But as he despaired of a cure
by mortal aid, soon by divine aid Felix,
implored, is present—Felix, whom, hanging in so great a wound,
he calls upon, pouring out his lament in such words as these:
"Woe is me! How great are the sins that weigh upon my troubles,
that I, wretch, should deserve to receive so great a blow, with Felix as my patron
and Felix my neighbor too, and, what is more, on Felix's very
birthday? Alas! I am a great culprit, guilty of a great
crime, since punishment strikes me at the very time when he is wont to set free.
Saint, I pray, help your own; I know you stand very near,
and, turning your ears here from the adjoining church,
you have heard, Felix, the weeping of your unhappy foster-child;
or if now you cling close to the side of the Most High,
before the throne of the great King, his friend and confessor,
you receive, revered one, this voice of your poor servant beyond the clouds
with God's own ear, and do not scorn it, but seek there
the healing that you may bring down to me by Christ's mercy.
So come, Felix, everlasting patron of my soul;
now run to me as physician in my bodily peril.
Run, I pray, and set your holy hands against the iron that threatens
my eye with ruin, and pull out the fixed iron that you see,
which I do not dare to draw back with my own hand, lest I
rob myself of sight while trying to free myself from the weapon.
For so deeply do I feel the bolt driven into me,
the nail thrust in beneath the hidden recesses of the eye.
Only do you, divine hand, which fashioned the very
eyes in us, the right hand that made you too powerful
with health-giving power, by which you tame the black demons
by tormenting them, by which you can drive out every
torment of the frail body by the lofty name of Christ,
mighty through the almighty Lord—under his protection now take me
up to be healed. Do not let my sins overcome you,
but rather let them fall, overcome by you. For I am more worthy of this
wound, I confess, than of the gift of gentle Christ.
But remember the word and deed of the Lord himself,
who by his coming redeemed the life of the sinner.
If you chose to judge me by the strict law of justice,
I deserve to be punished not in one eye only but in both,
so that I might be in my face what I am also within,
dark of heart, which is why I make ill use of my bodily
sight, blind to the just, sharp-eyed for the wicked;
and it is fitting, I confess, for a sinner to be one-eyed,
if it is fitting for such a one to be yours. Whoever is bound
by any crime becomes worthy of pardon once he has
begun to be yours, as I long ago began to be one of your own,
to whom I came, following not love of my native land
but the longing with which I had dedicated myself to you, O saint,
scorning the dangers of sea and land;
and, following the example of a good man, I broke the ties of my native land
to serve you, together with those companions
among whom I boast that I too am yours: show this now by your help,
so that I may not lose the eye pierced by so great a wound.
Give, I pray, so noble a gift to your unworthy servant
for the praise of the Lord; grant this as a glory to your day,
O saint, so that the day which the glory of Christ, whom you confessed,
made forever your birthday into eternal light,
I may keep as the birthday of my eye, and may celebrate together
Felix and the sight restored to me through Felix."
While the simple man wept out such words, behold, the hand of blessed
Felix was soon there with its favor, and, silently breathing upon him,
strengthened the wavering mind and hand of the frightened man,
so that he should not fear to dare to draw out the iron, now safely.
Scarcely had he tried, when, as if slippery, the hook
falls from the eye without the eye; only a flow of fluid followed,
which poured out in tears the inflammation that had festered there.
Soon the eye, cleansed of the night of so great a danger,
shone with as clear a mirror as it is seen now too, healthy,
shining by the gift of the eternal Christ.
And I think it shines more than usual today, because light
is added by the very day that restored it. So, you faithful,
consider now in your minds the measure of so great a danger,
and weigh likewise the working of so great a gift.
A man already weighty with mature years and tall of body
had stuck on the hook of a cord like a fish on a hook,
and, in place of the lamp, he hung with his eye open—
though not of its own will—an eye that the nail, hooking it, held apart,
fixed beneath the lid, and yet it caused no wound,
since the divine hand prevented it, which had made there
both the iron's point harmless and its weight light;
in that part where heavy rheum, or a hair, is unbearable, and where
we cannot endure the speck of the smallest grain of sand,
there—who would believe it?—a heavy iron with a curved point,
smeared besides with the caked grime of the lamp,
was fixed and long pressed its metal on the delicate
pupil without harm, and the sight was violated by no wound.
What hand so delicate in its fingers or in the art of healing
could have slipped itself into so fine a gap between parts joined together,
and, driven into the space between eyelid and eye,
between both paths, by a fragile passage through each,
have pierced in and hung the iron there with the eye unharmed—
the iron that, under the thick covering of the solid lid, filled the whole
orb of the eye, fixing it with its point yet not harming it with a wound?
What hand could do this but the hand that made all things?
That Spirit of God, who penetrates everywhere through all
the natures of things, subtler than anything fine,
who restored lost sight to the blinded, and who
made even the man blind from the womb have new eyes,
filling out the face of a body imperfect by nature
with the Creator's art, by which he perfects the whole world:
that Son of God, the hand and wisdom of the Father,
Christ, the all-begetting source and stability of things.
He himself had once fashioned that man, incomplete, in his mother's womb,
so that afterward, made man, he who was also the Creator
might add this wonderful work too to his divine signs,
filling the empty sockets with sight.
Then, spitting on the ground, he makes clay, and by it the sight
denied at birth he restores to his believing foster-child,
and with the same material by which he fashioned the whole body
he completes the half-finished man in the part that was lacking,
to prove that he himself had come in our flesh—
he who with God the Father, in the likeness of their shared image,
had formed Adam, composed of clay and breath.
He himself, the Maker, our Light, God, willed
to adorn the birthday of his friend Felix with so great a cure,
to show the lofty merit of the confessor by a mighty
gift—not to heap up honor
for the martyr by this work, for on him he long ago bestowed mighty
palms, with noble titles and a blessed name,
palms that the mercy of Christ the Lord renews in him at all
times through tireless mighty works.
But God wished to give us a special
joy at this time, and, by working some such sign of our own
patron, to grant it to his own servants,
so as to reveal us as the very own foster-children of heavenly Felix
and to teach us to live by his merit and care,
since, preserving our safety with Felix as guardian,
he often keeps the hostile enemy, in mishaps by night,
away from our limbs and our minds alike.
So now we rejoice in the honor of our danger,
and, seeing him shining with matching sight in both eyes,
whom we almost saw disfigured by the loss of one,
we rejoice, moved to the core, that this brother is safe,
whom Christ has given us by so great a gift.
Rightly I hold him as dear as my own eyes, for in his sight
the hand of Felix shines in Christ, my glory.
O happy chance, good wounds, sweet danger,
through which I learned that I am the martyr's care!
For it was worth it to me that my sight nearly perished,
so that now I might have sight by the gift of Felix.
24. Meropius Paulinus to Cytherius, his brother in Christ, greetings.
Martinianus, my brother in the spirit
and my true brother in one and the same faith,
whom you had sent off with an eloquent letter
to come to us,
we have now received, barely saved himself,
empty-handed, his letter lost,
but full, as a token of your love,
as though he were your own mouth;
and a letter truer than any writing,
sealed from your heart,
since he brought you back to us in a spiritual letter,
we have read with both mind and ear.
Now the two of us, joined together, give each other our right hands
in the kiss of holy peace,
and we offer to God a sacrifice of praise
and render thanks to Christ,
by whose deliverance he came safe out of the sea
to cross our threshold as a guest;
for he suffered dreadful things, and yet
in his dangers he experienced miracles.
Setting out from his homeland for a reason known to you,
he had chosen to travel on foot,
but reckoning the long stretches of land ahead of him,
he changed his mind about the route
and preferred the idle seasickness of tossing on the waves
to the labor of his feet.
He set sail from Narbonne along the savage road of the sea,
trusting himself to a fragile hull.
From then on this man, reluctant to walk, found the tables turned
and came to regret his sailing.
For when he had set out from the unbroken line of the coast
and advanced into the deep waters,
the night was already thick, but bright with clear skies,
the calm sea smiling,
and the stars alone were guiding their course,
since the moon was then absent from the sky,
when suddenly the ship, rotten with long years,
lost its power to carry them;
the joints of its sides worked loose and came apart,
and it took in the waves through the cracks.
The calm had lulled everyone to sleep;
only the helmsman was awake,
and, untroubled as the vessel glided over the gentle waters,
he was cutting his foamy path
and, to speed the course along, whistling
for stronger breezes.
Meanwhile the ship was sinking deeper
as the water filling it rose,
and as the planks spread ever wider apart,
the water rushed in more abundantly;
and for those who faced no waves from the open sea
a wave was born inside the ship,
and, already washing beneath the bodies of the sleepers,
it roused them with its wet chill.
When one felt it, and soon another, in all of them
fear shook off sleep.
They are terrified with dread of death, and still
do not know the cause of their fear.
By what way could the wretches escape the hostile sea?
They are drowning in their own ship.
If the waters were seething, whipped up by the winds,
safety would be found in the ship;
but with the sea poured into the very bowels of the hull,
where can life be found?
What harbor is there for them, when the sea is in the ship itself
and kills those trapped inside?
But God, the harbor and salvation of all,
stretches out a fatherly hand
and, amid the high ridges of the open sea,
spreads wide the bosom of his mercy,
in which he catches those falling over the precipice of death
and sets them in the shallows of life.
He had prepared a skiff that followed the great four-banked craft
for this very aid,
so that those whom God had chosen to save
from that crowd of voyagers
might be taken up by that skiff, which was floating close beside
the ship as it gaped open in the sea.
This skiff the ship's captain himself, even when he was first casting off
from the shore into the deep —
that Novatian, who carried a split faith
in a shipwrecked heart,
a man of death and therefore thinking thoughts fit for death —
had, as was his way, refused
to have as part of his load. Into his own ship
he hastens at once to climb,
and when the skiff was gripped by the final danger,
he tried to drive it off,
so that, with the rope that tied it to the vessel cut,
it would be cast adrift on the sea.
But, overcome by the opposing voices of the many,
he was thwarted on both counts,
because the judgment of all prevailed,
made stronger by Christ, its author,
so that soon the boat would be a saving refuge,
outliving the overwhelmed ship.
Strange was the face of that shipwreck:
death for the sailors, peace on the sea.
Outside, on the water, calm lay silent;
inside the ship there was a storm.
No rocks, no gale had broken the vessel;
but old age, stronger than these,
had loosened the firm oak timbers fastened with iron nails,
wearing them down over the years.
The sky was gleaming with bright clouds,
the sea was glittering with stars.
But what use to them was the happy stillness
of winds and sea alike,
when, in the depths of the sea, they were being abandoned
by the ship that carried them as it fell apart?
The water drinks the ship, the ship drinks up the water;
the waters are swallowed and they swallow.
The sailors, drunk on draughts of brine,
are killed by a grim intoxication.
The sea smiled gently on other ships
and raged against this one vessel alone.
But in the peril of the many one may discern
the working of heavenly judgment.
All those whom one ship carries
share a common peril of death;
and see, they are divided by differing fates,
assigned some to death and some to life.
And lest anyone perhaps think this was dealt out
indiscriminately to good and bad alike,
it is certain that no Christian perished
and that the faithless died.
For whoever perished was either a Jew of malicious heart
or one guilty of proud schism.
Whomever the right faith of Christ had sealed,
him life recognized as its own.
Yet there were some added to the Christians
who were not yet consecrated with that name,
whom flight in their company saved from the deep,
because they had clung to the Christians.
For while, of the faithless crowd of voyagers,
no believer was drowned,
so the clear truth of a great mystery
God showed in a few:
that at the end of the world, when the nations are divided,
there will be a distinction among all,
when the avenging angel passes over those
whose faces are marked beforehand with the banner of the cross.
So in that ship no one was handed over to death
who was endowed with the truth.
The ungodly who were joined to the Christians lived,
as light overcame the night.
For death was emptied of power
to gather Christians among the dead,
since on the foreheads of Christians gleams the sign
by which death was subdued and fell in ruin.
The shipmaster himself, the chief of the lost vessel,
was the first of those who perished.
For before he perished, shipwrecked, in the sea,
he had already suffered shipwreck in his mind;
he was sunk twice: the hull plunged him into the waves,
and his error into hell.
He could have torn himself free from the danger,
but his head, already owed to death,
his greedy mind, captive in the chains it deserved,
bound fast and tied to its end.
For rather than outlive his ship and his cargo,
he preferred death to safety.
Martinianus, already at the last thread of life,
mingled among the men who were going under,
was roused by the noise of the tumultuous crowd,
roused from the sleep of death.
He was then lying weary in a remote recess of the prow,
secure in his innocence,
like Jonah long ago, hidden in the belly of the ship,
breathing heavily in deep sleep.
But roused by the mournful cries on every side
of those who were perishing,
and battered in every limb by the feet of the crowd,
he leaps up from his hard bed.
While most were drowned inside, in the belly of the ship,
along the edges of its sides, where
the sailors are accustomed to run nimbly
to raise the sails or prop them up with poles,
the ship, though covered by the flood, was still floating
on its outermost planks;
by this way, to those searching out a way of safety,
Martinianus joins himself,
and, with Christ at work, fleeing the throng of death,
he becomes the companion of those escaping
and with a leap hurls himself far into the skiff,
which proved a harbor for many.
And he would almost have stuck there, left to death,
to be sunk in the sea with the ship,
had not Christ, as if grasping him with his own hand,
snatched him from the pit of death.
As Joseph once, shaking off his garment,
fled from the raging woman,
so this man, leaving everything behind, escaped naked in flight
from the faithless ship.
And as once the beast, at God's command, received Jonah
in its open mouth
and through its wide-gaping, slippery throat
sent him down into its belly,
devouring his body unharmed, its teeth held back,
and not eating the one it devoured:
so this man, falling headlong from the high ship into the waves,
the skiff came to meet and took up,
and faithfully carried him through the night in its safe hold
until it brought him back to port.
But since mention has been made of the great prophet,
in whom the image of a holy mystery
prefigured death in a three-day burial
and a return to salvation,
turning back the track of my song a little,
I would like to return to Jonah.
Wonderful are the Lord's devices: sunk in the sea,
he floats untouched by the waves.
He lives though devoured, and the one that swallowed him remains
fasting while its food lives on,
and though he is its prey, he is not the beast's meal,
but uses its belly as a home.
O prison worthy of God's holy fugitive!
He is caught by the sea to which he had fled,
and sent deep into the belly of a huge beast,
he is held in a living jail.
Thrown from the ship, he is lost, and yet he sails the waves,
an exile from the land, a guest of the sea;
he roams about in the cave of the beast's body,
a captive, and a defendant at liberty.
For, free of the waves, within the sea and outside the sea,
he swims inside a swimming beast,
and though shut up in a body, he goes out to God,
a prophet flying in the spirit.
Body is held by body, but the flight of the mind
no earthly chains can hold.
Enclosed in the belly, he breaks the prison by prayer
and reaches the ears of God;
free to pray and bound from fleeing,
he convicts himself by his own faith.
For he who had thought he could escape God by sea
and be hidden from God in a ship
must now believe that even inside a beast sunk in the sea
the Judge is present.
Now I must bring the foot of my pliant verse back
to my own Jonah,
whom, in the manner of the whale, the roomy skiff took up
and, shut inside its own belly,
carried trembling with cold and fear
and returned safe to land.
He tells of a wonder that happened at that time:
when, leaping headlong from the high stern,
he had fallen into that little boat
and had landed in the spot
where the skiff had taken in much water through its cracks,
a stinking pool of bilge,
at once, as God warmed his cold limbs,
lulled in a holy rest,
naked and wet — conditions from which sleep usually flees —
he slept more softly than in a bed,
and for the whole time in which he was carried back to shore
he was given over to sleep,
woken neither by the water in which he was soaked nor by the cold
that his nakedness had brought upon him;
for though the season of the year was mild autumn,
for the shipwrecked it was winter,
as they were shaken by the harsh loss of their clothing
and by icy shivering.
Here is another astonishing thing, from which you may gather
the grace that rewards Martinianus' faith;
beloved brother, hear it, and praise God,
and embrace our holy brother:
when he felt the boat gliding into port,
with the sand of the shore grating beneath it,
as sleep left him, he at last became aware of himself,
came to his senses, awoke,
and touched, lying against his breast,
the epistles of the apostle.
This book, in his fear, yet without knowing it,
he had picked up as he left everything else behind,
or else that book, living with the Holy Spirit,
had clung to him without his noticing.
Consider, I ask you: who but Christ
gave this guardian to his servant?
He testifies that it never even occurred to him
in that time of danger
to remember to take from there the little parchment
wrapped up in his baggage.
And even if it had entered his mind in his fear,
he would not have had time to look for it.
But in the body of his own letters
Paul the teacher was present,
and, loving his pure-hearted reader,
led him away from the hand of death;
once again God granted to Paul
men to be rescued from the bottom of the sea.
The power of grace that once
was in the apostle himself when he sailed
now, through the support of his letters,
for Martinianus and the others
who then clung to the Christians in their flight,
made ready a safe separation
from the peril, just as it had separated the faithful
from the ungodly among the shipwrecked.
So when the little boat had reached the shore
and set down the drenched men,
who were both holding on to life and still in need of it,
they begged for help to survive,
so that, delivered to a land crueler than the waves,
they might not perish of cold and hunger.
But nearby, set on Gallic soil,
Marseilles, daughter of the Greeks,
a city nurtured by a holy church,
opened its kindly arms.
Making for this city, the castaways tell of their disaster
and ask to be fed and clothed.
The brotherhood takes in Martinianus
and warms him with shelter and food.
Poor themselves, but with abundant love,
they provide a small gift.
Generous affection outweighs the scanty gifts;
they enrich their guest by their prayers
and, made rich with spiritual provision for the journey,
they send him off with their peace.
Yet he was given cheap boots,
so that he would not go about barefoot like a sailor —
he who would rather have been warmly clothed and barefoot
than shod and cold.
But, whatever he had suffered at sea, he refused to go by land
out of shame at his nakedness,
reflecting also that he might be thought to be feigning nakedness
out of love of gain,
if, like a ragged Teucer, he made his way through
forts, villages, and towns,
in the way that greedy beggars
are wont to wander over sea and land,
who, swearing falsely that they are monks or castaways,
make a trade of the name and the misfortune.
But this Christian of ours, however much
he truly was a castaway,
guarding against being thought like the deceivers
and refusing to let others be deceived about him,
does not want to be a wayfarer, lest he acquire
the new name of impostor,
and prefers to risk his life by sailing
rather than, by walking, endure the burning of his face.
So, shabby in his rags but shining in his footwear,
he chooses to take to the waves again,
goes back to the harbor, and to the safety of the land route
prefers the danger of the sea,
so that, hidden by the ship all the way to the shores he longed for,
like a lightly clad sailor,
he might, in the company of the sailors' nakedness,
escape the shame of being naked.
God the king, favoring faithful constancy,
attends his bold faith,
and, changing hard turns of fortune into those that follow,
balances adversity with prosperity,
and prepares a ship planked with solid oak
to carry him across;
he commands peace to the storms, puts the clouds to flight,
and directs the course with the breeze,
tempering sky and sea with such a calm
that the voyage would not stall in the stillness,
nor dangerous speed drive the vessel on
with a heavy blast.
So, with Christ gently favoring him,
he crossed the rough sea
and put in at a port some distance from the City,
whose name is Centumcellae,
since the ship was to go on further from there
to enter the harbor of the lighthouse.
Scarcely believing he had reached the shore
of the land he longed for,
he leaves the ship and joyfully leaps upon the ground
and hurries to Rome on foot;
there, a welcome guest, he finds the friendly homes
of his brothers and fellow citizens.
He breathes again in spirit and rests in body,
he gives and receives joy;
enjoying one another, they restore their homeland to each other
and give thanks to God.
Martinianus joyfully recounts his sorrows,
telling the brothers what he had endured.
In the midst of their very rejoicing
they mingle tears from overflowing hearts.
My Theridius was away from there at the time, here with me —
a man who is Christ's gift to me,
a man of peace, a man of the law, and a man of grace,
my repose, my delight, my very mind;
Paulinus, who shared his house and was one with him in pious mind,
was looking after his home in the City.
He strips Martinianus of his shipwrecked clothing
and covers him with his own,
and the gift of the tunic with which he had clothed his companion
he doubles with the gift of a hooded cloak.
The giver himself was then in turn left, like a castaway,
with a single garment.
After this he sets out on his way to us as well,
along the road where flint paves the causeway,
to which Appius, its builder, gave his name.
He treads the road that wears its travelers down;
he who had come as a sailor in worn-out clothes
now wears it down too as a traveler on foot.
But lest even this road be entirely free
and spared the usual mishaps,
he did not get away unpunished for the lazy notion
by which one is loath to press on on foot.
At the city of Capua, which lies twenty miles
from the place where I live,
finding a mule free of baggage — as pack animals
are usually sent back home —
he hires it for a small fee for the short trip and mounts it;
and soon, halfway along the road,
the rider, thrown far off when the mule took fright,
falls as his mount bolts out from under him.
Falling on his face, he did not injure his face;
sprawled on rocks and brambles,
he bruised neither his face on a thorn nor his limbs on a stone,
caught as he was by the hand of Felix;
who, as his brother was already drawing near to his dwelling,
would not allow him, through an encounter with evil,
to meet with danger within his own territory,
and drove off the envious enemy;
and him, his wish fulfilled, the faithful
confessor led into his precincts,
and Felix his patron brought him as a welcome guest
to our dwelling close by.
Asked here, he tells of his homeland, recounts his misfortunes,
and brings blessed news of you.
And by relating a few words from your writings,
as if he had sprinkled my lips with honey,
offering me thus a most sweet taste
from the drops of your honeycombs,
he made me long all the more for the letter
that he could not give me in my eagerness;
but since he himself came as the substance of your letter,
I have seen your letter after all,
written not with ink from a pen but with the stylus of the mind
upon a good brother.
Unknown before, as soon as he began to be known
he became very dear.
Grace shone out from within him,
his speech serving as the messenger of his mind.
"Every good man," Scripture says, "brings forth good things from what is good,
and you know the tree by its fruit";
so this man, pleasant in speech and chaste in faith
and bright with an honest face,
flowed in a sweet river of kindly love
into our inmost hearts.
Besides this, by rightly boasting that he was your friend,
he gave us more reason to love him.
For there is no concord between night and light,
nor is the wolf a fit companion for the lamb.
Hence the prophet too says: "As birds
of a kind flock together,
so justice always comes together with the good,
through a fitting likeness of character."
So a kindred mind has woven Martinianus,
far away though you are, into a match for you,
and the love of such men is a mirror of your mind
and an image of your faith.
God, the blessed author and fountain of the saints,
no longer chooses only the foolish
and weak things of this passing world
to destroy the lofty things of the world;
but, as he himself said, now drawing all things upward,
he claims the lofty things of the world as well.
Since he himself made both the small and the great,
grace joins them both,
and those whom as Creator he founded in one work
he re-creates by one gift.
A common unbelief has shut up all men,
so that faith might mediate for all,
so that the whole world might be made subject to God
and every tongue and every rank
might confess that Jesus, the one name above every name,
reigns in the glory of the Father.
To him now even the powerful of this age bend the knee
and bow their necks to God,
and princes confess Christ as king
and lower their scepters before the cross.
Purple and rags come together into one flock,
in harmony under God their shepherd.
The common kingdom, the one blood of all,
of the highest and the lowest, is Christ,
who, though you were adorned with the glories of this world —
rank, learning, and family —
enriched you with a humble heart, to bestow on you
an eternal loftiness,
so that you might be co-heir with the rich of heaven,
being here a lover of the poor.
Blessed are you now, poor in spirit but rich
in hope, in which the poor rejoice,
who, deprived of the slippery goods of the world,
will enjoy the joys of heaven.
Among them, deep in the bosom of father Abraham,
a place set apart from the fire of the rich
and refreshing with the dews of life
the God of the living prepares.
A sure token of so great a hope already
shines out for you in a great pledge:
the offshoot of your stock, planted for the Lord
in the courts of Jerusalem.
For to make you like the faithful father,
he asked of you a son,
enrolling your seed in the seed of Isaac
and seeking him like Isaac himself,
whom you, rivaling Abraham's love,
gave as a living victim,
and by handing him over to God you have already put him to death for yourself,
so as to keep him safe more securely.
Now he remains both outside your house and yours,
having no part in the earthly world.
Ready from his mother's womb, before
he knew his father and his mother,
or had any taste of good or could discern evil,
he blessedly chose the good.
And now as a little child he plays in the court of God
and sings with a mouth still nursing:
"From my mother's womb and from my first day
you, Christ, have been my protector."
You too have heard what is said to the blessed:
"Your seed shall be mighty."
You have this as well: "Of the fruit of your womb
I will set upon my throne."
This saying of David, though it speaks of Christ,
also sings, in Christ, of those
who, in the fellowship of Christ's body,
will be set upon the throne of God.
Fellowship with Hannah too is laid open for you
through the example of a holy child.
Like Samuel, this boy too has grown up in the temple of God,
a lamb now, and later a shepherd.
May his mother's diligent hand weave for him
an ephod fitted to his size,
which the spiritual teaching of God's word
may cover with sacred threads.
And may he himself be woven into the queen's robe on high
among its golden fringes,
and as a Nazirite may he adorn his head, holy to Christ,
with well-nourished locks,
and may the fair head of his soul, with the hair of virtue,
be armed with an active faith.
And may no razor ever, cutting,
come upon him to the loss of his hair.
And like the famous Samson, mighty in the strength of his hair,
long-haired with holy power,
may he lay low the lion, strangled by the strong
arms of prayer,
and pluck the sweet fruit of a noble victory
from the mouth of the dead beast.
But after this triumph, let him take warning from Samson's example
not to enter into foreign covenants.
The foreign woman is, to my mind, the law of the flesh,
deceitful with its alluring nets.
If this law should prove stronger than the law of the mind,
it will drag one into the dominion of sin;
tempting to evil with sweet words by the art of deceit,
it makes the manly spirit effeminate;
it blinds the eyes of the mind and shaves the head,
despoiling and disarming faith.
In this respect I do not want our boy to be a Samson,
lest he be joined in a union
which would be followed at once by captivity,
weakness, and blindness —
even though that strong man afterward recovered
his strength when his hair grew back,
and, led by the hand from the mill to be the sport
of his exultant enemies,
blind in body but seeing with his mind,
called upon God the avenger,
and, his strength soon restored with his hair,
brought down the house of his enemies;
when his hand, stronger than stone, had locked
its columns in a heavy embrace,
the roof, its supports pulled out, collapsed to the ground
and fell upon him; but even so,
even in death itself, God's mighty hero
buried his enemies in the ruin
and by a glorious death made amends to himself
for the disgrace of his enslaved life.
He who had lived as a slave while the enemy gloried
falls a victor, with the enemy crushed,
and in dying killed more thousands
than he had slain while alive.
I want our son to imitate this —
to overcome death by death — so that, remaining
in the flesh, he may conquer the flesh and live to God,
crushing the sins of the flesh.
But I do not want him, to the joys of the flesh,
overcome by the wiles of a harmful woman,
to surrender his soul and afterward become the enemies' prey,
stripped of the power of grace.
In this respect let him be Samuel: continually
holy, his hair unshorn,
through all the days of his life, with unbroken thread,
may he weave a sacred lifetime
and carry the infancy begun in service
right through to old age.
Let him slay Amalek, and, with holy ferocity,
sacrifice to God the sins of the flesh,
by whose slaughter the devil will have perished,
hateful to God forever.
In him let Saul fail and David reign;
let the small destroy the lofty,
so that he may not be lofty with the spirit of pride
nor livid with the evil of envy,
but, bearing lofty virtues in a humble heart,
may ascend the throne of the kingdom;
and let him follow those deeds of Samson
that came first, so that he may snap new ropes
like threads, and not betray his faith,
lest through cowardice he lose his hair.
Long-haired with the strength of heavenly works,
he will break the bonds stretched out against him,
he will pull up the stakes, he will lay low a thousand men
overcome by one right hand,
because our strength and our head is Christ, who is God,
who is the right hand and the power of God;
mighty through him, we conquer the serpent
that assails us with a thousand wiles.
Let the soul be strong, mortifying its ass,
the beast of burden that is the sluggish body.
With its moisture boiled away by sober labors,
let it turn the face livid with pallor,
and with the flesh afflicted, may victorious chastity
burn up the fires of sin.
For as our outer man is wasted away,
worn down by self-restraint,
then the man within is renewed, master of the one conquered
through the weakness of the body.
Then a thousand at our side and ten thousand at our right hand
will fall before the dried-up jawbone,
if our jaw is kept safe by resting —
the jaw that is kept busy by the habit of eating —
because the license of a well-fed body
is blunted by fasting.
And then triumph and a fountain spring up for us
in dried-out bones.
The jawbone that gave a weapon to the fighter
gives a drink to him when he burns with thirst,
as the bones of dead flesh, emptied of its juices,
are watered by the Holy Spirit.
But what was done by the saints of old as a figure
was written for us to put into practice,
so that what our forefathers performed in the body
we may carry out in the spirit.
The old things have passed away; all things have been made new;
the truth has done away with the shadow.
The day of salvation is now here; winter departs,
