and the earth is in springtime bloom.
Now the voice of the turtledove is heard, singing that the time
of pruning is at hand.
Let us keep the feast, then, not with the old leaven
but with the unleavened bread of truth,
because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,
and the kingdom of God is within us.
Therefore, released from the old laws,
we no longer live in shadow,
we whom, from the cloud of the law and the yoke of its statutes,
as from a burden of hair,
Christ himself, the Son of God, has set free,
having become the head of the redeemed.
With him as our head, we tread freely on the foul head
of the conquered dragon.
For them the encumbrance of hair was fitting,
and a shade over the crown of the head,
since a veil covered their hearts,
clouding over the sacred mysteries.
But we, with the veil of the letter removed,
in the light of his body
behold the truth unclouded,
our faces unveiled by faith.
So let our boy, a nursling of both the law and grace,
draw from both,
equipped for spiritual glory,
so that he may bring forth things both old and new.
Let him, strong in chaste deeds, let his hair grow long
and know no harmful blade,
so that from the sword of noxious doctrines
he may keep his faith untouched.
But again, let this same man, his mind unveiled
from above by the light of the gospel,
lay aside the hair of burden and of veiling,
a servant to faith, and free by faith.
Him, with first milk through the breasts of the prophets,
let the Law, his tutor, nourish;
him let sweet grace with the bread of angels
and with honey from the rock feed.
Let him be made drunk with the sobering cup
from the fountain of the Holy Spirit.
And you yourself, soon joined to your sons,
may flourish like a palm for God.
And see, your wife, in the yoke of Christ,
overflows like a fruitful vine;
for your home and for God, this strong rib of yours
stands at the sides of your house,
bearing a husband's cares, caring for the faith,
the crown of a holy spouse,
nurturing in chastity the children
who make their life new for God.
For this shoot, spread forth from your vine,
must, I believe, be so strengthened by God
that, a branch of its root, as a root itself
it may draw its own stock along with it.
As that boy once, by the providence of God
sold away into slavery,
was sent to the fields of grain, so that he might go before
both his father and his brothers,
and soon, in the famine that would follow throughout the world,
would be the one who fed his father and his brothers,
so perhaps into the holy house of bread
this son has gone before you,
to feed both his parents and his brothers
in the famine of this world,
where the earth, more lavish in bearing us thistles,
lacks the harvest of good things.
And he too can be said to have been sold to a eunuch,
since he is a servant of chastity,
and has been handed over into the charge and hand of Severus,
a eunuch for the kingdom of God;
strengthened by his nurture in faith
and in manly chastity,
the alluring pomp of the ensnaring world,
like a shameless woman,
he will spurn, proud in his chaste disdain,
and escape it in naked flight,
and will choose, rather than deadly pleasures,
to suffer saving punishments.
As that one once did, so now let this one endure
a prison for the sake of chastity,
so that from his youth, sitting alone
and shut away in a silent house,
he may love the dwelling of quiet solitude
and hedge his ears with thorns.
Let him prefer the house of mourning to houses of feasting,
so as to sow joy with weeping,
and let him willingly bind himself with hard laws
so as to free himself from the chains of guilt,
and put on himself the fetter of patience,
wandering neither in place nor in mind.
And then from lowliness he will win the heights,
for he who casts down the proud
exalts the humble, and, giving grace to the little,
resists the arrogant.
So that Joseph was first made small
that he might be great; and had he not
been a slave, he would not have been powerful
in the land of his slavery.
Where he had endured servitude and prison,
there he gained a kingdom and wealth,
and by enduring the chains of injustice
he took the rewards of justice.
Let this one too prove a guardian of his own body,
so that he may hold the keys of the prison.
If he binds the vices of the flesh in fear of Christ,
he will be set, as it were, over the prisoners,
and over others still shut in the prison of the world
and bound fast to this age;
being free himself, and now entrusted to himself,
he will be their teacher and keeper.
For he who has kept his own self
rightly has the keeping of others,
not that he wants them to stay in the prison's darkness
or free men to be put in chains,
but that he may teach those in his charge by his example
to throw off the chains of the world.
And, released from his own chains, he will easily
teach them to be loosed from sin,
and as a good man, the pilot of his own mind,
he will also steer the ship of the church.
For how will he preside over his neighbors
who does not know how to rule himself?
But my speech has slipped and run on too far;
I will return to my Joseph.
Chaste, let him bloom with the flower of blessed grace
like a lily of paradise,
and with a pure heart the draught of heavenly wisdom
let him modestly drink;
let him give answers to doubting mortals,
a secret interpreter of God,
and with the shining glory of a good name
become known in the king's house,
and, pleasing the king by the spirit of wisdom,
be taken up as leader of the kingdom.
Let him go forth as prince of the royal domain,
set over a great house;
but let him wear a robe of fine linen and a golden collar,
insignia fitting for Christ;
let him put on the woven garment of grace from above,
robed in innocence.
A garment woven of fine linen signifies unbroken faith
by its strong thread;
for threads of linen are said to be stronger
even than ropes of esparto.
In place of a collar, let him put around his neck
the most sweet yoke of golden love,
which, sweet in Christ and not troublesome in weight,
binds the neck but does not press it down.
Among these gifts let him also receive, the sign
of royal authority, a ring,
and, adorned with the threefold gift of the Trinity,
let him ride in the royal chariot.
For the royal chariot is the flesh of Christ
and his holy body, the church,
in which, amid thousands of rejoicing ones, rides
God himself, the charioteer of Israel.
Imitate Christ; do good, shun evil,
live the life of heaven on earth.
And the King himself will set you in his chariot
and make you a partner in his kingdom,
and will entrust to you the highest powers of his realm
and open his treasures to you.
But first he will bestow worthy pledges,
so that, with royal insignia
adorned, you may ascend the king's lofty throne
and unlock the royal storehouses,
wearing the necklace of wisdom, the robe of glory,
and the ring of faith.
But as that man was powerful throughout all Egypt
yet a stranger to Egypt's soil,
so let this one, mightier than the powers of the world,
be strong over Egypt,
but a pilgrim in the house of the Egyptians,
so mingled with them as to be unmingled;
and, though in a shared dwelling, let the holy race
stand apart from the unholy nation;
for now, placed in this world as though in Egypt,
let him so sojourn in this age
that he is a stranger to the business of the world,
a citizen of the heavenly city.
Living in the flesh, let him be an exile from the life of the flesh,
walking in the law of the mind,
and let him travel the whole land of the kingdom entrusted to him
in the sacred books.
And just as that godly man of God, Joseph,
went round the territories of Memphis
and, in enlarged granaries, the glad wealth
of plenty gathering,
rich with the goods of overflowing years,
fed the years of hunger,
so let this Joseph of ours, in the sacred writings,
walk through the kingdom of God.
For Scripture, breathed by the Holy Spirit,
is the mother of the everlasting kingdom;
and let him, providing with spiritual care,
build wide granaries of the mind,
so that in a heart made wide he may store abundant
food for unending life;
and when, with life-giving wealth,
he has made his land rich,
then you, to enjoy the power of your son,
will go like the aged Israel
and enter rejoicing, summoned along with
the whole company of your kin.
And in the king's house your son will feed your
old age with the bread he has gained,
as the young eagle is said to feed in return
its parents with care repaid,
when the force of old age makes them featherless again
and brings them back to the nest to be fed,
until their bodies are clothed in feathers once more
and they bloom with new plumage.
By a strange new turn of nature, roles reversed,
the old birds become nestlings to their young.
But when youth, purged of old age's torpor, has made them
swift flyers once again,
they begin anew the long-unused oarage of their wings
with their offspring as teachers,
and, mingled with the young who fed them, they fly together
with gentle impulse through the air;
in the clear sky, with slow sweeps, a liquid path
they delight to cut on high,
and, calmly fanning the cloudless air,
matched with motionless wings,
while they follow one another and lead by turns,
they form a crown in a wreathlike circle.
And unprompted, the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom
these mute birds proclaim:
the sacred likeness of the mighty cross is spread out
by their bodies poised upon their wings;
and their flight, wheeling round in a circle,
promises the reward of toil.
So let this nestling, a son of graces,
forerunner of your salvation,
of the birds that travel through the high clouds
be a spiritual imitator,
and, upborne by the arms and wings of the lofty cross,
fly to the crown of glory,
he who was drawn off from his own spring, so that
the whole spring may flow into his channel;
and you, bending forward, follow your little stream,
so that a river may go forth from you all,
blessed root of a holy offspring, like the fruitful
branches of a good tree.
You gave your son to God to be nourished,
and he so nourishes you
that the boy in turn feeds the grey-haired,
a little one become teacher to the old,
by a wondrous mystery of devotion
made a parent to his parents.
Then all, the whole company of the saints,
to that body on the heights
where, like eagles, the godly will gather,
you too will go flying,
which those will not be able to do who are kept from rising off the ground
by the weight of their inheritances.
When first the signal to raise the dead
the trumpet thunders from heaven,
these men, now bloated with the spirit of pride
and puffed up with hoary wealth,
will stay on the ground, shackled, and will not
free themselves from the chains
by which the faithless are now bound, as they wish,
and then will be held fast so that they cannot fly;
for, laden and weighed down with their goods,
the rich of the perishing world
the delicate clouds will not be able to carry
to meet God the King;
but, stuck in the mire of their own dregs
and crushed by the mass of their wealth,
in the noonday burning of the world, sudden
ruin of death will overwhelm them.
May God the Lord, I pray, not let the rod of such men
come into his own lot,
nor let us, toward the fruits of these rich men,
stretch out wicked hands.
You then, great care of my heart,
make yourselves light for Christ,
and now, rid of the burdens that weigh you down,
free your feet from their chains;
that you may be clothed in abundant light,
be naked to the world,
so that when the prince of this world comes he may find nothing
in you that is his.
And you, free from the weight of crushing things
and pure from the stain of sins,
lifting you easily, may they bear you in their light embrace,
the clouds that carry the godly;
and when you are borne to meet the Bridegroom King, may God
flood you with his radiance,
so that the bright glory of everlasting life
may swallow up what is mortal in you,
and that, restored to the heavenly image,
conformed to your Master's beauty,
enduring through everlasting ages like the angels,
you may live with God the King.
XXV.
Two souls in harmony are joined in chaste love:
a virgin youth of Christ, a virgin maiden of God.
Christ our God, lead this matched pair of doves to your reins,
and guide their necks, bowed beneath your light yoke.
For your yoke, O Christ, is light when a ready will
takes it up and love carries it with willing obedience.
To the unwilling, the holy burden of the law of chastity is heavy;
to the devout it is a sweet burden to overcome the work of the flesh.
Far from this bridal chamber be the wantonness of the foolish crowd,
Juno, Cupid, Venus — names of lust.
The holy children of a priest, in a covenant worthy of reverence,
are being joined; let peace, modesty and devotion meet together here.
For a marriage in harmony with God is at once the love of devotion, the honour of love,
and peace: these make the bond of wedlock.
God consecrated the work of this covenant with his own mouth,
and with his divine hand he established the human pair.
And to mark their love all the more as indivisible,
he made the two to remain out of one flesh.
For Adam was put to sleep and deprived of a rib that was taken from him,
and soon he received a partner made from his own bone;
nor did he feel the loss of his side, for flesh filled its place in turn,
and he recognized that he had been doubled;
and, seeing another self from himself in a companion body,
he at once became his own prophet with a new voice:
"This," he said, "is flesh of my flesh; this bone I know
to be from my bones; this is the rib of my side."
Now therefore, since under the ancient pattern a holy
covenant is being celebrated by the offspring of Aaron,
let sober joys be stirred with tranquil prayers;
let Christ resound everywhere in the voice of a devout people.
Let no crowd run riot through decorated streets;
let no one strew the ground with leaves or cover doorways with boughs;
let there be no pagan procession through a city that worships Christ;
I will not have profane display defile the devout.
Let no breeze be fragrant with foreign fumes;
let everything breathe the cleanness of chastity.
For the saints there is one ointment, which, poured out in the name of Christ,
breathes forth God in a chaste fragrance.
Let no trays be decked with needless gifts;
virtue is adorned by character, not by wealth.
Let the holy daughter-in-law of a priest, the wife of a consecrated
youth, now receive the dowry of light.
Let her shudder at garments embroidered with gold or purple;
her golden garment is the pure grace of God.
Let her also reject necklaces studded with gems of many colours,
so that she herself may be a noble gem for the Lord God.
A neck dedicated to bearing the yoke of Christ the Lord
must not be weighed down by hateful greed.
Rather, so as to please, let her be adorned with an inward adornment,
her character arrayed with gifts that bring salvation.
Let her not covet costly stones, nor the fleeces of the Chinese,
squandering her income to no purpose;
let her soul be adorned with chaste virtues, so that she may be
not ruinous but precious to her husband.
For where the glory of bodily display is cultivated,
a person grows cheap, devalued by vice,
and the mind, wretchedly blinded by the lust of perverse desire,
grows filthy amid the gleaming trappings of the body;
nor does the wicked one perceive what a shameful ornament he wears, so that
he who pleases himself with his clothing is lighter than his clothing.
God forbid that she should look like a daughter of an idol's temple,
she who has been made a daughter in the house of an apostolic people —
her skin falsely painted with cosmetics, her eyes with black
powder, or her hair dyed a golden colour.
The woman who scorns the pure beauty of nature by a proud
crime condemns in herself the work of God.
In vain would such a woman boast that she is chaste,
who adorns herself with so many kinds of adultery.
But you, young people of Christ, flee all those things whose
price lies in loss and whose use lies in ruin.
Believe the divine words: from these adornments
arises the stuff of punishment for those who covet them.
Isaiah threatens that a stiff rope will gird those women
who now wear silks interwoven with purple,
who trail tunics red with crimson and rustling with gold
in loose folds down to the ankle;
girded with ropes and wearing sackcloth without end,
they will grind great stones in the prison of the mill.
And those who heighten their heads with heaped-up, pampered tresses
will bear shameful baldness on a bare crown.
Shun being adorned with such dowries, O new bride
of a holy husband; these things please empty minds.
Do not wish, as you go about, to be recognized by people's noses
wherever you walk, from your perfumed clothes and hair,
or to sit with your head built up into a tower
by a pile and torture of plaited tresses,
lest, with many wickedly tempted by your splendour,
you become the wicked source of a deadly allurement.
Nor should you desire, by enhancing your body,
to please even your own husband, debasing your mind.
You too, holy youth devoted to the sacred books,
spurn the lover's concern for bodily beauty.
For Christ has richly repaid you, adorning
your beautiful soul with everlasting riches;
and he has adorned you both together with chaste dowries:
hope, devotion, faith, peace, chastity.
The word of God is silver, and the Holy Spirit gold,
and good works are bright gems for the mind.
If plain dress offends respectable minds,
and proud hearts delight in being courted with costly things,
let the examples of the saints remove that shame,
and the chaste simplicity of the first human beings.
Look at our ancient parents in their home in paradise,
to whom the whole world was a single field.
Yet sheepskins were their clothing;
are we now ashamed to wear cloth woven from spun wool?
When the beautiful Rebecca came as a bride to holy Isaac,
she was covered simply with the veil of modesty.
We do not read that she came adorned with jewels of many colours,
but provided with a little cloak drawn over her,
with which covering she modestly hid her face,
a virgin trembling at the face of the bridegroom set before her.
Or shall the dancing maiden Herodias please us more,
who won the death of the Baptist as the price of her feet?
The wicked girl so avenged the anger of her mother's lust
that she received a head as the price of her wantonness —
that very head, indeed, from which the herald voice had cried out
to the peoples that the Lamb of God was near.
How did the wicked dancer, a daughter worthy of her father, earn so great a crime
if not by her seductive attire?
Yet by this wickedness she overcame him and forced him, against his will,
into crime through the allurements of a pleasing body.
For the guests, worthy of the unjust king's banquet,
she led into assent, nimble in the art of her feet.
For had golden foil not covered her light soles,
so that she might sport more shamelessly on painted heels,
and had she not trailed a flowing gown with a rippling train,
her brow glittering with gems, her hair streaming down behind,
she would not, thus stealing into the corrupted minds of the onlookers,
cunning as she was, have prevailed to that unspeakable deed.
Herod himself too, proud in his royal robe,
madly swelled with sacrilegious arrogance,
and, elated by his attire and forgetting the honour due to God,
perished stinking from a wound swarming with worms,
paying the penalty he deserved: that he should die foul with sores
who had believed himself a god through the honour of his robe.
But granted that royal finery suits hearts puffed up with mad pride,
what dealings have we with Pharaoh?
The hollow glory of the world is at odds with our kingdom,
and holy light does not unite with the darkness opposed to it.
Let the cleric cherish a wife made comely by Christ's adorning,
and love her as beautiful in the light of the heart;
and let the reader learn from the heavenly history
that she was made by God's gift to be a help to her husband.
And in turn let the woman, that she may be equal to her holy husband,
receive Christ in her spouse with a humble mind,
so that she may grow, knit together in its joints, into a holy body,
and the man may be her head, whose own head is Christ.
In such a marriage the servitude of Eve has ceased,
and Sarah, a free woman, became equal to her devout husband.
Under such a law Jesus stands beside his own when they marry
as groomsman, and changes water into the nectar of wine.
It is fitting that Mary, the Lord's mother, be present at this wedding,
she who bore God with her virginity intact.
For God himself founded in the consecrated Virgin a temple pleasing to him
through a secret rainfall,
descending with silent gliding, as rain from a high
cloud falls upon a fleece in silent dew.
For no one was ever privy to this secret
by which God took on human nature from a virgin mother.
O new design of the Lord for human salvation!
Without intercourse a woman becomes pregnant in her womb.
She was only betrothed to a man, and not made subject to a husband;
a mother by childbirth, yet not a woman by intercourse.
She was a spouse by covenant, but not a wife in body;
untouched by a man, she was mother to a child.
A great mystery, by which the church is wedded to Christ
and is at once the bride and the sister of her Lord:
bride as a spouse, she is sister because she is not made subject.
Hence she remains a mother by the seed of the eternal Word,
conceiving peoples and bearing them at the same time.
Hence she is sister and spouse, since without use of the body
she unites in mind, she whose husband is not a man but God.
By this mother the old man is born just as the infant is;
this offspring has neither age nor sex.
For this is the blessed generation of God, which is not
of human seed but of heavenly stock.
Hence the Teacher says that there is now neither female nor male
in Christ, but one body and one faith.
For we are all one body, all members of Christ,
for whom Christ is the head of the body.
And since, having put on Christ, we put off Adam,
we press on at once toward the likeness of the angels.
Therefore this is the work for all who are born of baptism:
that both sexes may attain to the perfect man,
and Christ, the common head, may stand as all in all,
the King delivering his members into the kingdom to the Father.
Marrying and being given in marriage pass away with our frail age
when all have been formed into an eternal body.
So, remembering me, live always as an inviolable pair;
let the venerable cross be your yoke.
As children of that mother who is both bride and sister,
take on hearts worthy of those holy names,
and run together as brothers to meet Christ the bridegroom,
that you may be one flesh of the eternal body.
Let that love bind you here with which the church holds Christ fast
and with which Christ in turn cherishes her.
Let the bishop, your father, bless you himself; let him himself
lead the holy songs for the choirs that sing hymns.
Lead your children, kindly Memor, before the altar of the Lord,
and commend them in prayer with your sanctifying hand.
But what fragrance, flowing from heaven, steals into my nostrils?
From where does an unexpected light strike my eyes?
Who is that man approaching from afar with peaceful steps,
attended by the abundant grace of Christ,
surrounded by a blessed company of heaven's pupils
that recalls the likeness of the angelic host?
I know the man whom divine fragrances accompany
and on whose face a starry glory shines.
This is the man, this is he, rich in the manifold gifts of Christ the Lord,
a man of heavenly light: Aemilius.
Rise, Memor, revere a father, embrace a brother:
both names are yours in the one Aemilius.
Memor is both the younger and the elder. Wonderful gift
and work of the great God! The one who is younger is the father here;
born later, he is the elder, because as a priest of an apostolic see
he bears grey hairs in his heart.
Memor is son and brother; he rejoices that there is present
a father common to himself and to his children.
Justice and peace embrace one another in twofold exchange
when Memor is joined to Aemilius, one in heart with him.
The headband joins these bishops in divine honour;
devotion joins them as equals in human love.
So Memor, not unmindful of his duty, in due order
hands over his dear children into the hands of Aemilius.
He, yoking the heads of both under the peace of the marriage yoke,
veils with his right hand those whom he sanctifies with prayer.
Christ, hear your priests; Christ, as they pray,
graciously [?] grant assent to your holy suppliants.
Fill, O Christ, these newlyweds through the holy bishop,
and through his chaste hands strengthen their modest hearts,
so that there may be in both of them the harmony of virginity,
or else that both may be the seed of holy virgins.
This is the higher rank of their vows: that they keep their bodies
ignorant of the flesh; but if they come together in body,
may the offspring to come be a chaste and priestly race,
and may the whole house of Memor be a house of Aaron,
and may this house of Memor be a house of anointed ones.
Be mindful too of Paulinus and Therasia,
and Christ will be mindful of Memor for ever.
XXVI.
Look, the year has turned and run its course, and the day
brings back to us the light made famous by the name of Felix.
This would be the time to pour out our joy in happy words,
if anxious times allowed glad voices.
Yet this day, though we are in the midst of battles,
will be for us a day of joy and peace; let dreadful
wars roar far away, but let free peace dwell in our minds.
The sweet habit of joy is not forgotten
by a mind accustomed to open its heart in devout prayers
and to rejoice chastely in the Lord on feast days.
So, though the season is sorrowful, drive out
untimely sadness; good joys, sweet words,
all that is holy and glad, let us love on Felix's day,
a birthday without end, since on this day Felix
was born into everlasting ages, the day on which, his bodily span
completed, he passed into heaven to eternal life.
So let gloomy fears depart, and let joys return to hearts
refreshed; it is fitting that all sadness flee this holy
day, which the glory of so great a confessor
makes shine out, distinguished above all days through all time,
and adorns with thronging crowds.
This day I would celebrate gladly even if I lived as a wretched subject under Gothic arms
and among the savage Alans;
and if chains of many links weighed down my neck,
the enemy would not bind my soul together with my captive limbs;
with heart unbound, devotion would proudly trample on grim
slavery. Even amid barbarian fetters
my free love would sing its familiar song in pleasing words.
Now, therefore, though wandering rumour through many regions
strikes fearful ears with terrifying reports,
let steadfast trust in Christ the Lord
strengthen us and arm us, our minds fixed with upright foot,
and let no black panic draw clouds over this light,
which God makes serene with the heavenly honour of Felix.
As once, in the land of the Egyptian tyrant, the lawgiver
Moses consecrated the holy Passover under the first law,
and holy Judea then, though the wicked enemy
drove them with violent force to hasten their flight from home,
yet, bold with the freedom of a devoted heart
and undisturbed by fear, did not abandon the commanded rite,
but, though trembling and in flight, performed the divine
festival, feasting in glad companies on the saving lamb,
and, already victorious through the prefigured blood of Christ,
led joyful dances in triumph over the conquered Pharaoh
(hence, mindful of that flight, even now the Jews,
who keep their nationhood in name alone, eat unleavened bread,
because once, driven out with unleavened loaves,
they made their flight from Egypt; with like signs now,
through ancestral rites, but now through empty sabbaths,
they recall the welcome traces of their ancient fear;
for in vain they practise the old law under an empty image,
since for us the true Passover has been fulfilled
by Christ alone, given to the Father as victim for all,
and because the body of life is present, the shadow of the figure passes away):
so then let us now, glad in a troubled time,
all with devout mind keep the feast of the beloved martyr
with united zeal of cheerful devotion.
Perhaps this devotion will rather bring us safety,
if we are willing to lay aside our cares for this purpose,
that we may bring rejoicing hearts to the confessor,
in whose honour God rejoices, since the martyr despised
his own honour for the name of Christ the Lord,
cheap in his own eyes, so that he might be more precious to Christ.
Therefore let it please us to rejoice in such a patron
and, laying our cares aside, to spend in gladness the birthday
of the martyr who sleeps in blessed peace.
This too will be granted to the devout, if the feeling of joy
now proves stronger than the cause of fear
that would dismay our minds and cloud our hearts.
Believe me, it is not for their arms or strength that the foreign
peoples are to be feared; the wrath of an offended God moves them
because of our sins, so that by fear of death
he may rouse sluggish hearts to care for life.
So let us fear the gentle God in the savage enemy;
away with fear of the enemy, whom we deserve to dread
because we do not fear God; him whom, relaxed in calm peace,
we neglect, let us at least tremble before when force compels us;
let us humbly appease with grief him whom, when he brings us gladness,
we soon spurn, made proud by prosperity itself.
Let us reconsider the ancient examples of the holy fathers,
who, enduring deserved scourges in the wars sent upon them,
did not think that protection was to be found in arms or walls.
To hope for safety from human resources
is no safety at all. For mortal things will not drive away death.
So let those who have time for care make it their care to pray
to the heavenly Lord, by whom sad things and glad are prepared,
who alone by his supreme authority can grant
that, our cares driven out, joys may be renewed again.
For by this practice God the judge rules and varies
human affairs, so that clouds always follow clear skies
and rains flee once more when fair weather returns.
How great the power of prayer is, what a remedy it is to weep
before God our Father, let Nineveh teach, saved by its mourning,
and Amalek, conquered by the earnest prayer of aged Moses,
and accursed Haman, destroyed by the prayer of holy Esther,
who by a fitting reversal of punishment, wicked as he was, alone drank
the evils he had mixed for the saints, and on a just cross
himself hung, the cross he had set up for the Lord's servant.
So let faith leaning on God strengthen trembling
hearts, and in a sorrowful time count on a time of security,
trusting in God, since to fear God is the reason
for fearing nothing; whoever does not fear him alone
rightly fears everything. Let them trust in legions
and prepare fortifications for refuge by rebuilding walls,
those who have no trust in Christ the Saviour;
we are fortified by the sign and confession of the unconquered cross,
and, our minds armed by God, we do not seek arms
for the body; and though in limb we seem unarmed,
yet we bear arms, with which even in calm peace
we fight in spirit against bodiless enemies.
Now we need God as our helper, and he alone is to be feared,
without whom arms fall, and through whom arms are made firm;
he himself will be your tower within walls, and without walls
he will be your wall. Let us recall from this point the deeds of the fathers recorded
in the sacred books, and see who had the stronger
protection: those whom a city enclosed with great walls
but without God, or those whom, without city walls,
divine power fenced round with its allied favour.
I mean that city which fierce Joshua destroyed,
his own name changed to a name of power,
a city which that leader did not subdue in the usual manner of warfare,
toiling, as is usual, through a long siege;
but, brandishing weapons by divine aid through sacred mysteries,
his army not using its silent arms,
he went around the city with idle hands, for seven days
repeating seven circuits around its walls.
He took them captive by the power of the potent number
and by the priests' trumpets with their dreadful blare
imitating the lightning-thunder of heaven's wrath.
Then the people who trusted in their riches and their city
perished, their graves mingled among their homes.
Only Rahab the harlot, who kept chaste faith amid a wicked
nation, escaped, not by relying on her walls;
rather, through God's goodness she gained the reward of her devotion,
in that she was hostess to the Lord's servants under her safe roof
and, having devoutly hidden them, deceived the wicked citizens,
false with a good deceit, lying with a faithful heart.
Because she had proved faithful to holy guests and unfaithful to profane
citizens, life, homeland and home,
all of which she had despised in preferring God, she soon
found again in the kind Lord; had she placed her protection
in the city, she would have fallen, mingled in her country's ruins,
undefended by God; but the mystic harlot, foreseeing that Christ
would buy the defiled nations with his blood,
marked her own house with a scarlet cord
and received her own safety as her homeland perished,
signifying that those will be protected when the world falls
whom the blood of the unconquered cross marks. From this learn how much
that blood itself avails, whose mere image saved.
For every good it has always availed to trust in Christ,
to entrust all things to the God of hosts, to hold God alone
as the sum of all; such faith has always prevailed over all
arms; by such strength that little boy
was great, who, the stronger for spurning arms,
struck down the armed giant by the power of a stone.
We have known arms always in need of faith, but never faith
in need of arms. The rod of faith split the sea,
which drowned arms empty of faith together with their wicked prince.
Gracious faith clothes women too
with manly strength; by it a holy woman slew
terrible Sisera, his temples pierced with a tent-peg;
Holofernes, who terrified great peoples far and wide,
was deceived by the art of chastity and mocked by shrewd Judith,
who, undefiled in his impure bed,
victorious, beheaded their leader and put the barbarian camp to flight.
Naked faith is armed by God; by the power of faith
Hezekiah, with a few thousand men, was stronger than
Sennacherib, whose kingdom was Babylon and wealthy Nineveh.
He had set in motion the Assyrian forces and the Median realms,
and, crushing all the kingdoms round about with great legions,
he was making for the holy city of the Lord
and attacking that one city with the whole mass of war.
While he was preparing this, as wars held back his wicked designs
and God hindered him, he sent ahead a letter harsh
with proud threats; Hezekiah took it in grief and brought it before
the Lord at the altar, and, pouring out tears
as he read the savage words, washing them, lying prostrate and praying
with the people clad in mourning, he moved God, and with a single
prayer, victor over so grievous a destruction, he struck down the Assyrians while far away,
God fighting for him, having earned so great a shortcut
that he never even saw the enemy he conquered.
For after Hezekiah's plaintive weeping had passed beyond the stars
and the laments sent up above the heavens from a humble heart
had struck the ears of the highest Father with devout voice, as the lofty
doors of heaven opened, a winged angel glided down,
drawing fragrant air behind him where he glided,
armed with the sword of the Word, he struck the wicked camp
and, triumphing in a silent slaughter of sleepers,
gave a hundred and eighty thousand to a single death,
and one night alone witnessed so great a war.
In the morning the king rises, still threatening, and soon, wretched, his weapons
left idle, his soldiers destroyed, he flees with a thinned column,
fleeing Hezekiah, who was far away in another region,
whom, as if he were present, he had just been threatening with chains.
Then, as Isaiah was intercessor for Hezekiah,
so at this time let Felix be ours before the Lord.
Let us cast our cares and fears upon him
and transfer them to him. Our weight will be a light burden
to him, since what is a load to the small is light to the great.
So God himself bore the sins of men and was not swallowed up by them,
and, suffering death on the cross, he bore no guilt of his own.
He lost his life on the cross to restore mine;
he was made guilty, that I might not be guilty; among the wicked
he died condemned, that he might set us apart from the wicked.
By a holy death the Lord died for me, that I might live for him
and be worthy to live forever the life of the Living One.
So the martyrs are the nobler limbs in his venerable body,
among whom Felix, of outstanding strength,
shines among the sacred lights of the divine Head,
rightly powerful with God, since their sufferings came nearest to Christ's.
Let us run to this patron with united hope;
he will receive our complaints with calm kindness,
and while we joyfully celebrate his birthday,
he in his goodness will support our prayers with his lofty merits
and weep for us in return, because with devoted mind
we rejoice for him. This is no new concern for the saints,
to entreat God for sick sinners
and by the power of good merit to overcome evil desert.
For we read that Moses, praying when the people sinned,
quenched the heavy wrath of the eternal Avenger;
and when a fiery rain drenched the Pentapolis,
Lot in his flight set little Zoar apart from wicked Sodom,
and, mighty in chaste prayer, freed the city
and took it as his chosen home, because in his chaste dwelling
he had remained an upright inhabitant of an unchaste land,
living among the houses of Sodom but a stranger to its morals.
Why should I speak of heaven closed and opened again by Elijah's prayers,
and how, at the holy-speaking mouth of the lofty prophet,
famine stayed on the earth and well-being returned?
As the old age once had these men, so now let our
welfare, which has been granted Felix, ask for all it dares,
and hope for all it desires, trusting in such a patron.
Holy Felix, beloved of God, right hand of God,
be, I pray, a most strongly fortified tower for us.
For the God of Abraham is your God, and the God of Isaac
and the God of Israel is your God; he who divided
the Red Sea and sweetened the bitter spring,
he who gave manna from heaven and quail on the south wind,
and watered the thirsty ground by striking the rock,
he himself is your God, who went before the people
as they followed through the desert, and changed the pillar stretched before them
night and day by the alternating law of time,
and who for forty years in the desert
fed the people from heaven with the bread of angels
and refreshed them in their thirst by bursting the rock into rivers.
Ask, I pray, that Christ graciously take our
side; he is your God, by whose power mighty Joshua
commanded the sun and moon to stand still for his triumphs;
and when the Lord has granted you success for the Roman realm,
command the elements as your servants, Felix,
to serve our good; with the stars standing still, let the day
go on, lengthened; let the sun stand still for you, and the moon in harmony
stay fixed, holding the stars in their arrested course,
until Roman victory reaches its goal.
As in Assyrian Babylon Daniel tamed the lions,
victorious through outpoured prayer, so for you, Felix,
let savage barbarism be tamed, as Christ breaks it,
and let captives lie around your feet.
So once wild beasts lay around the prophet
and soothed the feet of the praying man with kindly tongues,
God changing their nature, so as to condemn
men savage in their bitter minds by the humane peace of beasts.
So too the flame confounded the cruel tyrant
as he watched the furnaces serve the holy boys,
the condemned singing and his own attendants burning.
How will wretched kings be able to defend themselves,
who, so degenerate from the human mind, raged against
those whom both wild beasts and flame spared?
But as, while the boys sang back eternal hymns,
a dewy breath scattered the kindled fires,
so for us may Felix's grace, with a calm breeze
breathed by God, temper the fires of war,
and, holding back the conflagrations that have risen in the lands of Romulus,
cool our anxious heat now with calm peace
and release our weary hearts, their cares quenched.
But why, foolish man, as though I were a guest unacquainted with you
and forgetful of you, do I petition you with the examples
of the ancient fathers, that you may grant help in our need,
help which, by God's gift, you will make come to us?
The examples of your own miracles are enough for me, Felix,
nor does Christ pour out heavenly gifts on you more meagrely
than on the fathers, whose noble offspring you are.
For, Felix, you are equally a son of the patriarchs and
of apostolic stock, no degenerate heir of so great
a seed; as confessor of the holy law and of the faith alike,
you, holy one, bear signs that rival the powers of your fathers;
and if the outward form of your works is different,
the power is not unlike; grace is diverse among us,
glory equal, since there is one fountain for all the saints
and a common kingdom of God; prophets and holy martyrs
do not have the same works, just as their times were different,
nor do deeds coincide in their signs when their causes differ;
through God's heavenly gifts they differ from one another
while equal in merit. If Felix did not do or suffer
all the same things as Daniel, and no pit held him,
nor did terrible lions surround him,
neither did Daniel suffer for his Master's name the same things,
blows, chains, terrors and the night of a black prison,
dreadful things which Felix endured. He who closed the jaws of the beasts,
making them tame before the praying prophet,
who made fires cool for the boys as they prayed
and kept their garments damp in the midst of the furnaces,
he himself has given Felix power, by lofty right,
to command the pestilent legions of Satan,
in whom he subdues all wild beasts and fires.
For what serpent, what beast is not found in this horde?
In short, I will tell of one out of many, so that from one
you may learn that demons have the natures of beasts.
A certain man, not long ago, was swollen by so monstrous
a demon that he not only consumed in an easy gulp
the ordinary food of men, even if a table heaped
with plentiful fare were set before him,
but also snatched hens from the doorsteps of the local people,
and as soon as he had seized them, tore them apart with rabid mouth
and devoured them raw, the feathers not choking him.
He even thirsted for the gore of corpses and licked
bones, gnawing the discarded carcasses of cattle,
a foul table-companion of dogs. This man, now freed from so great a demon,
look, sober, works a rented little field some way off,
and, healed by God in Felix's holy hall
and restored to himself, he shows by clear enough evidence
that Felix, strong by his merits and by the name of Christ,
tames monstrous beasts and conquers flames.
Speak, you who are present as witnesses of Felix's works:
does he not tame beasts and fires when he presses hard on the demons
who break souls with vices and bodies with diseases,
who burn a man with flaming desires
and devour him with sins? Tormenting and routing them,
does he not tame beasts and fires? Felix rages, a fiery avenger
against the fire-bearing host, and crushes the harmful flame
with the fire of God; the fire of darkness is conquered
by the holy fire of light; the demon flees, and God enters;
and the man becomes a house well changed, a happier hall,
with God as its owner, having disowned its foul tenant.
God is a bright and healing fire; with this fire my Felix
burns, to quench the inflamed demon
and to cool the man, set free, while the enemy burns.
Wondrous hand, potent rod, lofty power!
When spirits are mingled in a hostile pact within one body,
Felix intervenes within the hidden recesses
of the heart and, subtler still, separates the thin airs,
distinguishing the soul from the demon, so that when the demon is driven out the freed
mind takes back the man. This work is equal to that work
by which the image of the cross, through the sweetness of the sacred wood,
changed the bitter waters of Marah into drink for the people.
So Felix, mighty in his devotion, since he is the noble confessor
of the lofty cross, changes the man himself, as if he were the bitter cups
of Marah. He who but now, swollen by a bitter
demon, through foaming lips, with a viperous taste,
with heaving of his sides and sobbing of his wide throat,
often leaping up, belched out bitter blasts,
now wholly and solely a man, returned to his own control,
tastes sweet, breathes soundly and speaks calmly.
So the right hand of power girds Felix too.
By it he mightily devours the various arts of the prince of darkness,
as the rod of Moses devoured the magicians' serpents.
Look, we see that riches of the heavenly Lord are present
equal to Felix's merit, and that the forms of his works
correspond too; and whatever proofs of God the holy fathers
gave while in the body, Felix, living without a body
in Christ, performs; and his soul, powerful with distinguished
mind, while the bones of the body laid aside are at rest,
displays beforehand by clear signs, before the day of return,
what kind of crown it will wear for its merits
when Felix stands, alive again in his whole body.
All the saints will shine, each with his own light,
equal though differing in brightness, and with Christ as judge
none will grow at the cost of another's merit;
Christ will be kingdom, light, life and crown for all.
See the teachers of the Old and New Testaments,
distinct in their deeds but joined in honour,
in whom one Wisdom gave two laws.
And so equal glory balances varied powers.
Peter did not break the sea with a rod, nor did Moses
walk on the liquid surface; yet one honour shines
for both, since for both there was one author
of splitting the waters with a rod and treading the waves underfoot,
he who is God of the ancient saints and God of the new;
from the same Lord by whom the law was given came grace;
the God of Daniel and of the three boys
is himself Felix's God, and God is no less himself
in holy Felix, through whom he bestows good gifts
and exercises healing power on land and sea.
For every day we are witnesses, as frequent crowds come from everywhere,
either of the healed giving thanks and paying their vows
or of the sick seeking and experiencing various cures.
We see, too, many who have sailed from a foreign shore
lying prostrate before the holy hall of the holy martyr,
recounting, as they give thanks, the dangers they endured,
testifying that, when their ship was shattered by violent storms,
they were snatched away by God's mercy, and, led out by the very hand
of Felix, emerged from the depths of the sea
and peacefully found the safety they had despaired of:
by Felix's merits both waters and flames give way.
To pass over past proofs of his potent merit,
we know it by experience; dread from the recent terror
still shakes our minds as they remember, when we recall
the fire we endured when our houses were almost consumed;
though the flame is out, its traces still glow
in our minds and heap up our love for great Felix,
whom we saw, almost present in bodily action,
setting his hands against the flames and protecting our
doorways, which adjoin his own; the flame, almost touching them,
shrank back as though terrified by the face of the saint standing in its way,
and, driven back from seizing the roof of our house,
burned itself out close by, in the ruin of a neighbouring hut.
I will tell a wonder: the air stood still, without a gust,
and no breeze set the leaves of the groves trembling,
so that the swift fire could not advance further,
flying through the joined beams of the neighbouring houses,
but, abandoned by the dying winds, the flame refused to go on
and died, languid, its fuel consumed.
In the same way, Felix, release us from dangers by your help;
let evils not approach our homes, and, driven off by you,
let dreadful wrath sound far away with its bloody scourge.
Put on also, for warding off wars, that power
by which the river that flowed so harmfully from the neighbouring mountains,
and that, overflowing with a torrent swollen by sudden rains,
so often rushed headlong upon your threshold
that in its violence it shook with vast waters the dwellings
adjoining your buildings — you turned its stream
and made it change its course, so that now a new channel
leads it raging through an unaccustomed region,
avoiding our houses by a distant path:
so now turn away the battles coming in a war-resounding flood
from our lands. Let the impious hand keep away
from these sacred bounds, whose rampart is your grace,
and let enemies fear your hall as the demons do,
and let blood not violate what flame and flood have shunned.
XXVII.
Be born, O day, you who always return to me with slow rising,
and soon, hurrying toward your setting, flee, slow to return
but winged to depart. For while you linger through long
seasons, while the straining wheel of the slow year turns,
I wait for you with a longing heart and intent prayers.
How I would wish you to shine for me every day,
or, whenever you do come, to make up for your delays so
that you could stretch your light to summer's length,
or match that day which, when the stars were ordered
to stand still, wearied the world with its long light,
doubling human labours as the night was put off.
Now, dear day, in an all too swift sky, the law of winter
steals you from us, and winter, quick with light and sluggish with darkness,
forces the hours to be shortened.
But it is well that for you, Felix, whose grace is unending, the sun
shines with Christ as its illuminator, and you yourself flash
your own radiance on your birthday, and the splendour of eternal honour
is never buried by any setting fall.
Go, fleeting day, slip away; I will not call you back,
nor will I now complain that you are short, since without you Felix
always shines present to me with unquenched light.
If the birthday is absent, it is more that he himself,
the light of this birthday, is continually present. For he is not made
holy by the day; rather his honour is the reason for celebrating the day.
But if it is the crowd that makes a birthday surpass other days,
the crowd that runs more thickly than usual to the holy
thresholds, we see Felix's birthday kept almost always
with a packed throng. For what day, I ask, dawns
empty of prayers, or thinly attended by great crowds?
Yet I will admit that this day rightly keeps a special glory,
the day on which, when his life was once completed, it befell
Felix to lay aside his earthly garb and be called to the lofty
stars, to be kept in a blessed abode.
For that principle confirms the faith, which marks out the seasons with fixed
titles and through the yearly feasts sets its seal on holy
days on which the ancient fathers once trembled at the Lord's
wonders: days dreadful to the wicked
and ever to be celebrated by the godly, because they were kind to the saints
and harsh to the wicked. Witness the land of Memphis
and the sea, which then became dry ground for the saints and a flood for the unjust,
and the other deeds like these, done in Egypt and in many regions
by God, which we recall with mindful love.
So likewise the divine gifts of Christ are celebrated:
as the day revered by all on which, born of a virgin,
God took on manhood for all; and then
the day on which the magi, led by the star and bearing mystic gifts,
humbly beheld the child; or the day, rather, on which
the trembling Jordan washed him as John dipped him,
while he hallowed all waters for the renewal of the nations;
or whether that same day is made holy rather by the sign
by which God first performed a work, when, changing the stream,
he transformed water into the nectar of sweetest wine.
What of the paschal banquet? For certainly every
day, in every land, the Church proclaims the Pasch to all,
bearing witness to the Lord's death on the cross, and from the cross the life
of all; yet this great sacrament of great love toward all
the whole world everywhere, each year in the appointed month,
worships with equal service,
celebrating the eternal King in his risen body.
This solemnity is followed by the day (we count seven
weeks, and the festal light returns for the peoples)
on which the Holy Spirit, once sent down from high heaven,
divided tongues with fiery light,
and, himself one God, ran through diverse mouths
and then sounded every kind of speech from one mouth,
granting all to utter tongues unknown to them,
so that each recognised his own nation in a foreign mouth
and did not know the foreign speech in his own mouth.
The barbarian himself sang words known to others but unknown to himself,
speaking what was foreign to his own people; but in all of them one
Spirit praised the one God with varied voice.
As one who plays the lyre with the stroke of a single plectrum
moves strings of different pitch, or one who rubs his lips, blowing across
reeds joined together, though he produces one song from one
mouth, does not sound a single note, but tempers varied sounds
with masterly art, and governs the shrill holes with breath
and nimble fingers, closing and opening them,
so that in rapid alternation the sweet, tuneful air may go and return in the hollows,
running along its airy passage,
and the pipe, given life, may unfold unbroken songs:
so God, the one player and master of the all-sounding
harmony which he moves through all the bodies of things,
God, maker of all nature and all art, in every
work the source and the end, making good things and preserving what he has made,
abiding in himself in a mutual love,
by which the Father reigns in the Word and the Son in the Father,
he without whom nothing was made, through whom all created things
hold together in him, the same renews all things by the sovereign Word,
who, by the cross purpled with the dye of precious blood,
rose on high in swift ascent and pierced the heights,
flying on a cloud above the Cherubim, and sat at the Father's
right hand, and from there poured out heavenly gifts on his own:
the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Only-begotten and the Father,
who, himself God coming from God, though present everywhere,
yet rushed down in fire with visible descent there
where the harmonious company of the apostolic band was gathered;
and soon, when the new sound had drawn together out of the city many
men of every nation, he sat like flame upon them all
and, at once in all, sounding diversely with one breath,
as if playing lyre strings with a nimble plectrum,
sang the same proclamation in divided tongues,
striking out varied voices through human instruments.
When such drunkenness had filled those chosen minds,
hearts drunk with God belched out holy praises
from fasting throats. Who will take pity on me and give me to drink
from that river which makes sober by its drunkenness?
So, as the Lord has marked out the sky with stars, the fields with flowers,
and the years with seasons, so he has marked out the seasons themselves
with feast days, so that minds sluggish in daily
service, at least once a distinction has been made,
may gladly keep the holy solemnities with prayer when they return
after an interval, and idle minds may through the yearly
feasts make themselves ready for the Lord; for it is irksome to serve
righteousness continually without stain, and for those used to transgressing
it is hard labour to refrain from sin. One runs easily down any
valley; up a slope no one can escape at a run.
Hence the way of falling slopes more steeply down, and the way of life
is harder; the one holds many, the other is steep and for few.
Therefore the good Lord, to shelter all beneath the wings of his love,
gave to the weak, so that they might strive toward the citadel of virtue,
fitting intervals of holy days,
so that by modest observances they may at least touch the outermost
garments of Christ, and even the hem may heal those
who, not wholly banished from the realm of salvation,
lodge within the stalls of everlasting life,
far from the first rank, not far from the second.
For the first rank of life is to weave all
one's days through with unbroken goodness, and at all times
to celebrate Christ's holy Pasch with chaste worship.
But if my crop springs up mixed with thistles, and the thorn
of earthly toil pricks my untilled heart,
let me at least strive to offer myself to the Lord on feast days,
that with at least a part of myself I may touch the borders of life,
lest I be dragged with my whole body into the fellowship of death.
So, although we who dwell at our station close by
enjoy the continual honour of our holy patron,
whom a devoted throng always celebrates even without his birthday,
nevertheless, like household slaves on their master's
feast days, let us be released from cares and sing our prayers;
I shall go as leader of this rejoicing before the brothers as they sing psalms,
and lead the company like a standard-bearer.
For though crowds of people from various regions
pour out their pious joys today with like prayers,
yet it befits me to rejoice more richly and more notably on this
day, because no one is more bound to him as debtor
than I, for whom, under a private and more special star,
this day brought forth so great a patron without end.
Hail, dear day; hail, my light; hail,
ever festal to me! But this year you have risen and shone
more brightly for me, because together with the honour of Felix
you bring Nicetas back, so that through love of two saints
I may have a double birthday today, on which, celebrating the departure
of the martyr taken in the body, and the return of the bishop present in the body,
see, I worship, filled to the full,
welcoming Christ as he takes up lodging in a lowly heart.
Let my soul now exult and proclaim what once
the bride, loving and full of song, sang to her loving Lord:
'The rain is gone, the winter has departed, the voice of the turtledove on high
sounds in our land, the vine gives its fragrance';
and on earth we marvel at the flowering lilies of heaven.
Whence, I ask, has the year suddenly reversed the order of the seasons
and brought on spring, and flowers are seen in the frozen fields?
Nicetas is here, attended by friends of Christ the Lord;
this is why the winter turns to spring, why on every side
a quickening breeze breathes fragrant scents on us;
from this heart comes the breath of a blessed field.
A life of chastity and a mind shining with clear truth
make Nicetas the flowers and spices of Christ.
What worthy of so great a gift, with heart or lips,
can I, poor, foolish and small as I am, bring forth?
Now I need Felix himself, and herein lies his gift to me:
that he take from Christ riches which he himself may impart to me,
so that I may thank him worthily. And now I would wish
that living rivers of everlasting water might flow from my belly,
so that not by my own mouth but by Christ's gift I might
tell of my joy, which by Christ's gift
floods my peaceful heart more richly than usual
and doubles Felix's birthday for me through a manifold
love. I see before me, in the light of day,
Nicetas smiling at me; and, seeing my father,
whose love reigns in me above all others, I myself
become a Nicetas, bearing the likeness of his blessed name
in a mind that now triumphs, its prayer victorious.
Seeing him come from afar after so long a time
for your birthday, most glorious Felix,
shall I not confess that he has come under the guidance of your hand?
For who could fail to discern by so clear a sign
that this came to me through your prayer: that what I could scarcely
embrace in my prayers, or even imagine in sleep,
I should hold Nicetas once more, face to face, on the very
birthday of Felix, in sight and in embrace together,
and sing again in his presence what I owe, Felix,
with you as listener? But what am I to do, I ask? A poor man,
I sit at a rich man's table, and, wretch that I am, dare to put
my hand to great dishes; nor do I consider that it befits me
to prepare in return such things as I receive,
and to offer a word worthy of this judge.
So grant to your needy servant, holy one, that I may dare to speak words worthy of you, my patron,
and equally worthy of your friend.
I call upon your kindred, Felix, to join you at your festival.
The prayers I call yours are mine, and these are more truly
my prayers; for your lofty honour refuses earthly
joys. But since our joys belong to your palm of victory,
and you deign to count the prayers of your own as yours,
therefore, Felix, I implore your kindred too;
be present here as well, so that you may ask them, once called, to be present to me.
You who dwell in the joyful gardens of paradise in heaven,
and you who rest beneath the lofty altar of the Lord,
fair choir of the apostolic band, and you patriarchs,
the earlier race, both choirs of princes, whom in twofold rank
God marked out as fathers by twelve names,
for calling nations and peoples to the heavenly kingdom;
you too, holy prophets, I humbly entreat,
who foretold that God would come in our flesh;
you also, martyrs, who with bodies slain and blood poured out
bore witness to the Lamb slain and living;
all one offspring from divine springs,
whom pious Abraham, holy Isaac and gentle Jacob
begot for God through countless seed,
seed divided in two by heavenly and by perishable merits,
equalling with the one the stars of the sky, with the other the sand of the earth.
I believe indeed that you have gathered from everywhere
for this day in loving duty, out of love for Felix,
to celebrate as his comrades the honour of the confessor.
Yet I am not so presumptuous of such great honour
as to pray that all the saints should at once, for that reason,
breathe into my senses, as though I were worthy of so great a gift
that the voice of the turtledove might resound from my mouth,
the voice which the joyful earth heard throughout the world;
but because a divine voice befits the honour of Felix,
and because Nicetas, the Lord's servant and bishop,
sent to me just now from a distant land,
has come, see, for this day: a man as good in his teaching speech
as he is holy in his conquering soul and his conquered body.
Oh, if only a Cherub would take with fiery tongs
a coal from the very altar of the Lord and bring it out from afar
and burn the grossly fat lips of a sinner,
so that, my mouth purged of its caked filth,
not as from my own mouth but as from the mouth of my hearer,
I might more worthily bring forth with my mouth what I have drawn from him,
lest the harsh and sickly speech of a dull sinner
both defile chaste ears and assault learned ones!
But since my master himself sits at my side,
I shall often gaze with reverent eyes at him seated close by,
facing me; perhaps from the wise man's mouth,
like the worn-out flocks of the shepherd Jacob long ago,
I may conceive fruitful thoughts in my barren breast.
For Nicetas too, blessed by the Lord, like that
gentle Israel, a shepherd of sheep and of kids as well,
sits before the trough of living water; he too, with equal heart,
chooses for himself three rods from three kinds of tree,
and setting them in the water calls the flock, and as they mate
makes them conceive, and with the three rods colours what is conceived,
so that by the rods, their bark peeled in patches,
the marked offspring of the holy flock may be proved.
But on this flock it is not Laban's mark but the mark of life;
for the mark of death will be not to be marked by Christ.
So grace renews barren souls in the threefold Name,
and the Spirit, as husband, fills them by union with the Word,
and the Church marks inwardly the offspring conceived for God,
fruitful with virgin womb and mother of salvation,
while, intent on the three rods, she drinks in, moistened, the seeds of the Word
and is sealed with the light of the eternal face.
Hence the barren woman has borne seven, and she who abounded has failed,
as God enlarges the lowly and brings low the proud.
So I, on seeing Nicetas, as though I had found a spring,
ran like a thirsty sheep to the living streams,
parched, and at once felt my udders swell;
and, gazing long and intently at the face of my master as he fed us,
I looked on the varied rods in his learned breast
and drank in with fixed eyes the colour I beheld,
and his dewy mind sprinkled me with divine drops.
But since mention has been made of these three rods,
let us, if you please, look further into the mysteries of the kingdom.
The patriarch chose for himself three rods from three kinds of tree:
the fragrant one of storax, the light one of plane, the firm one of nut.
The Spirit is in the plane, the Virgin in the storax, Christ in the nut.
For the plane tree spreads its broad branches into shade;
the Holy Spirit formed Christ in the overshadowed Virgin;
and I think the storax rod must be the Virgin, who from the tree of David
brought forth, a virgin giving birth, the fragrant flower.
The nut rod is Christ, since in nuts the food is within,
the shell is outside, and over the green skin is the bitter rind.
Behold Christ, God veiled in our body,
who is fragile in flesh, food in the Word, and bitter in the cross;
his hard surface is the word of the cross, and the cross is food,
enclosing Christ's heavenly kernel within the flesh.
But again he is sweet through the cross, because on the tree
our God, who is Life, brought forth life; my Life hung on the wood
so that my life might stand firm for God. What, O Life, shall I repay
you, Christ, for my life? Unless perhaps I take the cup
of salvation which your right hand offers me to drink,
that I may be washed with the holy draught of a precious death.
But what am I to do? Even if I gave my own body to the flames
and held myself cheap, not even by shedding my blood
would I pay you my just debts, for I would only be giving myself back to you in exchange for myself;
and whatever I do in like return, I shall always fall short
of you, Christ, because you, Christ, paid for me my debts, not yours,
suffering for wicked servants.
What love could weigh against yours? You, the Lord, took my form,
so that I, the servant, might take your form. And is it thought a great thing
to buy one's own salvation with something that perishes,
to exchange the passing for the everlasting, to sell earth
and buy heaven? See how much more dearly God bought me
by the death of the cross! He suffered, brought low in the likeness of a slave,
to buy worthless slaves with precious blood.
But what am I doing? Recklessly I am carried out onto the unsafe deep,
daring to trust myself to the heights on a frail wing;
singing, as is my custom, the birthday of the illustrious martyr
on a lighter theme, I have suddenly soared to the summit,
flying above the stars, and have stretched my bold mind,
launching my speech, to the very source of things.
Where does this spirit in me come from? What breeze lifts me so proudly?
I do not recognise my swelling breast; a greater mind is driving it.
I feel Nicetas, as he sits close beside me and
touches me and breathes near me, pressed to my side.
The keen breath of the one breathing beside me enters me
and powerfully kindles an unaccustomed fire in me as I compose,
bringing its tinder close to warm my chilled vitals to life.
But I will check these swelling blasts, nor, small as I am, will I
aspire to speak things too great for me; I will return,
little, to the ground I left, and go on the level foot of modest song.
Although I cannot speak of Felix's sublime merit
without the praise of God, do you, holy Nicetas, receive me
into your fatherly bosom, and while I am upheld by your learned breast,
resting my head upon your gentle heart,
let your salt season my insipid self, and let your rich vein
water my thirsty thoughts with an unfailing stream.
I will say it again, rejoicing, and, still scarcely believing this gift,
I will ask it twice over: Tell me, please, have you returned,
and do I hold you, Nicetas, your very self, on whom until now,
sick at heart, I hung night and day with a wasting soul?
Have you come at last, restored to me in the fourth year?
But thanks be to Christ, who has brought you back, however late.
How I feared that the enemy might hold you cut off
in the lands between us by the opposing cloud of war!
But with longing overcoming all, you broke the chains
that stood in your way to us; neither the sea nor any toil
nor fear of the Goths nor the harsh cold of long
roads held you back. Truly, Nicetas, in such great
hazards you were conquered by affection and conqueror by kindness,
strong and weak alike, but mightily both.
Conquered by friendship, conquered by love of Felix,
you conquered harsh labours by tender devotion.
Come now, holy father, give me your ear and your hand;
let us knot our palms together in a mutual bond,
and, our right hands clasped in a reciprocal pact,
let us weave varied talk as we stroll along.
I would like to recount and also show to my anxious father
what we have done throughout the time he was
away. For to whom should I more rightly unfold my doings
and recount what has been accomplished for us by Felix's hand
than to one who cares for us? He, by the double right of master
and father, may approve what is well done and condemn what is wrong,
correct mistakes and calmly order what remains to be done;
he may help with his prayers what is unfinished, and, as bishop, dedicate
what is finished; and so he may move freely to and fro
in Felix's buildings, as one who bears Felix himself in his whole heart
and may take pride in them as in his father's hall.
So come, father, and keep step with me as my companion,
while I lead you round through each of the works.
Look: this portico, where the first gate receives you,
was formerly buried under a dark roof;
now it has risen anew with paintings and a higher roof.
And where the forecourt, enclosed all round by a squared covering,
lies open to the sky in its central space,
there used to be a little garden of poorly tended turf; the worthless plot
yielded scanty vegetables that served no purpose.
Meanwhile the desire came upon us to build this work
in this place; for the situation itself seemed to call
for this adornment, so that, with the doors thrown open on the facing front,
a more joyful splendour might light up from afar
the martyr's venerable hall, and the bright front, open
through double arches, might flood the interior with abundant
light, facing the conspicuous tomb
where the martyr lies asleep, his body laid to rest:
Felix, who from the threshold of his gleaming throne
gazes out over his courts through the twice-double doors thrown open to the light,
exulting, and rejoices that his walls are overcome by pious
gatherings, and his spacious halls by joyful peoples,
and that the dense crowds find relief through numerous doors.
And the hall itself, where the tomb of the holy martyr stands,
cleansed of its age, has taken on a new appearance.
Three hands, working with varied ornaments, have embellished it:
a pair of craftsmen in the coffered ceiling and the marble,
and a painter with images portraying holy faces.
Look, you see how great a splendour, as if in a temple reborn,
the carved coffering smiles with from its rippling vault.
In wood it imitates ivory, and from the roof above
hanging lamps are held by bronze chains,
and in the empty space between, the wandering lights sway on slack
cords, while a light breeze tosses their flickering flames.
The hall that once stood on piers, now propped on columns,
has spurned its cheap rubble for a nobler stone.
But let us return to the forecourt. Look up at the cells
set above the long porticoes under a double roof,
dwellings fit to be assigned to good men
whom, to pay due honour to holy Felix,
zeal for prayer, not a taste for drinking, has brought here.
For, like upper rooms joined on to the holy roofs,
they look down from their high windows upon the protected altars,
beneath which the bodies of saints have their resting place.
For apostles' ashes too, laid beneath the heavenly table,
give off a fragrance pleasing to Christ from their breathing,
sacred dust amid the holy offerings.
Here is father Andrew; here is he who, a fisherman sent to Argos,
taught vain-talking tongues to fall silent;
who, after he had freed peoples by breaking the nets
of wicked error and had drawn them into the nets of Christ,
condemned Thessalian Patras by shedding his blood.
Here too is the Lord's forerunner, John the Baptist,
the holy gateway of the gospel and the goal of the law;
he too, coming as a guest to the halls of my Felix,
honours his brother's tomb with a portion of his ashes.
Here lies Thomas the doubter, with his second name, Didymus, the Twin;
Christ let him doubt with the hesitation of a fearful mind
for the sake of our faith, so that we too,
strengthened by his lead and trembling before our Lord and God,
may confess that Jesus lives after death in a true
body, showing the living wounds of his flesh,
so that, when the day comes on which God will come, manifest in open
light, the rebels who nailed him may recognise him, trembling,
as he shines in the flesh that was tortured.
Here is Luke, a physician first by art and then by speech,
Luke, twice a physician: as once he cured those sick in body
with earthly aid, so now for sick minds
he has compounded the medicines of life in a twofold book.
With them, their companions in piety, faith, virtue and crown,
are the martyrs Agricola and Vitalis, joined with Proculus,
and Euphemia, the martyr who on the shores of Chalcedon
marks the coast hallowed by her virgin blood.
Bologna is the resting place of Vitalis, Agricola and Proculus,
whom sworn faith called to the arms of devotion,
and an equal victory covered with saving palms
their glorious bodies, pierced with nails as large as beams.
Here too is the martyr Nazarius, whom, by the faithful gift
of the noble Ambrose, I received with humbled mind;
he too deigns to share Felix's roof as a fellow guest
and adds his brothers' dwellings to his own abode.
Although all the saints together throughout the whole world are, through the one
God, everywhere, since through him they are everywhere presented
to God as members of his body, yet places have been allotted
to the bodies of the saints; and not only where a region holds
the whole body does the grace of those laid there live on,
but wherever there is any part of a holy body, there too, God bearing witness,
their power stands forth in proofs of their blessed merit;
and great power, even in the tiny dust of the saints,
proclaims the might of an apostle's body with telling voice.
So whoever lives chastely in the upper rooms
will be their neighbour, as will the stranger from afar who, moved by upright
affection, has hastened to the holy buildings;
when he wishes to approach Christ in private to pray,
whether by day or by night he wishes to pour out his prayers,
he may step out readily, as a guest, from the adjoining threshold.
Admire this too: that the martyr's lofty house,
by the law of the sacrament, opens through three doorways
(for it confesses one kingdom under a threefold name).
and the way the buildings, woven together with their structures joined to one another,
signify with holy right that, though the houses built
have many roofs, holy peace has only one
house, and harmony makes one body out of many members,
a body whose framework stands firm on Christ as its head.
Perhaps amid these sights you may eagerly ask
how this rich courtyard is to be filled with so many fountains,
since the city is far off and almost no aqueduct from the city
sends a meagre drop here along its thin channel.
I shall answer that we trust nothing to our own right hand
and rely on no earthly resources, but have entrusted everything to almighty
God and count on heaven for our fountains.
So we have built cisterns beside the roofs on every side,
to catch the rivers that God pours down from the clouds,
so that the hollow marble basins may all flow from brimming lips.
But if at times a shortage of water should occur,
the courtyard, laid out in ordered arrangement and marked with varied figures,
bright as flowers with shell patterns and painted cones,
will perhaps be worth seeing even with its basins dry.
For you know too how, in the great temple of Solomon,
the dry sea was an ornament, which the wise king
made of solid bronze and raised up on bronze oxen.
Look now at the other side: see how a single portico
and a wall, with a double opening between its central columns,
join by an entrance the halls that their roofs keep separate.
Now it is time to let our roaming eyes pass into this church,
which, opened along its long side, gains along with the light of the sky
extra space for its roof, which opens into the adjoining courts,
linking what was separate by means of inserted arches,
and offers the people the sight of a well-watered field,
which, however, walls set round it in a built enclosure
shut in, so that the holy buildings may not lie open to profane eyes,
and so that covered walkways may shield the open forecourt from the weather.
Do not wonder that the holy sheepfolds are growing in size;
everywhere the mighty glory of the eternal Christ is growing,
the honour of the saints is heaped up, and one God is known
by all, because the Holy Spirit illumines the world
and the Son, the heir, reigns with the coeternal Father;
hence holy grace, spreading abroad the light of truth,
multiplies among the peoples the seeds of eternal life.
And since the good shepherd increases his sheep, Christ on high is glad
to see the sheepfolds grow spacious along with the flocks of the redeemed.
Enter these buildings, bishop, singing psalms and hymns in response,
and carry my prayers to the Lord, and join your joys
to my prayers as you celebrate the feast of our common patron.
At the fitting time you will plead for a sinner
with the Lord, who rejoices at the honour paid to his confessor.
With Felix as guide, your prayers will be borne along an easy path;
Felix will go before you to the divine ears,
and while you offer holy rites and psalms together with devoted
service, Christ will descend with gracious power
to veil the people and the temple in a holy mist,
pouring a snow-white cloud through the covered sanctuary.
Now I want you to see the paintings in their long procession
along the coloured porticoes, and to tire your neck a little, bent back,
while with face tilted upward you read them all through.
Whoever sees these and recognizes the truths in empty figures
feeds his believing mind on an image that is not empty.
For the painting contains, in faithful sequence, everything
that aged Moses wrote in his five books,
and what was done by Joshua, who was marked with the Lord's name,
under whose leadership the Jordan, its flood held back and its waves
stopped fast, halted before the face of the divine ark.
A strange force divided the river: one part, its stream driven back,
stood still, while the other part of the river slid away and ran into the sea
and left its bed empty; and where the strong current rushed from its source,
it had heaped the gathered waves up high,
and a mountain of water hung menacing in a trembling mass,
looking down on feet crossing the dried-up depths,
and on the dusty footprints of men walking dry-shod
through the middle of the river over the hard mud.
Now run your attentive eyes over Ruth, who in a short book
marks the division of the times, when the Judges ended and the Kings began.
This story
seems short, but it signifies the mysteries of a great war,
in that the twin sisters part from each other in opposite directions.
Ruth follows the holy mother-in-law whom Orpah deserts;
one daughter-in-law shows faithlessness, the other faith:
one prefers God to her homeland, the other prefers her homeland to life.
