Does not this discord, I ask you, persist throughout the whole world,
with one part following God and the other rushing to ruin across the earth?
And would that the shares of death and of salvation were equal!
But the broad way takes in many, and error, beyond recall,
sweeps those who slip on the downward slope into easy ruin.
Perhaps someone may ask for what reason
we settled on this plan: to paint holy
houses, an unusual practice, with likenesses of living creatures.
Listen, and I will try to set out the reasons briefly.
What crowds the glory of Saint Felix draws here
is unknown to no one; but the larger throng here
is country folk, not lacking in faith but not taught to read.
Long accustomed to serving profane rites,
with their belly for a god, they are at last converted, newcomers to Christ,
as they marvel at the works of the saints made manifest in Christ.
See how many gather from all the countryside,
and how piously they go astray, misled by their untaught minds.
They have left distant homes and scorned the frosts,
not chilled, for their faith is fervent; and now, look, in crowds
they stay awake and prolong their rejoicing through the whole night,
keeping sleep away with gladness and darkness with torches.
But would that they celebrated these joys with sober devotion
and did not bring their own cups to mingle with the holy thresholds.
Although the fasting company gives back a better
service, as it chants holy hymns with chaste voices
and, sober, offers to the Lord the praise it has sung,
still I think such joys should be forgiven the little ones
who celebrate them with feasting, because error has crept into
their untaught minds; and their simplicity, unaware of so great a fault,
falls through piety, wrongly believing that the saints
rejoice when their tombs are drenched with fragrant wine.
So do they approve, now that they are dead, what as teachers they condemned?
Does Peter's table accept what Peter's teaching rejects?
Everywhere there is one cup of the Lord, one food, and one
table and house of God. Let wine go off to the taverns;
the church is a holy house of prayer. Give way to the consecrated
thresholds, serpent! In this hall it is not wicked sport
that is your due, but punishment; you mix mockery
with your own torments, enemy. At odds with yourself, you both
howl in torment and sing among the cups.
You fear Felix, and foolishly you scorn Felix;
drunk, you insult him; guilty, you plead with him; and, wretch, you revel
before the very judge whose vengeance punishes you in the flames.
For this reason it seemed to us a useful work to adorn
all the buildings of Felix with the play of holy painting,
in the hope that, through these sights, the painted forms
in their colours might capture the astonished minds of the country folk.
Inscriptions are written above them, so that the writing may show
what the hand has set out; and while they all point out the paintings
to one another in turn and read them over, they may be slower
to think of food, while a fasting that delights the eyes nourishes them;
and so a better habit may steal into them in their wonder,
while the painting beguiles their hunger; and as they read
the holy stories, the virtue of chaste deeds creeps upon them,
brought in by holy examples; the gaping drinker drinks in
sobriety, and forgetfulness of excess wine comes over them.
And while they spend the day gazing at length,
the cups grow fewer, since, with the time drawn out by the wonders,
only a few hours now remain to the feasters.
As for the rest of these things that we see done and painted,
I offer them to you as matter for prayer on my behalf, asking
that, as you carry on Felix's cause, you pray earnestly for me.
And it is fitting that the one you accompany with devoted mind
you should also resemble in the face of your mind and follow in spirit,
his equal in love for me; for, wretch though I am, I do not doubt that I am loved
by the martyr, granted at least the love one gives a little puppy,
since my life, home, property, grace, glory, and bread
are Felix, by God's gift. With him as leader, ask
that my foundations may be laid upon the holy mountains
and that the tower I have begun may be finished without interruption to the work.
From Genesis, I beg you, gather this meaning for your prayer:
that I may not remain an earthly Adam, but be born of virgin earth
and, having put off the old, be formed as a new image.
May I be led out of my own land and become a stranger
to my own kin, and hasten to the honeyed rivers of the promised land,
kept safe from the fire of the Chaldean furnace.
May I be ready, like Lot, to keep my roof always open,
so that I may be rescued from Sodom; and may I not turn my eyes back,
lest, lacking the salt of the heart, I be turned into a pillar of salt.
May I be offered to God as a living sacrifice, like the boy Isaac,
and, carrying my own wood, follow my kindly father beneath the cross.
May I find wells, but may Amalek, I pray, not choke them,
the envious one who blinds the springs of living water.
May I be a fugitive from the world, as blessed Jacob
was a fugitive from his brother Edom, and under my weary
head may I lay a stone to be consecrated, and rest in Christ.
May I have chaste love, and also a horror of sinful love,
so that, like Joseph unstained, I may flee the allurements of the flesh,
my body slipped free of its bonds, free
of sin, leaving my fleshly garment to the world as spoil.
For it is time to keep far from embraces; the last day
is at hand, the Lord is already near; it is time now to rise from sleep
and to keep watch, ready for the Lord's knock.
May my going out from Egypt be a good one, so that, with the law as my guide,
passing through the parted surges of my billowing heart,
I may escape the waves of the Red Sea and sing the Lord's triumph
once Pharaoh is drowned; to the Lord, with suppliant prayer,
exulting in trembling and rejoicing with fear,
I commend my labours, which are his own holy gifts.
Support with your prayer, Nicetas, what I pray for; and all of you as well
who have gathered here together for holy religion,
devoted to the Lord and giving thanks, say with me:
These things, Christ our God, with slight and fragile means
we make for our own sake; for you, supreme Creator,
cannot be contained by works made by hands, you whom the world with its whole body
cannot contain, for whom heaven is narrow and the earth a mere point.
But offering devoted service without end to your saints,
we honour great ones with our slight tribute,
hoping that, with them as our intercessors, you
may set in us the finished summits of your works
and be present to dwell in the minds you have built up.
XXVIII.
Into our old observance a new [?] theme is born for us,
and the customary solemnities grow with an unaccustomed vow;
at once the matter for my song and at once the birthday of kindly
Felix are doubled in his buildings by
these newly born works which, with lofty masses on every side,
you see have sprung up, shining with equal adornment.
Here, surrounded far and wide by long colonnades,
the forecourts open up, an open space enclosed by roofs,
and the courts lay open at once the stars to the eyes and passage to those entering.
There halls are joined by adjoining walls,
and, spreading wide in their layout and yet meeting together, open,
they join rival roof-ridges with interlocking beams
and stand out, beautiful in varied yet matching adornment
of marble, painting, coffered ceilings and columns;
among them the charm is varied also by small chambers,
which, in the colonnades, where a single
colonnade stretches in one line into a longer, confined space,
are set against its side; three openings close at hand disclose them,
and three doorways with running lattice-screens lay them open.
Holy names mark the middle one, with painted martyrs,
whom equal glory has crowned, though differing in sex.
But the two that open on the right and on the left
faithful painting adorns with two stories each.
The sacred deeds of holy men fill one:
Job, tested by wounds, and Tobit, by loss of sight;
but the other the lesser sex possesses: renowned Judith,
with whom powerful Queen Esther is also depicted.
The inner court smiles with varied ornaments,
glad above with its roofs, and open to the light, with serene
facades, and wreathed below with snow-white columns.
In its open center stands a gleaming cantharus,
which a bronze tower covers with a latticed dome.
Other vessels stand placed under the open air
as little fountains; set in a pleasing and varied order,
they differ in workmanship but agree in their vein of metal,
and a single water flows from different mouths into capacious basins.
This court, joined to the three basilicas, lies open to them all,
and from one point opens different entrances to all of them,
and likewise receives in one embrace the different
exits from the three, spacious with its central pavement;
yet a series of gleaming basins, set out in ranks
through five rows, densely packed in close-set
marble, makes it a marvel to the eyes but narrows it for those who stroll;
but in the surrounding colonnades there is ample room
to walk about, and at the lattices set between the columns
the weary may lean, and from there gaze at the flowing
waters, and with dry feet look upon the wet
ground without treading on it, and in pleasant rivalry
admire the fountains leaping with a gentle murmur.
Not only in wintertime is this convenience
ready to please; for just as the shade of the roof delights in the heat,
so sunny places please in the cold, and dry ones in the rain.
On the other side lies open an outer court, equally surrounded
by colonnades, lesser in adornment, greater in extent.
Before the sacred buildings it spreads a forecourt visible from afar,
which, with chambers built under a double roof,
through the converging beams of interconnected houses
imitates the look of a fortress with the appearance of a wall,
and opens a forum wide enough for assemblies to walk about in.
What sign venerable Felix lately gave in this place
I will tell in a swift account.
In the middle of the open ground, facing the threshold of the venerable hall,
there remained two huts built of wood,
awkward in position and ugly to look at,
which shamelessly destroyed all the beauty of the works, blinding
the view with a foul obstruction; for the door of the open
basilica, darkened by the little hovel set in front of it,
stood open in vain, as though its doors were shut.
When we wished to remove them, those who lodged in those huts
met us with defiant words
and swore that they could sooner bargain away their lives
than be forced to move from the place. Such talk seemed, indeed,
to deserve contempt; but this very thing was, I confess,
a cause of ill will to me, for I was loath to win even by a quarrel.
Meanwhile, one night, as those lulled to sleep were beginning
to take their first rest, behold, leaping from the abandoned
hearth, a spark kindled in one
hidden corner of those very huts, from the straw of hay
on which it had chanced to fall, a sudden fire; and soon, spreading through
the hut itself, it gathered strength from the dry fuel
and snatched an enormous flame from the brittle tinder,
then, bursting out with easy passage through the rotten timbers of the old
roof, it hurled the blaze in great
turbid whirls, churned a hot cloud through the air,
and hid the stars with black smoke.
Its very fury, moreover, gave out a terrible crash,
resounding with the heavier crackling of the brittle timber;
and on all the dwellings laid out round about for the village farmers,
and even on the fields set farther off from the village,
so did the heat blow, so did the dreadful light strike,
so did a fiery shower sprinkle roofs near and far
with sparks flying far and wide,
that we, suddenly roused by mournful laments on every side,
with the roofs all around bathed in a monstrous light,
seeing everything about us shining as in open daylight,
thought that everything had been seized by the flames and was burning,
and that the very palaces of the saints were at the same time
ablaze with so great a fire, and that those flashes were reflected from all the roofs at once —
flashes which filled even distant places with scattered
fires and scorched the countryside with great heat,
so that each man feared for his own roof, as though all the torches
were close to it, drawing in the burning heat at close quarters
and air infected with a dreadful reek.
We, trembling as though the danger were nearer to our own houses,
presumed nothing on our own strength; for whence would weak men have
force and hands enough to quench that great mass,
when the flame went on, more inflamed by its own
fuel, and, sprung suddenly from a little hut,
was drenching all the roofs at once with threatening fire?
So, relying only on faith and suppliant prayer, we run
to the nearby threshold of my Felix, and from there
we hasten with like prayers to the adjoining hall
and beg healing from the power of the apostles' ashes,
bowing our faces beneath the altars set above them.
Returning home myself, I bring out a piece of wood, small but great for salvation,
taken from a fragment of the eternal cross,
and holding it in my hand I thrust it from afar against the opposing flames,
as if holding a shield before my breast to cover myself
and ward off the enemy, beaten back by the boss thrust against him.
Believe it, and do not credit it to me, but render
thanks to Christ and give just praise to the Almighty;
for our salvation rests on the cross of Christ and on his name;
hence our faith, too, relying on the cross in this danger,
availed us, and the flame recognized our salvation.
It was not my voice or my hand, but the power of the cross that terrified
the fire, and in the very place from which it had risen
compelled the flame, as though fenced in by a prescribed boundary,
to sink down and be extinguished, its roaring dying away,
and the storm born from ashes to return to ashes.
How great is the power of the cross! Forsaking its own nature,
fire, which devours all wood, is burned by the wood of the cross.
Many hands then, dousing that blaze with vessel after vessel,
longed to conquer it with abundant water;
but although their showers matched the drained fountains,
yet with greater force, while those throwing it grew weary, the fire
had conquered all the water. We put out the fire with wood,
and a tiny splinter conquered the flame that water could not.
Afterwards, when fear had departed and the light that calls to labor
had brought back the longed-for day, we went out to see the doings
of the night and, though they still smoked far and wide,
to view with untroubled eyes the traces of the quenched flame.
And we believed that we would see very great damage to houses,
remembering the great terror and the fire;
but our expectation quickly shrank once we saw the facts,
and we see that nothing was burned except what ought to be burned,
and that one of those two
lodgings had burned — which our own hand, had the flame not taken it,
would have taken away. But Felix's grace also served us
with this gift: that, anticipating our labor
with useful flames, it afforded us a saving of work
there; for the flame had left standing a house like the burned one,
not so as to allow it to stand, itself
blocking the double doors with a like obstruction,
but so that the flame might punish that tenant with this too,
preserving for him what he himself would soon overturn.
For he who had lately preferred his hovels to the holy buildings,
first punished by the flame in one of them,
soon begins with his own hand to demolish the other hut
and completes his own losses with swift fury,
and laments his beloved dwellings and his empty affections.
Looking at once on the burned roofs and the demolished,
he marvels at unlike ruins in a like heap,
the two-colored wreck of rubble and ash joined together.
Seeing that this triumph had fallen to us without a quarrel,
the wretch accuses only himself, for whom no thanks
for compliance remained, and to whom the shame of punishment remains.
Now, since the facades lie open with the obstruction removed,
let us walk about in word and in spirit in these very
spaces, rejoicing, and let us be borne into the holy halls
and marvel at the sacred figures, monuments of the ancients,
and in three spaces let us read the two Testaments,
perceiving with right sight this reason too:
that the new law is painted in the old buildings, and the old law in the new;
for it is equally a useful beauty for us to have
newness in the old and oldness in the new,
so that there may be at once new life and hoary wisdom,
and that, being old men in gravity and little children in simplicity,
we may draw a balanced mind from both ages,
joining differing ages in our character.
There is also, in the inner part of the greater hall,
a chapel set deep within, like a daughter of that building,
beautiful with its starry dome and curving in a threefold recess
with spaces arranged around; in the middle it gleams with the font
of piety, and wondrously it both renews and is renewed.
For today a twofold renewal adorns it twice over,
while the bishop performs there two offices of Christ;
he dedicates the venerable sanctuary to a twofold use,
joining the holy sacraments to the purifying bath;
thus the sacrifice renews the temple, and grace the font,
and the new font, renewing the person it receives, both gives
a gift and, rather, the newness that it ceases to have through use
it begins, by divine use, to hand on to mortals.
For the font itself, once put to the use of renewing,
ceases to be new; but, being always used for such a gift,
it will never cease to renew the old.
This gift of the Lord, this image, by which through Christ's gift
the same man becomes new and the old man perishes — behold, see it
in the restored roofs of Felix's twin hall.
What had been old now appears to stand new as well;
for they had stood on a vast line of ugly piers.
Now, supported instead by better columns put in their place,
they have gained increase of both space and light,
and, putting off their decay, have taken on renewed youth.
For in these a twofold charm shines for the beholder,
in which renewed roofs vie with new roofs
in equal light; the age of the buildings differs,
their appearance agrees; the hand of the ancients and of the moderns
is in harmony; in like aspect a single beauty adorns both
works; what was founded long ago meets the new.
Nor is any difference visible to the eye; one and the same look shines
in the aged places and the raw; the black grime is hidden,
and painting has given back to the aged roofs a youthful brightness
with an infusion of the bloom of varied colors.
Hence the dates of the works are blended, and outside
newness gleams on the walls, while antiquity lies hidden, covered, within;
painted old age is veiled by the face of youth,
veteran age has blossomed again into a girlish face;
and they are at once old and new, and equally neither new nor old,
not the same and yet at once the same — which is a figure of the future
and present good; for now too it is profitable for us
to wipe away the squalor of the old life and be renewed
with a devout mind, to follow Christ and be made ready for the kingdom.
Then too, when it is granted us to rise again as life returns,
that rank of the risen will be counted the better
which, its flesh bathed from above in shining raiment,
will exchange the form of a servant for the image of the Lord
and, destined to reign with him, will receive an honor conformed to God,
like Christ, but by Christ's gift.
This same image warns us to put off the old form
and to wear the new, to blot out what lies behind,
and to turn the converted mind toward the things of God to come,
to bring fitting forgetfulness upon past cares
and bring into the mind care for the heavenly kingdom,
and to human affairs and the ways of this age
to die in mind before we die in death, and not to be freed
from the bonds of the body before those of sin. So let us be renewed
in our senses, and the muddy deeds of the earthly image
let us hasten to shake far from our body,
shaking out our garments, so that, the filth beaten off,
we may give back the garments of body and soul pure and shining.
And not only sin committed but sin contemplated
let us flee, as we would the plague-bearing air from a rotting corpse,
holding our noses against its foul smell.
Solomon warns that sins are to be feared like the face of a serpent
and shuddered at, and says they are armed with a lion's
teeth; and truly, as with the savage mouth of a lion
they cruelly gnaw [?] the soul which the sick pleasure of the body has conquered
and which the dragon has led away, vanquished, as his food —
he who devours the peoples of Ethiopia, not scorched by the sun
but black with vices and night-colored with sin.
Such Ethiopians the serpent eats; in them he has the food
which, condemned as he is, he is permitted to take, since God called the sinner
and the serpent's food by one name, earth;
and so by that name the one who feeds on sins is devoured by the dragon.
The time has come to change our ways, to rise from sleep
and at last to keep watch for God, and in turn to sleep
to those deeds over which a mind dead to Christ keeps watch.
If God does not open our understanding by the teaching of God,
by the light of the Word, let us at least take examples from the buildings
themselves, and let stones and timbers be teachers
to the dull, so that whatever work we have made here with our hands,
such a work we may make by faith; although the work of the mind
is far removed from the labor of the hands, yet from an unequal cause
a like principle of work is drawn. Look, see: I will prove
that unlike forms come together in a like appearance.
Many remember what the places were like where the new buildings now stand;
for it is only a short time since everything was begun
that now stands finished; what was toiled over for two years
a third year completed, by the prayer of the saints and the help of Christ.
Part of the space was a small garden, part a heap of rubble,
which many hands joined together, with the people's care, removed,
and they rooted out the cheap vegetables along with the briars,
so that the area, cleared, might lie open with a smooth surface,
which now, its acreage adorned with marble stones,
gleams, paved far and wide, forgetful of its former cultivation.
How well it has changed its appearance! After serving for dung,
the adornment of marble; after cheap cabbage it bears
Parian basins, and what once glistened with filth now gleams with water.
In what way, then, will this building now give me a pattern
by which I may cultivate, build, and renew myself
in my senses, and lay myself out as a site measured for Christ?
The reasoning is ready to hand: what my earth is, what in me
is rubble, and whence thorns spring up in my field.
The earth is the heart; the faults of a depraved heart are the rubble;
idle luxury, impure love, stained lust
are the rubble of the soul; so too anxious care for the body,
devouring envy and greedy hunger, heavy anger, fickle hope,
and ambition, lavish with its own and thirsting for another's,
are thorns to the mind, since with empty goads they constantly torment
wavering souls, which are continually burned
by the wretched fear of want and the wretched passion for possessing.
And so, even amid riches they are poor, and like that Tantalus
amid the waters they thirst, and do not have what they seem to have.
For they fear to use what they have gained, and leave behind what they have hoarded,
and while they lay up sustenance, they lose the time for living.
These thorns, then, this rubble, from our bristling minds
we must clear away, and tear out by its fibers this first
root of all crimes, from which the unhappy tree
sprouts; let it fall, struck at the root by the Lord's
axe, so that it may never sprout in our fields.
If this root withers, its source of nourishment cut away from us,
all wickedness will fall, every vice will perish,
all evils will follow the fall of their mother,
and as their tree dies, its fruits will perish with it.
Then, with the garden well cleared, the house will be built,
and, founded on living soil, the structure of the divine undertaking
will rise well on high. Christ himself will raise up columns
in us and will dissolve the old
piers of the obstructed soul, and the King will make room for himself
in our senses, so that he may walk about in them,
as in the five porticoes of Solomon
Wisdom used to direct its healing steps, with holy speech,
healing bodies by touching and hearts by teaching.
Let us not, then, be old amid new buildings,
so that Christ, who dwells in the heart, may visit new hearts.
For a worse tear results when new and old are forced together,
and new wine is rightly put into new wineskins.
Let the former life perish, lest the life to come perish.
Let us leave the world willingly, which we must lose unwillingly
unless we flee it willingly; let us die, so that we may not die;
let us bury a deadly life beneath a life-giving death.
Let the earthly image perish, let the heavenly take its place,
and let Adam be turned into Christ; let us be changed here
so that we may be changed there; whoever now remains the same
in himself will not be changed from himself for all eternity.
XXIX.
Come, [?] to songs; let my voice flow, articulate in modest
measures. Be present, O rich cause of my speaking,
Felix, and steal into my heart with your silent breath.
Your spirit will run through my mouth. Be the fountain
of my words, and I will be the pipe for your streams,
which you will supply to me from the river of the divine Word.
Rise, then, and with your gentle breath enter
my heart, O Felix, father and lord and patron;
you are my home, my medicine and my wisdom, Felix;
now sharpen my mind, dulled through long leisure,
quickening my heart with fiery light.
But I must not pour out my speech over that sea,
running through the merits or the miracles of the saints
and trying to unfold in verse all that, through all the saints
since the beginning of things, God bestows and performs,
which neither the human mind can grasp nor the tongue express.
And what wonder is it if paper, in a whole volume,
cannot hold what the whole world itself cannot hold?
For greater than the world is the world's Creator, God himself the King,
who fills earth and heaven; him whom this world
cannot contain the saints contain, not by the bulk of their bodies,
but humble in devotion and capacious through a pure heart.
Now, therefore, as I recount the divine good deeds of my patron
Felix — both the benefits for life he has conferred on me
and those which, providing them by heavenly help, he does not cease
to confer as gifts on the devout almost every
day, bestowing holy gifts through various signs —
the order of his merits demands that Christ be praised;
I shall seem to praise not a man but rather him
by whose authority Felix, mighty, holds his venerable name
and gives healing resources, by which he visits sick
bodies and frees souls held captive by the power of the black demon,
God prevailing. Nor is it in this help alone
that bountiful Felix works the gifts of Christ
and most mightily triumphs over the serpent enemy.
XXX. (Inscriptions of the Old Basilica.)

Felix's sanctuary, venerable for its ancient worship, now opens a new light through widened spaces. You who remember the narrow throne, rejoice to see how this throne now shines to the praise of the patron.

Before, the place was small, too narrow for performing the sacred rites, and it did not allow suppliants to spread out their hands; now it offers the people spacious altars for the sacred offices in the bosom of the martyr who lies in their midst. All things renewed are pleasing to God; Christ is always renewing all things and enlarging them to a fullness of light. So too, honoring the throne of his beloved Felix, he has enlarged it in splendor and in space alike.
XXXI.
Before, a boy of famous parents, bearing his grandfather's name,
he was Celsus; but now, as he deserved, he is "celsus" indeed, living on high,
for Christ the Lord heaped so great a gift on him
that, young in years, he came new to the waters,
so that, an infant twice over, both in the span of his age and in the font of washing,
he might be carried forward to God by a twofold grace.
Alas! What shall I do? I struggle, hanging between two kinds of love:
should I rejoice or grieve? The boy deserves both;
love urges tears on me, and love urges joy,
but faith bids me rejoice, and family love bids me weep.
I weep that so small a harvest from so sweet a child
was granted to his parents, and in so brief a time.
Then again, when I turn over in my mind the lasting goods of eternal life,
which God prepares in heaven for the innocent,
I rejoice that he has died, having finished his mortal course in a short life,
so that he might quickly enjoy the riches of God,
and not, mingled with the wicked, drag out earthly contagions for long
in the fragile lodging of the body,
but, stained by no crime of this world,
might go the more worthily to the eternal Lord.
So the infant was owed to God rather than to us,
and yet, for our sake too, he was pleasing to God.
The little one had begun to bring on his eighth year,
driving his first seasons round in swift laps.
Already he bore the yoke of boyhood on his tender neck,
subject to a schoolmaster's harsh commands,
and whatever he was taught, the noble boy, to his teacher's admiration,
drank in with a ready mind.
His parents rejoiced with anxious, foreboding hearts,
fearing that so great a gift might provoke envy.
Nor was the wait long: Christ, God, summoning from heaven
the soul that pleased him, took it up with the honor it deserved,
and snatched him suddenly from the earth, because it was more fitting
that he should live joined to the assemblies of the holy.
The cause of death was a fluid that flooded his throat,
by which a heavy swelling puffed up his milk-white neck;
then, driven back, it went away, but slipping inward it fled to the inmost parts
of the body and drove life from his vitals.
The earth received its share when the flesh was buried;
the spirit departed, carried in an angel's embrace.
His bereaved parents led an empty funeral;
Celsus lives joyful in the grove on high.
Spare yourselves, I beg, devoted parents, from sinning by many
tears, lest your love turn into a fault.
For it is an impious love that mourns a blessed soul,
and to weep for one who rejoices in God is a harmful love.
Is it not plain how much sin is incurred by such
love? We stand accused of holding our faith deceitfully,
or of rejecting God's laws in rebellious error,
unless what pleased the Lord pleases us.
It is more just to mourn these darknesses of mankind,
which we, our souls degenerate, create,
forgetful of our first origin in the heavenly image,
which the Father in his mercy calls back to his kingdom.
For love of it the Son took on my limbs,
conceived of a virgin, born of a virgin as man,
bearing all that belongs to men, and taking up all men in one body,
the Lord of all becoming a servant.
For he who was supreme was made in the form of a servant,
he who reigned in the form of God, God with the Father, the King.
He took the form of a servant and destroyed the guilt
by which man was once the slave of punishment and death.
And under the likeness of a servant the Lord restored the slave
to freedom, having been made our flesh,
so that through Christ the heavenly image might return to me,
Christ who on the cross stripped off the earthly Adam.
So my Creator bore my flesh and my death,
and by his death redeemed his beloved work.
He had given me much before, both promises of salvation
and precepts by which I might be guided along good paths.
But since, even when the remedy of the law was applied, I had not washed away
the long-festering wounds of the first father,
and had not trusted the prophets sent ahead from God's mouth
to wait for God's gifts,
and despair of salvation had sunk the human race everywhere,
without the light of faith, into darkness,
and sin reigned in our body together with them,
death in sin, and the devil in destruction,
and gloomy fear and wretched error were driving captive man
headlong ever deeper into death,
then the Father himself, pitying from high heaven
the deadly falls of wandering mankind,
and the serpent lording it over the fallen in cruel death,
could not bear it, and sent his Son to bring every good.
The Son obeyed willingly, God in full accord with the Father in all things,
caring for their common concern with equal love.
He came and became man, and, perfect in both natures, showed
that God was present, mingled with fragile flesh.
He performs the duties of a man, but with healing commands
he also displays the signs of the God hidden within.
With a man's voice he teaches divine things, while the things of mortals
he carries out in the body, apart from sin.
For, caring only to restore to himself the substance of his own work,
he came to take on nature, not vice.
For nature is good: the Good One made man for good things.
It was by his own will that man fell and corrupted himself.
Therefore the Maker of men came in a mortal body,
but was not made man with mortal guilt.
For he could not have wiped out sins unless he was free of them,
nor released the guilty if he himself were guilty,
nor would death have yielded to a sinner, since it would lawfully
hold him bound in the chains of sin.
So it rightly yielded to Christ as he broke open hell,
for in him it found nothing it could bind.
And death itself, made guilty in its turn of an unjust judgment,
was justly subjected to the man it had slain by a crime.
The serpent turned pale with envy, seeing the bars of hell
unlocked, man brought back, and the law reversed,
and seeing mortal man set free while death in turn was bound,
and the body shaken out of its soil and rising,
and seeing him, moreover, alive again and climbing the heavens,
livid with spite, he gnashed his savage teeth in vain.
And now he wastes away, as the host of the faithful grows
and the destroyer himself is destroyed through Christ.
So he healed the vices of my soul and took on the weaknesses
of my body, man from his mother, God from his Father.
The things he did were weak, it is true, but natural to the flesh,
and he displayed the feelings of the body.
With human senses he eats and drinks, and closes his eyes
in sleep, and tires himself walking the road.
As a man he sheds tears for a dead friend,
whom soon, as God, he himself raises from the tomb.
As a man he is carried in a boat, and as God he commands the winds,
and by the power of God, a man walks on the sea.
With a man's mind he trembles at the hour of approaching death;
with God's mind he knows the time of his slaying is at hand.
As man he is nailed to the cross; as God he terrified the world from the cross.
Man suffers death, but death itself suffers God.
Man hangs on the cross; God from the cross forgives crimes,
and by dying slays the life of crime;
counted among the guilty and thought worse than the robber
whom Judea preferred to the holy Lord,
he gives the heavenly kingdom to the robber who believes,
and while still confined on earth he already opens paradise.
It is fitting, then, for us to strengthen our souls, to lift up our minds,
and to thrust cowardly fears from our hearts,
since for our sake, see, he laid down his life and took it up again,
that Son of God, while remaining God in all things.
God the victor celebrated his triumph over our death
and carried our body with him to the stars,
not content to have drunk down all that is mortal for us,
to take away our wounds by his own.
But so that the anxious care of a doubting mind should not leave me
in suspense, he rose again in the same body in which he fell.
Clear proof lay open to mortal eyes: he himself
was seen after death just as he was before death.
For he freely presented himself to his doubting disciples
and offered himself to be examined by eyes and hands.
Nor was it without God's purpose that the apostle once doubted,
so that no one should be uncertain of life after death.
He strengthened faith by doubting: while the wavering Thomas
is refuted face to face, every man is taught.
From what Thomas is bidden to see in person and to touch,
I learn to believe steadfastly, with firm faith,
that the death of men has been conquered by the death of Christ crucified,
and that the hope of rising again has been planted in bodies,
in our bodies, because Christ the victor rose in this
flesh which I bear, in which I die.
And teaching me, for my sake he thrusts his limbs on the doubters,
and proves his flesh solid, built upon its bones;
moreover he shows the wounds of his side and of his hands,
and bids the doubter put his fingers into them.
"Look," he says, "here is my side, and my palms and feet;
here are the nails of the cross, here the track of the spear.
See, the very frame of the whole body stands
plainly alive, with sinews, bones, face, and skin.
Hold fast, then, to the faith that you see, and that you also
touch, and drive doubting thoughts from your hearts,
and be witnesses to all of so great a salvation,
and free the hearts of all men from fear.
Let the fear of death perish for all, and let this hope
of rising again give life to all peoples alike.
Yet this salvation belongs to believers, who with faithful hearts
will accept what you behold with your eyes.
See, in me, for all men without distinction,
death has been overcome and is gone; salvation stands restored to life.
I have given life out of death; by dying I have subdued death,
and restored the human race by my blood;
overcoming the sin of the flesh, in the flesh I destroyed
the stuff of guilt and brought forth righteousness.
Through a body death fell; through a body life rose;
in the flesh in which man had once died, he has come to life again.
And now, see, I carry Adam alive again in my body
and display him as victor over death and the serpent."
What consolations, I ask, will be enough for us, or what
rest will heal our weary souls,
if not even so great a medicine can heal the sick,
a medicine that teaches that lives return once death has been met?
Grief, be gone; fear, depart; guilt, flee! Death has fallen,
life has risen again, Christ calls us to the stars,
he who underwent my death, died for me and conquered for me,
so that the death of sin might be for me the life of God.
Indeed, from the cross he led the robber, now saved, along an open
path to where paradise lies,
and by this gift he gave a sign that sins can be atoned for
and the fences of the forbidden grove overcome by faith.
With such examples, with so great a guarantor of salvation,
it is fitting that we take heart and turn sorrow into joy.
Let us drive complaining griefs out of ungrateful hearts,
and let clear sight return to our dried eyes.
Let us believe Christ, as we have seen in him, that we
shall rise in the same bodies in which we fall,
and then, clothed over with a garment of divine splendor,
shall be changed and take on the likeness of angels.
But if so deep a night stands in the way of your darkened minds,
and your sluggish senses are dull in a blunted body,
so that, because divine things are hidden from bodily eyes,
you say the Scriptures deserve no belief,
then let Paul teach you that the things that are seen are not eternal;
eternal things are hidden from human eyes.
Foolish one, look at earthly things, but believe heavenly ones;
behold the world with your gaze, and God with your mind.
This is why faith is precious: for just as grace would no longer
be grace if it were credited to merits,
so there is no faith except that which believes what it does not see
and, with hope as its guide, pursues what is eternal.
Wretched mortals, race of complainers, at last
soften your minds and strip off your impious hearts.
Alas, how long, I ask, will you seek lies with hearts weighed down,
and love the slippery things of vanity?
Change your ways, break the chains of death,
and offer your freed necks to a yoke of perfect sweetness.
In place of your freedom take up divine chains,
which loose you from crime and bind you with devotion.
You who follow darkness wander about in the open light,
and you who see by night go blind in the daylight.
So let us open the eyes and ears of our minds to Christ,
so that the mind closed by sin may lie open to God.
For God already reveals his promises even to bodily
sight, and shows hidden things plainly.
All things rehearse the pattern of resurrection in every
body, both the seeds on earth and the stars in the sky.
Nights and days, risings and settings, take their turns
in succession; I die by night, I rise by day.
I sleep, lulled in the bodily image of death;
I am roused from sleep as from destruction.
What of the crops, the leaves of the woods, the seasons? Surely
all things die or come back by these laws.
When spring rises again, a new appearance returns to all things,
brought back to life after the death of winter.
What man, to whom the bodies of the world are subject, will do once,
all things under heaven do again and again.
But they ask in what body every dead person is restored,
or how a man is made out of ashes.
If what the holy prophets set down is not enough,
mute things cry out for belief: believe what you can see.
See how no seeds spring up in their fields
unless they first perish, dissolved in rotting decay.
You sow them bare, you gather them clothed; you cast dry grains,
and reap the same grains multiplied in fruit.
O how perverse our faith and our distrust,
that we trust the earth and doubt God!
And surely the earth neither dared nor was able to promise me
anything; indeed the field has often deceived me,
scarcely returning the seed entrusted to it; and yet, though deceived,
I do not hesitate to entrust it with my hope of a harvest,
nor do I regret sweating at certain toil for uncertain
crops, and entrusting bare seed to bare soil.
But if the earth can give back seed that has decayed,
which it does, after all, by the law of the eternal Lord,
is it believed that it will be hard work for the Almighty
to restore from something us who were made from nothing?
I was nothing, and by God's making I was born so that I might exist;
now I will exist again from my own seed.
For though even the bones are reduced to fine ash,
the dust holds the seeds of the whole body,
and even when the earth has soaked up the ashes from emptied tombs,
mingled with their kindred turf,
even then the Almighty keeps intact men who seem
to have vanished from bodily eyes,
and on the great day we shall see the bodies we now think
consumed rise whole for God,
for whom no nature perishes, since whatever exists anywhere
is all enclosed in the Creator's bosom.
Those whom water has swallowed in rivers and sea, and in the fish,
those whom birds and wild beasts have torn apart,
all of them the earth owes to God, because those whom the water drowned
the ground has received, laid out on the shore or the seabed;
and though it is one earth, yet, not gathered into one tomb,
it covers the scattered bones of a mangled corpse in many places;
and because consumed and consumer alike fall into the one
bosom of the earth when death carries them off,
or because through the excrement by which animals purge themselves
they give back the devoured limbs once the food is digested,
the human body passes over out of another's
body and does not lose the power of its own kind.
But though passed from the limbs of beasts into the soil,
the limbs of men remain safe with their living seed,
and when the beast dies that perhaps fed on a human
corpse, their substances are kept apart by reason.
For man is a rational animal, and therefore in him
the king surpasses other bodies in his body too,
so that, though he may be given as prey to dumb animals,
he still refuses to share their lot.
Only that flesh will receive the vigor of resurrection
which has been the vessel of a rational soul,
so that, its frame rebuilt, it may receive the soul as it returns to earth
in a covering that will never fall again,
and just as here mind and flesh are joined in every act,
so too they may be united for the eternal day,
so that they may reap the rewards of their deeds as a shared harvest,
partners in desert, in the place of light or of fire.
Therefore, although we and all breathing things
have been allotted one and the same matter in our bodies,
yet we are not, when dissolved by death, returned to nothingness,
left without a soul once the flesh has set;
but when the trumpet sounds, and the lands everywhere give back
our bodies from their hidden seeds,
with body, mind, and soul bound again in their own covenant,
we shall stand whole before God our Lord.
If you doubt that ashes can be gathered back into bodies
and that souls can return to their own vessels,
Ezekiel will be your witness, to whom long ago the whole
pattern of resurrection was revealed by the Lord.
There you will see, across the whole plain, coming to life
the dry remains of men of old,
and bones scattered far and wide over the outstretched field
running of their own accord, at command, to their joints,
and putting forth sinews from their marrowed depths,
and soon drawing skin over the flesh grown upon them,
and quicker than a word, with limbs completed in order,
new men standing up out of the old dust.
And lest you perhaps think that what the holy prophet's clear
vision reports was the empty dream of a sleeper,
accept a greater and complete witness on these matters;
for the Lord of the prophets himself speaks:
"I am the life; whoever believes in me will not be destroyed by death,
but will live in bliss, sharing my light with me."
Indeed, what he said in word he proved by power,
himself calling back his own man from the depths,
although at that time it was not only in his own body that Christ
gave signs, when he died as victor on the cross.
For when, as the earth was shaken, he laid hell open
and freed Adam, chained in the prison below,
the buried rose and burst out through the split rocks,
and a new rotunda flowered in the holy city.
Many saw the bodies of the holy men of old renewed,
brought to life by God's descent.
Then too the world, blinded as the light fled back,
feared it must atone for the crime with eternal night.
Then too, with the veil torn, the altars laid bare
lost the sanctity of the holy sanctuary,
to show that the temple was to be emptied of God's presence
and that its holy things would be profaned by an enemy's hand,
as the great catastrophe later taught under a Roman general,
when temple, citizens, city, and rites were overthrown.
For it was right that Judea, for whom Christ was not
her sacrifice, and through whom Christ was made a victim,
robbed at once of the seat and place of her ancient rites,
having denied the faith, should lose everything sacred.
For Christ is the end of the law, since, foretold by the faithful law,
by coming he became the law for the law,
setting an end to the old law and laying down the law of faith,
establishing for the nations the law of the prophet.
Hence the teacher says: "The old things have passed away, their times
fulfilled; all things everywhere are being made new."
And now with unveiled face we behold God revealed
in Christ, in the glory of his own light.
And I think the mysteries of the veil torn in the temple
also signified this gift that grace bestows.
For just as the sanctuary lay open when the veil was torn,
so faith unlocks for us the hidden things of the law.
So Moses is read beneath the ancient veil
by the Jews, still covered by the mist of their hearts,
a mist that Christ, in whom I have believed, takes from the eyes of my mind,
dispelling the shadowy figures,
and showing himself veiled in the ancient shadow of the law
and now unveiled in the face of a body,
just as the prophets sent before him sang that he would come,
just as he appeared before the apostles' eyes,
just as the Jews, though seeing him, did not perceive him,
their minds dulled by their own impiety,
and just as we, though we have not seen him in the body,
behold him by believing, with an inward light.
For what the truthful teachers report that they saw
and touched, I touch and see by faith.
And by believing, all may come to know Christ,
who blinds the impious hearts of the faithless
and pours his light through faithful hearts,
that he may dwell in the souls that please him and make them shine.
Therefore, my brothers, my care, my heart, gladden
your grieving souls in this faith.
Drive away sadness, made teachable by faithful devotion,
and, trusting in God, put on joy.
Unhappy mourning and senseless grief befit those
for whom no hope remains, because no faith remains,
and for whom the whole good is only to live in this world,
to despair of God and to trust in bodily things.
Let inner stupor besiege the inconsolable hearts
of those whose senses have abandoned the truth,
whom their mind, faithless toward God, disinherits, and whose lot,
cut off from Christ, falls into the darkness below.
For us, let the apostle be present to console us with God's own words,
let Christ in his love teach us through the Gospel;
let the examples of the fathers and the proclamations of the prophets,
let the book of the history of the apostles strengthen us,
in which we see Christ returning in his body to the stars
and carried into heaven in the lap of a cloud,
and we are bidden to hope that he will return from heaven just as
we saw him go to heaven, to the Father.
On his coming all things now hang;
all hope and faith yearn eagerly toward this King.
And already the ages, soon to be changed into new ones,
are in labor with the end drawing near in the last time.
The true oracles in the sacred books warn all
to believe what was foretold and to prepare themselves for God.
Hurry, I beg you, while there is opportunity here
to provide for good things and guard in advance against evil.
Turn your heart around and turn away perverse cares;
faith shows us how to weep with profitable tears.
It is good to mourn for sin and with streaming tears
to wash away the wounds contracted through our faults,
with tears like those with which David watered his bed every night,
groaning greatly, mighty in his humble heart.
If that man, beloved of God, ate ashes like bread
and mingled his drink with tears,
what, alas, is fitting for wretched me to do? How shall I be cleansed?
How shall I make amends? By what help shall I be saved?
My heart of pumice has no tears, I shudder at ashes for food,
and delicacies delight my hungry soul.
Who would give me a fountain for rivers of tears,
with which to weep for my deeds and my days?
For, as the deserts of a life spent in crimes demand,
I need a river to weep for my huge wounds.
Break the stone of my heart, Jesus my Savior,
so that my softened inner parts may flow with a holy spring;
I pray you, O Christ, the spring, rise up within my innermost being,
so that the living vein of your water may well up in me.
For you are the spring from which life flows, from which grace streams,
from which light pours out on peoples of every kind.
Those who drink you, Christ, refreshed by your sweet torrent,
will thirst no more, and yet they will thirst.
For those whom the abundance of the divine word has satisfied,
its sweetness, once tasted, makes thirst the more.
So, Lord God, bread and spring of salvation,
may souls forever hunger and thirst for you.
Neither starving hunger nor parching thirst
will consume our life if the mind eats and drinks you.
Ever-flowing, you are always being drunk, and though drained you more generously
surpass both the crowd and the thirst of those who drink.
For you are wholly sweetness, God, and love, O Christ;
so you can fill rather than glut.
And always to be thirsted for with greedy longings,
you flow in and are taken in, and love is never sated;
and so devotion is made perfect, that you are loved without end,
Christ, who will give life without end to your own.
Grant me now to mourn, O God, and by wholesome weeping
to sow beforehand the seeds of eternal joy;
let this, I pray, let this rather be my time of mourning, in this age
in which whatever is present passes by on a brief road.
Away with you, merrymakers; I prefer the company of those who weep,
so that through brief tears I may reap long joys.
If only a heavy sackcloth, a shaggy covering of goats'
hair, should prick me as it covers me in my mourning,
then, once the father is appeased, the ring of the honor I had earned
will be restored to me, and the robe of gladness will clothe me;
then the father will rightly kill the fatted calf for me,
if only, fasting, I hunger for righteousness.
I would rather suffer hunger for bread than for the holy word;
I want no house of wine, I thirst for the water of light;
here let dire hunger torment me, here let shameful poverty
besiege me, huddled in wretched rags,
here let the rich man pass me by in front of his house,
scorning to fill me even with his crumbs.
I do not want a silken robe now to blaze on me with Tyrian purple,
drawing envy to a body that is destined to burn,
lest after purple garments the everlasting flame
should wrap me round and I pay the price of the garment in fire.
Rather let us lie here in misery on a foul heap
of dung, and let dogs lick our sores,
so that, released after a sad life by a peaceful death,
a gentle angel may come to meet and receive us
and set us down rejoicing in the bosom of the patriarchs,
far from where Gehenna rages with its gaping chasm.
I am not speaking of fictions that frighten little children:
the dog barking at the gates through three muzzles,
and Charon terrifying the shades with his grim squalor,
the Furies, savage with snaky hair,
Tityus, eternal food for the deadly vulture,
and Tantalus parched with thirst amid the waters,
the wheel turning without end and the stone that rolls back,
and the useless jars of the toiling Danaids.
These things poets who lacked the truth sang in empty verses,
for they did not hold Christ, the head of truth.
But God has taught us true things, the Creator himself
recounting to us the whole truth about his works.
Learn from the Gospel the places of the poor man and the rich man:
the poor man lies in Abraham's bosom, the rich man in fire.
As justice reverses their lots, he who had wept here
rejoices there, and the poor man is full while the rich man is in want.
The one enjoys good rest, the other groans in the flames;
the rich man receives punishment for his riches, the poor man receives riches.
The rich man begs a little dew from the poor man,
whom he had spurned when he begged in the world above.
Then upon him as he burned, not even a small [drop] from the tip of the poor man's [?]
dripped from his fingertip a drop of cooling relief,
because from the great feasts of the glutted man not even a crumb
had fallen into the mouth of the hungry poor man.
Taught by these warnings, let us learn to live for Christ a life of holy
justice, and to set aside a share for the poor.
You who find the needy loathsome, who shudder at the sight of a beggar
and take meeting a devout suppliant as an evil omen,
who admire yourself gleaming in costly clothing
and do not see that you are filthy in your inner dress:
you carry in your mind all that you shudder at in the poor man's body,
a rich man fouler than rags and sores.
You despise the blind, you avoid touching the leper,
greedy rich man, yet you love your own leprosy.
He is wretched and crippled in the eyes of men; but you
are hideous before God in the crippling of your soul.
Shameless man, you spurn the needy who shares your nature,
and by your greed you shut him out from his share.
Whatever overflows to you, unjust man, beyond any use,
whatever you hide away in a hole dug in the turf, is the share of the poor.
Why do you hold what belongs to others? With what hope do you keep what you must leave behind,
neither given back to its owners nor yours to enjoy?
You who find the needy loathsome, who, made senseless by the name of rich man,
raise a grim eyebrow on a wrinkled forehead,
and do not deign even to call by name
those whom you do not see awash in luxury like yours:
look in what form the Son of God came,
who, though he was rich, was poor on earth.
And God, when he came, chose not the lofty but the lowly things of the world,
so as to destroy the strong by the weak.
Let the rich man no longer rejoice in riches, nor the strong in strength,
nor the wise in great intellect.
Let no one trust in his own resources or applaud himself,
since all things are sown or given by God, their source.
Christ, made the refuge and the very person of the needy,
is a shame to the rich and a glory to the poor.
Let us run eagerly toward his ambrosial fragrance,
so that the odor of death may flee far from us.
Who will grant me to pour precious nard from an alabaster jar
and, weeping, to wash the Lord's sacred feet?
You, my dear ones, I pray, give your efforts to holy concerns,
and give yourselves in mind to God, your boundless Bridegroom.
The time is at hand, the Lord is now near; hasten to make ready
to meet the King, while the brief hour lies open.
Use your wealth with kindly devotion
and tear the root of evil from your hearts.
Store up the price of your life in the hearts of the needy,
and anoint your heads with devout spending.
And kissing the pure footprints of Christ the Lord,
wipe both his feet with your hair, wash them with your eyes.
If you long to enjoy Celsus without end,
act so that the same hall may lie open to you.
For one whom holy faith, an age that knows no sin,
and a devout mind in a chaste body have kept,
it is a sure belief that he dwells in that region above
where God's fiery altar shelters the saints.
So, good brothers, we do not want you to grieve over our dear child
like men who have no hope;
for if we surely believe that Christ Jesus
died and now lives in the citadel of God,
so too all those who rest in living faith
the Father will bring with Christ when he returns.
For this is what that teacher teaches by the word of the Lord,
under whose guidance we strive to walk the starry paths:
that those whose life has been lived out in Christ
will have eternal life with Christ.
And when the chief angel gives the trumpet signal of the Lord's coming
from the lofty throne of the Father,
those who died in Christ will rise first,
counted worthy to go in the clouds to meet God.
And though all will live again in the flesh in which they lived,
not all will become light with bodies transformed.
For we shall rise, but we shall not all be changed;
this will be the distinction among the nations before God.
The bodies of the ungodly too will rise incorrupt
from their tombs, fodder for long punishment.
For them life will be dying without end, and death living in torment,
and feeding their own crosses with enduring flesh.
The sinner will beget from his own body
his own executioners and will be food for his own worms.
But those whom devotion has raised up by heavenly conduct
will wear crowns shared with God the King,
and, their bodies clothed in divine light,
will live forever conformed to Christ the Lord.
Since this is so, take comfort from these words
and refresh your faithful souls with the hope of the truth;
and believe that Celsus, our common pledge, in the light on high
enjoys the milk and honeycombs of the living.
Either kindly Abraham cherishes him, taken into his bosom,
and gentle Lazarus feeds him with the dew of his finger,
or with the infants of Bethlehem in paradise,
whom wicked Herod struck down in his envy,
he plays in the fragrant grove and weaves
crowns as rewards for the martyrs to be honored.
Mingled with such as these, he will attend the Lamb, the King,
an infant added to the virgin ranks.
Celsus, pure boy, dweller in the land of the blessed,
Celsus, grief of your parents, Celsus, glory of your fathers,
Celsus, love and longing and light of your family,
Celsus, a brief grace to us, a long one to yourself.
Yet your grace can live long for us too,
if you remember us before the Lord.
For in you, small in years but vast in merit,
life was brief in time but mighty in holiness.
For the kingdom of heaven is shown to belong to such infants
as you were, a child in age, in mind, and in faith,
and as that child of ours was too, who bore your blessed
name, called away at the very time he was given,
an offspring long desired and not granted to us,
unworthy as we were to rejoice in devout posterity.
We believe, Celsus, that he plays with you in the eternal green meadows,
sharing in joy and life,
he whom we entrusted, in the city of Complutum, to the martyrs nearby,
joined to them by the bond of a shared tomb,
so that from the neighboring blood of the saints he might draw
something with which to sprinkle our souls in that fire.
For perhaps one day, for us sinners too,
this little drop of our blood will be a light.
Celsus, help your brother, working with him in shared devotion,
so that there may be a place for us in your rest.
Live as companions, live forever, brothers,
and, a worthy pair, dwell in places of joy;
and with your innocent merits, equal infants, overcome your parents' sins
by your pure intercessions.
As many years as you had, Celsus, so many days of life
did he drink in; but he, the younger, is the elder in that he went first.
For he is younger in that he lived less; and yet the same child,
since he departed first, is now your elder there.
Celsus, with your brother, stand by your own family, to which we are joined;
for we are a vein of your ancestral blood.
Together with your father Pneumatius and your mother Fidelis,
name Paulinus and Therasia too as your own,
so that through your prayers, by the mercy of Christ, we too may have a shared
protection, Celsus, we who are yours.
Yet it remains for us, too, to strive so that
we may follow you with a like simplicity.
Then we shall be able to live as companions of our Celsus,
and to be forever the fathers of a sweet pledge.
XXXII.
I, Antonius, have examined, I confess, every sect;
I have looked into a great many and run through each one in turn,
but I have found nothing better than to believe in Christ.
I have resolved to set these things out in gentle verse,
and so that no one may be displeased that I compose such songs:
David himself entreated God with a tuneful voice,
and after his example we will sing small things in place of great,
telling what is to be shunned, what followed, what revered,
while in every case both the matter and its reason are proved.
First, the Jewish people was not moved even by the wondrous
grace of God; for though it was then rescued from wicked Pharaoh
and crossed the sea on foot by the light of the shining pillar,
with a leader who saw the hostile horsemen drowned,
a people that never lacked anything in the desert lands,
for whom manna ran down from heaven and a spring from the rock,
after all this it denied the God who had bestowed so much,
and while with a mad heart it sought another deity,
it lost in the kindled fires the gold it had thrown in.
The pagan is no better: he worships the stones he carves
and makes for himself what he himself must fear.
Then he worships images that he fashions out of bronze in such a way
that, whenever he pleases, he can send them broken up to the mint,
or rather, as often happens, turn them into shameful shapes.
Next he slaughters wretched cattle, and the minds of the gods,
whom he thinks angry, he searches for in a warm lung,
and prays for a man's life through the death of a beast.
Why does he ask to be forgiven, who seeks pardon with blood?
And this, what sort of thing is it, how foolish, how deserving of censure!
Though almighty God once formed man,
man dares to form a god; and so that crimes may not be lacking,
he even sells him, and the buyer purchases himself a lord.
Am I to believe that the philosophers have any reason,
who lack reason, whose wisdom is vain?
There are the Cynics, like dogs, as their name betrays;
there are also the followers of the uncertain teaching of Plato,
who are troubled by the long-sought substance of the soul,
forever discussing it and never able to define it;
hence they love to copy out Plato's book on the soul,
which, apart from its title, contains nothing certain within.
There are also the Physici, named after nature,
who delight in the ancient, rough and unpolished life.
For one of them once carried a staff and an earthen vessel,
which alone he thought useful and alone worth having,
the one for support, the other for drinking;
but when he saw a farmer standing and scooping up in cupped hands
water to drink, he broke the earthen vessel,
and, throwing it far away, said that superfluities must be removed.
A peasant taught him that he could spurn even this.
These men neither drink wine nor are nourished by bread,
nor recline on a bed nor ward off the cold with clothes,
and, ungrateful to God, they refuse what he has provided.
What shall I say of the various rites, and of the temples built for gods
and goddesses? I shall speak first of what the Capitol is:
here there is a god and the god's wife, and they will have her
to be his sister too, as Virgil, their authority, notes
when he says "both sister and wife." More is told of Jupiter:
that he violated his own daughter and gave her to his brother,
and that to seduce other women he changed his own shape:
now he was a serpent, now a bull, now a swan, and a tree,
and by changing himself he shows what sort he was;
another's form pleased him more than his own.
More shamefully than these, he took the guise of an eagle and came into the unspeakable
embraces of a boy. What does the crowd of worshippers say?
Let them either deny it was Jupiter or admit this disgrace.
He certainly bears a name that reason cannot approve.
They offer sacrifices to Jupiter and say "Jupiter most good,"
and pray to him, and put "Father Janus" in first place.
This Janus was a king who named after himself
the Janiculum, a prudent man, who, since many future things
he could look back upon, they painted him with a double face,
and the ancient Latins called him twin Janus.
Because he came to the Ausonian shores by ship,
a coin was first struck in his honour in such a way
that one side bore a head carved on it, the other a ship;
in memory of this, whatever coins are now stamped
they call, from that ancient practice, "heads" and "ships."
What do they hope from Jupiter, since he comes second to a king
and is placed after him in the sacrifices by the lips of those who pray?
He also has a mother captivated by love for a shepherd;
for the shepherd comes first, ahead of Jupiter, or of Jove himself [?];
but the shepherd did better, who wished to keep his chaste modesty
and spurned the goddess; and in her cruelty she cut off his manly
parts, so that he might never touch
another's bed, he who [?] would not approach hers.
Yet was this, was this what the just judgment of the gods achieved:
that he who had not become an adulterer should not become a husband?
Even now half-men lament in these shameful mysteries,
and there is no lack of men perverted by this contagion,
and inside they worship some secret thing as if it were greater
and call it holy, so that if a chaste man wished to go there
he would be profane. So the priest himself, being stricter,
shuns intercourse with women and submits to that of men.
O blind minds of men! Their rites are forever
a source of laughter on the stage, yet they do not turn back from this error.
They claim that Saturn was Jupiter's father, and that he devoured
his children before him and soon vomited from his belly that unspeakable
meal, but that afterwards, through his wife's cunning,
he swallowed into his bowels a stone substituted for Jupiter;
had she not done this, Jupiter would have been devoured.
They call him Cronos, and by a fiction Chronos, because time
consumes what it creates and promises again what it has consumed.
But why do they invent a roundabout name in place of "time"?
They also say that, because he constantly feared for himself from his offspring,
he was cast down from heaven by Jupiter and hid in the fields
of Italy, and that Latium was therefore given its name then.
Mighty gods, both of them! One is hidden on earth,
the other could not discover the earth's hiding places.
Hence the ancient Quirites established the Latian evil,
so that a slaughtered man might satisfy an empty name.
What night of the mind, what heedless hearts!
What is worshipped is nothing, and bloody rites are performed.
And what of the fact that they hide the Unconquered One in dark caves,
and dare to call him whom they cover in darkness the Sun?
Who would worship the light in secret and hide the star on high
in the underworld, unless he were the cause of evil things?
And what of the fact that the Isiac rites, the sistrum and the dog's head,
they do not hide in the same way, but set out in public places?
They are certainly looking for something, and they rejoice when it is found,
and then lose it again so that they can look for it again.
What wise man would put up with this: that those people, as it were, shut the sun away,
while these openly display the monstrosities of their own gods?
What has Serapis done to deserve this, that he is torn apart by them
through various shameful places? In short, he is forever
made a beast, made a dog, made the rotting carcass of a little ass,
made a man, now in rags, now weak with a sick body.
And while they do such things, they admit that he feels nothing.
What shall I say of Vesta, of whom her own priest admits
that he does not know what she is? And yet deep within the innermost shrine
a fire is feigned to be kept forever unquenched.
Why is she a goddess and not a god? Why is fire said to be female?
This woman, indeed, as Hyginus records,
was the first long ago to weave a garment from new thread,
called after her own name, which she herself gave
to Vulcan, who had then shown her how to guard
the covered hearths; he in turn, delighted with the gift,
offered it to the Sun, through whom he had earlier discovered
the adultery of Mars; now the whole credulous crowd
hang up garments to the Sun at the Vulcanalia.
And to honour Venus, Adonis too is then carried about;
then they throw out dung, and fling him out as if he were dung.
If you look into it all, it seems all the more laughable.
Something else is added here: those whom they call the virgins of Vesta,
I hear, carry a feast every five years to a serpent,
which either does not exist or, if it does, is the devil himself,
the enemy of the human race and its tempter of old;
and they venerate him who now, at the name of Christ,
trembles and hangs suspended and confesses all his deeds.
What minds men have, that they speak falsehoods in place of truth,
worshipping what should be abandoned and abandoning what should be worshipped!
But it will be enough now for me to have recounted these empty fears.
All these things I myself once held, before I attained the clear light;
and when I had long been uncertain and driven by so many storms,
the holy Church received me in her saving harbour
and, after the wandering waves, set me in a tranquil place,
so that now, with the cloud of evils wiped away,
I may hope for serene light at the promised time.
Now that former salvation, which heedless Adam lost,
driven then by an evil wind, will now, with Christ at the oar,
be rescued from the rocks and rise again to endure forever.
For our helmsman so steers all things on every side
that he who has just removed the error from our minds
will by a better way open the threshold of paradise.
Happy is our faith, dedicated to the one, the certain God.
For God is one, and the Son is one in one substance
with him; in both is one strength, one power.
For Christ, the Word of God, shone forth from the Father's heart
and always was; not as if born,
but going forth from his mouth, he removed that empty chaos
and took away the formless gulf of close-woven night,
and assigned to their places sea, lands, air and sky,
and, the darkness driven off, gave them a twofold light.
But when all things gazed in amazement at the new sun rising,
he enriched these four first principles with various things:
men were added to the earth, stars to the sky,
the bird hangs in the air, the fish swims in the flowing sea.
Thus he adorned each element with its own forms;
he bound them together, different though they are, joined what was separate
and separated what was joined, so that now, though divided, they hold together.
For Ocean encloses the earth, and the sea is itself enclosed by the earth,
and the air between is enclosed beneath the vault of the ether.
This sky, too, which we see on high,
lies beneath six others rising at equal intervals;
and beyond the seven thrones, beyond so many heavenly realms,
all the remaining part, which towers beyond them all,
which rises above, which stretches on every side into the heights,
which lies open without end, which no mind can grasp,
is the home of unapproachable light and the holy seat
of almighty God, from where he looks down from afar on what he has made beneath him.
So all things stand firm, while the Spirit encompasses all.
Likewise these things whose use is granted to us,
which the lower heaven embraces in its great circle,
though all are far apart, are held together in a single peace,
and in short they have one name: all of them are the world.
The Greeks of old called it "cosmos";
and so, in naming what was thus put together, each language
called it "cosmos" from its adornment, and "mundus" from its light.
For all this where the sun now shines lay foul in shadow,
and an example of it remains whenever night defiles all things,
and teaches from the darkness what a grace was given in the light.
He who made so many good things, who worked thus everywhere,
is the Lord from the heart of God, the Spirit of his mouth,
the Word of the holy Father, the builder of all these great things.
Let no pagan praise himself if he avoids idols
or thinks it enough that he believes in a single deity.
Does he worship God who does not worship his Word,
who does not venerate his Power with equal honour?
Whoever confesses that God is invisible and incomprehensible
will find, if he reflects, that Christ too is the same,
since no one can grasp the Word,
no one can see him; only his works are seen.
For the Son in the Father, and the Father in the Son, made all things,
and whatever he gave by his power he protects by his love.
So he was, is and will be the true Saviour forever,
who took away errors, who made the truth visible,
and, having appeased the Father, restored the perishing world.
No wonder if he rules all things who created all things,
who brought forth the whole from nothing, drove back the darkness
with light, and commanded day to follow night,
and, because he was in the flesh, forgives the sins of the flesh;
for he sees that frail man easily falls into error,
and though he rebukes, he will grant to all a single pardon;
and I will say something new, and shall not regret having said it:
he will be more merciful than just. For if he
chose to be just, no one would escape punishment as free of guilt;
for the just one condemns wrongs, the merciful one forgives everything.
He does this so that the gifts of the life to come may be assured,
and indulgence may restore what guilt took away;
if this were not granted to the people who ask for it,
then scarcely anyone would be free of every fault.
Who could by his own merit win the promised light?
Then the joyful will be allowed to reach the kingdom of heaven,
then death itself will be able to die, when for all time
life will be everlasting, when in that blessed abode
there is no room for sin, where there is no desire.
So great a glory remains in store for the faithful people.
He has granted still more; he has given this greater gift as well:
the sinner who repents of his earlier fall
he does not count among the crowd of sinners.
Indeed, it is punishment enough for one whose guilt is his grief;
fear is his own punishment; he suffers the torments of guilt
just as one who confesses that he has deserved them.
What could be better, or what more moderate?
He judges, inquires, chastises, spares and honours,
he who conquers all things and is not conquered even by anger.
What will happen in the future we already see from the present;
for when, threatening, he often gathers bristling clouds,
and in a holy terror flashes all too brightly with ruddy fire,
and thunders with gloomy rains and black clouds,
every living kind fears destruction; but the living Power
relents and calms the sky and our minds alike.
So too he bids us hope for this hereafter, he who now proves
that he could destroy all things, but refuses to will their destruction.
Thus a renewed salvation is shown for the age to come,
and the mercy of the eternal God will remain eternal.
XXXIII.
O blessed man, whose iniquity is forgiven,
and whose sluggish delay in believing has not been counted against him,
to whom faith, though empty of works, brought life!
Behold, this man, whom beneath the gold of the lofty ceiling
a painting portrays with the wonders of [?],
renowned for the proud name of the Verii
and for his consular blood, Baebianus,
is himself the bountiful grace of mighty Christ.
Formerly this man, held captive by mortal bonds,
and poor toward God amid the riches of the world,
had run through a life made pleasant by ready wealth,
unmindful of his mortality.
When he sees himself, a mortal, brought low by his end,
with weary gaze he seeks the kindly God.
And at once, enlightened, he finds Christ;
he begs for pardon and, a suppliant, reverences the feet
of the priests, his own accuser,
and by denying he is worthy of grace, makes himself worthy.
He vows a blameless life, if any life remains to him,
and rejoices to die, if he may meet death reborn.
The bishop trusted his prayer and, as he thirsted for the rivers of life,
girded for the rite, drenched him in the pure stream.
And when the bishop had soon performed the holy rites in their accustomed order,
he, partaking of the divine sacrament and fragrant with chrism,
declares himself awestruck by a wondrous majesty;
but what is this scent, he asks, that he feels gliding into his
breast and healing his inmost being with sweetest nectar?
Then his devoted wife [?] explains that the ointment breathes
of the name of Christ; and the priest gives his pledge
and urges him to ask for himself a long span of life.
He, now wholly God's, replies: "This gift is enough for me,
which I now possess; now death is gain to me, and life is Christ!"
Behold the grace given to the earth through the eternal Christ!
This is that happy thief who at the very end
confessed Christ and, though guilty, won the stars by his faith;
this is the one who goes away rewarded with a full day's wage,
the late labourer hired at the eleventh hour.
So when, renewed, he shone from the sanctifying wave,
sinking his heavy limbs back on soft cushions,
with heart refreshed he addresses his devoted wife:
"My span of years had reached nine lustres,
and my life had begun to run a year beyond,
a life blessed for me in a harmonious marriage,
sweet in its children and distinguished by honours;
and now, washed clean of deadly stains,
it passes by a holy end to the merciful God."
At these words, with loving tears, his devoted
wife implores him to pray to go on living.
Then he: "O woman, you do not know what you ask;
do you know already whether I could live so devoutly
as to keep so great a gift unblemished?
And what good is a life in which salvation dies?"
When he had said this bravely, his eyes flashing fiercely,
gazing up at the sky in amazement, he says:
"I see a flaming circuit of light,
a circle into which no woman comes.
O happy the man to whom it is granted, while still in the body,
to behold the form of the eternal age,
in which there is no need of marriage,
