and sex vanishes in everlasting bodies!"
When he had said this, then, as if released by sudden death,
he draws a bloodless stiffness through his outstretched limbs.
But his wife, trembling and terrified at such a sight,
swoons into the likeness of death; now, speechless, she stretches
trembling hands toward his face and, intent on the limbs of the man lying there,
hangs over her lifeless husband, paler than he.
The very delay made his death believable; for twice
the sky turned round, a double day revolved and twice was closed by evening,
while the image of death deceived mortal eyes.
But he, caught up through the clouds by the hands of angels,
had left the lodging of the body to which he would return, and then
was gazing on the secrets of the ethereal heaven and the blessed seats,
as God showed them to him; and, deemed worthy by Christ,
his devout soul, while mourned on earth, was rejoicing among the stars,
grieving only at this, that it [feared] it must still return.
Sent back from its departure, it returns, to report what it had seen
and strengthen the faith of those who doubt that the dead live.
And when, restored to his limbs, he saw the face of his wife
close beside him, he promised that he would tell
something wonderful, and put off his account until the following day.
So when the morrow shone forth at the first dawning of the day,
early in the morning the priest (for he happened to be present)
performs the sacred rites; and when he had completed the solemnities with devout worship,
the man, gazing up at heaven, spread out his hands, and then, drawing
his arms in toward himself, as though clasping gifts sent from heaven,
he presses them in an eager embrace, asking, "Are all these mine?"
All were astonished at his words and ask
what it is he sees that is closed to mortals. He
said, "All is well," and, often calling to mind the patriarch Isaac,
he repeats in Greek, "Divine, sweet and divine to behold,"
shuddering and full of reverence; and how an angel
had lifted him up and carried him through the void, how he saw
many thousands mingled with the hosts of angels and of the Lamb,
and Christ reigning as God over all things with the Father,
he tells; he tells of the eternal city with its jewelled gates,
he tells too of the heavenly grove of the ethereal paradise.
And amid all this he laid his right hand on the hidden breast
of his wife, saying: "We two are one and the same"; and
repeating these words, and so completing in holy order a peaceful
end, he breathed out his life in the words of the gospel.
And now he enjoys God, and still holds in his care his blessed
wife, bound to her by an eternal love;
yet he has snatched away the comfort of one son,
a father unable to bear being without all his children.
But when you have closed your days at a fitting age,
renowned mother, once your children are reared,
then that boy of yours, wearing a crown blooming with light,
will come to meet you together with his father;
with him as companion, your husband, coming joyfully from heaven,
will hold out his right hand to you with tender words:
"The time has come! Be released now from cares, released from the body!
You have lived for your children; now be given back to me.
No longer is our marriage mortal, as it was when, in frail
bodies, grudging brevity once granted it to us,
a marriage that swift time took from us with slender fruit,
adding scarcely two lustres to three years;
for your life had added twenty years to a lustre
when my life ran ahead of your course,
while my age had run on twice ten years beyond yours;
and yet one love had made us equal in age.
Now, steadfast under a better yoke, and on the lips of the devout,
we shall live through golden ages with God as our king.
Rise, follow your husband and son; see, open lies the gate
of the serene heaven, by your merit [?]
[?] an angel flying on ahead;
God himself stretches out a loving hand from a cloud, and
with beckoning right hand calls you into heaven."
Happy Apra, who were granted, on earth and in heaven,
to keep forever the blessing of a husband who was your only one,
through whom you have bright honour on earth, and under the same name
your glory in heaven too will be everlasting!
POEM I.
Come now, I pray, inseparable companion
in all my fortunes,
let us dedicate our anxious and brief life
to the Lord God.
You see how, in swift rotation,
the hurrying days pass by,
and the members of this fragile world
diminish, perish, and slip away.
Everything we hold flows away,
and what has flowed away does not return;
eager and wandering minds
it draws on with empty show.
Where now is the outward show of things?
Where is the wealth of the powerful,
whose delight it was to take possession
of the souls they had ensnared?
He who once turned the earth with a hundred ploughs
now toils anxiously to own a pair of oxen.
He who often rode in carriages through magnificent cities
now goes, sick, on weary feet to an empty countryside.
He who once furrowed the seas with ten tall ships
now boards a tiny skiff and steers it himself.
The fields are not in the same state, nor are any cities,
and all things rush headlong to their end.
By sword, plague, famine, chains, cold, and heat,
one death snatches wretched men away in a thousand ways.
Everywhere wars roar; madness stirs everyone; with arms
kings press hard upon countless kings.
Impious discord rages through a world in confusion;
peace has left the earth; you are seeing the last of all things.
And even if time should remain beyond the closing of this age,
or the world could have long days,
it would still befit us to keep watch for our own setting,
and for each to look to the end of his own life.
For what good is it to me that rivers in their long course
always flow downward with unfailing waters,
that aged forests have outlasted many centuries,
and that the flowering fields endure in their places?
These remain, but our parents have not remained.
I live my life as a guest for a brief time.
So we were not born to no purpose for these ages,
which perish for us and in which we die,
but so that in this life we may earn eternal life
and long rest may follow brief labor.
And yet this labor may perhaps be harsh to the rebellious,
and savage hearts may think its laws severe;
but this burden is not heavy for a gentle back,
nor does the kindly yoke chafe a meek neck.
God is to be loved with the whole mind, with all the strength of the heart:
so it is commanded; and let the second concern, for one's fellow man, thrive.
What one would not want done to oneself, let him do to no one;
when wronged, let him not know how to exact revenge.
Content with little, let him avoid being thought lofty;
let him not fear being despised, nor be in the habit of despising.
Frugal, truthful, chaste in mind and body,
let him, a lover of peace, lead a blameless life.
Generous from his own to all he sees in need,
let him not covet what is not his, and let him give away what is his.
What, I ask, is thought hard in these commandments?
Or what will there be that faith cannot undertake?
Those who believe that the holy prophets sang the truth,
and who do not doubt that the words of God endure,
who see Christ, who suffered the penalty of the cross, the utmost of death,
now in the full honor of the Father on high,
and who await Him, awesome in great majesty,
keeping watch with lamps full of oil —
to them earthly things are worthless, heavenly things lie open, and they
do not live as captive slaves of this present time.
The deceitful wisdom of the world has not caught them,
nor have they fixed fruitless studies on the stars.
Commands and fasces, the gifts of the ignorant mob,
and the wealth that the world has made the seed of crimes,
they have trampled underfoot, seeking heaven with holy ambition,
with the votes of Christ and the applause of angels.
Neither harsh labor nor alluring pleasure overcomes them.
They desire to gain nothing; they fear to lose nothing.
He who is Christ's hates all that is not Christ's, establishing
himself in Him, since he longs to bear Him within himself.
He, the God of all things, Creator of heaven and earth,
for my sake was born a man of a holy virgin.
His back to scourges, His cheeks to blows, His face to spittle
He offered, and He did not refuse to be nailed to the cross.
Not that such great endurance brought anything to God,
whose riches neither grow nor diminish;
but so that what had been conquered in me might conquer in Him,
I was made part of Christ's body, and He of mine.
Dying, He bore me; rising again, having conquered death, He bore me,
and with Him He carried me to the Father above the stars.
What, then, should I refuse to endure for so great a hope?
Or what will there be that can separate me from the Lord?
Bring fire, torturer; search my entrails with your hand;
my limbs, once set free, will escape your torments.
If I am shut in a dark prison and bound with chains,
I shall go free to God in ecstasy of mind.
If the lictor prepares to cut through my neck with his blade,
he will find me unafraid: death is quick, the pain brief.
I do not fear exile: there is one home for all;
I scorn hunger: the word of the Lord becomes my food.
Yet this confidence does not arise in me from myself;
You, Christ, grant me to speak, and You grant me to suffer.
In ourselves we dare nothing, but we trust in You,
we whom You command to fight and enable to conquer.
My only hope, then, is God, in whom to believe is life,
who has made me a citizen of another homeland.
Bidden by the lot of my fathers to pass through this perishing world,
I go as a stranger, a soldier under the standard of Christ,
and, not doubting that I hold earthly things by a brief title,
I shall use my own as though what is mine were not mine.
I shall not marvel at wealth; I shall pursue no honors;
I shall not fear poverty while Christ is rich.
With the same mind with which I stand in adversity I shall meet prosperity;
evils will not overcome me, nor good things ensnare me.
I shall always give thanks to Christ, always give Him honor;
the praise of the Lord shall always live in my mouth.
Only you, faithful companion, gird yourself with me for this fight,
in which God has given help to the weak.
Watchfully restrain me when I am proud; console me when I grieve;
let us both be an example of a godly life.
Be the guardian of your guardian; return the care in turn;
raise me when I fall, and rise with the help of the one who lifts you,
so that not only our flesh may be one, but our mind
also may be one, and one spirit may nourish us both.
POEM II.
The festal day wants to be honored with sacred pages;
put away profane books;
with a hymn we must hallow the first beginnings of the Name,
which Christ commands us to observe.
Christ is nectar in the mouth, honeycomb on the tongue,
living ambrosia in the throat,
a blessed lotus in the breast, from which, once you have tasted it,
you would never wish to depart;
honey in the marrow, serene light to the eyes,
the sound of life in the ears.
The lyre or plectrum of sweet eloquence
returns when this Name is heard.
In wandering journeys, in slippery misfortune,
in the temptations of evil,
to those dying of thirst and hunger, heat and cold,
it is offered as a powerful salve.
Dire despair shakes the inner shrine of the mind
because of the mass of its sins;
inherited depravity rages in the inmost being;
lust kindles its torches;
greed for gold drives the soft heart
to amass by right and wrong;
the soul swallows the gorge of a stinking gullet,
ruined by Venus and Bacchus;
the bloody avenger drives wrath
to slake itself with a ready blade;
fear bids one inflict misfortune on others
as a wicked way of guarding oneself;
violence that cannot master itself casts out patience
and seeks out ruinous weapons;
perverse obstinacy shakes faith,
fortunate among the guilty [?] — but not for long.
This Name, once heard, comes to bring salvation;
this takes away every poison.
Limbs possessed, and a spirit
tormented by a most impure demon,
by this, by this Name obtain their healing,
and come back up from the underworld.
Bodies bewitched by a dire spell, and by the chant
of a witch devoted to the tombs,
shake off the treacherous force of the binding plague
and return home healed.
He whose joints, loosened limb by limb, compel him
to sit helpless on his bed,
he whom blindness, the most wretched cross of all,
has made dependent on another's feet,
he whom the whole city sees walking lame
in both his knees —
they can all return home on their own feet,
celebrating the name of God.
Hail, O true Apollo, glorious Paean,
who drove off the infernal dragon!
The sweet quiver of Your testimony,
which is made up of four men,
the arrow dipped in prophetic honey,
feathered with the oracles of the fathers,
the bow resounding mightily with the Father's power,
the string strong in miracles,
have laid the old serpent low in his own death.
Hail, noble triumph!
Hail, blessed victory of the world,
parent of a blessed age!
Hail, Name which all in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth
hear with bended knee!
Hail, one, one, one God in three;
hail, Trinity one in One!
This blessing, when the light, raised from the eastern pole,
begins its daily journey,
this, when in the west the sun sinks with his chariot into the sea,
hallows me.
Crucified Victor, atoner for sins,
Life all-powerful in death,
grant that, when I am called away at the final hour,
from this chaos buried in evils
this blessing may carry me across to You;
meanwhile, grant what is good for me,
and let not the restless delay of my mind torment it,
bound in this stinking prison.
POEM III.
Holy God, light of light, harmony of all things,
who by Your Word founded an eternal kingdom,
without beginning and not subject to end, from whom
comes all that now is, that was, and that will be;
unknown to the eyes of the body, scarcely known to the mind,
not easy for tongues, nor to be grasped by souls;
indulgent, holy, just, patient, merciful,
full, perfect, supreme, almighty,
alone and not alone, thrice one and one in three,
ever greater the more richly You are believed!
Let him consider whether he may hope for pardon who hesitates
to speak Your praises because he fears he is unequal to them.
Surely he will know that he may rightly be forgiven,
and he will be guilty only of foolish simplicity.
Only one who might attempt and manage to number things beyond number
could count up all Your powers.
What we feel is more than the tongue can speak,
and what we feel, when we speak it, becomes less.
All the elements in their various forms, which from of old
we believe, hear, touch, and see —
broad in the sea, heavy in the earth, shining in the sky,
mobile in the air, gloomy in black night,
planted on leafy ridges, settled on the plains,
sown with vineyards, fit for every crop,
trackless in deserts, congealed by sluggish cold,
fiery in the stars, living in the rivers —
You created by the power of Your Word as soon as it pleased You;
and what for others means doing, for You it is enough to will.
Nature brings forth nothing unbidden, and to You,
the Beginning, all things owe their beginning:
the moon, rendering her service in the dark night,
and the sun, bidden to shine in the bright day,
ages of ages, months, days, year, and hours,
whatever we do at any time, or the means by which we do it,
the angelic people, the patriarchs, and the throng of the godly
whom devout faith has gathered into heaven,
wherever the Roman lives, wherever the barbarian world rages,
whatever the encircling ocean holds apart,
things made of joined limbs and things that have no limbs,
those that answer with words and those that gape without a voice,
those that fear preserves by flight or courage defends,
that caves hide, rivers roll along, or wings lift up —
all render to You one hymn in their different voices,
and long to unfold what they cannot.
Even brute beasts tremble before You, the dumb speak to You;
and how they do it the mind of man does not know.
Of what we know, we know that all things rest on hidden causes,
and nothing You do can be without reason.
Me alone among all my guilty heart terrifies,
lest I speak Your praises with an unworthy mouth,
lest my sins weigh me down, lest a burden heavier than lead
hold me captive in the lowest darkness.
But while I wander through the many windings of my cares,
a path for us to follow meets me in my fear.
If I defend myself, I am guilty; if I confess my crimes, I am saved;
I hope for Your pardon rather than deserve it.
Whatever crimes I committed without a witness, You have examined;
for since You see what is yet to be done, You can see what has been done.
If heaven, Holy One, is rightly believed to be Your throne, and the earth
the footstool of Your feet,
crimes are not uncertain to Him who penetrates the whole world,
wherever it lies open to approach by foot or by sea.
Whatever the west wind sees in the west, the east wind in the east,
whatever grows warm under the south wind or stiff under the north,
lies under Your eyes, though no witness be present
and night, faithful to it, cover the crime committed;
though it be shut in caves, sunk in a river,
or hidden under the weight of a mountain cast down upon it,
or veiled by the dense roofs of houses — he alone
will escape a witness who does no wrong.
It is said that, such was the keenness of fortunate Lynceus' sight,
a wall could not stop his searching eyes.
If this is thought to have been possible for human sight,
do we believe that anything is unknown to You,
who rule the sea, the heaven, the earth, and whatever is in them,
pervading all things, outside them and within?
Nor do I wonder: the elements obey their own Father,
and all things, pierced through, lie open to their Lord.
If anyone could sin without himself, he would remain hidden;
but if he sins, his own mind stands by as witness.
So I, wanton always from my earliest years,
whose love mixed the lawful with the unlawful,
bold, perjured, a pretender and a dissembler,
ambitious, fickle, envious, impatient,
cruel, lacking reason, raging, greedy,
a squanderer of my own and a seeker after more of others' —
whatever crimes are plotted, accomplished, and dared by
a polluted body, a guilty mind, a chattering tongue,
all this I have done; yet, since the Judge is appeased,
punishment has no place for so great a crime.
But praise to You, to You, holy Father, praise at every time,
who can bring a condemned soul to life,
spare the humbled, pour light into darkness,
and make saints out of senseless rocks.
Sunk in the midst of death, in the whirlpool of vices,
I am rescued, purified by holy waters,
and I who but now deserved the torturers' chains and flames,
the same and yet not the same, now live as one set free.
Why do I say 'free'? My crimes rein in that word;
even after pardon I am held as a slave of sin.
For the old enemy, all the readier through his zeal for fighting,
harasses the unwary with various arts,
pleasing to hearing, sight, taste, and touch,
always cunningly casting allurements in my way,
so that, if any ill-secured part of my members should waver,
he may break in like a wolf ravaging an open sheepfold,
or like a lion bursting swiftly from his hidden den
if the flock lies open to roam unguarded.
But You, holy God — if my words speak what I feel,
and my mind does not say one thing and my tongue another —
anxious, eager, devoted, with heart and mouth
I knock: bid the door open; give, I ask; I seek; teach me,
as far as it is right and holy for a mortal to know, how
ready You are to hear suppliants, and in how many and what ways.
Forgive my sins — I use milder
names than the weight of my deeds deserves.
Forgive rather my crimes; and let the raging serpent himself now feel
the darts he is forging against me,
and on countless hooks with deceiving bait
may his own devices hold him captive, I pray.
I would not want gold and gems, nor the rich realms
of kings, nor the immense wealth the world holds,
nor to ride behind crowded fasces and curved axes,
conspicuous on lofty horses,
nor that the annals to be preserved should record my name,
and a crowd of nobles wear down my threshold,
nor that alluring pleasure should creep in even by such means;
but let me, content, have what is enough.
I do not seek a long course of life, nor joys
all too suited to bodily delights,
since all of it passes more swiftly than wintry shadows
and flowers that the harsh south winds have swept away.
In these, life is brief; after death, punishment is everlasting.
He condemns himself who asks for things that perish.
Give rather a teachable understanding; give light to my mind;
give death to the members that destroy the soul.
Instruct me in my anxiety, direct my faltering steps,
and to one who believes add, in Your fullness, a fuller faith.
Let me have zeal for justice and a guarding of the truth;
let my body be pure, my soul without stain;
let there be simplicity, integrity, patience, a mind conscious
of its own uprightness; let there be piety, let there be love that counsels well.
I shall not seek what belongs to others; the loss of my own will come easily;
let me be foolish to the world, that I may be wise to You.
Let pleasure die, with an end set upon it forever,
and let my senses not recall what it does harm to remember.
Let a good conscience fear no witness;
let what we say be sure, and what we do be seemly.
Ambition, drunkenness, hatred, pride, anger, lust,
and envy, the mother of every kind of crime,
be far away; and may my life earn by constant prayer
that, once their yoke is shaken off, they never try my neck again.
So, humbly, now at the fresh morning, now when evening has come,
may I keep the hours of the service I have undertaken,
so that whatever night comes may always be thought my last,
and I may live each day in the world as one about to die.
Frauds, perjuries, thefts, and robberies will cease
if I fear the judgment that impends so soon.
Let a wholesome measure govern my prayers, my speech, my deeds;
let a measure beyond all others be found in my love for You,
so that into my whole heart and all my marrow,
if I deserve it, You may pour Your whole self, Father.
Night and day, every hour and every moment, every scruple of time,
even every instant, let them make our faith grow;
and to keep it I need the help of Your goodness.
All the power is Yours; in me there is scarcely even the will;
and since I stretch out manifold anxieties to no purpose,
I shall settle the matter more fully in a few words:
there are those who often ask for things that contradict their own words;
grant us, O God, what You know is good for us.
If a woman, grieving, lights a lamp and searches for her drachma,
and rejoices that it is not lost to her;
if the sheep left behind was no cheap concern
to the shepherd who counted a hundred sheep,
so that, though its loss might have seemed easy to bear,
it is a sweet burden on his bent shoulders;
if a father, when the son he lost returns to him with interest,
bears witness to his joy with a lavish feast:
why should I doubt that Your care throughout the whole world is
that no one who has believed in You should perish?
For if one whom long ago, to enjoy the world with reason,
the holy right hand formed from moist clay
were taken from nothing only to be thought fashioned for nothing,
it would be the work of one at play rather than of one who makes.
Then, when man, condemned by his own just charge,
having transgressed the law, had perished in death,
by changing the person You made the case give way,
neither too harsh nor too lenient,
deigning, as Lord, to send the Lord down to earth,
to make the shame of the cross into power,
so that whatever He could have commanded by His majesty
He might rather do as one subject to command;
to take chains from captives and captives from the enemy,
and to tear away the fixed snares of death,
so that what belief in the deceitful serpent had bound
a better belief might now be able to loose.
He who was begotten of You without time or sequence, through You
so received the whole that You lost nothing by it;
one man [?], alike in power, equal in substance,
holy from the Holy, good from Goodness,
full from the Full, just from the source of justice,
true from the True, and God from God.
A nature born of a marriage might seem
a third thing, when two have produced something between them;
but You, Lord of nature, sower of all things, through whom all things are,
beget nothing other than what You were.
Him who would afterward take on for us the weight of flesh,
whose beginning the ages had not known,
a mother without a husband, giving back the Lord poured into her,
a virgin pregnant in an untouched womb, brings forth.
He is born on earth; all things recognize the light
(and yet neither the world nor the darkness comprehends it).
He is true man and true God, not something between the two;
nature denies the one, His works prove the other.
Christ, at last the new joy of a world made secure,
long since written of in countless volumes;
Christ, light of the blind, cleansing of leprosy,
hearing for the deaf, rest for the troubled,
walking for the lame, a tongue for the mute, Redeemer
of the world and true salvation of a condemned people,
though eternal, endured the confinement of the common tomb,
and He whom the grave held remains eternal.
He was immortal; He died, and now He lives;
before, God became man; now God, out of man,
has ascended to heaven, received into the holy seat;
the everlasting Lord is, and was, and will come.
You are the unbegotten Father; begotten of You is the Son; from You,
not begotten, the Holy Spirit proceeds,
who, ever between the Son and the Father,
is felt and feels, is given and received,
sanctifies, breathes, rules, is wholly everywhere,
cleanses by His coming, and is held by the pure.
Provided only that he who joins together three names and three persons
does not, when questioned, deny that they are one God,
alike in power, alike in goodness, the very same,
let him believe them not merely 'one' but rather 'the same.'
This I have said, not as much as I wished, to match the weight of the subject,
but as much as I could, entangled as I am in vices.
Grant, Father, that there may always endure in me
this one faith in the threefold names.
POEM IV.
Hear the words of Your servant, highest King, and serenely
look with mercy on my state of heart.
I am wretched, as I deserve, as scarcely anyone in the world is;
grief is always with me, and every hour is sad.
The seventh year has come since a new cause
began to breed manifold sorrows and to shake my heart.
Since then my brother has been a captive in foreign lands,
naked and needy, his heart afflicted.
His pitiable wife, at home, goes through all
the streets begging food with trembling lips.
By this shameful trade she supports four children,
whom she can barely cover, as best she can, with rags.
I have a sister, consecrated to Christ in her early years,
who keeps her vigils in remarkable simplicity.
She, sharing the same lot and keeping up her grief without end,
has now almost lost her eyes through weeping.
Our household goods, small as they were, have been plundered,
and alas, there is no one to bring help to us in our misery.
My brother's wife has been shut out of the family property,
and now we are already half reduced to the level of peasants.
Our noble rank has perished in our misery; poverty has taken its place.
We deserved, I confess, to suffer harsher things;
but have mercy, mighty Ruler, have mercy on those who pray to You,
and at last, merciful One, put an end to these evils.
Restore the captive to his homeland and his native fields,
and with modest means restore our roof as well,
so that our minds may offer praises to Christ forever,
who alone can give worthy rewards.
